Quote: “Cheongsong: a green treasure”

Introduction EN: Explore Damyang Gamagol Valley, where volcanic landscapes of dacite and rhyolite create a striking natural environment.Visit Juknokwon Bamboo Garden, a 160,000-square-metre park featuring natural bamboo forests, ecological exhibits, and scenic trails. From the observatory, enjoy panoramic views of Damyangcheon Stream, the historic Gwanbangjerim Forest, and Metasequoia Road, home to trees over 300 years old.Discover the roots of Gasa literature at pavilion sites such as Soswaewon and Hwanbyeokdang in the Mudeungsan area. These historic locations reflect the region’s long-standing literary tradition, blending classical poetic forms with folk rhythms and inspiring generations of Korean scholars.
Description: Mudeungsan UNESCO Global Geopark is located in the southern part of the Korean Peninsula near the city of Gwangju. It is centred around Mount Mudeung, a prominent granite mountain rising to 1,186 metres, overlooking Gwangju and the surrounding lowlands. The geopark is a heavily forested area within the Mudeungsan National Park. The climate, influenced by the mountain terrain, is warm and temperate, with significant rainfall throughout the year. Mount Mudeung was formed by volcanic activity during the Cretaceous period, approximately 87 million years ago. The geopark includes 20 geosites spanning seven distinct geological periods. These include five large colonnades of Mudeungsan Tuff shaped by ancient eruptions, extensive block streams and cryoplanation surfaces formed by periglacial processes, and talus slopes with distinct microclimatic environments. Other features include dinosaur footprints and trackways, as well as diverse geological and geomorphological formations such as scenic cliffs and waterfalls. A notable geological feature is the Gwangju Uchiwa-shaped Rock Formation—a large, fan-shaped eroded sandstone formation known for its distinctive shape and size. It is a popular destination for both visitors and geology enthusiasts.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Mudeungsan has preserved its rich cultural heritage thanks to the active engagement of local residents who have long valued and protected the natural environment. In the 1990s, a grassroots conservation movement emerged to safeguard the area. Mount Mudeung is affectionately known as the “Mother Mountain,” reflecting the deep respect and emotional connection the local community holds for this natural landmark. Numerous temples are nestled within the scenic landscape of Mudeungsan, which features volcanic colonnades, steep cliffs, block streams, caves, and waterfalls. Among these, Muryangsa Temple—located on the western foothills of Mudeungsan and first established in the 7th century—is one of the region’s oldest and most significant temples. The Buncheong celadon pottery technique also developed on Mount Mudeung, using the region’s naturally weathered, coarse soils. Unlike traditional pottery clay, the surface was decorated with white kaolin to enhance quality. Clean water, abundant forests, and mineral-rich soils created favourable conditions for pottery production, leading to the spread of kilns throughout the region. The technique became a defining feature of local craftsmanship. Mudeungsan watermelons are recognised as a GEOfood product of the geopark. Grown at altitudes above 500 metres for over 400 years, they are shaped by the region’s distinct geology and climate. Today, nine farms in Geumgok Village collaborate to preserve this agricultural tradition as part of the area’s living heritage.
Quote: “Mt Mudeung stands tall in the centre of a spiritual route through the Honam region”

Introduction EN: During the annual Nordland Regatta each June, the four-oared bindalsfæringen, the Viking boats, are shown sailing on the Bindalsfjord.See petroglyphs at Vistnesdalen and soapstone quarries at Talvik that trace coastal settlement back to the Stone Age.
Description: The world’s northernmost UNESCO Global Geopark is also the mythical land of the trolls and the immemorial homeland of the indigenous Sámi people. The extraordinary landscape of Trollfjell Geopark, a vast territory dominated by water and thousands of small islands, skerries, fjords, exposed crystalline rocks, but also a rare boreal rainforest, has sparked the imagination of the local populations for centuries. They believed that the stone mountains along the coast, unfriendly to humans, were in fact living creatures that chased beautiful maidens. The trolls, as they are known have inspired dozens of legends, some related to the geopark’s geosites. An example is Torghatten, a stone promontory with a unique feature: it is pierced from one side to the other. The hole on the iconic landmark, one of Norway’s most popular tourist attractions, revered by kings who carved their names on its walls, was formed by marine abrasion of a cave created during periods of higher sea level during the last 2-3 million years. For long periods, the waves, frost and salt eroded the hard granite rock until the caves on either side met and became one. Local legends, however, have a much more interesting explanation in which the hole was created by an arrow during a spectacular quarrel amongst the trolls.   Trollfjell UNESCO Global Geopark displays a 600-million-year-long geological history with chapters of closing oceans, the collision of continental plates, mountain building and erosion. In this period two events were of great importance: the shrinking and closure of the ancient Iapetus Ocean, with the creation of the Caledonian mountain chain, granitic batholiths and uplifting of the oceanic crust that formed the Leka Ophiolite, a rare geological occurrence; but also, the several Ice Ages of the last 2.6 million years. The latter left a glacially sculpted landscape and, along the coast, a sub-horizontal plateau, one of the world’s best-developed strandflat, with numerous islands and shallow seas and up to 60 km wide. One of the best ways to explore the strandflat is by kayak allowing the diverse birdlife of the region to be observed undisturbed.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The Trollfjell UNESCO Global Geopark is dedicated to raising awareness about the cultural heritage of the South Sámi people, an Indigenous group with deep ties to the region. This includes highlighting Sámi cultural monuments and intangible heritage such as traditional reindeer herding, which has shaped the landscape and identity of the region for centuries. Though reindeer herding ceased in the mid-20th century within the geopark boundaries, herds continue to migrate seasonally in nearby areas, including the Jillen-Njaarke and Voengelh Njaarke reindeer grazing districts. The Trollfjell UNESCO Global Geopark boasts a cultural heritage spanning over 11,000 years, beginning with the earliest human settlements on the Vega Islands. The Vega Archipelago, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, is home to the eider duck and an ancient way of life based on fishing and the sustainable harvesting of eider down, a tradition that has continued for more than 1,500 years. With evidence of human settlement from the Stone Age onwards, the islands are home to small fishing villages, quays, warehouses, eider houses built for ducks to nest in, lighthouses and beacons. Hundreds of cultural monuments within the geopark offer a window into the evolution of coastal communities, including Stone Age petroglyphs at Vistnesdalen, soapstone quarries at Talvik, and remains of historical mining operations such as the Brønnøy Kalk Quarry, which provided essential resources for tool-making and construction. A current project at Stein Recreation Area in Sømna focuses on interpreting the historical significance of water mills and water-powered operations. This area was once a hub for agricultural processing and early industrial activities, and the geopark is developing interpretive panels and directional signage to guide visitors through its history.
Quote:
“Trollfjell Geopark aims to provide world-class activities and thrills based
 on the unique geological history and localities in the area”

Titre EN: Jeonbuk West Coast UNESCO Global Geopark
Introduction EN: Sample local flavours rooted in the geopark’s coastal environment, where fresh seafood from the sea and tidal flats features in dishes such as seafood porridge, kalguksu (chicken noodle soup), and seasoned vegetables, followed by desserts made with wild mulberries and black raspberries.Join the Masil Walking Festival in May, where participants of all ages explore coastal geosites with geopark guides. The walk combines geological insights with cultural and historical heritage, concluding with local food experiences.From April to October, visit the Gochang Ecotourism Market, held each weekend at the Gochang Dolmen Site, offering local crafts, agricultural products, and traditional snacks.
Description: The Jeonbuk West Coast UNESCO Global Geopark presents 2.5 billion years of well-exposed geological history in the western part of the Republic of Korea. The area is already internationally recognised through multiple UNESCO designations: as a natural and cultural World Heritage site (Gochang, Hwasun and Ganghwa Dolmen Sites), a biosphere reserve (Gochang Biosphere Reserve), and a Ramsar site (Gochang and Buan Tidal Flats) for its exceptional coastal wetlands. The vast tidal flats, interspersed with volcanic features and islands, offer a journey through geological time. Known in Korean as getbol, the Gochang tidal flats are among only 19 coastal wetland areas worldwide with a tidal range greater than 5 metres (macrotidal). With mud layers reaching up to 40 metres in thickness and forming over the last 8,500 years, this site holds one of the thickest Holocene sediment records globally, preserving a rich archive of environmental change since the beginning of the Holocene epoch, 12,000 to 11,500 years ago. Along the coastline, an unusual volcanic feature is the presence of peperite—a rock formed by the interaction of hot magma with wet, unconsolidated sediment. This site provides key geological evidence of synsedimentary volcanism, with distinctive lithofacies and internal textures shaped by magma fragmentation and steam explosions. The geopark is also home to important fossil sites. The dinosaur egg site at Gochang includes the holotype for Faveoloolithidae, the key specimen used to define this type of dinosaur egg. It provides evidence of colonial nesting behaviour in a repeated sedimentary environment.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Jeonbuk West Coast UNESCO Global Geopark preserves a rich cultural heritage, including one of the highest concentrations of dolmens in the world, some dating back to the 3rd–4th century BCE. The Gochang Dolmen Site demonstrates early communities’ understanding of local geology, as they selected and shaped rhyolitic tuff and feldspar porphyry blocks, often naturally fractured by volcanic activity. Beyond the dolmens, the region's historical depth is reflected in celadon kiln sites from the Goryeo Dynasty (918–1392 AD) and temples nearly 2,000 years old. These cultural assets are actively promoted through geopark initiatives that integrate geological heritage with local traditions, encouraging sustainable tourism and education. The geopark supports local communities through the development of geovillages. In Gochang, Geovillage Hoam—located near the Dolmen Site and Ungok Wetland—features eco-friendly lodges designed by local residents, serves locally grown food, and offers guided geotrail tours and clay craft experiences. In Buan, Geovillage Yuyu near Jeokbyeokgang offers geo-eco tours and traditional cuisine while preserving Buan’s Silkworm Farming system, designated as a Korean Important Agricultural Heritage System. Visitors can learn about silk production and explore mulberry-based products at the Buan Mulberry Promotion Hall. Through these efforts, the geopark ensures that tourism contributes directly to local livelihoods and cultural preservation.

Introduction EN: Explore the Cuesta landscape shaped by Mesozoic rock formations and Himalayan uplift, creating two distinct parallel ridges across the geopark.Visit the petrified wood sites of Chaloem Phra Kiat and Mueang, revealing fossilised trees dating back millions of years.Experience cultural heritage through the Sikhio Tai Yuan Indigenous community’s weaving and building traditions, and the Rueankorat-Chalermwatana folklore project.
Description: Khorat UNESCO Global Geopark, located in Nakhon Ratchasima, Thailand, is recognised as a significant palaeontological site, earning the title of Paleontopolis (City of Ancient Life). Its fossil record spans from 16 million to 10,000 years ago, showcasing an extraordinary diversity of prehistoric life. Among its most remarkable discoveries are fossils of dinosaurs, ancient elephants, and other vertebrates, as well as extensive deposits of petrified wood found in the Chaloem Phra Kiat and Mueang districts. The geopark has been internationally recognised through the scientific classification of several new fossil species discovered in its territory. Notable examples include Khoratosuchus jintasakuli, a prehistoric crocodile, and Sirindhorna khoratensis, a newly identified dinosaur species. These findings underscore the importance of Khorat as a key site for vertebrate palaeontology. Geologically, Khorat UNESCO Global Geopark is underlain by Mesozoic rock formations, primarily the Khorat Group, Maha Sarakham, and Phu Thok formations. These consist of sandstone, conglomerate, siltstone, shale, claystone, and rock salt. The uplift of the Himalayas 65 to 55 million years ago led to the folding and elevation of these rock layers, shaping the current plateau and basin structure. This geological evolution contributed to the formation of two distinct rows of cuestas in the western and south-western regions of the geopark, lending the area its distinctive topography. The Early Cretaceous Khok Kruat Formation has yielded an abundance of fossilised reptiles, including three new species of iguanodont dinosaurs, as well as a carcharodontosaurian theropod dinosaur, a crocodile, and a turtle. In the eastern part of the geopark, fluvial deposits from the Neogene to the Quaternary period have preserved fossils of rare prehistoric mammals, including an ancient orangutan, an anthracothere, and a hornless rhinoceros. These discoveries are complemented by an extensive collection of fossilised plants, with ten genera of ancient elephants identified among the 55 known globally, along with more than 20 other mammal species. The exceptional diversity of mammalian fossils from the Miocene to Pleistocene periods is considered the primary geological highlight of the geopark. With its parallel ranges of cuestas and extensive fossil record, Khorat UNESCO Global Geopark stands as a crucial site for understanding the region’s geological and palaeontological history, solidifying its reputation as Cuesta and Fossil Land.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The Khorat UNESCO Global Geopark is deeply intertwined with the Thai Khorat culture, encompassing the region’s distinctive language, traditions, and musical heritage. The geopark fosters strong connections between geological heritage and cultural identity, as seen in its integration of geosites with historic and religious landmarks, such as the Khao Chan Ngam Cave and Prehistoric Paintings and the Sikhio Sandstone Historical Quarry and Phanom Wan Stone Sanctuary. The geopark has taken an active role in preserving cultural traditions, particularly in collaboration with the Sikhio Tai Yuan Indigenous community, where efforts have been made to record traditional weaving, construction methods, and other intangible heritage elements. The Rueankorat-Chalermwatana Project showcases local folkloric traditions, including traditional building techniques and the Khorat song style. The major economic activity is agriculture, including the cultivation of rice, cassava, and sugar cane, and the raising of cattle, pigs, and chickens. Nakhon Ratchasima is a regional highway and railway transportation centre. In the city centre of Nakhon Ratchasima and the surrounding district cities, the majority of the population is engaged in industry, commerce and services.

Introduction EN: Explore Kolbingen Cave, the only show cave in the south-western Swabian Alb, where thousands of years of geological activity have created extraordinary dripstone formations.Experience the Swabian-Alemannic carnival, an Intangible Cultural Heritage tradition celebrated with elaborate wooden masks, local parades, and centuries-old customs unique to the region.Discover castles perched on limestone cliffs, including Hohenzollern Castle and Lichtenstein Castle, alongside significant Celtic heritage sites such as the Heuneburg and the Heidengraben.
Description: The Swabian Alb UNESCO Global Geopark covers a 220-kilometre-long mountain range south of Stuttgart, shaped by gentle hills, juniper heaths, woodlands and river valleys. Its most striking feature is the Albtrauf, a steep escarpment marking the northern edge of the plateau, home to clifftop castles such as Lichtenstein, Reussenstein and Hohenneuffen, and waterfalls like Gütersteiner and Sirchinger. The region’s limestone was formed during the Jurassic period, between 200 and 145 million years ago, when the area lay beneath a warm, shallow tropical sea. Fossils from this time, including ammonites, sharks, and marine reptiles, are abundant. A notable site is the Ofterdingen Ammonite Pavement, where a 200-million-year-old seabed is exposed in the streambed of the Steinlach River. Near Nusplingen, the finely layered limestone preserves remarkable detail—from fish and frogs to feathers and leaf veins—offering a rare window into Jurassic life. The geopark is also rich in karst landscapes, with over 50 caves open or accessible to visitors. Sites such as Wimsen and Falkenstein Caves reveal underground worlds of stalactites, mineral formations, and clear pools. The region also records more dramatic events: two meteorite impacts around 15 million years ago, including the Steinheim crater, still visible today.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The Swabian Alb is shaped not only by its geological history, but also by a rich and layered human presence. Caves throughout the region offered shelter to Palaeolithic communities and were sites of cultural expression, evidenced by the oldest known art sculptures and musical instruments. The geology also influenced settlement patterns and resource use, from Stone Age flint extraction to early Celtic iron smelting. Volcanic chimneys with water-retaining basaltic fillings provided rare access to freshwater, leading to the emergence of villages around rain-fed basins known as “Hühlen.” The region hosts three UNESCO World Heritage sites: the “Caves and Ice Age Art”, the “Upper Germanic-Rhaetian Limes”, and one component of the “Prehistoric Pile Dwellings around the Alps.” Castles built on fossil reef cliffs, Celtic oppida - large, fortified settlements - such as Heuneburg and Heidengraben, and medieval towns like Reutlingen and Bad Urach reflect a long continuum of cultural adaptation to the land. Traditional land use practices also contribute to cultural continuity and landscape stewardship. Intangible heritage recognised nationally includes the Köhlerhandwerk (charcoal burning), transhumant herding systems of southern German pastoralism, and Streuobstanbau (traditional orchard cultivation). These practices, rooted in centuries of local knowledge, sustain biodiversity, conserve cultural landscapes, and continue to play a role in regional identity and economy.
Quote: “Few places in the world were ever home to as many volcanoes as the Swabian Alb 200 million years ago”

Introduction EN: The historic Podzemlje Pece Mine, with over 800 km of tunnels, can be visited by taking an old mining train, by mountain bike, or even by kayaking the flooded galleries 700 m below the surface.'The Castles of King Matjaž' is a unique snow-castle-building competition, taking place on the last weekend of January in the region of Koroška, Slovenia.One of the longest mountain-biking flow trails in Europe – the Petzen Flow Country Trail, an 11 km journey starting at 1,700 m above sea level.
Description: Depending on how one looks at it, geography can either divide or connect. In the cross-border Karawanken–Karavanke UNESCO Global Geopark, Austrian and Slovenian communities decided that their common geological heritage was one of many reasons to come together. Right on the border between Austria to the north and Slovenia to the south, the limestone peaks of the Karavanke/Karawanken mountain range, aligned in an east–west direction, follow one another like a long queue of caravans. The range, with a total length of 120 km, is one of the longest in Europe and the geopark lies right at its centre. Covering a timespan of more than 450 million years, from the Ordovician to the Miocene, most of the mountainous landscape is a direct result of the collision between the African and Eurasian tectonic plates that gave rise to the Alps. The tectonic forces squeezed, twisted and changed the composition of the sedimentary rocks deposited millions of years earlier at the bottom of a warm ocean called Tethys. In the process, intense volcanism gave rise to the Smrekovec and Olševa/Ouschewa volcanoes. Later, glacial, fluvial and karstic processes shaped the landscape into what it is today. When hiking on the highest peaks of the Karavanke, one can still find the remains of sea snails, sea lilies and even ichthyosaur bones—evidence of life in the ancient Tethys Ocean. The geopark features several peaks over 2,000 m, and forested areas that form part of the European Natura 2000 network of protected habitats for rare and threatened species.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The geopark is defined by its rich mining heritage and long-standing ironworks tradition, which have shaped the region’s development both in the past and into the present. Today, visitors and scientists are drawn to the area by the abundance of minerals found in historic mines, its exceptional natural resources and the unique stories of its people. The Podzemlje Pece mine is one of only five areas worldwide to host a specific type of lead–zinc ore. It was in operation for nearly 350 years, until its closure in 1994. At its peak, the mine employed over 2,000 people. Its tunnels extended for more than 800 km through the Mežica Valley. To preserve this technical, natural and cultural heritage, it was transformed into a tourist mine and museum in 1997, and can now be visited by mining train, by bike, or even by kayak through its submerged galleries. The Obir dripstone caves in Bad Eisenkappel (Železna Kapla) were discovered by chance in 1870 when miners opened a new gallery in search of lead–zinc ore. Delicate stalactites—some as fine as silk thread—hang above crystal-clear waters in this karst system, which stretches for more than 800 m and resembles the entrails of a gigantic sea creature. The Hemmaberg–Juenna Museum opens a window onto one of Europe’s oldest pilgrimage routes. Twenty years of archaeological excavation have uncovered evidence dating back to the Ostrogoths, a Roman-era Germanic people. Among the discoveries is a recently unearthed burial ground. The geopark offers a wide range of geo-experiences and educational programmes. Interpretive panels provide geological context, while schoolchildren benefit from hands-on learning designed to foster a deeper connection with the region’s geological and cultural heritage.
Quote: “Secrets written in stone”

Introduction EN: Explore the lowland landscapes of Czechia’s first Protected Landscape Area, home to deer, wild boar, foxes, and protected bird species like the peregrine falcon.Follow the 119 km Golden Path trail linking rock towns, castles, river gorges, and historic battlefields.Discover local legends that connect gemstones, mountain spirits, and jewellery-making, brought to life through the geopark’s narrative trails.
Description: With a geological record spanning an impressive billion years of Earth's history, the Bohemian Paradise Geopark territory holds evidence of remarkable events that have shaped the planet. From its origin near the South Pole to its present location, the landscape reveals signs of monumental geological events, such as the collision of two vast continental masses: Laurentia (now North America) and Gondwana (now Africa). The area also preserves traces of the later fragmentation of the supercontinent Pangea, accompanied by intense volcanic activity. Within the geopark, numerous monogenetic volcanoes—volcanoes that erupted only once—stand as testimony to these ancient geological processes. These are accompanied by a suite of internationally significant features, including columnar jointing, volcanic tubes, and above all, intricate mineral veins that reveal treasures such as quartz, agates, and jaspers. Another striking feature of the geopark is the presence of so-called rock towns, with examples including the Prachov Rock Cliffs, Klokočí Rocks, and the Příhrazy Rocks. These awe-inspiring sandstone formations have been sculpted over time by water into towering structures reminiscent of abandoned castle turrets. Over the centuries, dense pine forests have grown around these formations, creating a natural labyrinth where water flows from the summits, feeding streams and waterfalls below.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Known for its jewellery tradition, medieval castles, and sandstone rock towns, the Bohemian Paradise UNESCO Global Geopark is where remarkable landscapes and rich geological history converge. The quartz, agates, and jaspers formed by ancient monogenetic volcanic eruptions have supported a renowned jewellery industry with a heritage spanning over three centuries. As a result, Turnov, a medieval town founded in 1250, has become the centre of Czech jewellery-making craftsmanship. Bohemian Paradise features a dense network of well-maintained and clearly marked hiking and cycling trails. The most famous is the 119 km Golden Path of the Bohemian Paradise, which connects the sandstone rock towns, the Jizera River canyon—navigable by boat—and several castles and palaces across the region. Another trail recounts the history of the Prussian-Austrian War of 1866. Geology and storytelling are deeply intertwined in the geopark. East of Turnov lie the Kozákov Mountains, long associated with legends; one such tale speaks of goblins dwelling deep in the mountain, teaching the people of Turnov how to work with precious stones. These mythical gnomes are said to have polished and ground gems under the watchful eye of the righteous king of the gnomes, Garnet. The Jizerské Hory Mountains also hold their own legend—where, in a dense forest of beeches and oaks, a dark-red ruby is said to have appeared in the Jizera River as a sign of the love between Petr and Leontýnka. These and ten other legends have been curated by the geopark into a narrative trail, offering visitors an immersive journey where geology and imagination come together.
Quote: “A more than 300-year-old stone-cutting tradition links many small workshops to the natural geology of the region”

Introduction EN: Explore the region’s medieval castles, such as that of Fülek and Hollókö.Discover fossilised remains of 17-million-year-old habitats at the Ipolytarnoc Fossils Nature Reserve.Marvel at the columnar basalt outcrop formations of Somoska, where solidified lava created stunning geological features.
Description: Shared between Hungary and Slovakia, the Novohrad–Nógrád UNESCO Global Geopark is one of the few cross-border geoparks. It showcases a remarkable geological history spanning the last 30 million years. Situated at the northern edge of the Pannonian Basin—a vast sedimentary basin formed during the Miocene (23 million years to 2.58 million years)— the region’s geology captures the opening of this basin and the tectonic processes that followed.  At Somoska, visitors can marvel at a striking columnar basalt outcrop, created when lava solidified inside the vent of a volcano thought to have been active during the Pliocene or Pleistocene periods. Nearby, the Bone Ravine exposes 3.3-million-year-old sediments containing fossilised remains of dozens of mammals, many related to modern-day species like tapirs, elephants and rhinoceroses.   The Ipolytarnoc Fossils Nature Reserve, often referred to as a "prehistoric Pompeii," preserves 17-million-year-old habitats destroyed by a volcanic ash cloud. This lagerstätte site, a term used to describe a location with exceptionally well-preserved remains, features fossils of extinct animals, such as the Amphicyonids (bear-dogs), along with thousands of leaf impressions, shark teeth and petrified trees. These extraordinary finds are protected within a state-of-the-art museum, which enhances the visitor experience.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The Novohrad-Nógrád UNESCO Global Geopark represents a unique cross-border collaboration, where geotourism drives economic growth while preserving the region’s geological and cultural treasures. The people of the geopark have made great efforts to preserve and present the many sites of cultural heritage, such as the area around Hollókő, particularly its Old Village with traditional Palóc folk architecture. This important centre of the Palóc people’s folk art and living traditions has been recognised as a UNESCO World Heritage Site for its exceptional preservation of a traditional settlement and representation of rural life before the agricultural revolution. The region’s fossils have inspired local legends, attributing their petrified forms to the magic of a cruel wizard. According to folklore, touching the petrified trees could grant wishes to those pure of heart, or curse those with ill intent by turning their hearts to stone. Fossilised shark teeth were believed to be the tongues of birds silenced by the wizard’s curse. This captivating blend of science and storytelling highlights the geopark’s unique ability to preserve both geological wonders and cultural traditions. The geopark actively promotes education and raises awareness about the value of both natural and cultural heritage. It focuses on harmonising the natural and cultural landscapes by maintaining geosites, developing new ones, and creating interpretive infrastructure such as study trails and paths for hikers, bikers and horse riders. Additionally, the geopark supports landscape revitalization programmes, particularly in wet habitats, and contributes to the European Landscape Convention’s national initiatives, ensuring sustainable management of the territory.
Quote: “Ancient world without borders - geoscientific and other natural values”

Titre EN: Ore of the Alps UNESCO Global Geopark
Introduction EN: Visit historical mines such as Larzenbach/Hüttau, St. Veit im Pongau, and Mitterberg.Hike the Copper Trail and enjoy the beautiful alpine landscape.Attend the spectacular nocturnal procession of terrifyingly clad Krampus figures and Perchten elves during Advent.
Description: In the Austrian alpine region, the Ore of the Alps UNESCO Global Geopark, also known as Erz der Alpen, follows the course of the Salzach River southward. Once the most important prehistoric copper mining area in the region, its mining legacy is celebrated today through several visitable mine shafts and a hiking trail offering breathtaking views. Most of the geopark lies within the Alpine Greywacke Zone, a band of metamorphosed sedimentary rocks dating back 485 to 300 million years, which forms the geological basis of the region’s copper mining tradition. During the last ice age, the area was covered by the Salzach glacier, with only peaks and ridges above 2,000 metres free of ice—giving the mountains their rounded appearance. The only range that rose above the ice was the majestic Hochkönig, a 2,941-metre limestone massif and landmark of the geopark. It is home to a permanent glacier, the Übergossene Alm, a remnant of the Little Ice Age of the 16th to 19th centuries. Until the 19th century, ships navigated the Salzach River—named after the German words Salz (salt) and Aach (running water)—transporting salt mined from the region. When the glaciers retreated, a new landscape emerged, with valleys filled by debris flows, slides, and rockfalls. The slopes of Fritztal, largely composed of till, offer some of the best examples of these post-glacial formations, including the distinctive ice-age “earth pillars” near Hüttau. The deeply incised valley, cut into soft greywacke bedrock, separates the Hochkönig range in the west from the Hochgründeck mountain in the east. These alpine ranges are cloaked in dense forests of conifers at higher altitudes, and beeches, maples, oaks, and spruce at lower elevations. Deer, chamois, and marmots are common sights, while alpine meadows support traditional pasture and dairy farming.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The copper ore of the Mitterberg–Mühlbach region has been mined since prehistoric times. The so-called Tauerngold—the “gold of the Hohe Tauern” mountain range—was the most valuable mineral resource of the Middle Ages. While mining has now ceased, the region’s connection to its geological heritage endures. Sustainable tourism within the geopark raises awareness of nature and geosciences, notably through programmes focused on environmental education and urban mining. The Copper Ore Trail links the visitor centre in Bischofshofen with museums and significant mines across the geopark’s villages, nestled beneath the imposing Hochkönig Massif. Along the trail, visitors encounter remnants of ancient mining, impressive geological outcrops, cascading waterfalls, steep rock faces, and deep ravines. The route connects the four communities of the Ore of the Alps UNESCO Global Geopark: Bischofshofen, Mühlbach am Hochkönig, St. Veit im Pongau, and Hüttau. Each December during Advent, the region comes alive with the dramatic Krampus and Perchten processions. This centuries-old pagan tradition sees young men donning animal hides, carved wooden masks, and clanging cowbells, roaming the streets in organised nighttime parades. The Bischofshofen parade takes place annually on the evening of 4 December.
Quote: “A wide diversity of geology, nature, culture, wellness, culinary experiences and memorable moments”

Introduction EN: Take the 900-metre-long wooden footpath for views of the immense Palfau Wasserloch Gorge.Walk the Lynx Trail, a 200 km path with 11 stages taking you through three internationally recognised protected areas.
Description: In the very centre of Austria, amid the Northern Calcareous Alps, the Styrian Eisenwurzen UNESCO Global Geopark showcases mountains up to 1,000 metres, the broad valleys of the main rivers Enns and Salza, and the deep gorges of their tributaries. The Styrian Eisenwurzen UNESCO Global Geopark is rich in caves, sinkholes, underground streams and dolines. Its standout feature is the largest gypsum cave in Europe, the 350-metre Kraus Cave, known for its small gypsum crystals and stalactites. This natural spectacle was formed by thermal, sulphur-rich waters flowing through carbonate rocks and transforming them into gypsum, a soft sulphate mineral. This water still flows from a spring at the bottom of the gorge, now contained between concrete walls. Opened as a show cave in 1882 by Franz Kraus, it was the first cave in the world to be illuminated by electric light. The region is world-renowned for the outcrops that enabled geologists to define a specific stage within the Triassic Period (251–201 million years ago). The Anisian Stage, named after the Enns River where limestones outcrop, was studied in the late 19th century by Wilhelm Waagen and Carl Diener. Using ammonite fossil assemblages found in the area, they identified this stage as distinct from older and younger geological periods. This global time-marker, now referred to as a stratotype, defines the period between 247 and 237 million years ago.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: With just over 5,500 inhabitants, the Styrian Eisenwurzen UNESCO Global Geopark is a region of idyllic villages, green valleys, and mountains covered in spruce and fir, home to lynx, foxes, ibex and chamois. Countless tributaries flow from the high mountains to the valleys, where, particularly in the communities of Wildalpen, Palfau and Gams, the geopark supports the conservation of orchards growing old and rare varieties of apples and pears. In some of these rivers, strong water flow allows for high-adrenaline experiences such as rafting, canyoning and kayaking. The Upper Styrian region, where the geopark is located, has been a centre for mining and iron ore processing for centuries. At its peak in the 1950s, it was the largest iron ore mining region in Central Europe, with up to 5,000 miners. This long and rich heritage, inscribed on UNESCO’s Intangible Cultural Heritage list since 2018, has been passed down through generations in the form of dances such as the Eisenerz Miner’s Dance, songs, traditional miners’ workwear, and initiation rites like the Ledersprung, which involves jumping over a leather miner’s apron. Today, this heritage can be explored along the Styrian Iron Trail, which links 18 municipalities. The 100-kilometre trail includes numerous historical sites and museums that tell the story of the region’s centuries-old mining, metallurgical and industrial traditions.
Quote: “The gypsum-bearing Kraus Cave of Gams was the first cave in the world to have electric light installed for the public in 1892.”

Introduction EN: The 14 km Han Cave can be accessed via a vintage tram and features a beautifully curated museum.Explore picturesque towns like Durbuy, known as ‘the smallest city in the world’, and its surrounding castles.Try the world-famous Trappiste de Rochefort beer, brewed at the Abbey of St. Remy.
Description: The Famenne-Ardenne UNESCO Global Geopark lies in Wallonia, southern Belgium—a French-speaking region known for picturesque medieval towns, castles, and craft beer made by monks. The geopark offers more: fascinating caves, preserved forests, and ancient history. Three distinctive units divide the landscape: to the north, the Famenne, a large depression with schistose substratum characterised by hay meadows and wet grasslands; in the south, the Ardennes, a vast sandstone plateau from which several rivers flow; and the Calestienne, a central calcareous region where water has carved numerous karstic features. These geological formations date from the Paleozoic era (541 to 251 million years ago), when sandstone, limestone, and clay were deposited in a marine environment depending on climate and continental proximity. These deposits were folded during the Hercynian mountain-building event (around 295 million years ago) and later flattened during the Meso-Cenozoic. The Ardennes are composed of Lower Devonian sandstones (419 to 393 million years old), forming a distinct relief in the southern part of the geopark known as the Ardennes Plateau, which includes the region’s highest elevation at 560 metres. The central Calestienne consists of Middle Devonian limestones (393 to 383 million years old), perforated with karstic channels and marked by cliffs. Finally, the northern schists of the Famenne depression date to the Upper Devonian (383 to 359 million years ago), and also include synclines of Carboniferous limestones (359 to 331 million years ago). This juxtaposition of rock types creates a contrasting landscape directly tied to the underlying geology. The geopark is renowned for its underground world of caves and sinkholes. The caves of Han, Rochefort, and Hotton are internationally recognised not only for tourism but also for their value to scientific research. The 14 km Han Cave, accessed by vintage tram, includes a beautifully curated museum.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The educational role of the geopark, in close collaboration with scientific research across the territory, is key to improving understanding of geological systems and their interactions with the atmosphere, biosphere, and hydrosphere. This approach supports sustainable management and valorisation of the territory’s geological heritage—scientific and touristic alike—including the stewardship of underground resources. The region’s rich cultural and archaeological heritage is showcased through key sites. The Megaliths Museum in Wéris is devoted to the Neolithic period, highlighting the cultural, spiritual, and ceremonial significance of megaliths—large stone structures often used for religious or funerary purposes. The area also preserves important Roman heritage. One of Northern Gaul’s largest Roman villas can be visited at the Malagne-Rochefort Archaeopark near Rochefort town centre. The geopark also holds more recent historical significance. The rolling hills of the Ardenne Massif were the site of the 1914 Battle of the Ardennes, where German forces defeated the French with nearly 60,000 casualties. Today, the geology of the region underpins diverse activities, including tourism, sport, and local industries. A well-marked trail network allows visitors to explore the geopark on foot, linking geosites and some of Belgium’s most picturesque villages—such as Ny, Sohier, and Wéris—as well as several medieval castles, including the celebrated Castle of Jemeppe. For those seeking refreshment along the way, the world-famous Trappiste de Rochefort beer, brewed at the Abbey of St. Remy, offers a satisfying stop.
Quote: “The largest number of karstic phenomena in Belgium ánd in Europe”

Introduction EN: Visit the medieval Manderscheid Castles, which overlook the narrow valley of the Lieser River.Explore the Eifel Maar Museum in Manderscheid, offering insights into the region’s unique geological history.Join geo-active experiences including guided tours to volcanic sites, volcano-themed events, and workshops on volcanism, geothermal energy, and ecosystems shaped by volcanic activity.
Description: Located in the northwestern part of the Rhenish Slate Mountains, the Vulkaneifel UNESCO Global Geopark is defined by its volcanic legacy, with over 350 eruption centres that have shaped its landscape. The region is particularly renowned for maar volcanoes, low-relief craters formed by explosive phreatomagmatic eruptions when groundwater contacts hot magma. Vulkaneifel’s volcanic activity occurred in two main phases: the first, between 45 and 35 million years ago, and the second beginning around one million years ago, culminating in the Ulmener Maar eruption 10,900 years ago. Many of these maar craters have filled with water or developed into bogs, offering a continuous sediment record of the last 150,000 years. These deposits provide detailed reconstructions of past climates and ecosystems, with current research extending the timeline of climate records to approximately 130,000 years, establishing Vulkaneifel as the most important climate archive for Central Europe. Paleontological discoveries, such as the well-preserved primitive horse and the world’s oldest known honey bee found in the Eckfeld Maar, contribute to the global significance of the region. These findings, along with ongoing geoscientific research, underscore the region’s importance. Geologically, the area remains active, with surface uplift continuing at a rate of about one millimetre per year.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Vulkaneifel UNESCO Global Geopark is deeply rooted in the local and regional cultural heritage, from Celtic and Roman relics to medieval castles and chapels. Sites such as the Celtic ramparts of Steineberg and Barsberg, the Roman villa complex in Duppach, and the walkable town fortifications in Hillesheim reveal the ancient layers of this landscape. Notably, the “Saviour Church” in Gerolstein stands as a symbol of the Protestant community in the early 20th century. These protected monuments serve as venues for public and private events, such as the annual medieval festival at the Manderscheid Castles. The geopark is actively engaged in supporting regional tourism and plays a key role in developing local and regional tourism strategies. Local guides, under the direction of the geopark, help enhance visitors' experiences and understanding of the area. One innovative approach has been the creation of the Vulkaneifel-Pfade (Volcano Eifel Paths), a series of leisure trails designed to encourage mindfulness while telling authentic regional stories, fairy tales and myths. These trails provide hikers with an opportunity to pause, reflect, and engage meaningfully with the landscape. Local customs continue to play a significant role in the region’s tourism. The Rhenish Carnival, now part of UNESCO’s Intangible Cultural Heritage, is celebrated across the region, with vibrant parades and events attracting large crowds. Other traditional activities such as May Day celebrations, Epiphany singing, and the presence of local choirs enrich the region’s cultural offerings. Additionally, the geopark supports the Viez (apple cider) culture, with the annual crowning of the Cider Queen, who serves as an ambassador for the region, promoting local traditions and products.
Quote: “The Earth below the Vulkaneifel is still in motion, pushing the surface one millimeter higher each year”

Titre EN: Thuringia Inselsberg - Drei Gleichen UNESCO Global Geopark
Introduction EN: Hike the 'Geo and Pleasure Trail,' starting and ending at the Arnstadt brewery, showcasing local food traditions and stunning views, with sculptures connecting the land's fertility to the famous Rostbratwurst sausage.Visit the Bromacker Fossil Site, a key European site for Permian tetrapod tracks and fossils, with significant palaeontological discoveries.Explore the GeoMuseum at Castle Ehrenstein, home to the Böttcher collection of Muschelkalk fossils and dinosaurs, and learn about the region's ancient marine life.
Description: Thuringia Inselsberg - Drei Gleichen UNESCO Global Geopark is named after two of its most prominent features: Inselsberg, a mountain peak that rises to 916 meters, formed through the erosion of softer surrounding rocks, and Drei Gleichen, a medieval castle complex built between the 8th and 11th centuries atop the region’s mountain peaks. The region’s geological history stretches back millions of years, starting with the merging of landmasses to form the supercontinent Pangaea. As time passed, the land began to break apart, leaving behind fascinating rock formations and fossils. One of the standout sites is the Ruhla Crystalline Complex, where the ancient foundation of the region can be seen in exposed rocks. Millions of years ago, this area was surrounded by an ancient sea, creating fossil-rich reefs that were discovered in the early 19th century. The Thuringian Forest Mountain Basin, a valley nestled between mountains, contains a thick layer of rock formations from the Late Carboniferous and Early Permian periods. This area is significant not only for its fossils but also for the early study of plant life, which began here over 300 years ago.  The youngest rocks in the region, found in the Drei Gleichen area, date back to the Triassic and Jurassic periods. This area features dramatic landscapes, including colourful badlands, shaped by the Earth’s movements. It is also home to the only site in central Germany where the boundary between the Triassic and Jurassic periods can be seen.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Thuringia Inselsberg - Drei Gleichen UNESCO Global Geopark is deeply interconnected with the cultural heritage of its local communities, preserving centuries-old traditions and fostering new research initiatives that bridge the past with the present. The region’s rich cultural heritage is visible in historical sites such as the Marienglashöhle Friedrichroda, a former gypsum mine that operated from 1778 to 1903. The mine is now a site where visitors can explore the evolution of the Thuringian Forest and learn about the 400-year mining tradition around the town of Friedrichroda. The Bromacker fossil deposit in the Thuringian Forest is also at the heart of a significant ongoing research project led by the geopark in which systematic excavations and geological studies are taking place. The aim is to enhance our understanding of early land vertebrates and their habitats. The research, conducted by a collaboration of institutions, also invites the public to witness the work firsthand, connecting community and scientific knowledge. The Metal Craft Museum, Steinbach-Hallenberg, preserves the technical and cultural history of iron processing, once the region’s most important industry. Through interactive exhibits, visitors can learn about local dialects, traditions, flax processing, and the farming lifestyle that intertwined with metal crafts. The museum vividly depicts the working conditions of past centuries and celebrates the community’s heritage.

Introduction EN: The Ridge Trail is rich in cultural heritage, taking you past Bronze-Age burial sites such as the Verhøj, a 121 m burial mound which marks the highest point in the whole of the geopark territory.Explore richly forested areas around the Vejrhøj Arch and the Rørvig Peninsula.Learn how the geopark promotes awareness of biodiversity and geodiversity through school visits, public outreach, and restoration projects like the dead ice landscape on the Egebjerg Peninsula.
Description: Stretching over a peninsula on Zealand Island and facing the Kattegat Sea, Odsherred UNESCO Global Geopark preserves an exceptional glacial landscape shaped during the latter part of the Weichselian glaciation, around 17,000 years ago. The ice sheet flattened the terrain, carved out glacial depressions, and deposited sediment that gave rise to the region’s distinctive topography. The most dominant landforms are three end moraines known as the Odsherred Arches. These large ridges form the spine of the geopark and are regarded as a textbook example of glacial geomorphology. Together with meltwater plains and kettle holes, they offer insight into the dynamics of the last glaciation and are considered of high scientific value by both Danish and international geologists. The Ridge Trail (Højderygstien), a seven-kilometre hiking route, follows one of the Odsherred Arches and offers sweeping views across Sejerø Bay and Lammefjord. Lammefjord is a former fjord that has been partially reclaimed for agriculture, illustrating the interaction between geological heritage and land use. Since the end of the last Ice Age, coastal and postglacial processes have continued to shape the landscape, especially along the irregular coastline of white sand beaches and in the formation of numerous lakes. This ongoing evolution of landforms adds to the scientific and educational value of the area.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Since the end of the last Ice Age, the Odsherred landscape has supported continuous human activity, with archaeological traces from multiple periods still visible today. The region is home to approximately 1,000 sites of cultural and historical interest, including one of Europe’s most significant Bronze Age discoveries: the Sun Chariot. While the original artefact is housed at the National Museum of Denmark, the Solvognens Fundsted (The Sun Chariot Site) in the geopark offers a curated visitor experience. Through a 30-minute audio-guided walk, visitors explore the landscape and an interpretive art installation that commemorates the archaeological find. The geopark integrates its rich agricultural traditions into educational programming and visitor engagement. At the Visitor’s Field, local pupils participate in guided tours to learn about traditional farming methods, particularly carrot and potato cultivation. These visits often culminate in outdoor cooking sessions, which freshly harvested ingredients. Contemporary art continues to shape the cultural identity of the region. In the early 20th century, groups of painters were drawn to the unique Odsherred light and landscape, forming what is now known as the Odsherred Painters. Their work, much of it inspired by geosites, is exhibited in the local art museum and integrated into an art history trail across the geopark.
Quote: “Feel the presence of history”

Introduction EN: Over 200 caves, along with pinnacle morphologies and poljes, bear witness to the relentless action of water over time.A guided biology tour of the Abrasion Platform provides a close look at the flysch and shows how a variety of species have adapted to live in this complex ecosystem, including starfish, octopuses, sea cucumbers, hares, and more.
Description: The Basque Coast UNESCO Global Geopark is located in the Basque-Cantabrian Basin, west of the Pyrenees. Its geological evolution is related, therefore, with the opening and closing of the Bay of Biscay (Lower Cretaceous – Eocene), the rise of the Pyrenean Mountain Chain (Oligocene – Pliocene) and, lastly, the modelling of the landscape conditioned mainly by its closeness to the sea (Pliocene – Quaternary). During the Lower Cretaceous (115 – 105 million years ago), the geopark was under a shallow tropical sea where large deposits of limestone of reef origin formed. Today, those limestone formations from the Aptian – Albian age form the main inland terrain of the geopark, with mountains very close to the coast that exceed 600 m in height. The opening of the Bay of Biscay fractured the seafloor, giving rise to a deep basin where more than 5,000 m of pelagic sediment and flysch were deposited continuously between the Albian (110 million years ago) and the Lower Eocene (50 million years ago). The most recognisable part of this gigantic outcrop is located on Zumaia Beach, where one of the most important and well-known stratigraphic outcrops in the world can be found. This geological open book unveils ancient global crises and catastrophes that have shaped our planet. Notably, one of the layers marks the last of the five mass extinctions that have occurred throughout Earth’s history. Referred to as the K/Pg or P/E extinction event, it took place approximately 65.5 million years ago when a large asteroid struck Earth near Chicxulub, Mexico, resulting in the extinction of the dinosaurs.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The archaeological heritage of the geopark is among the best in the Cantabrian area. There are more than 40 caves containing archaeological remains from the Lower Palaeolithic to the Neolithic. Cave paintings in the Ekain Cave, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, must be highlighted, but there are many other sites of great interest with a surprisingly continuous record. They allow for a detailed reconstruction of the evolution of humans, forests, and palaeobiota in the valley during the last 200,000 years, linked to climate variations. The Nautilus Didactic and Research Classroom houses an internationally significant collection of giant ammonites in Mutriku. Developed over six years, this initiative brought together the entire ammonite collection under one roof, enhancing its scientific and educational value. Geoparkea collaborated with the University of the Basque Country to investigate the collection’s scientific importance while also working with the Mutriku City Council to develop educational programmes, making palaeontology accessible to children. Cultural heritage, particularly intangible heritage, holds great significance for both the Basque Country and the Basque Coast UNESCO Global Geopark. The Basque culture is deeply rooted, with ancestral customs, traditions, and its unique language, Euskara, serving as a key element of its intangible heritage. The conservation and promotion of this heritage are fundamental to the geopark’s strategic objectives. A recent initiative, The Enigma of the Basque Language Euskara guided tour, was developed by a well-known linguist and TV presenter in response to public interest. This tour offers visitors insight into Basque culture and language and has become a regular feature of the geopark’s annual geotourism programme. The Maritime Heritage Festival showcases the region’s seafaring traditions through live demonstrations, the construction of a traditional wooden boat, an exhibition of historical fishing artefacts, and navigation in traditional boats. The geopark’s maritime heritage is also highlighted in the Coastal Walk Georoute between Deba and Mutriku, which explores Mutriku’s historic connection to the sea through eight themed stops on an app-based tour.
Quote: “Spectacular coastal formations marking various chapters of the history of the planet”

Introduction EN: At Los Roques, impressive towering cliffs—formed by intense volcanic activity and subsequent erosion by the sea—showcase the island's dramatic coastal scenery and provide a glimpse into its geological history.Explore the archaeological heritage of the Canary Islands at El Julan, a significant pre-Hispanic site with architectural structures, burial caves, worship sites, shepherds' shelters, and engraved panels known as "Los Letreros" and "Los Números."Discover other notable heritage features such as the rock engravings of La Caleta.
Description: The smallest of the main islands in the Canary Islands Archipelago, El Hierro is the most recent volcanic island of the archipelago to emerge above sea level, 1.2 million years ago. Still in its early stages of construction, it has the greatest density of volcanoes in the Canary Islands, with over 500 open craters and another 300 covered by more recent lava flows. It is known as the “island of 1,000 volcanoes.” The island is home to the youngest active volcano in the Canary Islands, known as Volcán de Lomo Negro, which last erupted in 1793 and has remained dormant since. It also features impressive volcanic landforms, such as volcanic cones, lava flows, and craters. The most prominent of these is the El Golfo volcanic complex, which includes the El Golfo Valley, a vast semi-circular depression created by a massive landslide. El Hierro’s geological history also includes recent volcanic activity. On 10 October 2011, an underwater eruption occurred at a depth of 300 m, 1.5 km off the southern coast, adding to El Hierro’s rich geological heritage a new, still-submerged volcano called Tagoro. This geological milestone led to the implementation of a project that culminated in 2015 with UNESCO declaring the island of El Hierro a geopark. The island has three impressive amphitheatre-shaped escarpments open to the ocean, where viewpoints have been strategically placed to observe the El Golfo Valley, the arches of Las Playas, and El Julan. The presence of these amphitheatres at the junctions between each pair of the three ridges gives El Hierro its characteristic three-edged pyramid shape.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: El Hierro’s cultural identity reflects its history of isolation and adaptation. The island was first settled by Amazigh or Berber communities from North Africa, who developed distinct traditions in animal herding, water harvesting, whistled language, gastronomy, and toponymy. Archaeological traces such as the geometric ideograms of El Julan and Libyco-Berber texts—the highest concentration in the Canary Islands—provide insight into this heritage. The arrival of Norman conquerors in the 15th century led to a blending of Bimbache traditions with European influences, shaping the landscape and economy. Cultural heritage includes rural stone constructions, salt flats, winepresses, and religious sites such as the Santuario de la Virgen de Los Reyes. Rock art at La Restinga, Guinea Village, and the Mirador de La Peña by César Manrique are key protected sites of interest. Three more sites—Los Carneros de Tigaday, Fiesta de la Cruz, and the Hotelito de Puntagrande, the smallest hotel in the world—have been newly recognised. El Hierro’s intangible heritage is deeply rooted in community traditions. The Bajada de la Virgen de Los Reyes pilgrimage, held every four years, is a key cultural event, alongside the shepherds’ Caracol Cave festival and the Los Carneros de Tigaday carnival. The island also preserves its unique Silbo Herreño, a whistled language once used for long-distance communication. Sustainability is central to El Hierro’s development. The island has promoted eco-tourism, focusing on scuba diving, natural pools, and an extensive certified footpath network. Gorona del Viento, its hydro-wind power plant, has made El Hierro a model for 100% renewable energy, attracting researchers and policymakers worldwide.
Quote: “The island of a 1000 volcanoes”

Titre EN: Molina- Alto Tajo UNESCO Global Geopark
Introduction EN: Try local traditional products such as honey from the Caldereros Range, sausages from El Pairon, truffles, or wine, promoted through fairs and local markets.Visit one of the geopark’s museums, such as the Cubillejo de la Sierra Historic Museum, the Hombrados Open Air Ethnographical Museum, or the Peñalén Mining Visitors Centre.
Description: Molina-Alto Tajo UNESCO Global Geopark, located in the Castellana area of the Iberian Mountain Range, lies between the Ebro and Tagus rivers. The region features mountains reaching up to 1,900 metres and preserves a continuous sedimentary sequence spanning over 400 million years, recording key geological events such as the formation and breakup of Pangea. Several significant geosites highlight the region’s geological history. The Lower Palaeozoic of Checa village provides evidence of the Ordovician glaciation, shedding light on ancient climatic conditions. The Lower Triassic continental sediments of Barranco de la Hoz del Río Gallo reveal sedimentation processes from the time when Pangea was still intact. Additionally, the Fuentelsaz GSSP stratotype serves as a globally recognised reference point for studying the transition between the Early and Middle Jurassic periods. The geopark is primarily composed of Mesozoic formations, particularly from the Triassic and Jurassic periods, which cover much of the Molina region and the province of Guadalajara. These sedimentary sequences include clastic and carbonate materials, deposited under alternating continental and marine conditions. Structural features, such as northwest-oriented compressive folds, developed due to the geological forces shaping the Iberian Range. Cretaceous formations, particularly in Comarca de Molina, consist mainly of carbonate rocks like limestone and dolomite. Dispersed Neogene outcrops, though limited in extent, add further stratigraphic complexity to the region. The Shire of Molina is characterised by remarkable geodiversity, containing a well-preserved stratigraphic sequence of significant continuity. Its tectonic, lithological, and geomorphological features reflect the area's long and complex geological evolution. Additionally, the region hosts palaeontological sites with fossiliferous deposits spanning multiple geological periods, providing crucial insights into past ecosystems.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Molina-Alto Tajo UNESCO Global Geopark has a rich cultural heritage spanning from the Palaeolithic to the Iron Age, reflected in its archaeological sites, historical architecture, and traditional industries. Casares Cave, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, contains engravings from the Upper Palaeolithic and palaeontological remains from the Middle Palaeolithic. Other significant prehistoric sites include Rillo de Gallo, which preserves Neolithic remains, and the Caldereros Range, an active research site. The region also has an exceptional number of Iron Age hillforts, some of which have been excavated and turned into museum exhibits. Traditional industries such as mining and salt extraction have shaped the region’s history. The salt works of Saelices de la Sal were vital to the provincial economy for centuries. Iron ore and other metal mining, active since the Iron Age, played a significant role in local development. Intangible cultural heritage is also a key part of the geopark’s identity. Religious pilgrimages to hermitages, such as the La Hoz Virgin Loa, continue to be practised. Local festivals include the Luzón Bulls carnival tradition, and the ringing of bells in Alustante was recently recognised as an official cultural heritage practice by the regional government. One initiative includes advising schoolteachers on integrating local heritage into curricula.
Quote: “Rocks of more than 400 million years old are found next to rocks in the process of being formed”

Introduction EN: Modern history in the Chablais dates to the 19th century during the industrial era with the large-scale quarrying of gypsum, slate and building stone in the towns of Armoy, Morzine and Meillerie.From the late 19th century, until the beginning of World War I, the Lake Geneva Riviera was one of the most frequented European destinations by high society. A distinctive Art Nouveau architectural identity was established and lakefront promenades, grand gardens, thermal spa buildings, hotels, theatres and casinos were built.From the 1950s, winter sports tourism became very well established and numerous famous ski resorts such as Chatel, Morzine-Avoriaz and Les Gets are now the annual destinations for millions of visitors.
Description: The Chablais Massif offers a rare and exemplary geological model of how the Alps were formed. Its stacked rock sequences reveal key stages in the region’s geological evolution—starting from the time when landmasses were separated, through continental drift, and culminating in subduction and continental collision processes that gave rise to the Alpine orogeny. This long and complex history has made Chablais an important reference point for geologists studying mountain formation. Later, during the Quaternary period, successive glaciations reworked the landscape, carving deep valleys and depositing vast volumes of sediment. One striking result of this glacial history is the 600-metre-thick Evian Natural Mineral Water aquifer. Visitors can learn about its formation and hydrological cycle at the spa town of Évian-les-Bains, or explore its catchment areas at geosites such as Tréchauffé and Champéillant, where rain and glacier meltwater begin their slow underground journey through the rocks. Geological processes have also shaped dramatic events in recent history. On the night of 11 March 1943, intense rainfall and unstable bedrock triggered a landslide that blocked the Brenon River, creating Vallon Lake. This newly formed lake submerged farmland and displaced families. Today, Vallon Lake, the youngest lake in the Chablais region, lies beneath the Roc d'Enfer in a tranquil forested setting, with the submerged foundations of former buildings still present beneath its surface. The retreat of glaciers at the end of the Last Ice Age also left behind numerous smaller lakes and wetlands that now serve as biodiversity hotspots. These include the Chilly Marsh, fed by waters from Mont de Boisy, and the Vouas of Lyaud, home to carnivorous plants, dragonflies and grey herons.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Situated between Lake Geneva (Lac Léman) and Mont Blanc, the Chablais UNESCO Global Geopark covers a 50 km stretch of remarkable natural landscapes that have shaped the cultural and economic life of its inhabitants and attracted generations of visitors. The region’s human presence dates back to the final retreat of the glaciers, around 12,000 years ago. Notable archaeological sites include the extensive Neolithic necropolis at Genevray in Thonon-les-Bains, which contains over 220 sepulchres dated between 2850 and 1350 years BCE. Later, in the Neolithic and Bronze Age, communities built stilt houses along Lake Geneva and other Alpine lakes. The site at Tougues, with its exceptionally preserved artefacts, is part of the UNESCO World Heritage listing “Prehistoric Pile Dwellings around the Alps.” From the 12th century, Chablais became part of the Duchy of Savoy, a Franco-Italo-Swiss territory that remained under Savoy rule for eight centuries. Remnants of this era include the Castle of Ripaille on the shore of Lake Geneva, once the residence of the Dukes of Savoy. Religious orders also left a lasting mark on the territory, founding abbeys in the valleys of Haut Chablais, including the 12th-century Abbey of Abondance, which remains open to visitors today. Geotourism plays a vital role in supporting the region’s sustainable development. Excursions for the public, guide-led tours, and a coordinated network of local tourist offices promote the geopark’s values and heritage. The Chablais UNESCO Global Geopark also supports the development and visibility of local products through branding initiatives, including protected designations such as AOP cheeses and AOC wines, as well as artisanal crafts.
Quote: “Rich geological history, lots of lakes and a wealth of renowned mineral waters.”

Introduction EN: The South West Coast Path runs the entire 22-mile stretch of the geopark coastline taking in Berry Head National Nature Reserve, Cockington Country Park, woodlands, and farmland.Torre Abbey holds significant archaeological value as a nationally recognised scheduled monument. Established in 1196, it is one of the finest-preserved mediaeval abbeys in Devon and Cornwall.Sit beside the Dame Agatha Christie CBE sculpture on a harbour-front bench in Torquay, unveiled in 2025 and depicting the iconic author, who grew up in the area, with her dog Peter.
Description: Stretching over more than 100 km², from rich undulating hills down to an intricate coastline of sandy and rocky coves, cliffs, caves, sea stacks, and arches, the English Riviera UNESCO Global Geopark tells a story of more than 400 million years. It begins in the Devonian period (419–358 million years ago), when grey limestones were deposited in warm tropical seas south of the equator. During the Carboniferous period (358–298 million years ago), a collision between two continental masses created a vast mountain range. Over time, erosion exposed the underlying limestone, which can still be seen today at prominent sites such as Hopes Nose and Berry Head – the latter an internationally recognised heritage site and National Nature Reserve, home to a variety of coastal wildlife and restored Napoleonic fortifications. Around 500,000 years ago, the region had shifted further north, and flowing water played a major role in shaping the landscape, carving cave systems into the limestone. Among these is Kents Cavern, one of only two caves worldwide where three or more human species have been found. Homo heidelbergensis, Neanderthals, and Homo sapiens left behind traces here dating back over half a million years, making it one of Europe’s most significant prehistoric caves. With its accessible caverns, Kents Cavern has attracted Earth scientists for generations, including Rev’d Buckland, Charles Darwin, Alfred Wallace, and William Pengelly. Pengelly developed a pioneering method of stratigraphic recording still used in archaeology today. Torquay Museum preserves his notebooks and many artefacts discovered at the site, including the oldest human fossil found in northwestern Europe – a jawbone dated to 41,000 years ago.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The English Riviera has long inspired stories that blur the lines between history and legend. After his defeat at the Battle of Waterloo in 1815, Napoleon was held aboard HMS Bellerophon in Tor Bay. Granted permission to view the coastline, he reportedly compared its tranquil beauty to the Mediterranean shores of his homeland. In the Victorian era, the story resonated with the growing trend for coastal leisure, and the English Riviera emerged as a resort destination associated with elegance and escape. The resort towns of Torquay, Paignton, and Brixham are situated around one of England’s most scenic bays, each offering a distinct experience: Torquay’s continental charm, Paignton’s traditional seaside atmosphere, and Brixham’s maritime heritage. The area has welcomed generations of visitors and remains one of the country’s most popular holiday destinations. The Riviera continues to support the local economy through tourism, sport, culture, and cuisine. Sailing is a major attraction, with over 50 events held annually, including the Brixham Heritage Race and regattas across the three towns. The coastline also receives visits from tall ships, cruise liners, and international rallies. South Devon’s culinary reputation is equally notable, with a high concentration of organic producers and fresh seafood landed daily in Brixham, one of the UK’s busiest fishing ports. The region's most famous cultural figure is Agatha Christie, born in Torquay. With over two billion books sold worldwide, she remains a major draw. Visitors can follow the Agatha Christie Mile, explore her personal collection at Torquay Museum, and visit her former home, Greenway, now a popular attraction.
Quote: “With tales going back 400 million years and a spectacular coastline the area has much to discover and enjoy”

Introduction EN: Discover traditional shepherd shelters (mitata) and learn about dry-stone building techniques that are still in use today.Hike to the summit of Psiloritis, Crete’s highest peak, and take in panoramic views shaped by ongoing tectonic uplift.Watch the bearded vultures (kokkalas) glide above Psiloritis, where the species is known to maintain one of its last viable populations in southeastern Europe.
Description: At the heart of Crete, Psiloritis UNESCO Global Geopark encompasses the Psiloritis and Talaia Ori mountain ranges and the surrounding valleys. It presents an almost continuous rock sequence from the Permian period (around 298 million years ago) to the present, making it a key site for understanding regional geodynamics. Crete is located at the intersection of the Eurasian, African, Arabian and Anatolian plates. As the island drifts away from Europe at 3.5 cm per year and Africa simultaneously moves northwards at over 2 cm per year, intense tectonic convergence drives the uplift of Psiloritis and the fragmentation of the island. These processes have shaped a dramatic landscape of high mountains, deep gorges and active faults. The area’s limestone bedrock has led to the development of a dense karst system, with caves, dolines, sinkholes, and one vertical cave reaching over 950 metres in depth. Three major show caves—Sfentoni, with richly decorated chambers; Melidoni, with archaeological significance; and Idaion Andro, a sacred site from the Neolithic to Roman periods—highlight the region’s geological and cultural links. Distinctive tectonic folds are visible in the Vossakos Open Air Fold Museum, where a range of well-preserved structures is exposed along the road between Kato Doxaro and the Vossakos Monastery. These outcrops attract students and researchers each year and offer direct access to textbook examples of rock deformation.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Psiloritis UNESCO Global Geopark lies at the cultural and geographical crossroads of the Mediterranean. For centuries, diverse cultures have shaped the region’s identity, leaving behind a rich legacy of architecture, land use, and traditions—closely tied to the island’s geological setting. Local limestone has been central to building practices across the geopark. Dry-stone architecture reflects a deep relationship between people and their environment. A key example is the mitato—a circular shepherd shelter that typically includes a space for maturing cheese and a yard for livestock. Their form reflects a collective way of life that continues today in the mountain communities of Psiloritis. To support the preservation of this tradition, the geopark collaborates with local associations to offer dry-stone construction workshops in the village of Margarites. Led by experienced craftspeople and supported by the geopark’s scientific team, the workshops combine hands-on training with geological knowledge and field visits to key stone structures. This initiative strengthens the link between geological heritage and sustainable land use while encouraging intergenerational knowledge transfer. The geopark also includes several important archaeological sites, such as ancient settlements, sacred caves, and classical-era cities. These are integrated into educational and tourism activities, helping to reinforce local identity and connect visitors with the long-standing interaction between landscape and culture.
Quote: "That connection has endured for thousands of years I’d say, and still holds true—for me and for many others who continue to live and work in these mountains." Nikolaos Kapsalis — Local resident and truffle hunter

Introduction EN: The iconic Reykjanesviti Lighthouse, standing proudly on the peninsula’s edge, is a symbol of maritime heritage with panoramic views.Birdwatchers can spot a variety of species, including puffins, at the seabird colonies along the coastal cliffs. The nearby Kleifarvatn Lake is home to unique fish species, making it a popular fishing destination.Reykjanesbær showcases traditional Icelandic architecture and local culture.Photos courtesy of © H0rdur (Photos 1-3).
Description: Reykjanes UNESCO Global Geopark, located in southwest Iceland near the capital, Reykjavik, is a dynamic landscape where new crust is constantly being created. Volcanic eruptions and earthquakes, the most recent occurring in the 14th century, are part of the region's geological story. The Reykjanes Peninsula features a rift volcanic system with a fissure swarm that stretches across the land, forming volcanic craters, lava fields and fissure eruptions. As one of Iceland’s most active volcanic regions, Reykjanes also boasts remarkable geothermal activity, including hot springs, geysers and mud pools. The Gunnuhver mud pools offer visitors a unique encounter with the region's geothermal activity. Located near Reykjanes Lighthouse, Gunnuhver is named after a female ghost, Gunna, who, according to legend, terrorised the area until a priest trapped her, causing her to plunge into the boiling mud pools. These pools form when steam from a boiling geothermal reservoir condenses and mixes with surface water, creating acidic conditions due to the presence of carbon dioxide and hydrogen sulphide, that transform fresh lava into clay. Among the Gunnuhver group, the largest mud pool spans an impressive 20 meters and boils vigorously, offering visitors a mesmerising glimpse of the Earth's power. The Reykjanes Peninsula, a geologically young part of Iceland, represents the volcanic counterpart of the North Atlantic Ridge. This is where two tectonic plates, the North American and Eurasian, diverge at a steady rate of 2.5 cm per year, resulting in a fascinating interplay of geological forces that continuously reshape the landscape. Recognised as one of the IUGS 100 Geological Heritage Sites, it stands as a remarkable testament to the planet's ever-changing nature.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Reykjanes UNESCO Global Geopark fosters strong partnerships with local communities and educational institutions, creating a foundation for sustainable development and geotourism. Educational initiatives include the development of materials for all school levels, with the aim of raising awareness about the region’s geological heritage while promoting environmental stewardship.
