Local communities must be at the heart of such projects, as our story is best told in our own voice.— Abdullah bin Ibrahim Al-Eisa, native resident

Introduction EN: See the iconic Dodamsambong Peaks, three cone-shaped limestone pillars rising from the river, shaped over time by water and weathering.Take part in outdoor activities like paragliding, hiking, and sightseeing that highlight Danyang’s dramatic geological and mountainous landscapes.Visit Suyanggae Exhibition Hall to discover archaeological artefacts from the Palaeolithic era.
Description: Located at the heart of the Korean Peninsula, Danyang UNESCO Global Geopark lies along the Baekdu Daegan mountain range and showcases remarkable geological diversity. The landscape features folds and thrusts within 1.87-billion-year-old granite gneiss, alongside limestone, quartzite, shale, and sandstone from the Palaeozoic and Mesozoic eras. These rocks record a complex tectonic history spanning three major geological events that are superimposed in this region, making it a key site for understanding the geological evolution of East Asia. The sedimentary sequences in Danyang provide valuable information on ancient marine environments, while the middle Darriwilian carbon isotope excursion—recorded here for the first time in the Sino-Korean Craton—offers a globally recognised reference point for correlating rocks of Ordovician age. Research conducted on the region’s limestone caves has contributed to knowledge of large-scale palaeoclimate variation in East Asia and has strengthened awareness of cave conservation. Additionally, fossil evidence in the Hari area represents the first discovery of a mass extinction event from the Permian period in terrestrial sediments in East Asia. With a balanced distribution of igneous, metamorphic and sedimentary rocks, and a well-preserved sequence of geological layers—excluding only the Devonian—Danyang provides a rare window into both regional and global Earth history. The area also contains features such as karst topography, unconformities with a 1.2-billion-year gap, and fossil-bearing formations, all of which form the basis for a network of geosites that support geotourism and public understanding of Earth sciences.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Today, Danyang UNESCO Global Geopark attracts visitors with a range of recreational and educational opportunities. Hiking trails, cruise tours along the Namhan River, and panoramic views from the Mancheonha Scenic Observation Deck offer ways to engage with the region’s striking topography. The area is also home to the Republic of Korea’s largest paragliding facility, providing aerial views of the geopark’s diverse landscape. The region is known for its distinctive variety of garlic, cultivated on limestone terraces. This local product has become a popular souvenir and reflects the close relationship between agriculture, geology, and community identity in Danyang. Education is a central pillar of the geopark’s activities. An annual environmental programme encourages students to take part in conservation initiatives, including clean-ups at key geological sites. In collaboration with the Sobaeksan Observatory, the geopark is also developing integrated astronomy and geology education programmes. These aim to position Danyang as a national hub for school field trips and educational tourism, strengthening local engagement with the region’s geological heritage.

Introduction EN: Try local specialities made with star anise, one of the region’s most extensively grown crops, supported by Lang Son’s mineral-rich soils and covering more than 34,000 hectares.Explore the Na La cave system in Van Quan district, where visitors can navigate glittering stalactites, underground streams, and narrow passages that reveal thousands of years of geological formation.Hike to the Na Duong basin, an extraordinary site preserving tropical fossils from 40–20 million years ago, offering rare insights into ancient ecosystems and mammal migration across Southeast Asia.
Description: Set within the rugged limestone peaks of northern Viet Nam, Lang Son UNESCO Global Geopark tells a remarkable story of shifting seas, volcanic eruptions and evolving ecosystems. The geopark is a natural archive, preserving evidence of life’s evolution through the ages. Its oldest rocks reveal traces of an ancient seabed, once home to trilobites – marine creatures that resembled large woodlice – and graptolites, early sea animals that lived in colonies. As the sea receded, it left behind layers of shale, sandstone and limestone, and volcanic landscapes emerged. The geopark lies at a geologically significant crossroads, where two ancient continental fragments once collided around 245 million years ago. This tectonic collision shaped much of the region’s landscape and formed part of the broader geological structure of Southeast Asia. The area contains a nearly continuous sedimentary record stretching over 245 million years, helping researchers reconstruct past environmental changes and tectonic events. One of the geopark’s most remarkable geological sites is the Na Duong Basin – a natural depression that formed during later tectonic rifting around 56 to 34 million years ago. The fossils preserved here reveal a lush tropical ecosystem of ancient forests, swamps and lakes. Vertebrate and invertebrate fossils provide key insights into how mammals and other species moved across the region, making this site internationally significant for understanding biodiversity and evolution in Southeast Asia. The geopark’s dramatic limestone landscape, shaped by the region’s subtropical climate, features extensive karst formations and cave systems.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The geopark is home to diverse ethnic groups including the Kinh, Nung, Tay and Dao peoples, who uphold unique languages, crafts and traditions. Central to the region’s spiritual life is Đạo Mẫu, the worship of Mother Goddesses, a syncretic belief system that honours deities associated with different realms of the universe—heaven, earth, mountains, forests and water. Recognised by UNESCO as Intangible Cultural Heritage, Đạo Mẫu rituals often include hầu bóng (spirit mediumship), an empowering performance combining music, dance and storytelling that continues to shape the cultural identity of local communities. Lang Son’s rich intangible heritage is also reflected in Then singing, a spiritual musical tradition likened to a fairy rhythm, and the use of the Dan Tinh, a traditional gourd lute. These forms of expression are passed down through generations and remain part of everyday life and seasonal festivals, where traditional dress and customs are proudly displayed. The interweaving of geological and cultural heritage makes the geopark not only a site of natural importance but also a living cultural landscape.

Introduction EN: Learn about geothermal processes, volcanic gases, and thermo-medicinal waters at Puela Hot Springs, a geosite combining therapeutic benefits with geological education and scenic surroundings.Visit the GeoAmigo Cafeteria “Casa del Volcán,” owned by local resident, where local identity is celebrated through ancestral dishes and volcanic-themed cuisine using ingredients from nearby farmers.Explore Las Caras Tourist Complex, where petrified roots and ancestral carvings revealed after 2006 volcanic activity are now part of community-led tours, horseback rides, and volcanic mud treatments.
Description: Located in the Ecuadorian Andes, Tungurahua Volcano UNESCO Global Geopark displays a geological history spanning over 417 million years, shaped by volcanic eruptions, tectonic uplift, and glacial activity. The landscape features deep canyons, crystal-clear rivers, icy waterfalls, and towering rock walls carved over millennia. At its heart rises the imposing Tungurahua Volcano—still active and a key site for volcanological research. Beneath its surface, magma heats underground water, creating mineral-rich thermal springs that have long been treasured for their therapeutic properties. The geopark spans five cantons across Tungurahua and Chimborazo provinces—Baños de Agua Santa, Patate, Pelileo, Guano, and Penipe—where its creation has supported sustainable development through conservation, education, local production, and community-based tourism. The region also bears witness to a dramatic seismic past. Major earthquakes in 1797 and 1949 devastated towns such as Guano, Pelileo, and Patate, leaving a legacy of resilience that continues to shape the territory. Baños de Agua Santa, located at the foot of the volcano, endured a series of eruptions between 1999 and 2016, during which the community became internationally recognised for its effective risk management and recovery efforts. Today, Baños thrives as a centre of innovation and diversified livelihoods, with a vibrant adventure tourism industry, agroecological farming, and geotourism initiatives playing key roles in the local economy.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The geopark's cultural richness is reflected in the traditions of the Salasaca and Puruhá Indigenous peoples, who preserve their identity through distinctive clothing, music, dance, and ancestral storytelling. A cultural icon of the Puruhá people and ambassador of the geopark was Baltazar Ushca, widely known as “the Last Iceman of Chimborazo.” From childhood, he upheld the ancestral tradition of harvesting ice from the mountain’s glaciers, shaping a living legend that remains part of the region’s cultural heritage and symbolising the deep connection between people, place, and nature. The intersection of geological heritage and cultural identity is also visible in innovative sustainable development initiatives. One notable example is the GeoAmigo Cafeteria “Casa del Volcán,” owned by local resident Indira Medina. The café celebrates local identity and cuisine with a volcanic theme inspired by Tungurahua, using ingredients from nearby farmers and serving ancestral dishes with a contemporary twist. Another example is the Las Caras Tourist Complex, where visitors can explore petrified tree roots and carved rock faces attributed to the ancestral Killuyakus people. Discovered by Manuel Rosero after volcanic activity in 2006, the site is now managed by local residents who offer educational tours, horseback rides, and volcanic mineral mud treatments. The Guamag Protected Forest conserves 207 hectares of forest near Sangay and Llanganates National Parks, providing educational programmes, guided tours, and eco-friendly accommodation that strengthen environmental awareness and conservation in the region.
Quote: The geopark is our window to the world. Through it, we share our history, knowledge, and the importance of preserving our environment. — Myriam Masaquiza, Salasaca community entrepreneur and leader.

Introduction EN: Changshan UNESCO Global Geopark, located at the junction of the Yangtze and Cathaysia massifs along the Jiangshan-Shaoxing tectonic belt, stands out as an exceptional natural geological museum and laboratory for paleontological studies. Showcasing over a billion years of geological history, the mountainous landscape has a subtropical monsoon climate and is rich in biodiversity, featuring evergreen broad-leaved forests and a complex terrain sloping from the north and south towards the centre.
Description: The geopark preserves well-developed stratigraphic sequences and abundant, diverse fossils, which support global biostratigraphic studies, providing key insights into early life evolution and long-term tectonic processes.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Changshan boasts a history of over 1,800 years, and today around 300,000 people from nine ethnic groups live in the area, contributing to the stewardship of the region’s cultural and natural heritage. Cultural heritage is closely intertwined with the region’s landscape, as Changshan was an important link in the Maritime Silk Road, and during the Song Dynasty it was an important traffic artery which became renowned for its flourishing literary scene. The continuous study of Song poetry with over 4,000 recorded poems reflects the people’s deep connection to the land. The land continues to support local livelihoods, with the strata of the geopark meaning the soil contains a high content of nutrient elements beneficial for agriculture. Changshan is known in China as the hometown of citrus changshan-hayou and tea-oil camellia, and the geopark actively encourages the development of this characteristic agriculture, playing on its local advantages and bringing shared prosperity to the local community.

Introduction EN: Nisyros UNESCO Global Geopark, located in the southeastern Aegean Sea at the heart of the Dodecanese island group, encompasses the volcanic island of Nisyros and its surrounding islets.This compact geopark is remarkably diverse, shaped by one of the youngest and most active volcanic systems in Greece, and features one of the best-preserved calderas in the Aegean.
Description: The geopark presents a natural open-air geological museum, including the Stefanos hydrothermal crater, one of Europe’s largest and most accessible, alongside a series of hydrothermal craters, fields, lava domes, volcanic cones, and submarine volcanic centres. These features make Nisyros a natural laboratory for studying active volcanism, geothermal systems, and the evolution of young volcanic islands within the Hellenic Volcanic Arc.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Ecologically, the geopark hosts a diversity of habitats, with its volcanic soil supporting endemic and rare plant species, while terraced landscapes, dry-stone walls, and small-scale agriculture reflect long coexistence between people and nature. Villages such as Nikía and Mandraki preserve volcanic-stone architecture, and monasteries like Panagia Spiliani highlight spiritual heritage. In Nisyros, geology and human history are inseparable, and the geopark has encouraged the community to participate in heritage preservation through collaborations with local schools and research institutions, encouraging the next generation of environmental stewardship. Visitors are drawn to Nisyros for its cultural authenticity, with vibrant traditions of festivals, music and gastronomy very much still alive.

Titre EN: Joyce Country and Western Lakes UNESCO Global Geopark
Introduction EN: The rocks and landscapes of Joyce Country and Western Lakes UNESCO Global Geopark tell a story that spans 700 million years, linked to the mountain-building event of the Grampian-Taconic Orogeny (a major period of mountain formation over 450 million years ago).
Description: This has created great geodiversity in the park, displaying a wide range of igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks, and a rich fossil record. It is also home to Ireland’s only fjord at Killary Harbour. Limestone terrains in the east have developed extensive karst and epikarst systems, including the Cong isthmus, where you can find one of the world’s fastest flowing spring complex and multiple cave systems.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Around 60% of the geopark lies in a Gaeltacht area where Irish is a living language for home, education, business, and social life, making Joyce Country and Western Lakes the first UNESCO Global Geopark on the island of Ireland to include a Gaeltacht area. Irish is deeply embedded in local culture and has influenced the language of science itself, with terms such as “drumlin” derived from the Irish “droimainn”, now used internationally in glaciology. Communities across the region continue to participate in music, storytelling, crafts and cuisine, helping to keep the Irish language and associated cultural practices alive, such as Gaelic football, handball and traditional basket making using locally grown willows, with the geopark promoting sustainable development by supporting local businesses to keep the area’s intangible heritage alive.

Titre EN: Miné-Akiyoshidai Karst Plateau UNESCO Global Geopark
Introduction EN: Miné-Akiyoshidai Karst Plateau UNESCO Global Geopark features a diverse landscape of mountains, valley plains, and the Akiyoshidai karst plateau, known for its dolines and extensive limestone caves. The plateau’s grasslands, shaped by centuries of traditional burning, support unique limestone-adapted flora and fauna.
Description: The Akiyoshidai Karst Plateau, a key feature of the Miné-Akiyoshidai Geopark, is formed from the Akiyoshi Limestone, offering an 80-million-year record of marine ecosystems. This limestone, along with the fossil-rich Mine Group, preserves evidence of terrestrial life on land after the Permian extinction around 250 million years ago, including recently discovered plant and insect species. Nationally significant geological heritage includes skarn copper deposits formed by magma interacting with limestone around 100 million years ago, with this copper historically used in the Great Buddha of Nara, which is part of the UNESCO “Historic Monuments of Ancient Nara” World Heritage Site.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The geopark lies within a “satochi satoyama” zone, a transition area between wilderness and urban spaces, rich in biodiversity and agricultural heritage. Historically, the economy centred on agriculture, forestry, and mining. While coal mining declined about 50 years ago, limestone mining continues, alongside a copper mining festival. Today, modern manufacturing and tourism is supported by the region’s unique natural and cultural landscape. In this way, the geopark links Earth science with local culture, with sustainable tourism initiatives leading to economic development in the area, the geopark running educational programmes, and local universities conducting scientific research on the land.

Introduction EN: Lenggong UNESCO Global Geopark, located in Perak, Malaysia, is nestled between the Titiwangsa and Bintang mountain ranges. Its diverse landscapes include river terraces, limestone hills, and granite peaks. The region's tropical climate fosters dense rainforests rich in biodiversity, including endangered and endemic species like the Malayan tiger and Lenggong rock gecko, while limestone forests host rare plant species.
Description: The Lenggong Geopark also highlights outstanding geological heritage, including the Lawin Tuff, evidence of ancient volcanic activity linked to the supercontinent Gondwana, and granitic magmatism tied to major global tectonic collision. The region hosts rare granites, major faults such as Bok Bak, and suevite formed by a meteorite impact around 1.8 million years ago, as well as the thickest Toba super-eruption ash deposit outside Sumatra, left by one of Earth's most powerful volcanic eruptions about 74,000 years ago.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The population is ethnically diverse, including Orang Asli Indigenous Peoples. Agriculture, aquaculture, and tourism are key economic drivers, with the region known for freshwater fish, cultural heritage, and preserved forest ecosystems supporting unique wildlife and traditional livelihoods. The geopark includes the Lenggong Valley, a UNESCO World Heritage Site with one of the world’s longest archaeological sequences, where stone tools, burial sites, and ancient settlements reveal a deep history of human adaptation to changing environments. Community-led initiatives and partnerships with researchers and educational institutions promote geotourism, heritage conservation, and traditional knowledge, ensuring that local people benefit from increased visitation while safeguarding both archaeological and natural sites.

Introduction EN: Located in western Sarawak, Malaysia, the Sarawak Delta UNESCO Global Geopark sits at a major geological boundary where two ancient landmasses came together more than 200 million years ago, during the breakup of the supercontinent Gondwana.
Description: This collision shaped the foundations of Borneo and has led to the Kuching Zone suture, which is a key piece of evidence for how Southeast Asia's landmasses have shifted over time. Today, the geopark is defined by a warm tropical climate and exceptional biodiversity, supported by an extensive river delta system and a landscape that transitions from low-lying plains to higher ground inland. The area preserves a long record of Earth’s history, spanning over 250 million years, during which shifting plates and tectonic forces gradually reshaped Borneo.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Home to over 600,000 people, this geopark includes Kuching – the UNESCO City of Gastronomy, where traditional street food and kopitam culture blend with fine dining and festivals. Kuching and neighbouring towns showcase the region’s ethnic diversity and harmony, and locals partake in cultural dances, such as the Eagle dance of the Bidayuh Indigenous Peoples. Traditional agricultural, aquaculture and craft-making practices, along with more modern ecotourism practices, are supported by the region’s strong transport network which links the region nationally and internationally, meaning visitors can experience the Sarawak Delta’s rich geological history and sustainable land usage, showcasing the dynamic environment and traditions of the delta.

Introduction EN: Dahar UNESCO Global Geopark in Southern Tunisia becomes the third in Africa, and offers a remarkable geological record spanning the last 250 million years, highlighting the earth’s evolution.
Description: Situated on the northeastern edge of the Saharan Platform, Dahar features well-preserved, flat rock layers from the Mesozoic Era (about 250–66 million years ago) and diverse petrographic, mineralogical, and morphological features shaped by erosion and alteration, and marks the site where the Great Rift opened around 200 million years ago, initiating the formation of the Tethys Ocean and the breakup of the supercontient Pangaea into Gondwana and Laurasia. A key highlight is Jebel Tebaga, which hosts Africa's only known marine Upper Permian outcrop, featuring marine fossils formed over 250 million years ago.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: In the geopark area, agriculture and livestock shaped by arid environmental conditions form the main economic activities. Human adaptation to this challenging environment is evident in traditional water systems, oil mills, ksour (fortified granaries), and troglodytic dwellings, which link geology closely with cultural heritage and ingenious responses to scarce water and extreme temperatures. As tourism grows, supported by an improving road network and proximity to an international airport, the geopark works to provide visitors an authentic experience, exposing them to traditional crafts, food and practices.

Introduction EN: Visit the prehistoric rock art of Sunmalelen in Misool, created thousands of years ago by early inhabitants.Hike the geotrail to The King's Crown, a stunning landscape where the emerald waters and karst archipelago of Wayag Islands reveal stories dating back millions of years.Embark on an underwater adventure by diving into Raja Ampat’s stunning marine world, home to 75% of the world’s reef fish and breathtaking coral reefs, earning its reputation as 'the last paradise.’
Description: "The Emerald Karst in the Equator," Raja Ampat UNESCO Global Geopark, consists of four main islands: Waigeo, Batanta, Salawati and Misool. The geopark area is home to the country’s oldest rock formation, dating back 443.8–358.9 million years to the Silurian-Devonian era, nearly one-tenth the age of the Earth. This ancient rock unit, along with overlying Mesozoic rocks that include ocean floor ultramafics, forms the foundation of the region’s karstic limestones. Notably, karst topography flourishes in both older (Eocene) and younger (Miocene-Pliocene) limestone units. The archipelagic karst formation in the geopark is believed to have been influenced by rising sea levels during the Quaternary Period, followed by ongoing karstification. This process has resulted in numerous caves, some located below sea level, making them popular diving destinations. Prehistoric cave paintings, created by inhabitants thousands of years ago, have been discovered on steep limestone cliffs and eroded coastal cavities, highlighting the deep connection between geological and cultural heritage in the Raja Ampat UNESCO Global Geopark.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Raja Ampat is rich in intangible cultural heritage in the form of dances and traditional ceremonies that illustrate the connection of local people with the natural surroundings. The Sasi Ceremony, recognised as a national cultural heritage is a remarkable example of cultural preservation in Raja Ampat. Rooted in ancestral wisdom, this traditional practice aims to sustain the populations of marine animals and plants on land, ensuring ecological balance and abundance for future generations. Sasi is carried out in distinct seasonal phases. During the Sasi Closing Ceremony, the community is prohibited from harvesting seafood or certain plants, allowing nature to regenerate. This period is followed by the Sasi Opening Ceremony, where the community comes together to celebrate and harvest responsibly. These ceremonies are not only a way to manage resources sustainably but also serve as an expression of gratitude to nature for its generous provisions. The Raja Ampat UNESCO Global Geopark was established through a collaborative effort, involving the regional government, local communities and stakeholders. The geopark's focus lies in safeguarding various Earth heritages, both geological and non-geological. Education plays a crucial role in nurturing a sense of responsibility towards the planet and its diverse treasures.

Introduction EN: Discover the Mandela Rock Paintings on Mandela Mountain, with 4,234 identified artworks dating to the Xixia, Yuan, Ming, and Qing dynasties, spread across 16 km² and depicting local wildlife.Learn about the Alxa carpet weaving technique, developed over 280 years ago during the Qing Dynasty and recognised on China’s national intangible cultural heritage list.
Description: Encompassing a vast timeline of Earth’s geological history, the geopark’s rich tapestry of landscapes ranges from granite mountains to sand deserts and wetlands. Towering at a remarkable height of 1,611 m, the Bilutu mega-dune in the Badain Jaran Desert has earned the title of Desert Everest. Surrounding this colossal dune, countless other dunes have intrigued researchers for years. Although their formation remains a subject of debate, they share an intimate relationship with the lakes nestled among them. The water stored within the dunes continuously replenishes the lakes, resulting in a fascinating correlation between the size of the dunes and the expansiveness of the lakes. Stretching between the Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region and the Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, the Helan Mountains are a result of a series of north-northeast trending folds and faults shaped by tectonic forces. The highest peak reaches an impressive elevation of 3,556 m, making it the highest point in the Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region. Notably, the Helan Mountains act as both a geographical and climatic boundary, separating the river basins of China and serving as a barrier against the Gobi Desert, yellow sand, and frigid Siberian currents. The mountains bestow upon the surrounding Yinchuan Plain its remarkable fertility. The standout geological feature of the geopark is the stationary mega dunes of the Badain Jaran Desert, reaching staggering heights of nearly 500 m. These dunes have earned the desert the moniker Singing Sand Kingdom due to the melodic rumble emitted when the wind sweeps across their slopes. Though the exact mechanism behind this phenomenon remains a mystery, it is believed the electrifying song emerges as the wind unveils layers of sand, generating an enchanting low-pitched resonance.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The Alxa area is home to a rich cultural heritage shaped by diverse Indigenous populations and centuries of nomadic tradition. Numerous cultures have flourished here, including the Di, Hun, Serbi, Rourao, Dangxiang, Huihe, Turks, and Mongolians. Today, Mongolian and Buddhist customs continue to shape daily life. The geopark features 15 nationally recognised cultural heritage sites, including the South, North, Yanfu, and Badan Jaran Temples, as well as the ancient ruins of Black, Red, and Lvcheng cities. The Mandela Mountain Cliff Paintings, carved over 6,000 years ago, display remarkably smooth surfaces and vivid depictions of local life and wildlife. Intangible heritage plays a central role in the region’s identity. Nomadic communities have long passed down folk songs, heroic poetry, dance, music, wrestling, and horse and camel racing. These traditions are actively promoted through geopark-supported festivals and geotourism activities. Carpet weaving and camel-based crafts also reflect the area’s enduring relationship with the desert environment. The geopark collaborates with local schools and research institutions to support geo-education. Summer camps and science festivals introduce young people to desert landscapes, water resources, and fossil discoveries, helping to connect geological heritage with local knowledge and community engagement.
Quote: “An ocean of singing sand”

Introduction EN: Explore the “Kalksporet” (Lime Trail) in Hjerm, featuring an open-air amphitheatre, interpretive panels, and audio installations on local geology.Visit Holstebro Museum to see a 1,000-year-old Byzantine jewellery piece linked to local oral traditions and scientific folklore.Discover the traditional craft of clinker-built Viking boats at the harbour in Struer, recognised as UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage.
Description: In Vestjylland UNESCO Global, landscapes bear witness to a dramatic geological past shaped by repeated glaciations during the Quaternary period. The core of the geopark consists of impressive ice age landforms sculpted when enormous ice sheets covered northern Europe. During the last glacial advance, between 23,000 and 21,000 years ago, the Scandinavian Ice Sheet reached its maximum extent, spreading from the mountains of Norway down to Denmark and leaving behind the varied terrain seen today. This glacial heritage was mapped over a century ago by Danish geologist N.V. Ussing, who identified the Main Stationary Line – a marked boundary between the hilly glacial landscapes and the flat meltwater plains. These features, along with other landforms shaped by postglacial rivers, coastal processes, and the strong westerly winds of Denmark’s west coast, form a diverse and scientifically valuable landscape. The geopark contains 48 inventoried geosites, including Bovbjerg Cliff, a site of international geological importance. Other key sites are situated within eight nationally recognised areas of geological interest and five designated National Coastal Landscapes. Some of the cliffs in the geopark reveal geological deposits from both the Tertiary and Quaternary periods, further adding to the richness of the area’s Earth history. The geopark provides a comprehensive record of glacial and postglacial development, offering valuable insights into the forces that have shaped western Jutland over hundreds of thousands of years.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Vestjylland UNESCO Global Geopark supports its communities through a strong focus on education, cultural identity, and the integration of local knowledge. A wide range of interpretive trails has been developed to highlight the connections between geology, culture, and the everyday life of the region. These include the coastal trail from Trans Church to Bovbjerg Lighthouse, the “Kalksporet” (Lime Trail) with its amphitheatre-shaped viewing platform in Hjerm, and a countryside trail linking four villages, where visitors encounter geological and cultural heritage. The geopark provides educational materials and in situ interpretation across its territory, including exhibitions, guided tours, and multimedia content. The Geopark Family – a set of seven mascot characters – serves as narrators for educational films that present life in the region across time, from prehistory to the future. These resources are available in accessible language and formats designed to engage children, schools, and the wider public. Cultural heritage is closely linked to the sea and farming traditions. Initiatives include work with museums and local experts to interpret archaeological finds and folklore. In Holstebro Museum, for example, a 1,000-year-old Byzantine jewellery piece is on display, accompanied by storytelling activities rooted in West Jutland traditions. The geopark collaborates with artists and researchers to preserve and share these cultural expressions. The geopark also supports traditional skills such as clinker-built boatmaking. In Struer, the “Nordvestjysk Fjordkultur” organisation builds and maintains Viking-style boats, a practice inscribed on the UNESCO list of Intangible Cultural Heritage. Joint efforts are underway to offer public trips in the boats on the Limfjord. Demonstrations of hunting with falcons are offered in partnership with Nature Park Nissum Fjord. The technique is used both as cultural education on this tradition, and as an act of local conservation, managing populations of invasive barnacle geese.

Introduction EN: Explore the historic mining tunnels of Lavreotiki with expert volunteer guides, who provide insights into ancient mining techniques and the region’s world-renowned mineralogical diversity.Learn about the geopark’s underwater treasures, including the vital Posidonia oceanica seagrass beds, and their role in supporting marine biodiversity.Visit cultural landmarks such as Mycenaean chamber tombs, Roman baths, and Byzantine monasteries, set within the geopark’s striking geological landscapes.
Description: The Lavreotiki UNESCO Global Geopark is a hidden treasure, situated just 60 kilometres from Greece’s capital, Athens. The Lavrion deposit, a historically significant mining area rich in mineral resources, spans approximately 150 km². It includes primary ore mineralization of sulfides and sulfosalts, as well as native metals such as silver, lead and arsenic. The deposit consists of five interrelated styles of ore deposits, a unique feature not observed in any other known mining district. Furthermore, oxidation and water movement through these deposits over the past million years have mobilised elements to form secondary minerals like smithsonite, azurite and malachite. Nearly 12% of all known mineral species on the planet can be found here, making Lavrion the most mineralogically diverse location on Earth. The Lavreotiki Peninsula, located in southeastern Attica, is part of the East Attica sub-region and is distinguished by its unique natural landscapes. The region features fertile agricultural lands, scenic coastal zones, and significant archaeological sites. Its hilly terrain, with the highest point at 258 meters (Megali Vigla), is divided into eastern and western sections by the Legraina Valley. Key valleys, such as the Valley of Potamos—formerly linked to the Athens-Lavrion railway—and the Plaka-Adami Valley, further enhance the area’s diverse geography.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Lavreotiki has been a centre of human activity since antiquity, largely driven by its rich geological resources which were central to industry and commerce. This mining legacy is reflected in Lavreotiki's numerous cultural landmarks, which span millennia. These include Mycenaean chamber tombs, Roman villas and baths, Byzantine monasteries and architectural remnants from Venetian rule. Together, these sites tell the story of a region shaped by its geology and deeply intertwined with the development of civilizations throughout history. A standout example is the Holy Monastery of St. Paul the Apostle, located near the settlement of Upper Plaka in Palaiokamariza. This Byzantine-style monastery, with its cruciform architecture and dome, is dedicated to the Apostle Paul. It preserves the traditional fresco technique, using natural pigments ground from rocks, exemplifying the region’s intangible cultural heritage and Orthodox monastic traditions and the link between geological and cultural heritage. The geopark is home to rich biodiversity, supported by agricultural lands, covering 27.7% of the Lavreotiki Municipality, and extensive forest. One key conservation effort is led by the Environmental Educational Center of Lavrion, which runs programmes to raise awareness about biodiversity and sustainable development. One initiative focuses on the Posidonia oceanica beds, valuable underwater ecosystems critical to the region’s marine biodiversity. These programmes educate young people, aged 5–15, about protecting these habitats and fostering a healthy, sustainable lifestyle.

Introduction EN: Visit the Mapuche Indigenous Religious and Ceremonial Complex in Icalma, including the Eltuwe cemetery and Nguillantuwe ceremonial site.\Explore the house of Poeta Tellier, a renowned poet from the commune of Lautaro.Take one of the spectacular trails that wind through the slopes of glacial valleys, including the Lagunillas Trail, where relatively recent (4–2 million years ago) volcanic-sedimentary records can be observed.
Description: From Vilcún, on the western border of the geopark, and following the S-31 to the east, it’s not long until an almost perfect conic mountain, its top covered in snow, will come into view. It’s the 3,200-metre-high Llaima Volcano, one of the most active in the country. Surrounding it is Conguillío National Park, a 60,832 ha protected area of outstanding beauty considered one of the last natural refuges in the world. The area’s conditions, with wide temperature variations that can reach up to 40°C in summer and nearly -20°C during the winter months, have nurtured a diverse forest. Araucarias—ancient conifers from the time when dinosaurs still roamed the Earth and now surviving only as relicts—are the most important species and are protected by the Araucaria UNESCO Biosphere Reserve. In the lower areas of the geopark, the Andean prairies provide communities with summer grazing areas known as veranadas. This diverse landscape and ecosystem is home to dozens of species, many of them endemic and protected, such as the monito del monte, a marsupial native only to South America and considered a living fossil; Darwin’s frog; the culpeo fox; and the quirky vizcacha. Although the geological record goes back to 300 million years ago, volcanoes and traces of volcanic activity dominate the landscape of the Kütralkura UNESCO Global Geopark. These giants are the result of an active tectonic margin, where an oceanic plate moves beneath the South American continent. This tectonic activity produces intense seismic and volcanic activity, exemplified by the Tolhuaca, Lonquimay, Llaima, and Sollipulli volcanoes. Aside from Llaima—the region’s largest and most active volcano—Sollipulli is particularly striking. This dormant stratovolcano, at 2,282 metres, features a 62 km² caldera that contains a massive glacier with more than 2 cubic kilometres of ice. But Kütralkura is not only made of volcanoes. The Malleco Lagoon in Tolhuaca National Park is a glacial relict with its own waterfall. Several trails wind through the slopes of its glacial valleys. One particularly special trail is the Lagunillas Trail, where relatively recent (4–2 million years ago) volcanic-sedimentary records can be observed.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The creation of the Kütralkura UNESCO Global Geopark is a collaborative effort led by Chile’s National Service of Geology and Mining (SERNAGEOMIN), in partnership with local organisations, Indigenous representatives, and municipal governments. At its heart are the Mapuche-Pehuenche communities, whose deep connection with the land—known as Ñuke Mapu (Mother Earth)—underpins conservation and sustainable development efforts. Their worldview, built on the principle of küme mongen (living well), emphasises harmony, respect, and balance with nature. This philosophy influences the geopark’s governance and planning, fostering a unique model that integrates ancestral and scientific knowledge. The inclusion of local women and youth ensures that Mapuche identity and knowledge are preserved for future generations. Agriculture and forestry are central to the livelihoods of the region’s communities. Traditional practices such as veranadas, the seasonal migration of livestock to high-altitude pastures, support sustainable livestock farming and help maintain the cultural identity of Mapuche families. These practices are complemented by the collection and use of piñón (Araucaria seeds), a highly nutritious local resource harvested since pre-Hispanic times and now used in food products sold year-round. Additionally, forest-based activities such as crafting with native wood and the production of honey and jams provide essential income while preserving natural resources. Cultural heritage is another vital aspect of the geopark’s work. Sites like Ruka Kuze, an ancestral ceremonial house preserved by a single family for over 200 years, represent the resilience of Mapuche traditions despite social and religious pressures. The preservation of these sites, along with local craft industries, agricultural practices, and storytelling traditions, ensures that the region’s heritage remains vibrant and relevant.
Quote:
“The geopark has brought better living conditions and created an environment of respect and wisdom among communities, entrepreneurs, and institutions. It’s a privilege to live where we feel the heartbeat of the earth.” 
—Camila Jara Quilapan, a Mapuche community member and part of the geopark’s Technical Committee

Introduction EN: Learn about the region's geoheritage at the Guangwushan-Nuoshuihe Geopark Museum, located in Tieluba.Walk part of the ancient Micang Road, a section of the historic Shu Dao network, which has been recognised on China’s Tentative List for World Cultural and Natural Heritage.
Description: The Guangwushan-Nuoshuihe Geopark is not only a geological heritage site with great aesthetic value but also an open-air museum and a region of high scientific importance for the study of karst and granite landforms and the geological evolution of eastern Asia. The unique landscapes of the geopark include karst peak clusters, cave deposits, granite mountains, valleys, ponds, and waterfalls. Here, visitors can observe a wide variety of fossils that accompany a complete record of the sedimentary evolution sequence along the northern rim of the Yangtze Plate. Among the many important palaeontological finds, one of the most significant is Shuotherium dongi, discovered in 1982 at Ganchang Town, which is considered one of the oldest mammal fossils in the world. Among the geopark’s highlights, the Jiaguoshan Peak Cluster stands out, and embarking on the Jiaguoshan Mountain Investigation Route is the ideal way to observe it. Located in Nuoshuihe Valley, this route offers views of the sedimentary evolution profile of the overlying strata of the Yangtze Block and several karst caves. Along the way, visitors can also explore Cambrian, Ordovician, and Permian karst caves, as well as large-scale travertine landscapes, such as Rock Falls. Beech trees grow on both sides of the road, and their leaves turn a vibrant red in autumn, adding an extra layer of beauty to the landscape.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The geopark is home to a rich and layered cultural heritage. Sites such as the Micang Ancient Path, the Bazhong Grottoes, and remnants of ancient cities from the Qin, Han, Tang, and Song dynasties reflect centuries of regional development. These are closely linked to broader traditions, including Sichuan-Chongqing culture and the legacy of the Red Army. The region is recognised as a “long river of tea and horse culture” and is considered a tangible repository of historical heritage, contributing to research on Chinese history and culture. Indigenous Ba communities continue to live within the geopark area, maintaining a strong connection to local traditions. Their folk songs and dances are still performed today, reflecting enduring cultural knowledge passed down through generations. Important heritage sites include the Red Army Stone Carving Slogans at Xiong Ancestral Temple, former battlefields, historic bridges, and other sites preserved across Bazhong City. Local institutions promote this heritage through exhibitions, educational signage, and cultural forums. The geopark also safeguards diverse forms of intangible cultural heritage. Among the most prominent are the Mountain Climbing Hymn and the Bashan Bei’erge folk songs, both nationally recognised. Traditional skills such as brewing, paper-cutting, shadow puppetry, and food processing—including bean marinating and fish preparation—are supported through performance events and the development of cultural products, contributing to local creative economies.
Quote: “Discover traces of Earth and human history along the winding Ancient Micang Road”

Introduction EN: Explore the hallowed grounds of the Wulanbutong Ancient Battlefield, where the renowned 1690 battle unfolded, leaving an indelible mark on Hexigten Geopark's history.Step back in time at the Yingchanglu Ruin Site, once a splendid summer resort of the Yuan dynasty. This national cultural relic offers a captivating glimpse into the opulent lifestyle of ancient nobility.Discover the Hexigten granite stone forest, a rare geological formation with well-preserved granite mortars and egg-shaped landforms, known as a “museum of granite landforms.”
Description: Nestled in the enchanting landscapes of inner Mongolia, Hexigten Geopark stands as a testament to the harmonious interplay between geological marvels and vibrant cultural heritage. The region is famous for its spruce forest, a sacred place that locals believe confers safety and peace—one of the reasons why the forest is so well preserved. The heart of the geopark is adorned by the vast expanse of the Mongolian grassland, a picturesque tapestry of rolling plains and boundless beauty known as the “backyard garden of Beijing.” Beyond its lush vegetation, the geopark is home to renowned geological heritage. Situated at the crossroads of China, Korea, and Siberia, Hexigten is intersected by the Xilimiao–Daqing Ranch Great Fault and the Wendu'ermiao–Xar Moron River Deep Fault. These fault lines divide the region into three distinct areas, each bearing the imprints of well-defined tectonic events. Hexigten Geopark thus serves as an ideal destination for studying structural movements in northern China and unravelling the mysteries of our planet's geological evolution. The geopark is geographically divided into eastern and western regions, structured along the Beidashan–Mount Huanggangliang–Mount Obo–Mount Erlongshan axis. The eastern region presents a rugged mountainous terrain, while the western part is predominantly characterised by expansive plateaus. To the northeast lies the Greater Khingan Mountain, an imposing range that commands attention, while in the southern reaches, the Yanshan Mountains unfold. Finally, the southwestern region beckons adventurers to traverse the Otindag Sandy Land, one of the largest sandy areas in China, where endless dunes create a surreal landscape. The Hexigten granite stone forest represents a rare and unique geological formation. The shapes and origins of these horizontally jointed granite stone forests are seldom seen elsewhere. Mount Qingshan is home to numerous granite mortars with well-preserved evolutionary stages, and typical egg-shaped granite landforms are also highly developed. These features rival the granite peak forests of Mount Huangshan, earning Hexigten the title of a “museum of granite landforms.”
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Hexigten UNESCO Global Geopark is located in the Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region of China, in an area named after a historic unit of the Mongolian army. While the majority of the population is of Han heritage, Mongols make up a significant portion of the community, alongside 14 other ethnic groups, including the Hui, Manchu, Korean, and Daur peoples. The area preserves numerous cultural relics from the Liao and Jin Dynasties, and the Mongolian community maintains distinct traditions and customs. Four cultural systems emerged from the Xilamulun River valley: the Red Mountain Culture, the Grassland Bronze Culture, the Ancient Qidan–Liao–Jin Culture, and the Mongolian Yuan Dynasty Culture. Sections of the ancient Jin Great Wall traverse the grassland, linking geological landscapes with a long human history. Today, Hexigten UNESCO Global Geopark serves as a centre for scientific education and research, hosting institutions such as the Research Centre for Quaternary Glaciers of China, the Research Centre for Granite Landforms of China, and the Teaching and Research Base of China University of Geosciences.
Quote: “The junction of mountains and desert creates a unique landscape home to a unique culture”

Introduction EN: The Tortoise Back Stone reveals a pattern resembling a tortoise shell, formed by weathering of fine-grained red sandstone.The Danxia Perforate Natural Bridge, also called Elephant Trunk Hill, was shaped by erosion into a stone arch resembling an elephant’s trunk.The region is the birthplace of Taoism, with key sites including Tianshi Mansion, Shangqing Palace, and Zhengyi Temple.
Description: Longhushan UNESCO Global Geopark in Jiangxi Province spans nearly 1,000 square kilometres and showcases striking mountainous terrain, scenic valleys, and dramatic waterfalls. The park’s centrepiece is Longhushan Mountain, rising to 1,474 metres. It features a late-mature stage Danxia landform, with granite peaks, deep gorges, and meandering rivers that provide valuable insights into regional geological evolution—particularly erosional processes. One notable geological feature is Fairy Maiden Rock, a vertical cave formed through long-term water erosion along vertical joints. It has a distinctive funnel-like shape, narrowing at the top and widening gradually toward the base. The lower section resembles feminine contours, which has inspired the feature’s name. The geopark encompasses the integrated Longhushan, Xiangshan, and Guifeng parks, combining geological, geomorphological, ecological, and cultural landscapes. Geological vestiges in the geopark record key information about Earth’s history since the Cretaceous period (around 145 million years ago). They reveal significant events, such as the deposition of red beds, followed by tectonic uplift and erosion that produced some of the region’s most intricately sculpted landforms.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Longhushan UNESCO Global Geopark is a living centre of Taoist tradition, deeply embedded in the local landscape and cultural identity. The geopark is home to nationally protected cultural sites such as the Tianshi (Heavenly Master) Mansion, Shangqing Palace and Zhengyi Temple. Longhushan is considered the cradle of Taoism in China and remains the only site authorised to award official Taoist certificates. These are issued through events attracting thousands of Taoists from both within China and internationally. Taoist culture is made accessible to the public through exhibitions, performances, and digital outreach. Taoist musical traditions are actively preserved and promoted, including performances at international festivals. A Taoist musical drama from Longhushan has been staged in Egypt, and special products—such as musical instruments and books—are produced and sold to support the cultural economy. In addition to Taoist heritage, the geopark also protects ancient cliff tombs dating back over 2,600 years. These funerary sites of the Ancient Yue Nationality are presented with daily interpretive performances that align with the geological features of the surrounding Danxia landforms. Longhushan UNESCO Global Geopark cooperates with universities and archaeology institutes to ensure proper conservation and public understanding of these sites. The geopark also supports the transmission of local intangible cultural heritage. This includes the Yiyang Opera Tune, a nationally recognised form of traditional drama known as the “living fossil” of Chinese opera. It has been brought into communities, schools, and geotrails through partnerships with the Yiyang Opera Tune Art Protection Centre. Additionally, Taoist music of the Zhengyi tradition has been recognised as a representative national intangible heritage and remains a central element of both ritual and cultural life in the geopark.
Quote: “The Geopark is multicultural, which involves Taoism, Buddhism and Confucianism. It is where Cliff Grave culture and Taoism originated”

Introduction EN: At Aoya Folk Museum, the charm of singing sand, the craftsmanship behind Inshu Japanese paper, and the legacy of Ama women divers are celebrated in special exhibitions that connect visitors to the area’s rich history and culture.At Genbudo Park, visitors can explore the origins of the Genbudo Cave, famed for its striking basalt formations, while interactive exhibits reveal the geological history that shaped this natural wonder.
Description: The San’in Kaigan UNESCO Global Geopark on Japan's northern coast reveals a landscape of striking contrasts. From coves with white sandy beaches and calm crystal waters, like Takeno Beach in Toyooka or the Uradome Coast in Iwami, to the golden sands of the Tottori Sand Dunes—unique in Japan—the region offers an unexpected diversity. The dunes, stretching 16 km long, 2.4 km wide, and up to 50 m high, are formed by sand carried by the Sendai River and shaped by sea currents and winds, creating a spectacle that defies traditional images of Japan. Granite outcrops date back 70 million years to when Japan was part of the Asian continent, while sedimentary and volcanic rocks trace its rift from Asia 25 to 15 million years ago—a process that continues today. The geopark’s hundreds of bays, cliffs, caves, and rock formations narrate this ancient history through their natural beauty. The northwesterly monsoon, combined with the Tsushima Warm Current, brings heavy precipitation and snow to the mountainous areas, carving dramatic coastal landforms. This interaction of climate and geography has also created unique ecosystems like the wetlands of the Toyooka Basin. Formed by basalt from the Genbudo Cave and the poor drainage of the Maruyama River, these wetlands have become a sanctuary for the Oriental White Stork. Once extinct in the wild, the species now thrives, with over 300 individuals residing in Toyooka City, thanks to dedicated conservation efforts. The geopark not only celebrates natural heritage but also highlights how human intervention can harmonise with nature to protect and preserve it.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The San’in Kaigan UNESCO Global Geopark demonstrates a remarkable synergy between natural conservation, cultural preservation, and community engagement. Its history is deeply intertwined with the geological features of the region, which have shaped the lives, livelihoods, and traditions of its people for centuries. Ports and towns along the coast, once thriving maritime hubs, used the topography for trade, transportation, and even burial practices, as seen in the Ohnaru Burial Mounds dating back to the 5th to 7th centuries. The geopark is also a treasure trove of intangible heritage, with 11 nationally designated cultural properties, including the Kirin Shishimai Dance—a Japan Heritage-recognised folk tradition linking the region’s natural environment, landscape, and local culture. Today, the geopark continues to inspire innovative uses of its landscapes. Mountain terraces prevent landslides while serving as rice paddies, recognised as both cultural and ecological heritage. Formerly barren dunes now sustain specialty crops like Chinese shallots, and lava-carved land doubles as scenic trekking routes. These practices exemplify the harmonious relationship between the community and its environment, balancing sustainability and cultural pride. Geotourism plays a vital economic role, with approximately 65 groups offering activities such as sandboarding, snorkelling, and sea taxi tours that highlight the area’s unique geography. These ventures not only attract visitors but also involve local fishermen, small business owners, and guides, fostering sustainable economic growth and preserving the geopark’s heritage. Through its collaborative efforts, the San’in Kaigan Geopark serves as a model for community-driven conservation. Initiatives like the reintroduction of Oriental White Storks in Toyooka City exemplify the impact of local governments, citizens, and organisations working together. Regular roundtable meetings bring residents and practitioners together to exchange ideas, address challenges, and envision the geopark’s future.
Quote: “Beautiful natural environments, people live in geodiversity from the formation of the Sea of Japan”

Introduction EN: Although the wet season from May to October brings daily showers and high temperatures, it is also when the geopark's waterfalls are at their most spectacular.Visit EXPLORASOUND, Viet Nam’s first museum entirely dedicated to sound, featuring musical instruments inspired by the five elements—metal, wood, water, fire, and earth—integrated with interactive technology.Walk along a preserved section of the historic Ho Chi Minh Trail, a logistical network used by the Viet Cong and the People's Army of Viet Nam during the American War, which runs through the geopark.
Description: In southern Viet Nam, about 200 km north of Ho Chi Minh City, Dak Nong UNESCO Global Geopark covers a landscape shaped by volcanic activity and intense tropical weathering. The geopark's oldest geological formations date back to the Early–Middle Jurassic (200–163 million years ago), but it is the volcanic activity of the last 16.5 million years that defines the area's distinctive geomorphology. Fertile volcanic soils support rich agricultural traditions, including coffee, tea, and rubber plantations, while beneath the surface lie substantial deposits of bauxite—Viet Nam holds the third-largest reserves of this aluminium ore globally. Volcanism has sculpted dramatic geological features, including volcanic cave systems, craters, and waterfalls. The Nam Blang volcanic cave lava field, discovered in 2007, is Southeast Asia’s largest volcanic cave system, spanning over 10 km and including approximately 50 caves. These lava tubes were used as shelter by prehistoric communities between 6,000 and 10,000 years ago. The caves and surrounding terrain provide visible evidence of volcanic phenomena such as ash deposits, volcanic bombs, and both pahoehoe and ‘a‘ā lava flows. The geopark also features the Nam Kar volcano, a young volcanic complex comprising scoria cones, spatter cones, and lava flows. Initially mined for cement additives, operations were halted when its geological significance was recognised, and the site is now protected. Among the area’s scenic highlights is the Dray Sap waterfall—a 100-metre-wide cascade plunging 12 metres—surrounded by pristine primary forest.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Dak Nong UNESCO Global Geopark encompasses the ancestral lands of the M’Nong, Ma, and Ede peoples. "Dak," meaning "source of water" or "source of life" in the M’Nong language, reflects the deep cultural connection these communities maintain with their land and waterways. Recognised in 2005 by UNESCO as part of the “Space of Gong Culture in the Central Highlands of Viet Nam”—a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity—the geopark is a living repository of intangible heritage. For the seventeen Austroasiatic and Austronesian ethno-linguistic groups in the region, gongs are central to social rituals, daily life, and seasonal celebrations. These instruments are seen as a channel to the supernatural, expressing communal identity, spiritual beliefs, and cultural continuity. Through initiatives like the EXPLORASOUND museum, the geopark promotes innovative ways of engaging both visitors and communities, building awareness and appreciation of local traditions through sound and interactive cultural experiences.

Introduction EN: Travel on the Qinghai–Tibet Railway, the highest railway in the world and the longest to cross permafrost, which passes through the geopark.Cycle along the scenic 109 National Highway, a popular route from Nanshankou to Kunlun Mountain Pass with breathtaking views.Discover traditional Haixi Mongolian crafts and cultural practices preserved by local artisans and recognised as provincial intangible heritage.
Description: Mount Kunlun UNESCO Global Geopark is located in the southwest part of Golmud, Qinghai Province, at the northeastern edge of the Qinghai–Tibet Plateau. The Kunlun Mountains, one of the longest mountain chains in Asia, stretch over 3,000 kilometres along the southern edge of the Tarim Basin, the Taklamakan and the Gobi Desert. This region is among the first areas of the Tibetan Plateau settled by humans. The geopark spans wide fault and glacial valleys across extremely high mountains covered by ice and snow, holding geological heritage from the Mesoproterozoic (1,600 million years ago) to the Quaternary (2.5 million years ago to present). It is particularly known for glacier landforms—such as the Jade Everest modern glacier—and earthquake relics, including a major surface rupture caused by the M8.1 Kunlun earthquake in 2001. These features offer insight into ocean–continent transitions, the uplift of the Qinghai–Tibet Plateau, and five major glaciations. Geologically, the geopark lies within the Kangxiwar–South Kunlun–Madoi–Maqin collision zone. It has undergone multiple cycles of crustal evolution marked by ocean development and land–ocean transformation. The area hosts a tectonic mix of Mesoproterozoic, Neoproterozoic, and Jurassic strata, along with evidence of intense magmatic activity. It is considered a key area for understanding the geological evolution of inland Asia and the Eurasian continent. The geopark retains rare geological relics linked to both the Palaeo-Asian and Tethyan tectonic systems. Suture zones and ophiolitic remnants preserve records of oceanic closure, crustal extension, subduction, and continental collision, making Mount Kunlun an irreplaceable site for studying large-scale tectonic processes in China and Eastern Asia.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Mount Kunlun, known as “the Ancestor of Mountains,” holds a unique place in Chinese civilisation. Regarded as the birthplace of Kunlun mythology and the origin of the Kunlun Sect of Taoism, the area continues to play a symbolic and cultural role in the national imagination. An important archaeological legacy of early human activity is preserved in the form of microliths—small stone tools—discovered at sites such as Naij Tal and Sanchakou. Other protected heritage sites include the Yematan and Wild Yak Valley cliff paintings, the Yidaogou and Sandaogou stoneware relics, and the historic Sanchahe Bridge. Intangible cultural heritage is also present in the daily lives of local communities. The geopark recognises Haixi Mongolian traditions such as the kid hair-cutting rite, folk fire-worship ceremonies, traditional weddings, and costume-making. The town of Guolemude, within the geopark, has been designated a national “Hometown of Woodcarving and Embroidery.” Local artisans continue to produce and sell traditional costumes and woodcarvings, preserving cultural practices while contributing to the local economy.
Quote: “Mount Kunlun, known as “the ancestor of mountains”, holds a special place in Chinese mythology and culture”

Introduction EN: Explore the distinctive miarolitic granite peak clusters of Taimushan, featuring stone egg landforms shaped by volcanic activity.Watch local women prepare Kanzong, a traditional She ethnic rice cake, using ancestral techniques passed down through generations.Discover the intricate art of Zherong paper cutting, crafted into unique souvenirs by local artisans.
Description: At the heart of the Taimu and Jiufeng mountain ranges and with panoramic views of the South China Sea, the Ningde UNESCO Global Geopark is an igneous rock paradise with towering peaks of rhyolite rising above the forest. It is formed by three scenic areas – Baishuiyang in Pingnan County, Baiyun Mountain in Fuan City and Taimu Mountain in Fuding City – and is famous in the country for its waterfalls, deep pools and other coastal and island attractions. Located in northeast Fujian Province, the geopark spans mountainous and coastal landscapes shaped by complex tectonic, magmatic, and erosional processes. It lies within the Mesozoic Southeast China igneous zone, part of the Pacific volcanic rim, and features extensive Late Jurassic to Early Cretaceous dacitic–rhyolitic rocks. Among its defining features is the Taimushan miarolitic granite peak cluster. These epithermal granites, formed during crustal extension, exhibit distinctive “stone egg” landforms—some of the best-developed in southeast China. Additional granite bodies, such as the Zhuzhou outcrops, preserve a full magmatic sequence, contributing to Ningde’s value for understanding continental magmatic evolution. Ningde also holds a number of volcanic structures including Baiyunshan and Bijiaoshan dome volcanoes and the scattered volcanic fields of Yiyang. These offer insight into bimodal volcanic rock assemblages, significant for reconstructing tectonic and magmatic activity along the southeast coast. Erosion features are equally prominent. Baishuiyang Scenic Area hosts an exceptionally rare flat bedrock riverbed, while Longtingxi Canyon cuts deeply through granite terrain. The Mandarin Duck Stream Canyon showcases river incision within a well-preserved ecological environment. Streams such as Chanxi and Longting reveal groups of potholes and grooves, ideal for studying fluvial erosion. The coastal zone displays a bay with scattered beaches and a variety of sea erosion landscapes. Dayushan Island, one of the ten most beautiful islands in China and the highest island in Fujian, features central lakes and over 10,000 mu of grassland, forming a unique ecosystem within the coastal landscape.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Ningde UNESCO Global Geopark supports a broad range of cultural preservation, education and sustainable development initiatives that reflect the deep connection between its geological landscape and local traditions. The geopark is home to several nationally protected cultural relics, including the corridor bridge in East Fujian, the Fuxia building complex in Pingnan and Wu’s mansion in Fengqi. These historical sites are complemented by five nationally recognised cultural towns and villages such as Shuangxi, Xitan and Puyuan, which showcase traditional architecture and community life. Restoration and conservation projects are supported by local and national authorities, with a focus on integrating heritage protection into tourism and rural development. In She ethnic villages like Xita and Hutou, demonstration projects link geological heritage with cultural ecology and promote the protection of minority cultural identity. The region is also rich in intangible cultural heritage. It includes three elements recognised by UNESCO: the traditional wooden arch bridge construction technique, the watertight compartment blessing ship, and Zherong paper cutting. Other nationally recognised traditions include silver forging, lion dances, folk operas, marriage and haircutting customs, and the preparation of white tea and red rice wine. Local artisans continue to produce and sell traditional crafts and food products, including Fuding white tea, Fangjiashan green snow bud, Muyang honey peach, she silver jewellery and Zherong paper cuttings. These products are promoted through festivals and tourism partnerships, and partners are encouraged to use the Ningde UNESCO Global Geopark branding to support visibility. The geopark organises and hosts events such as the Ningde UNESCO Global Geopark Cultural Tourism Festival, the Peach Blossom Festival, the Fishing Tourism Culture Festival, and the “March 3” She traditional festival. These events provide platforms for promoting local products and heritage while engaging residents and visitors alike.
Quote: “The many landforms create an ornamental landscape”

Introduction EN: The Shengshou Temple in Nanwutai is where ancient Chinese Emperors worshipped, monks and Taoists devoted themselves to spiritual practice, and people made pilgrimages from the Qin (221–207 BCE) to the Han (581–618 CE) Dynasties.The Lantian Ape Man Site Museum offers a wealth of material contributing to the study of paleontology, paleoclimatology, paleogeology, and Quaternary geological activities.Take a walk through alpine meadows and along clear mountain streams in Heihe, where Quaternary glacial features and cultural relics meet in a landscape shaped by ancient plate tectonics.
Description: Qinling Zhongnanshan UNESCO Global Geopark is located in the central section of the Qinling Mountains, one of China’s most important mountain ranges. The range marks a significant natural boundary dividing the north and south of the country in terms of geology, climate, water systems, ecology, and even human culture. Situated within the Qinling composite continental orogenic belt, the geopark preserves exceptional orogenic geological heritage and Quaternary geoheritage, making it a major site for geological research. The geopark is home to the third-largest concentration of landslides in the world. These landslide relics form varied and well-preserved landforms and are of great scientific value for the study of geomorphological evolution and Quaternary geology. Also of note are the Taibai glacial relics, which provide valuable insights into Quaternary glaciations and palaeoclimatic change across East Asia. Fault activity also characterises the region’s geological significance. The northern piedmont fault, with a displacement of up to 13 kilometres, has been active since the Late Cretaceous and is considered a key site for the study of neotectonics and Quaternary geological evolution. Qinling Zhongnanshan UNESCO Global Geopark comprises six scenic areas, including the Lantian Man site, where important fossil remains of Homo erectus were discovered. The skull fossil, dated to approximately 1.15 million years ago, represents one of the earliest human ancestors found in East Asia. The Lantian Ape Man Site Museum includes a relic protection zone, a cultural relic display area, and a comprehensive service zone. It plays a vital role in scientific research on human evolution, paleoclimatology, and Quaternary-era geological processes.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Located just a few kilometres outside Xi’an, the Qinling Zhongnanshan UNESCO Global Geopark connects the region’s rich natural heritage with deep cultural and historical roots. Xi’an, once the eastern terminus of the Silk Road, was the seat of power for successive ruling dynasties including the Zhou, Qin, Han and Tang. The geopark contributes to preserving and revitalising this legacy. Religious and cultural heritage is central to the identity of the geopark. Sites such as the Shengshou Temple in Nanwutai have long served as destinations of pilgrimage and worship, with emperors, monks, Taoists and lay people alike engaging in spiritual practice from the Qin to Han Dynasties. The geopark also promotes local intangible cultural heritage, ranging from Xi’an Drums Music and Shaanxi cuisine to Huayin Laoqiang opera, puppet shows, shadow puppetry, embroidery, and folk customs. These traditions are showcased through events, exhibitions and educational initiatives. The geopark also serves as an educational hub, hosting national study trip bases and university field schools, including from Peking University and the Chinese Academy of Sciences, to promote geoscience learning through hands-on exploration.
Quote: “Abundant geological heritage sites, splendid landscapes, varieties of biological species, favourable environment and plentiful historic culture”

Introduction EN: The Jiuhuashan Global Geopark Museum tells the geological history of the park. Moreover, it is part of the Jiuhuashan Museum which has the largest comprehensive exhibition on Ksitigarbha culture and art in China.Every spring, the park is covered with rhododendrons in full blossom. In the summertime, Jiuhuashan is both beautiful and cool. And in autumn, the forests are covered with red and yellow leaves.
Description: Jiuhuashan is part of the southeastern hills of the third step in China’s four-step terrain classification, a system used to identify regions based on topographic features. It is adjacent to the Middle–Lower Yangtze plains in the north and the mountainous area of southern Anhui in the south. Landforms within the park include middle to lower mountains, hills, and basins, with elevations ranging from 50 to 1,344 metres above sea level. With a geological history dating back to the Neoproterozoic (around 800 million years ago) and a sedimentary record spanning more than 500 million years, the region bears witness to a significant tectonic event: the collision between the Eurasian and Pacific plates during the Cretaceous period (around 140 million years ago). This collision led to the formation and upwelling of magma that gave rise to the Qingyang massif. Much of this history is visible in the geosites of Jiuhuashan UNESCO Global Geopark. Many are especially representative of the magmatic activity resulting from oceanic–continental plate collisions in East Asia. The most outstanding geoheritage features of the geopark are its dramatic granite peaks and striking geodes filled with quartz, feldspar, and purple and green fluorite crystals.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Jiuhuashan, “the mountain of the nine lotuses,” is a sacred site where, according to legend, Ksitigarbha lived for decades and attained Buddhahood in the renowned “Flesh Hall.” The area is home to numerous temples and shrines that reflect its continued religious and cultural significance, particularly among the Han community. Jiuhuashan’s Buddhist heritage is rooted in centuries of cultural exchange, notably between China and Korea, and reflects a unique integration of Chinese Confucian and Buddhist traditions. This heritage is jointly protected and maintained by local monks and residents, and is expressed in distinct Hui-style architecture and cuisine. The region is home to approximately 3,000 monks and nuns who live in over 350 temples and shrines. Among them, Qiyuansi—or Tending Garden Monastery—is the largest. Originally built during the Ming dynasty and remodelled in the Qing dynasty, it remains a centre for religious practice and Buddhist studies.
Quote: “A Model Site of Integration of Geo-landscape and Culture”

Introduction EN: Marvel at the iconic granite peak forest of Sanqingshan, including formations like the Oriental Goddess and Python Slithers out of Mountain.The geopark is considered to be a cradle of Gan Opera and Madeng Drama, both of which have been passed down over hundreds of years.
Description: Sanqingshan UNESCO Global Geopark, located in Jiangxi Province, features a remarkable granite peak forest shaped over hundreds of millions of years. The region’s geological history begins around 800 million years ago, before the formation of the Rodinia supercontinent. The current landscape formed through the rapid uplift of a granite fault block, gradually shaped by erosion into a striking cluster of granite peaks. Among the most distinctive formations is the “Oriental Goddess Peak,” a granite column that closely resembles a seated figure with long flowing hair. According to local legend, this peak represents Yao Ji, the Oriental Goddess and daughter of the Queen Mother of the West. In the story, Yao Ji falls in love with a mortal woodcutter. When their union is discovered, the Queen Mother transforms the man into a python, and Yao Ji, in grief, becomes the mountain itself. A nearby formation, “Python Slithers out of Mountain,” a 128-metre-high granite column, is also linked to this tale. These legends, deeply rooted in local culture, are intertwined with the park’s geological features, offering a layered understanding of both natural history and cultural interpretation. Across the seasons, Sanqingshan’s landscape shifts with dramatic weather and light, making its geomorphology and associated stories a visible part of daily life and visitor experience.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Sanqingshan UNESCO Global Geopark is deeply rooted in Taoist tradition and Jiangnan civilisation. With over 1,600 years of history, the Sanqingshan ancient architectural complex is nationally protected and includes 238 Taoist cultural remains such as temples, palaces, stone carvings and cliff inscriptions. These are concentrated around the Sanqing Temple, forming a 2-kilometre north–south cultural axis that is a key site for cultural preservation and tourism. In terms of intangible heritage, the geopark safeguards five listed traditions, including the Yushan Zihu Lantern—an elaborate New Year custom featuring various lantern types—and the Yushan Performing Art, a form of religiously-rooted drama dating to the Tang Dynasty. The Yushan Rib Inkstone Production Technique, with a history of over 1,300 years, continues to be passed down for its historical, artistic and economic value. Promotion of this cultural heritage is an ongoing priority. The geopark invests in interpretation materials, films, educational outreach, and repair work—such as the restoration of Huaiyu Academy. It also organises events such as the Yukeng Village folk customs event, Yinjiang She Ethnic Cultural Event, and the Huaiyu Lantern Show.
Quote: “Outstanding scenery of granite peaks and pillars surrounded by clouds and rainbows”

Introduction EN: Shennongjia is the best place in China to see golden snub-nosed monkeys.The Baishou Dance is a collective dance that incorporates singing, music and opera elements, part of the Tujia ethnic heritage.
Description: Located in Hubei Province, the Shennongjia UNESCO Global Geopark covers over 1,000 km² in the southwestern part of the Shennongjia Forestry District. It preserves one of the most comprehensive geological records in China, spanning more than 1.6 billion years. The region documents key phases of Earth’s evolution, including continuous strata from the Proterozoic (1,600–1,000 million years ago), evidence of the Rodinia supercontinent's breakup, and sedimentary sequences of glacial origin linked to global climate change events. Particularly significant are the carbonate formations containing fossilised stromatolites—early cyanobacteria responsible for oxygenating the Earth’s atmosphere around 540 million years ago. The region’s tectonic history is equally remarkable. Shennongjia’s current mountainous landscape was formed by the folding and fracturing of rock layers as tectonic forces uplifted the area from an ancient seabed. The result is a complex terrain of alpine ridges and subalpine valleys, with thirty-two peaks above 2,500 metres and six over 3,000 metres, including the Shennongding range—the highest point in central China.
