In addition to its geological significance, the geopark lies within one of China's key zones for biodiversity conservation. It includes part of the Shennongjia World Biosphere Reserve, a World Heritage site, and a Ramsar Site. Each of the five subareas—Daijihu, Shennongding, Tianyan, Guanmenshan, and Laojunshan—hosts distinct ecological landscapes, from sphagnum marsh wetlands to alpine meadows and high-altitude forests. Shennongjia is the best place in China to observe golden snub-nosed monkeys and giant salamanders, alongside other endangered species such as leopards, forest musk deer and golden eagles.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The Shennongjia UNESCO Global Geopark is deeply linked to the legacy of Shennong, the "Divine Farmer" or Yan Emperor, who is credited in Chinese mythology with introducing agriculture and medicine. For many, visiting this landscape is akin to making a pilgrimage to the roots of Chinese civilisation. The region is home to the Tujia ethnic group, who trace their cultural heritage back over two millennia. The Tujia are known for their rich traditions in song, storytelling, and performance. Among their most celebrated expressions is the Baishou Dance—a large-scale ritual involving up to 1,000 performers. Dancers wearing traditional xilankapu brocade garments use more than 70 symbolic gestures to represent aspects of life such as farming, hunting, and courtship. The Tujia also maintain art forms such as Xiagu Shadow Puppetry, which uses handmade figures and translucent screens to recount folktales, and continue to preserve the epic poem Legend of Darkness, one of China’s important National Intangible Cultural Heritages. The poem, passed down since the Tang Dynasty (618–907), recounts creation myths and the formation of the five elements—Metal, Wood, Water, Fire and Earth.
Quote: “Roof of Central China”

Titre EN: Holy Cross Mountains UNESCO Global Geopark
Introduction EN: Kadzielnia geosite is a former quarry and geological reserve situated in the centre of Kielce, and is one of the most important geosites in Europe documenting the biodiversity loss seen in the geological record of the Devonian (419 – 358 million years ago).The region is home to an extensive network of caves, such as the Jaskinia Raj geosite, one of the most important paleontological sites documenting Late Pleistocene (2.58 – 0.011 million years ago) vertebrates.The Raj cave is abounding with stalactites, stalagmites, columns, draperies, curtains, ribs as well as basins and dumps, with pisoids (“cave pearls”).
Description: In southern Poland, between Warsaw and Krakow, the Świętokrzyskie (Holy Cross) Mountains are among the oldest mountain ranges in Europe, formed during the Caledonian Orogeny, a major continental collision event in the Paleozoic era that ultimately contributed to the formation of the supercontinent Pangea. Over millions of years, the landscape has evolved, showcasing a variety of fascinating geological formations and structural features that define the geopark today. Visitors can explore diverse geological formations, including middle and upper Devonian limestone outcrops that reveal the ancient history of the region’s marine environment. The area is also home to tectonic features shaped by Caledonian, Variscan, and Alpine movements, offering insights into the dynamic geological processes that have shaped the landscape. Karst formations, representing terrestrial periods from the Permian-Triassic to the Cenozoic, are another key feature of the geopark. These formations include sinkholes, caves, and underground drainage systems that add to the area’s geomorphological diversity. Rocky limestone crags perched on hill ridges provide a dramatic contrast to the surrounding landscape, highlighting the intricate relationship between geological structures and topography. The Holy Cross Mountains UNESCO Global Geopark is home to a remarkable diversity of plant and animal life, with over 1,100 species of vascular plants—46% of Poland's flora—alongside rich populations of insects, amphibians, birds, and mammals, many of which are protected or endangered. The landscape features diverse forest habitats dominated by Scots pine, oak, fir, and beech, providing crucial ecosystems for species such as the endangered smooth snake and several Red List fish species.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The Holy Cross Mountains UNESCO Global Geopark has an important mining legacy, dating back to medieval times, that has shaped the local economy and identity. Copper and iron mining have provided livelihoods for generations, and remnants of historical mining and quarrying, such as those found at the Góra Miedzianka geosite, offer valuable insights into the development of these industries and their lasting influence on local communities. The name of the geopark is rooted in the historical and cultural heritage of the Świętokrzyskie (Holy Cross) Mountains. The name originates from the Benedictine abbey established on Łysa Góra, where relics of the Holy Cross were brought back by the Benedictines. This pilgrimage site, which was once a centre of pagan worship until the 11th century, became a focal point of religious significance in Poland and gave rise to the names Świętokrzyskie Mountains, Świętokrzyskie Region, and Świętokrzyskie Voivodeship. Beyond mining, local communities sustain their livelihoods through a variety of traditional and modern practices. Agriculture, forestry and small-scale industry provide economic stability, while tourism has become an increasingly important sector. The geopark attracts visitors with its natural beauty, cultural heritage and educational opportunities, supporting local businesses and creating employment. Cultural heritage initiatives within the geopark, such as the “Night at the Castle” event in Checiny and the activities at the Mining Heritage Museum in Miedzianka, offer opportunities for local communities to engage with their heritage while benefiting from tourism. The geopark also collaborates with local associations to preserve intangible cultural heritage, including traditional music, dances, and crafts such as those promoted by the Pottery Tradition Center in Chałupki.

Introduction EN: Seridó’s cultural heritage is diverse, and the geopark preserves the memory of ancient prehistoric peoples in more than 120 archaeological sites. The most outstanding are in the Carnaúba dos Dantas municipality, where 90 sites—particularly Xiquexique—show hunting and ritual scenes.Other cultural expressions of the region include cordel literature, mamulengos theatre, puppet performances like those of the guignol in France or the Italian pupazzi, and a strong religious heritage of Sephardi Judaism, Catholicism, Protestantism and Afro-Brazilian syncretism.
Description: In north-eastern Brazil, where the state of Rio Grande do Norte borders its neighbour Paraíba, the Seridó UNESCO Global Geopark is in the Caatinga domain. Caatinga ('white forest’ in the Tupi language) is an exclusively Brazilian semi-arid biome characterised by small, thorny trees that shed their leaves during the dry season. With only two seasons—of which the longest is dry and only a few months bring sparse rain—it is dominated by cacti such as the mandacaru (Cereus jamacaru), thick-stemmed plants, thorny brush, and arid-adapted grasses that make up the ground layer. Appropriately, the geopark adapted the Tupi word “ceri-toh”, meaning “little or no foliage, little shade,” as its name. A small part of the geopark lies within the UNESCO Caatinga Biosphere Reserve and is home to endemic mammals such as the mão-pelada (crab-eating raccoon), the brown brocket, the nine-banded armadillo, and the mocó or rock cavy—a large rodent that lives in the rocky areas of the geopark. Due to the presence of ancient igneous and metamorphic rocks, the landscape is marked by inselbergs and other landforms caused by the differential erosion of surrounding softer rock formations. The geopark’s geological record spans more than 2 billion years and documents major events such as the amalgamation of the Gondwana supercontinent—when several scattered landmasses joined together—multiple episodes of magmatism important for the formation of tungsten ore deposits, and later events that carved the landscape into canyons. The complex volcanic and subvolcanic history of the region gave rise to the largest scheelite mineralisation in South America, an important tungsten ore that can be visited in the Brejuí Mine. Located near the town of Currais Novos, the mine has operated since 1940 and remains the main site of scheelite exploitation in South America. Its importance to the region is such that Currais Novos, a town of only 45,000 inhabitants, was the first to have a cable TV operator in the North–Northeast of Brazil. In 2000, a theme park was created by the company, featuring a well-curated exhibition about the mining history of the region and the role of scheelite in the local economy, a memorial to the mine’s founder, and visits to the deactivated underground galleries. The park is currently the largest visitor attraction in the state of Rio Grande do Norte.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: "But beautiful to me is a grey sky With a thundering light intoning its refrain A harbinger that brings encouragement Of the rains coming to sertão" When Maria Bethânia praises the incoming rain in the Brazilian Northeastern hinterland (sertão), she captures the lifeblood of a region where land and people are intertwined. Her words echo the hopes of millions who endure the sertão's cycles of drought, awaiting the life-giving rains. At the heart of this challenging yet deeply connected landscape lies the Seridó UNESCO Global Geopark. The Seridó UNESCO Global Geopark bridges its rich geological significance with the lives and livelihoods of local communities, fostering sustainable development through education, culture, and tourism. Home to over 120 catalogued archaeological sites, it preserves treasures like ancient rock paintings and engravings that reveal the lives of early populations in northeastern Brazil. Legally protected sites such as Xiquexique, Poço do Arroz, and Cânions dos Apertados stand as symbols of the region’s enduring cultural and scientific heritage. The geopark's cultural vibrancy is enriched by traditions like cordel literature, mamulengos theatre, and devotion to Nossa Senhora de Sant’Ana, which boasts over 210 years of festivity in Currais Novos. Through interpretive projects such as "Os Cinco Sentidos do Geoparque Seridó," the community is engaged in understanding geodiversity through experiential learning that employs the five senses, creating strong ties between local heritage and environmental conservation. Education lies at the heart of the geopark's mission, with initiatives such as "Vem Passarinhar," which connects children and adolescents with the region’s avian biodiversity, fostering environmental stewardship. The "Itinerant Seridó Geopark" project brings exhibitions, lectures, and workshops to different communities, promoting knowledge exchange and deeper engagement with the region's unique features. Tourism plays a vital role in strengthening local economies. The geopark’s strategies intertwine geological heritage with cultural and gastronomic traditions, offering visitors a holistic experience that supports local artisans and producers. Geoproducts, such as crafts and souvenirs linked to geological features, provide new income streams for residents, enriching both livelihoods and cultural identity.

Introduction EN: Explore the Guaritas geosite, where sandstone formations and traditional sheep farms create a unique blend of natural and cultural heritage.Discover the Serra do Segredo Municipal Park, offering geo-trails and conservation initiatives for climbers, hikers, and students.Visit Fazenda Santa Marta, a rural experience-tourism destination showcasing natural wool dyeing and sustainable farming practices.
Description: Caçapava UNESCO Global Geopark is located in the southernmost part of Brazil, within the administrative boundaries of the municipality of Caçapava do Sul. The unique physical and natural features of the territory make it an important site for investigation and teaching for a number of Brazilian universities and research groups. The geopark's mineral resources have played a crucial role in the economic development of the region, with sulfide metals and marble being mined for lime and cement products. The geology of the Caçapava UNESCO Global Geopark is characterised by the Ediacaran to Cambrian volcano-sedimentary deposits of the Camaquã Basin, which provide a complete and well-exposed record of the transition stage of the South American Platform between 600 and 500 million years ago. The Serra do Segredo and Minas do Camaquã geosites are particularly notable for their well-preserved records of sedimentary and volcanic activity during this period. These geosites display features such as fault-controlled basins, ancient volcanic flows, and sedimentary deposits that reveal details of the tectonic and climatic conditions during the assembly of the Gondwana supercontinent. The Guaritas geosite stands out for its highly dissected plateau of fluvio-eolian sandstone and conglomerate formations. These structures are prime examples of cavernous weathering phenomena, including tafoni, honeycombs, and arches, which are of international interest to geomorphologists. These formations not only reveal the region’s complex geological past but also contribute to its current landscape dynamics, highlighting the ongoing interaction between natural weathering processes and geological structures. Together, these features make the Caçapava UNESCO Global Geopark a critical resource for advancing the understanding of Earth’s geological history and processes. These geosites are world-class examples and promising study areas in the field of geomorphology, particularly in cavernous weathering research. The sedimentary hills and ranges of the Caçapava UNESCO Global Geopark are also of unique ecological importance, hosting a diverse range of endemic species of cacti, native flowers, and bees.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The Caçapava UNESCO Global Geopark actively integrates the needs and traditions of its local communities into its framework for sustainability. The region’s Indigenous Guarani people, quilombola communities, and family-based cattle ranchers form the backbone of the Southern Brazilian Pampa’s cultural and ecological identity. These groups, whose lifestyles are deeply tied to the land, benefit from the geopark’s efforts to balance conservation with socio-economic growth. Cattle ranching in particular—a practice sustained for over 300 years in the Guaritas area—demonstrates a model of co-existence that has preserved the integrity of the landscape and its resources. In addition to supporting these traditional ways of life, the geopark is a growing centre for outdoor recreational activities. Rock climbing, hiking, and free flight activities take full advantage of the region’s diverse terrain, while the Serra do Segredo Municipal Park provides geo-trails and eco-tourism infrastructure to visitors, creating local employment opportunities. The region’s unpolluted night skies also attract stargazers and astrophotography enthusiasts, adding another dimension to its tourism offerings. Economic activities such as olive oil production further highlight the potential for sustainable local development. The Pampa’s olive groves produce high-quality oil that has gained national recognition, emphasising the region’s ability to merge traditional agricultural practices with modern markets. By fostering such initiatives and linking them to conservation and education, the geopark provides a robust model for how local communities and natural heritage can thrive together.

Introduction EN: Lingyan Temple, Nengren Temple, and Guanyin Cave reflect over a thousand years of history, preserving traditional architecture and spiritual heritage.The Nange Archway, Nanxijiang Ancient Village, and the Ancient Quarry of Changyu Dongtian are key cultural heritage sites within the geopark.
Description: Located on the southern edge of the Pacific Rim, Yandangshan UNESCO Global Geopark preserves a significant geological record shaped by tectonic and volcanic processes. Between 128 and 108 million years ago, the oblique subduction of the Kula-Pacific Plate beneath the Asian continental plate triggered extensive rhyolitic volcanic eruptions. These eruptions formed the prominent peaks of the region and contributed to the geological development of Mount Yandangshan. One of the key features is Guanyin Peak, which has a distinctive form that resembles a seated figure. Its exposed cross-section reveals multiple phases of volcanic activity, including a substantial layer of rhyolite formed during the second eruptive stage. Another notable formation is Scissors Peak, located within the Dalongqiu Scenic Area. Its summit appears split in two by a vertical joint, creating a shape reminiscent of a pair of scissors. Like much of the surrounding landscape, it is composed of rhyolite formed by volcanic activity. Northwest of Scissors Peak, a viewing platform near the Jinxi Stream provides a view of the Giant Dragon (Dalongqiu) Waterfall. Geological studies identify this site as a former volcanic vent, where magma once rose to the surface. The rhyolite surrounding the waterfall originates from this vent and contributes to the broader understanding of Yandangshan’s volcanic history.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Mount Yandangshan has long held cultural significance, inspiring more than 5,000 poems since the Tang and Song dynasties and over 30 books exploring its landscapes, ecology, and heritage. The tradition of stone carving, especially at Changyudongtian, reflects local knowledge of the area's varied volcanic rocks. Craftsmen use different types of lava to produce distinctive carved stones, now displayed at over 400 locations across the geopark. Since its designation in 2005, Yandangshan UNESCO Global Geopark has prioritised heritage protection, science education, and sustainable tourism. A 23-acre Geological Museum was established to support science outreach, and interpretation systems have been developed across the park, including dedicated science galleries in each area. Educational activities have expanded into schools and community spaces, reinforcing public engagement with geological knowledge.
Quote: “More than 5,000 poems have been inspired by Mount Yandangshan”

Introduction EN: September and October are the golden autumn season in China. The leaves of the trees turn gold, making the views absolutely breathtaking.Enjoy hiking on one of the many trails, such as the Yuntaishan geo-tourism route or the Shennongshan geo-tourism route.
Description: Delving into the park's mesmerizing geomorphology reveals an array of gorges, peaks, valleys, and cliff terraces, collectively known as the Yuntai Landform. These captivating features have been shaped by the interplay of tectonic forces and the relentless force of natural erosion. The towering cliffs of Yuntaishan, composed of quartz sandstone and thick carbonate rocks, reach staggering heights of up to 600 metres. Within the geopark, Hongshixia Valley, Dragon Ridge Great Wall, and Whale Bay stand as prominent geosites. Hongshixia Valley's formation traces back billions of years, marked by geological movements, orogenic activity, and the relentless erosion caused by water. Over the past 2.6 million years, the valley acquired its distinctive zigzag shape as surface water carved its way along two sets of fractures in the red quartz sandstones. Stretching approximately 1.5 kilometres long and boasting depths of over 60 metres, Hongshixia Valley reveals breathtaking vistas of red cliffs juxtaposed against pristine waters, a testament to the oxidation of iron-bearing minerals. Dragon Ridge Great Wall, as its name implies, emerges as a majestic ridgeline nestled between two gorges. Composed of limestone, this natural stone wall extends 11.5 kilometres in length, reaches heights of 100–200 metres, and spans tens of metres in width, showcasing the grandeur of piled-up stones.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Yuntaishan UNESCO Global Geopark lies at the southern piedmont of the Taihang Mountains in northern Jiaozuo City, Henan Province. The name “Yuntaishan” first appears in a tablet inscription from the reign of Emperor Kangxi during the Qing Dynasty. “Yun” means “clouds”, reflecting the region’s frequent fog and mist across its mountainous terrain. The park is home to a rich collection of traditional narratives and cultural sites. Among them is the legend of Shennong, known as the "Divine Farmer", who is said to have introduced early agricultural techniques, farming tools, and Chinese herbal medicine. This legend is closely linked to the park’s lush environment, where vegetation covers over 90% of the area. Yuntaishan has long been a place where Confucianism, Buddhism, and Taoism intersect. Cultural heritage sites include Jiayingguan, Miaoleli Pagoda, Tianning Temple, and Sansheng Pagoda, all of which are designated national key cultural relic protection units. The geopark also contains sites such as the Fucheng ruins, Dangyangyu kiln site, and various temples, altars, and cave sanctuaries, including the Northern Wei Dynasty cliff stone carvings and Yaowang Cave. The tunnel group of Diecaidong has been awarded a Guinness World Record and is an internationally recognised protected site. Intangible cultural heritage also plays a significant role in the region’s identity. Taijiquan and paper cutting have been inscribed on the UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage list. Yuntaishan Bajiquan martial arts, Huaibang rice wine brewing, and Jishantang traditional Chinese medicine practices have been recognised at the provincial level. These traditions reflect the connection between cultural expression and the natural environment.
Quote: “It is said that visitors encounter a spring every three steps, a waterfall every five steps, and a pond every ten steps”

Introduction EN: Explore Indonesia’s largest natural amphitheatre, complete with stunning waterfalls and ancient rock formations, at the Ciletuh Amphitheatre.Visit Kampung Batik Purwasedar to discover the tradition of Pakidulan Batik-making, inspired by the geopark’s rich heritage.
Description: Sitting just south of Jakarta, the Ciletuh–Palabuhanratu UNESCO Global Geopark is a rural region shaped by its location atop a tectonic subduction zone. Java hosts more than 45 volcanoes and sits on the Sunda plate, where the Indo-Australian plate subducts beneath it. This area is part of a complex geological setting where three major tectonic plates—the Eurasian, Pacific, and Philippine Sea—converge with several microplates, resulting in both intense volcanism and high seismic activity. The area is characterised by a rare geological diversity that can be classified into three zones: the subduction zone uplifted rocks, the Jampang Plateau landscape and the ancient magmatic zone shifting and fore arc evolution. This geological diversity is vividly showcased in the Jampang Plateau, which features sandstones, volcanic ashes, and lava flows that were once on the ocean floor before being uplifted by tectonic forces. The Ciletuh Amphitheatre, Indonesia’s largest horseshoe-shaped natural amphitheatre, was formed by the collapse of the Jampang Plateau and is now home to nine stunning waterfalls, including Awang, Cimarinjung, Sodong, and Puncakmanik. Another highlight is the Cisolok Geyser, where geothermal activity creates a fascinating display of water jets and steam. Since the Pleistocene (about 2.58 million to 11,700 years ago), volcanic activity has been shifting to the north, resulting in hot springs, geysers and geothermal resources in the northern area. The geopark’s tropical forests are home to some of the most threatened creatures on Earth, such as the Javan leopard, Javan gibbon, Javan surili, Javan Slow Loris, Wreathed Hornbill, Javan Green Peafowl, Javan Hawk-eagle and the Java Sparrow.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The Ciletuh–Palabuhanratu UNESCO Global Geopark takes its name from the Ciletuh River and Palabuhanratu, meaning "Queen Harbour." According to local legend, Palabuhanratu was the Queen of the Indian Ocean and a guardian of the southern coast, a figure deeply embedded in the region’s cultural identity.  Communities in the coastal regions of the geopark are sustained by fisheries, benefiting from the Indian Ocean's rich marine resources. Meanwhile, the mountainous areas offer fertile grounds for cultivating vegetables, ornamental plants and other crops. A striking example of culture and economy working hand in hand is Kampung Batik Purwasedar, located in Purwasedar Village. This initiative empowers over 20 artisans to produce Pakidulan Batik, which draws inspiration from the region’s natural beauty and cultural heritage. Using eco-friendly dyes made from roots, leaves and tree bark, Pakidulan Batik features three iconic motifs that capture the essence of the geopark: Curug, meaning waterfall; Panenjoan, the upland scenery with rice fields, trees, and serene clouds; and the ancient Jampang motif, honouring the 65-million-year-old rock formations in the geopark. Beyond batik-making, the intangible cultural heritage of the Ciletuh–Palabuhanratu UNESCO Global Geopark includes traditional dances like the Jipeng dance, folk tales, and ancestral customs preserved in traditional villages like Kasepuhan Sirnaresmi, Ciptagelar and Ciptamulya.
Quote: “The first land of the western Java Island”

Introduction EN: Explore the stunning karst landscapes of Rammang-Rammang Eco Village, where mangrove forests, diverse wildlife, and traditions like boating on the Pute River offer an unforgettable experience.Discover the Mallawa Hot Spring at Reatowa, a geothermal marvel caused by geological faults.Visit the Simbang Celebes Mushroom Farms to learn about sustainable oyster mushroom cultivation and enjoy locally produced mushroom-based delicacies.
Description: Maros Pangkep UNESCO Global Geopark is located in the southern part of Sulawesi Island, intersected by the Wallace Line, a biogeographical boundary that separates the species native to Asia from those native to Australia and Oceania. The geopark covers the Bantimurung Bulusaraung National Park on land and the Kapoposang Water Tourism Park and Liukang Tupabbiring Local Marine Conservation in the ocean.  The Thrust Mélange of the Bantimala Complex consists of metamorphic rocks ranging from low to ultra-high grades, deep marine sedimentary rocks, and tectonic blocks of oceanic crust. This formation dates back 70-135 million years and provides essential evidence of Sulawesi Island’s early evolution, contributing to the understanding of pre-tertiary global tectonics. The Karst of Maros Pangkep is another remarkable feature of the geopark. The area contains 572 caves, both horizontally and vertically, which are renowned for their impressive speleothem characteristics. The longest cave stretches for 27 km and forms part of the hydrological system, connecting an underground river to dolines, which serve as cave entrances. Over 332 types of prehistoric artifacts have been discovered in these caves, including 45,500-year-old pig paintings in Leang Tedongnge.  The region’s intensive geostructural system, which drives karstification and subaerial exposure, plays a key role in the formation of underground rivers that link various caves. Additionally, the karstic formations are crosscut by Neogene volcanic rocks, further enhancing the site's geological complexity. Lastly, the Coral Reef Islands of the Spermonde Archipelago hold significant geological value, showcasing the interconnectedness of terrestrial and marine features within the geopark. The modern carbonate platform is extensively exposed, highlighting the development of hundreds of patch reefs. These reefs are covered in sandy marine sediments that undergo morphological changes during the monsoon seasons, driven by the geodynamic process of the Indonesian Throughflow (ITF) ocean currents. These reef islands are part of the global coral triangle and represent modern equatorial carbonates, offering valuable insight into Sulawesi’s paleogeographic evolution.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The geopark area is predominantly inhabited by the Bugis and Makassarese ethnic groups. The local communities' way of life is deeply influenced by ancestral customs, encompassing moral and social values towards both fellow humans and the natural environment. These customs are reflected in the regional characteristics, including language, arts, and daily life patterns.   The area is known for recognising a unique gender system comprising five categories: men (bura'ne), women (makunrai), feminine men with social roles like women (calabai), masculine women with social roles like men (calalai), and gender-neutral individuals balancing traits of both men and women (bissu).  The Bissu community, as exemplified by the Sere Maggiri dance in Segeri-Pangkep, serves as a living testament to the ancient pre-Islamic Bugis civilisation that thrived centuries ago. During the era of the Bugis kingdoms, Bissu played key roles in important ceremonies, including the seven-day and seven-night ritual of descending into the fields (Mappalili), which was accompanied by the recitation of an incantation known as Mattedu Arajang. The Bissu’s social functions included guarding, nursing, carrying ritual objects (arajang), leading rituals, serving as shamans (sanro), and teaching those preparing for marriage. The ancient Bugis manuscript called Lontarak, specifically the I La Galigo text, tells stories about the Bissu and their history. This manuscript is an important representation of the rich cultural heritage of Bugis civilization in South Sulawesi, with origins dating back to the 19th century.

Introduction EN: Visit the Prambanan Temple UNESCO World Heritage site, a magnificent 9th-century Hindu temple complex of 240 structures.Enjoy the picturesque coastline of white sandy beaches, coral reefs and rocky shores across Gunung Kidul, Wonogiri and Pacitan.
Description: Gunung Sewu UNESCO Global Geopark, also known as the Thousand Mountains, is a striking karst plateau in Central Java, Indonesia, featuring unique geological formations, rich cultural heritage and prehistoric settlements. The geopark extends 120 kilometres from west to east and is bounded by a depression zone in the north, shaped by the active Merapi and Lawu volcanoes, and by the Indian Ocean in the south. The region’s geology represents a classic tropical karst landscape with features including conical hills, dolinas, uvalas, and irregular valleys. Gunung Sewu is located on the edge of an active subduction zone and tectonic activity has shaped the region, creating river terraces in the Sadeng dry-valley and coastal terraces along the southern coast. The southern part of Gunung Sewu boasts a series of beaches that attract visitors with their combination of rocky shores, coral formations, white sand, and vibrant reef ecosystems. These beaches stretch across Gunung Kidul, Wonogiri, and Pacitan regencies, making them a significant draw for geotourism. The karst hydrogeological system of Gunung Sewu is another key feature, with numerous underground rivers, springs along the southern coast and hundreds of caves. These caves feature formations such as stalactites, stalagmites, limestone pillars, and flowstones, showcasing the area’s rich geological processes.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The region of Gunung Sewu is steeped in a rich cultural and historical heritage, marked by Hindu and Buddhist influences. Among the most significant cultural landmarks is the Prambanan, a complex of 240 Hindu temples built in the 9th century, designated a UNESCO World Heritage site. Another key site is the Candi Gana archaeological site, dating back to the 6th century, which features Buddhist stupas and statues. The region preserves traces of prehistoric settlements spread across an area of approximately 1,800 km². These settlements, dating from the Paleolithic to Neolithic periods, include evidence of cave dwellers and open-space communities, representing the Pacitanian stone-culture, a notable prehistoric cultural heritage in Southeast Asia. Education plays a vital role in sustaining and promoting the region’s heritage. The "School to Geopark" programme enable students, accompanied by geography and biology teachers, to visit geosites and engage in learning activities that connect geology, biology and culture. These programmes aim to foster an understanding of the region’s unique identity and its interconnected natural and cultural heritage. Institutions like the Indonesia Karst Museum and the Gunung Sewu Etalase further provide platforms for shared learning and community engagement.
Quote: “Although all Gunung Sewu beaches have a common geological formation, they each have their own characteristics”

Introduction EN: The region is a trekking haven that has become increasingly popular, especially amongst those who are willing to make the strenuous hike to the summit.The geopark is rich in Sasak culture, with local communities practicing traditional ways of life and preserving their cultural heritage.The Gili Islands are renowned for their vibrant coral reefs and marine biodiversity, making them a popular destination for underwater exploration.
Description: The Rinjani-Lombok UNESCO Global Geopark, located on Lombok Island in Southeast Asia, features the towering Rinjani volcano and its 50 km² caldera. The caldera contains Segara Anak lake, a stunning body of blue water that locals call the "Child of the Sea." This dramatic landscape was shaped by the catastrophic eruption of the Samalas Volcano in 1257, an event that buried ancient civilizations, triggered a worldwide cooling period, and reshaped the island's geography. The eruption formed a massive caldera and pyroclastic flow, while remnants of the volcanic system gave rise to Mt. Barujari and Mt. Rombongan, young volcanic cones that now sit within the caldera. The volcanic complex of Lombok developed due to the subduction of the Indian Ocean Plate under the Southeast Asia Plate. The geology is dominated by Quaternary calc-alkaline volcanoes, Oligo-Miocene volcanic rocks, and Neogene intrusive igneous rocks. The island’s volcanic features are classified into an older complex (Mt. Punikan, Mt. Nangi, and Mt. Sembalun) and a younger complex led by Mt. Rinjani, the tallest peak at 3,726 m above sea level. The diverse landscape of the geopark includes savannahs, semi-deciduous forests, and tropical montane evergreen forests, which support a rich ecosystem of protected species. Preserved within the Mount Rinjani National Park, the geopark is a biodiversity hotspot. The caldera's hydrothermal and meteoric waters, paired with lush tropical vegetation and stunning waterfalls, create a unique environment for scientific exploration, conservation, and geotourism.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The Rinjani-Lombok UNESCO Global Geopark spans five districts whose local economies are closely tied to their traditions and natural resources. Handwoven crafts like tenun ikat, songket, and ketak, made from Lygodium ferns, are created using traditional techniques and natural dyes, supporting local artisans and contributing to the tourism sector. Visitors to the Rinjani-Lombok Geopark can engage in a wide range of outdoor activities, including trekking up Mount Rinjani, rafting, river tubing, camping, biking, snorkelling, diving and sightseeing. The geopark also features seven geotrails and more than ten geotourism packages which actively involve the local community, emphasising local knowledge and highlighting the geological and natural significance of the region, while creating economic opportunities through household product sales and geohomestays. To further enhance local engagement, the Rinjani-Lombok Geopark and Science Technopark have been initiating a partnership to support young entrepreneurs, particularly high school students, in developing geoproducts that integrate geological and geopark interpretations.
Quote: “The tropical bridge between Asia and Australia”

Introduction EN: Take a trip to Hengam Island to see dolphins, or go snorkelling to witness the diversity of tropical fish swimming in the coral reef.Visit Bandar Laft on Qeshm’s north shore, popular for its Lenj Shipyard where traditional boats are still built and for its badgir (windcatchers), an ancient Persian architectural feature used to ventilate houses.Visit the Namakdan Salt Complex and the Namakdan Salt Cave, a 7-km chasm of multi-coloured galleries and beautiful salt crystals.
Description: While for some Qeshm is shaped like an arrow pointing towards mainland Iran, others see a dolphin just like the ones that swim the turquoise waters of the Persian Gulf. Regardless, the position of the largest of the Iranian islands, at the border of two different marine ecosystems - the Persian Gulf and the Sea of Oman - together with its geological characteristics led to the formation of vast coral reefs, mangrove forests, and beautiful sandy beaches.  Qeshm is at the southern edge of the Zagros Mountain range, an 1800 km fold and thrust belt formed by the collision between the Arabian and Eurasian tectonic plates, initiated in the Miocene (25 – 5 million years ago) and still ongoing. These mountains, a series of elongated ellipsoid-shaped ridges, are mostly formed by sedimentary rocks that folded over a layer of salt, acting like a sliding surface, and by subsequent erosion that removed the softer layers. The thick salt layer, less dense than the surrounding rocks, has formed domes such as the Namakdan Salt Complex, featuring a variety of salt-related landforms, including salt flats, springs and sinkholes. The most impressive is the Namakdan Salt Cave, a 7-km chasm of multicoloured galleries and beautiful salt crystals considered to be the longest salt cave in the world and recently inscribed in the International Union of Geological Sciences “First 100” geological heritage sites list.  The cave's pure and dry air is also used to help patients with respiratory issues. The geopark is also rich in erosional landforms such as the Valley of Stars, an impressive labyrinth of sandstone canyons with tall columns and flat-topped mounds that locals believe to have been formed by a shooting star. Another notable feature is the 10 metre-deep Chahkuh Gorge, which gets narrower the further one adventures into it, until only a glimmer of sunlight enters through the top of the canyon. At the bottom, several wells were carved into the rock by locals in search of water.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Qeshm Island UNESCO Global Geopark empowers its local communities through innovative initiatives that preserve cultural heritage while supporting sustainable livelihoods.  Folk music is an integral part of Qeshm Island’s cultural identity. Several groups of local musicians play traditional instruments and pass down this heritage to the next generation. The lute, typically played by the lead singer, is a key instrument in these performances. Geo-products crafted by local artisans reflect the connection of local communities to Qeshm's natural resources. The Namakdan Salt Cave Candle is an eco-conscious souvenir that promotes the cave while discouraging the removal of natural samples. Indigenous artist Avatef Khashabi creates ceramic geoproducts inspired by the vibrant layers and formations of the Namakdan Caves. These initiatives provide sustainable income for local communities and students while promoting conservation. The Gouran Maritain Park-Museum showcases Qeshm’s maritime heritage by preserving and showcasing traditional wooden boat-building techniques, known as "Lenj." Established in collaboration with the Gouran Village community, the museum features 28 pictorial displays and 14 original vessels. The craft of constructing these boats, inscribed on UNESCO’s Intangible Cultural Heritage list, connects visitors to the Persian Gulf’s rich sailing culture and supports the continuation of this centuries-old tradition.
Quote: “The land of erosion, the art of erosion”

Introduction EN: Sample local honey harvested at geopark sites like the Messel Pit and the international Forest Art Centre, produced through a sustainable beekeeping partnership with the Glückshonig company.Cycle through the cultural landscape of the western Bachgau along a signposted trail that passes Roman and medieval archaeological sites with views as far as Frankfurt.Discover the mining history of the region at “Marie in der Kohlbach,” a historic lead and silver mine southeast of Hohensachsen, now open to visitors.
Description: Bergstrasse-Odenwald UNESCO Global Geopark, located south of Frankfurt between the Rhine, Main and Neckar rivers, preserves over 500 million years of Earth history. The region is marked by the striking contrast between the flat Upper Rhine Plain and the ancient Odenwald mountains, where landscapes, geological formations and human history intersect. One of the geopark’s most iconic features is the Felsenmeer, or "Sea of Rocks," in the Odenwald. Here, thousands of boulders—some the size of trucks—lie scattered across the slope, formed from granite-like crystalline rocks deep in the Earth’s crust. These rocks were uplifted by tectonic forces during the formation of the supercontinent Pangea (490–250 million years ago) and later shaped by freeze-thaw processes during the last Ice Age. Roman stoneworkers exploited this resource between the 2nd and 4th centuries, leaving behind more than 15 workshops and around 300 unfinished or damaged boulders. Today, visitors can explore the site and its geological history at the Felsenmeer Information Centre. Another outstanding site is the Messel Pit Fossil Site, a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1995. Located near Darmstadt, this former oil shale and coal mine holds the most significant Eocene fossil deposit in the world, dating back around 47 million years. The exceptionally well-preserved fossils—some with fur and soft tissue—offer insight into the evolution of mammals, including early horses, pangolins, marsupials and bats. Over 1,000 species have been documented, making Messel a global reference for understanding life in a subtropical forest ecosystem during the Eocene.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Bergstrasse-Odenwald UNESCO Global Geopark is rich in cultural heritage, particularly from the Carolingian empire, a vast Frankish-dominated empire in western and central Europe during the Early Middle Ages. Sites such as Lorsch Abbey, a UNESCO World Heritage site, Einhard’s Basilica in Michelstadt-Steinbach, and more than 200 castles reflect the historical importance of this landscape as a corridor of power and movement. Mining heritage is also a central part of the region’s identity and history. The “Marie in der Kohlbach” visitor mine, southeast of Hohensachsen, preserves over 500 years of lead and silver mining. Ore extraction began in the 1530s, and by 1771 a drainage tunnel was constructed to support intensified operations. The mine follows a hydrothermal ore vein associated with Tertiary volcanic rocks, and guided tours introduce visitors to black powder blasting techniques and the harsh working conditions of miners in the 18th and 19th centuries. Today, the territory remains a centre of cultural life. In the southern part of the Geopark, the city of Heidelberg is recognised as a UNESCO Creative City of Literature. With a literary tradition stretching back to the founding of Heidelberg University in 1386, the city became a major centre for humanist and Romantic literature. It remains home to around 200 writers, 45,000 students, and a dense network of publishers, bookshops and translators.
Quote: “Between granite and sandstone – continents on the move”

Introduction EN: Discover the striking fairy chimneys of Kula-Salihli UNESCO Global Geopark, shaped by erosion processes and capped with basalt or sandstone.Visit Gökeyüp village, where over 100 families continue a centuries-old pottery tradition using Roman-era methods.Explore the Emir Hot Springs, a site of ancient Roman and Ottoman baths once known as “Thermai Thessos” for its healing waters.
Description: In western Türkiye, the Kula-Salihli UNESCO Global Geopark extends across three distinct geological units: the Kula volcanic province, one of Türkiye’s youngest volcanic areas; the Bozdağ Mountains, stretching east of Izmir to the Anatolian Plateau; and, situated between them, the Gediz Graben – a major depression formed by the extension of the Earth’s crust due to the subduction of the African Plate beneath the Anatolian Plate. The geopark features a large lava plateau, lava caves, and basalt columns, as well as a range of morphological features associated with graben formation, including faults, fan deposits, and earthquake-related landforms. Kula-Salihli UNESCO Global Geopark has a complex geological structure resulting from the active tectonic regime of the Aegean extensional province – one of the most seismically active and rapidly deforming regions in the world. This region is shaped by converging plates and subduction-collision-related geodynamic processes. The geopark rests on the metamorphic basement of the Menderes Massif and the ophiolitic mélange units of the İzmir-Ankara Zone, a remnant of the Tethyan Ocean. Quaternary volcanism in the area occurred in three eruptive phases, dated to approximately 1.1 million, 300,000, and 15,000 years ago. The outstanding volcanic features of the geopark have been recognised since antiquity. The ancient Greek geographer Strabo (63 BC–24 AD), in his work Geographica, referred to Kula as Katakekaumene (“the burned land”) due to its coal-black lava.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Kula is one of the few settlements to survive the Greek invasion of Anatolia in the wake of World War I, and its historical centre features original Ottoman architecture. Gökeyüp village, an important pottery centre in western Anatolia, has over 100 families creating beautiful clay artefacts using methods dating back to Roman times. The geopark includes significant cultural heritage sites such as the Homoerectus Valley, the Çakallar human footprint fossils, the Kanlıkaya rock paintings, and the ruins of Sardis—the ancient capital of the Lydian Kingdom, where money is believed to have been invented—as well as a temple dedicated to Artemis dating to the 3rd century BCE. Kula-Salihli UNESCO Global Geopark supports sustainable tourism and education through dedicated infrastructure, including the Kula Geopark Visitor Centre “Katakekaumene” and over 12 km of marked geotrails with interpretive panels. Guided tours, school programmes, and geo-education activities are regularly offered. To strengthen scientific collaboration and support sustainable development, the geopark has partnered with Celal Bayar University to establish the JARUM-Geopark Research Centre. It has also created the GeoCycle bicycle society, combining sport with geotourism outreach.
Quote: “The region that was ‘fire-born’”

Introduction EN: The Fossa Magna Museum tells the story of Itoigawa’s jade and unlocks the mystery of how the Japanese islands were formed.At the Nou Fishing Port, the centre of one of Japan’s largest crab fisheries, and at Marine Dream Nou Roadside Station, browse one of the region’s largest seafood markets.The Spring Festivals of Amatsu Shrine and Nou Hakusan Shrine feature ancient ritual dances.
Description: As if being northeast Asia’s only major source of jade were not enough, the Itoigawa UNESCO Global Geopark—the first in Japan—also tells the full story of the formation of the Japanese islands and hosts a vast forest that is home to some of the country’s most important species. Named after Itoigawa city, which translates as ‘Thread-Fish-River,’ this geopark—with a name hard to pronounce even for native Japanese speakers—is centuries, if not millennia, old. Contrary to expectation, its river is nowhere to be found. One theory suggests the name derives from the plentiful three-spined stickleback, a freshwater fish called itoyo. The geopark’s territory, almost entirely covered in pristine forests and home to protected species such as the Japanese serow, Japanese black bear, Japanese macaque, and several birds of prey, extends from the heights of the Kubiki Mountains (part of the Myoko Togakushi Renzan National Park) and the nearly 3,000-metre peaks of the Northern Japanese Alps (part of the Chubu Sangaku National Park) to the coastal lowlands and offshore waters to the west. This impressive altitude difference has created turbulent rivers that carved deep valleys and ravines, such as the Himekawa and Umidani Gorges. At the Kotakigawa Jade Gorge, a National Natural Monument of Japan, deep in the mountains of southwestern Itoigawa beneath the towering limestone face of Mount Myojo (1,188 m), massive boulders of jadeite lie strewn about the Kotaki River. These boulders are washed downstream to the coast, where they have been collected for over 7,000 years, helping Japan’s prehistoric Jomon civilisation—one of the world’s oldest jade-working cultures—to flourish. At the Choja Gahara Archaeological Site, a Jomon village that thrived between 5,000 and 3,000 years ago is preserved. But there is more to Itoigawa. Around 20 million years ago, the Japanese archipelago began to separate from the Asian continent, forming an island arc centred on the geopark. The Japanese islands fractured, creating a deep geological trench through the centre of Japan called the Fossa Magna. Tectonic movements along the Itoigawa–Shizuoka Tectonic Line gave rise to the massive Kubiki Mountains, the Japanese Alps, and active volcanism at Mount Yakeyama, which first erupted only about 3,000 years ago. At Fossa Magna Park, visitors can observe an exposed section of this tectonic line, making it an excellent site for learning about geological faults.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Known as the "World’s Oldest Jade-working Culture," the region's historical significance begins with a remarkable 7,000-year-old jadeite jade hammer unearthed at the Ogakuchi Site. This discovery highlights Itoigawa’s legacy as a centre for jade production, with decorative jade beads crafted up to 5,000 years ago and traded as far as the Korean Peninsula. The Chojagahara and Teraji sites, pivotal centres of jade production during the Middle Jomon Period, are now protected as National Historic Landmarks, ensuring that this unique cultural legacy is preserved for future generations. Cultural traditions further enrich Itoigawa’s identity. The "Oumi Take-no-Karakai" New Year’s Festival, celebrated for over 500 years, features vibrant tug-of-war competitions over bamboo poles, culminating in massive bonfires along the coast. To ensure its continuity, a "Children’s Karakai" now engages younger generations in this cherished tradition. Traditional dances, such as the "Bugaku Court Dances of Amatsu Shrine and Nou Hakusan Shrine" and the "Nechi Yamadera En’nen Festival" of Nechi Hiyoshi Shrine, are equally significant. Dating back roughly 500 years, these dances—primarily performed by children—are believed to bring good harvests, family safety, and long life. Their similarities to dances from Kyoto and Osaka suggest the influence of historic trade routes like the Hokuriku Road. The Itoigawa dialect reflects the region's geographic isolation, with its unique accent, grammar, vocabulary, and pronunciation. This linguistic heritage stands as a testament to the community’s resilience and distinct identity. Education and disaster preparedness are also integral to Itoigawa’s sustainability. At Shimohayakawa Elementary School, a Disaster Risk Reduction Programme focuses on the active volcano Mt. Niigata-Yakeyama. This initiative has inspired students, with one alumnus pursuing volcanology at university and returning to share his knowledge. The Fossa Magna Museum complements these efforts with lectures and workshops on natural disasters, climate change, and volcanic phenomena, fostering a culture of awareness and resilience.
Quote: “The diversity of the land from 0-3,000 meters made the world's oldest jade culture and varieties of traditional culture”

Introduction EN: With a long whaling heritage, former fishermen now offer whale watching cruises.The Onda Festival, held biannually in May at the Kiragawa Hachiman Shrine, has been celebrated since the 12th century.Kiragawa town, located in the western part of the geopark, preserves an important architectural heritage that has largely disappeared elsewhere on the island.
Description: Muroto UNESCO Global Geopark is a land where one can find a millennia-old Buddhist heritage and walk an ancient coastline that has been raised by tectonic forces to over one hundred metres above sea level. Divided into five regions, each with distinct geological features, Muroto UNESCO Global Geopark is particularly known for the outcrops along the Gyodo-Kuromi coastline, where highly folded turbidites, trace fossils, and sand dykes—considered “fossils of liquefaction” caused by earthquake-induced vibrations—can be observed. On the west coast of the Muroto Peninsula, marine terraces hundreds of metres above sea level bear witness to the island’s ongoing tectonic uplift. Meanwhile, the Mikurado Caves, formed by wave erosion at sea level, are revered as the place where the monk Kūkai is said to have practiced asceticism and attained enlightenment. The geopark is covered by coastal subtropical vegetation adapted to strong sea breezes and a mild climate, thanks to the Kuroshio Current. These forests, home to dozens of native tree species, have long provided Ubame oak wood—the raw material for Tosa binchotan, a long-burning, odourless and smokeless charcoal highly prized by chefs. Within the geopark, 37 kilns still produce this traditional charcoal.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Muroto UNESCO Global Geopark integrates conservation, education, and cultural heritage, offering visitors and residents a unique connection to the region’s natural and human history. Its renowned marine terraces, among the most prominent in Japan, serve as a living classroom, showcasing tectonic uplift and providing insights into the Earth’s geological processes. These are complemented by disaster prevention education programmes that use real-world examples—such as the Tsuro Tsunami Evacuation Shelter—to teach earthquake and tsunami preparedness. The geopark supports enduring local traditions, such as the Onda Festival in Kiragawa Town, which preserves 12th-century performances and highlights traditional architecture like Tosa plaster walls. Heritage industries, including the production of Tosa binchotan charcoal, continue to thrive. Initiatives like Sumigen’s binchotan culinary ventures and BBQ camps help preserve this craft while contributing to local innovation and economic resilience. Intangible cultural heritage is reflected in unique food practices, including kashikiri tofu, made from edible acorns—rooted in the local ecosystem. Fishing practices such as fixed-net fishing promote sustainable livelihoods and marine conservation, while community responses to rising seawater temperatures demonstrate adaptability and resilience. Seasonal festivals like the Wasuke Jizo Festival and Apoi Fire Festival bring people together to honour both tradition and nature, creating vibrant cultural experiences. On Shikoku, the smallest of Japan’s main islands, a 1,200 km pilgrimage route leads walkers through 88 temples and numerous sacred sites associated with Kūkai, the founder of the esoteric Shingon school of Buddhism. The Shikoku 88 Temple Pilgrimage is one of the few circular pilgrimage routes in the world, and passes through Muroto UNESCO Global Geopark.
Quote: “Where the ocean and the land meet for the birth of a new habitable land”

Introduction EN: The Kuniga Coast Trail, one of the most scenic routes in the Oki Islands, passes through traditional farmlands where cattle and horses graze freely. The trail begins near the top of Matengai Cliff and descends to sea level near the Tsūtenkyō rock arch.On Nakanoshima Island, the Akiya Coast showcases dramatic geological formations created by volcanic eruptions and erosion, making it one of the island’s most impressive coastal landscapes.
Description: The Oki Islands UNESCO Global Geopark tells a geological story stretching back 250 million years to the formation of the Pangaea supercontinent. Formed by the summits of two massive stratovolcanoes that erupted approximately 5 million years ago, this archipelago of about 180 islands—only four of which are inhabited—is a striking example of geological and natural diversity. The islands boast lush forests, turquoise waters, and rust-coloured sea cliffs, offering insight into Earth's dynamic history. The islands originated from tectonic collisions that transformed ancient marine sediments into the Oki gneisses, the oldest geological units in the region. Around 20 million years ago, additional tectonic activity along the back-arc of the Japan and Pacific Plates led to volcanic eruptions that shaped the islands’ dramatic topography. Subsequent erosion and rising sea levels submerged much of the calderas, leaving today’s islands as remnants of these ancient volcanoes. Among the most notable features is Matengai Cliff, which rises 257 metres above the sea, providing panoramic views of the coastline. Mt. Akahage offers visitors a glimpse into one of the volcanic calderas that formed the archipelago. The islands’ volcanic past also produced obsidian—a natural glass valued by early settlers 30,000 years ago for both practical and aesthetic purposes. Isolated from the mainland, the Oki Islands developed unique ecosystems home to endemic species such as the Oki hare and Oki salamander. Fishing, farming, and cultural traditions like sumo wrestling are integral to the islands’ way of life, illustrating the deep connection between geology, biodiversity, and human activity.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The Oki Islands UNESCO Global Geopark is a living example of the close relationship between people, culture, and the environment. Its cultural heritage dates back 30,000 years, beginning with the use of obsidian tools and evolving through phases such as its role as miketsukuni—a provider of food for the emperor and Shinto rituals—,its use as a place of exile for aristocrats and emperors, and its prominence as a port on the kitamaebune trading route. This heritage is preserved in 101 designated Cultural Properties, including nationally important sites like Oki Kokubun-ji Temple and Takuhi Shrine. Intangible heritage is equally valued. The region has 27 designated Intangible Folk Cultural Properties, such as the nationally recognised Oki Dengaku and Niwa-no-mai dances. These traditions continue to connect the local population with their ancestors while offering cultural insight to visitors. Education plays a vital role in sustaining this legacy. The geopark has developed picture-story shows for preschool children to introduce the geological, natural, and cultural heritage of the islands. This creative approach has inspired further learning, including study sessions and original plays exploring the islands' history. Tourism also plays a key role. Local associations of hotels, guides, restaurants, and other stakeholders collaborate to offer "geo experiences" that showcase the islands’ distinctiveness. These efforts are based on the idea that tourism development should begin with local knowledge and pride.
Quote: “Search for the keys that will unlock the mysteries of the islands”

Introduction EN: Visit Hwajeogyeon Pool, where 13-metre granite formations rise above clear waters. This striking geological site was once used for sacred rain ceremonies, reflecting ancient cultural traditions.Explore the Jeongok Paleolithic Site, where well-preserved archaeological remains—including the renowned Acheulean hand axe—have been uncovered, thanks to the unique soil conditions.
Description: Hantangang UNESCO Global Geopark presents a complex geological history shaped by tectonic activity and volcanic processes. It comprises Precambrian and Paleozoic metamorphic rocks, Jurassic and Cretaceous granites, Cretaceous volcanic rocks, Quaternary basalt, and a variety of soils, including glacial-period deposits. The geopark lies within the Imjingang Belt, a major tectonic province formed by the Paleozoic collision of the Sino-Korean and Yangtze cratons. This belt is considered the lateral extension of the Qinling-Dabie-Sulu Belt in eastern China, one of East Asia’s most significant tectonic features. A defining element of the geopark is the Late Quaternary Hantangang River Volcanic Field, created by fissure eruptions of basaltic lava. The lava flowed along the paleo-channel for over 110 km, forming a broad volcanic plateau. Subsequent river rejuvenation carved deep gorges into the solidified basalt, giving rise to distinctive volcanic landforms, including steep cliffs with columnar joints. These contrast with V-shaped valleys shaped by fluvial erosion in granite and metamorphic rock areas, illustrating the lithological control on erosion processes in the geopark. Spanning Gyeonggi-do and Gangwon-do provinces, the geopark also features dense forests that enhance the region’s ecological importance. The Hantangang Basalt, formed by historic lava flows, defines the area's unique landscape as an undulating lava plateau known for its striking geological characteristics.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The Hantangang River has supported human settlement since the Paleolithic era, providing vital water resources and fertile plains. Archaeological remains—including Paleolithic stone tools and Bronze Age dolmens built from local basalt and tuff—reflect a long-standing relationship between people and the landscape. The area’s strategic location also made it a key site for military activity, with natural columnar joint formations historically used in defensive structures. Modern infrastructure began shaping the region in 1914 with the construction of railway lines and irrigation systems. However, the Korean War brought severe destruction and loss of life. Due to its proximity to the Demilitarized Zone, the region remained underdeveloped throughout much of the 20th century. Today, the geopark is working to revitalise the area by promoting its geological, cultural, and historical significance, fostering sustainable development through conservation, education, and geotourism. Geotourism has become a key driver of local economic growth, particularly through the development of the columnar joint-themed Geotrails (Jusangjeoli-gil), which attract visitors year-round, including in winter. The geopark also plays an active role in preserving and promoting intangible heritage. The Pulpiri grass flute tradition, designated as Provincial Intangible Cultural Heritage, is featured in geopark events and supported by a dedicated cultural centre in Pocheon-si City to ensure its preservation and transmission.

Introduction EN: Visit the Ries meteorite crater, a rare geological feature with characteristics also found in impact craters on Mars.Take the 7-Hills Way, a circular hiking route linking geological, archaeological, and cultural history sites, with panoramic views and interpretive panels.Explore medieval towns in Bavaria built using meteorite impact rocks, with architecture shaped by the region’s unique geological heritage.
Description: Around 15 million years ago, during the Miocene epoch, the world's continents and oceans were in familiar positions, but significant geological changes were underway. The collision of the Arabian Peninsula with Eurasia cut off the Indian Ocean from the Mediterranean, eventually drying it out. As the climate cooled, mammals and birds thrived, and apes began to dominate. Amid these gradual changes, a dramatic event occurred—a cosmic stone, about 1 kilometre wide, entered Earth’s atmosphere and struck Bavaria at speeds over 70,000 km per hour. The impact lasted only seconds but reshaped the landscape, generating pressures of millions of bars and temperatures exceeding 20,000 °C. Pulverised material was ejected as far as 450 km. The resulting Ries Crater, Europe’s best-preserved meteorite crater, is one of the most intensively studied impact sites worldwide. At Wallerstein Cliff, visitors can see Ries-Lake limestones, including travertines and stromatolites, offering insights into the area's ancient environment. The shockwave altered the Earth's crust, forming new rocks, including suevite, which has been quarried for centuries and used in local architecture. A prime example is St. George’s Church in Nördlingen, built with these impact rocks, linking the region’s geological past to its architectural heritage. The suevite in Ries Geopark is extremely significant for research and used to identify similar rocks in impact craters worldwide, including the Moon.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The geopark’s long-standing connection to space exploration is an integral part of its identity. Since the Apollo 14 astronauts trained in the Ries meteorite crater in the 1970s, the area has continued to serve as a geological training site for NASA and the European Space Agency. The Ries Crater Museum, housed in a 16th-century barn, showcases impact-related features, including a sample of moon rock collected during NASA’s Apollo 16 mission, highlighting the connection between Earth’s impact craters and lunar exploration. Cultural traditions also thrive in the geopark, with festivals and events that celebrate the region’s medieval heritage, such as the annual medieval festival in Nördlingen and the rich culinary traditions tied to local ingredients. These traditions, along with the geopark’s commitment to sustainable tourism, ensure that the region remains vibrant and connected to its geological and cultural roots. The Ries Panorama Way, a 128-km trail that follows the crater rim, offers a complete perspective of the region's geology, biodiversity, and medieval history, including significant sites such as Oettingen Castle and the Harburg fortress.

Introduction EN: Climb Gunung Raya, the highest peak in Langkawi. Visit Kampung Kilim, a popular tourist attraction known for its boat rides, eagle feeding, and mangrove tours. Watch the Mek Mulung theatre, regularly performed at the Kota Mahsuri Cultural Complex.
Description: Ninety-nine, the magical number that gathers all the islands in the Langkawi Archipelago, a tropical paradise of white sand beaches, forest-covered mountains, and mangroves, thirty kilometres off the coast of Malaysia in the Malacca Strait. Malaysia’s first UNESCO Global Geopark, Langkawi, is a fascinating place. There are dozens of beaches, like the expansive Tanjung Rhu Beach or the secluded Datai Bay; the richest mangroves in the country, such as those in the Kubang Badak Reserve or the Kilim Karst Geoforest Park, where dramatic limestone formations carved by running water have helped create one of the most important ecosystems in the region; and forest-covered limestone and sandstone peaks, such as those in the Machinchang mountain range, home to the Machinchang Cambrian Geoforest Park. Here, Cambrian rock formations, estimated to be over 550 million years old, form the substrate of one of the oldest rainforests on the planet. In addition to numerous mountain trails, Mt. Machinchang can be accessed via the famous SkyCab, one of the longest and steepest free-span cable car rides in Southeast Asia. Another of the geopark’s gems is the Dayang Bunting Marble Geoforest Park, just south of the main island, where a large collapsed cave has given rise to a freshwater lake surrounded by dense tropical forest. Nearly 300-million-year-old marble formations, some of the finest in the world, can be found here.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The Langkawi UNESCO Global Geopark actively fosters the well-being of its local communities through innovative programmes, cultural initiatives, and environmental conservation efforts, ensuring a harmonious balance between tourism, tradition and sustainability. The geopark celebrates the island's cultural diversity, showcasing the rich stories of its people through channels like Orang Langkawi, which highlights the unique lives and traditions of Langkawi's residents. Initiatives such as Kopi Puteh, where a couple crafts aromatic coffee using generational recipes, and Mahsuri Gold, a natural balm inspired by local folklore, demonstrate how tradition fuels modern entrepreneurship. Datai Valley’s virgin coconut oil showcases the use of natural remedies, while the 'Two Pie Craft' initiative innovatively upcycles coconut husks into art. Educational programmes such as GeoMangrove and Geocoral invite participants to engage directly with conservation. The GeoMangrove programme, conducted in the Kilim mangrove sanctuary, teaches participants of all ages to plant mangrove seedlings, contributing to coastal ecosystem protection. The Geocoral programme, led by local experts, demonstrates how to establish coral breeding sites, fostering a deeper understanding of coral reef conservation. These initiatives are complemented by weekly Geosite Cleaning events, where participants clean geosites and learn their unique stories from Geopark Rangers, promoting both environmental care and cultural appreciation. To cultivate future generations of conservationists, the geopark has established GeoClubs in schools, offering students opportunities to learn about Langkawi’s unique heritage. The GeoTeacher (GeoCruise) programme equips educators with the tools and experiences needed to inspire their students about the geopark’s natural and cultural wonders.
Quote: “Rocks from the oldest continent: where geological wonder and legend meet”

Titre EN: Dong Van Karst Plateau UNESCO Global Geopark
Introduction EN: Visit Quan Ba’s "Heaven’s Gate" for panoramic views over winding roads, mist-covered mountains, and lush valleys.Travel along the stunning Ma Pi Leng Pass, rising to 1,200 metres, and admire sweeping vistas of deep canyons, dramatic limestone peaks, and the winding Nho Que River.Explore Dong Van in bloom: from October to November, the hillsides and rice terraces burst into pinkish-white buckwheat flowers, and from January to February, peach and plum blossoms transform the landscape into a romantic spectacle.
Description: Dong Van Karst Plateau UNESCO Global Geopark is located in Ha Giang, Viet Nam’s northernmost mountainous province. Dominated by limestone formations (approximately 60%), the region features dramatic landscapes of towering peaks, deep canyons, and extensive karst systems. Its geological history spans more than 550 million years, beginning in the Cambrian period, and includes evidence from two major extinction events: the Frasnian–Famennian (around 360 million years ago) and the Permian–Triassic (around 250 million years ago). The geopark contains sedimentary, igneous, and metamorphic rocks, offering significant stratigraphic and paleontological value. Fossil discoveries include ancient fish, flora, brachiopods, bivalves, trilobites, foraminifera, corals, conodonts, crinoids, and fossilised mollusc traces. Key geological features include the Tu San canyon, one of Southeast Asia’s deepest canyons at 700–800 m, and Mieu Vac Mount, the highest peak at 1,971 m. Two protected conservation areas within the geopark safeguard rare flora and fauna, including conifer species, Asian black bears, Southern serows (mountain goats), and diverse birdlife. Notably, the critically endangered Tonkin snub-nosed monkey—once thought extinct—was rediscovered here in the 1990s.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Dong Van Karst Plateau UNESCO Global Geopark is home to 17 ethnic groups, including the Mong, Lo Lo, Pu Mong, Co Lao, Bo Y, Dao, and Tay—some of whom have lived in the region for 500 to 800 years. Over 60% of the geopark’s population belong to the Mong ethnic group, the largest Mong community being in Viet Nam. These communities actively preserve their cultural identity through language, traditional customs, crafts, and festivals. Folk literature and performing arts continue to flourish. Mong oral traditions include folk songs, fairy tales, riddles, and proverbs, while Tay cultural expressions include lullabies and stories such as the “Legend of the Flute.” Traditional musical practices—such as the Art of Leaf-Blowing, Lip-Blowing, and flute playing—form a key part of intangible heritage. These expressions are supported by education and sustainable tourism programmes that promote cultural pride and strengthen local livelihoods. Cultural landmarks include the Vuong Family’s Palace in Sa Phin commune, constructed from green stone, Po mu wood, and terracotta tiles. Its carved motifs—dragons, phoenixes, and bats—symbolise royalty and prosperity. Dong Van Ancient Quarter, with around 40 preserved houses dating back to 1890, showcases a distinctive architectural complex combining traditional market spaces with residential areas, reflecting ethnic identity and local interpretations of feng shui.
Quote: “About 200 Tonkin snub-nosed monkeys live in the Geopark, the only place in the world where one can still find them”

Introduction EN: Immerse yourself in Salpausselkä's rich history, with over 220 Stone Age settlement sites, including the significant Ristola site dating back 10,500 years.Kapatuosia hillfort, located in the historic centre of Hollola, is a nationally significant archaeological site. Once an island, the hill dates back approximately 8,000 years.Discover local traditions and stories through cultural events like the Hollo & Martta International Folklore Festival, which celebrates music, dance and the legend of the giants of Hollola.
Description: The most prominent geological features of the Salpausselkä UNESCO Global Geopark, are the Salpausselkä ridges, which extend across southern Finland for more than 600 kilometres. These formations—composed of sand and gravel—were deposited by glacial meltwaters at the edge of retreating ice sheets during the Younger Dryas period, a cold phase that occurred roughly 12,900 to 11,600 years ago. The ridges interrupted the warming of the Northern Hemisphere and marked the end of the Pleistocene Epoch. Today, they remain among Finland’s most studied and recognised geological features. To the north of the ridges lies a dense network of lakes, including Lake Päijänne, Finland’s second largest lake. The region also includes internationally significant eskers including Kelvenne Island and Pulkkilanharju in Päijänne National Park. These narrow, winding gravel ridges were formed by meltwater rivers flowing within and beneath the glaciers. The name Salpausselkä comes from the Finnish word meaning "to block," reflecting how these ridges shape the landscape and water systems of the Finnish Lakeland. Formed by retreating glaciers, these glaciofluvial landforms not only define the landscape but also play a vital role in water supply. The porous structure of the ridges acts as a natural reservoir, filtering and storing high-quality groundwater that serves as a clean and sustainable source of drinking water for the region. Another key geosite of international value is Pirunkirkko, or the “Devil’s Church.” This steep, smooth cliff was shaped by ice movement along a fracture in the 1,632–1,643 million-year-old Ahvenisto rapakivi granite pluton. The term rapakivi was first introduced by Finnish geologist J.J. Sederholm in 1891, and today designates a granite type known internationally. The Pirunkirkko cliff, 40 metres wide, sits in the Paistjärvi nature reserve in Heinola and can be reached via a four-kilometre hiking trail.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Salpausselkä UNESCO Global Geopark is home to a rich cultural heritage that is closely tied to its geological features. The area includes numerous Iron Age settlements, providing valuable insight into past human activity. Stories and legends tied to geological landmarks are also part of the region’s cultural fabric. In Hollola, a local legend tells of two giants, Martta and Jalle, whose tale of love and heartbreak is linked to the construction of the medieval church. This legend lives on in the Hollo & Martta International Folklore Festival, an annual celebration of folk music and dance that keeps local traditions alive. Local identity is strongly influenced by natural features, as seen in the region’s coat of arms, which features Vellamo—a mythological water spirit—symbolising the lakes and winding ridges of Salpausselkä. The provincial song, The Land of the Green Ridges, celebrates the same geological landmarks in both name and lyrics. Pure water, a defining feature of the geopark, plays a vital role in preserving traditional practices such as sahti brewing. Sahti, a traditional Finnish beer, is considered one of the oldest surviving beer traditions in Europe and represents a living expression of intangible heritage tied to the landscape and its resources.

Titre EN: Muskauer Faltenbogen / Łuk Mużakowa UNESCO Global Geopark
Introduction EN: Ride the Waldeisenbahn Muskau, a historic narrow-gauge railway that winds through forests and villages, offering scenic journeys and seasonal events.Explore Babina Grube, a former lignite mine transformed into a nature reserve and geosite showcasing the area’s geology and post-mining ecology.Visit Teufelsstein, a glacial boulder linked to local legend, said to have been hurled by the devil at the church in Bad Muskau.
Description: Muskauer Faltenbogen / Łuk Mużakowa UNESCO Global Geopark is a transnational German-Polish territory located between Berlin, Dresden and Zielona Góra. Its central geological feature is the Muskau Arch, one of Europe’s most striking push moraines, formed during the oldest of the three European ice ages approximately 340,000 years ago. The advancing glacier compressed the subsoil to depths of around 300 metres and deformed horizontal layers of sand, gravel, clay and lignite from the Tertiary period. These unconsolidated deposits were pushed upwards to form a terminal moraine rising up to 150 metres above the surrounding terrain. During the most recent ice age, meltwater reshaped the landscape further, carving a valley 30 metres deep with meanders and terraces. The geopark also contains features such as dunes, cold iron-sulphate-mineral springs, and visible lignite deposits that reflect its glacial and post-glacial history.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Muskauer Faltenbogen / Łuk Mużakowa UNESCO Global Geopark celebrates cooperation and the rich local identity of the border territory between Germany and Poland. The historical glass industry dates back to the 16th century, when the first glassworks were established using local sand and wood resources. It flourished in the 18th and 19th centuries, producing a wide range of glassware including bottles, jars, glasses and vases. These products were traded beyond the region and contributed to the artistic and craft traditions that continue to shape the cultural identity of the area.
