Lignite mining is another key element of the geopark’s cultural heritage, reflecting both the economic development of the region and its impact on the landscape. In the 19th and 20th centuries, mining operations exploited rich brown coal deposits formed during the Tertiary period. Former mining areas have since been transformed into nature reserves, scenic lakes, and interpretive sites, linking geological heritage with community revitalisation and ecological restoration. Rich cultural practices include the preservation and celebration of the Sorbian language, folk music, dances, and Easter egg painting. Local cuisine and traditional products also reflect the culinary heritage of the region, including Muskauer butter cake, Lusatian fish soup, smoked eel, local honey and jams, and herbal teas.
Quote: “A landscape shaped by warm and cold climates”

Introduction EN: Explore over 300 million years of geological history, with exceptional fossil records ranging from giant Carboniferous insects to ammonites, reptiles, and dinosaur footprints.Hike the expansive woodlands of the Teutoburg and Wiehen Hills, shaped by tectonics, glaciation, and centuries of cultural interaction with the land.Visit the Varus Museum at Kalkriese, near the site of the Battle of the Teutoburg Forest (9 AD), where Germanic tribes halted Roman expansion—an iconic moment linking natural and human history.
Description: Located in northwestern Germany, the TERRA.vita UNESCO Global Geopark spans the wooded Teutoburg Forest, the Wiehen Hills, and the glacially shaped Ankum Heights. The geopark’s geological story begins in the Carboniferous Period, over 320 million years ago, when the region was part of extensive tropical wetlands. These swamp ecosystems later formed coal and shale beds that were mined for anthracite until the late 19th century. Exceptional plant fossils, giant arthropods, and early flying insects from this period are preserved at the Piesberg Cultural and Environmental Park, the Museum for Industrial Culture, and the museum at Schölerberg. The region continued to record changing environments through time. In the early Permian, around 290 million years ago, it became a restricted lagoon where early reptiles were preserved with rare anatomical detail, including scales and stomach contents. During the Jurassic Period, shallow coastal plains were frequented by dinosaurs. Today, visitors can explore the Dinosaur Track Site at Bad Essen-Barkhausen, an abandoned quarry containing more than 130 fossilised footprints of long-necked sauropods. In the Cretaceous, approximately 50 million years later, the area was submerged under a tropical sea, home to large ammonites. These fossils can be seen in the Heimathaus Borgholzhausen and the Natural History Museum in Bielefeld. The limestone deposits from this period remain visible along the southern slopes of the Teutoburg Forest, offering further insight into the dynamic geological history of the geopark.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The TERRA.vita UNESCO Global Geopark highlights the long-standing interaction between people and landscape. It is home to around 50 megalithic tombs dating back over 5,000 years and numerous burial mounds from the Iron Age, offering valuable insight into northern European prehistory. These archaeological remains include the Karlsteine, a rare megalithic tomb built from local quartzite, and are part of international initiatives such as the Megalithic Routes network. At Kalkriese, the site of the Battle of the Teutoburg Forest in 9 AD, visitors can explore Roman history at the Varus Museum, including the discovery of the only complete Roman segmented armour ever found. Cross-border heritage collaboration is also present in the 326-kilometre Hünenweg trail, developed jointly with De Hondsrug UNESCO Global Geopark in the Netherlands, following a myth-laden route once thought to be created by giants. The region’s agricultural landscape is marked by Plaggen soils, formed through centuries of sod farming. Practised from the 12th to 20th centuries, this method of transporting fertilised turf created distinctive terraced farmland, which today remains ecologically and historically significant. TERRA.vita has raised awareness of this cultural legacy by opening a dedicated Plaggen Soil Information Centre in 2022. TERRA.vita also documents and promotes living traditions. The geopark’s intangible heritage includes practices such as indigo dyeing (Blaudruck), falconry, organ craftsmanship, and the Swabian-Alemannic carnival. Local craftspeople, artists, and associations are featured through profiles and videos on the geopark’s website, supported by an interactive cultural map.
Quote: “The rocks of TERRA.vita tell magnificent stories”

Titre EN: Cabo de Gata-Níjar UNESCO Global Geopark
Introduction EN: Playa de los Muertos, Playa de Monsul, and Playa de los Genoveses are just a few of the many beaches that attract visitors with their crystal-clear waters and picturesque surroundings.La Isleta del Moro is a volcanic formation that rises from the sea, offering panoramic views of the surroundings.The region is fertile with charming coastal villages, such as San José and Las Negras.
Description: Sitting near the boundary between the European and African tectonic plates, Cabo de Gata-Níjar UNESCO Global Geopark is one of the few sub-desert areas in Europe and was the first maritime and terrestrial Protected Area in Andalusia. The exceptional weathering conditions and sub-desert dwarf vegetation allow visitors to appreciate geological features such as domes, lava flows, columnar jointing, alluvial fans, coastal cliffs, dykes, and fossilised reef structures. The geopark encompasses two distinct geological units: the Sierra de Cabo de Gata and the Bay of Almería, each shaped by different geological processes. The Cabo de Gata Volcanic Complex is part of a larger submerged area beneath the Alboran Sea, which formed 13–14 million years ago. Magma ascended through the crust, creating numerous submarine volcanic structures, influenced by the Carboneras Fault, a major tectonic fault resulting from the collision between the African and European plates. Over time, an archipelago of islands, volcanic domes, and coral reefs developed in a subtropical climate, leaving behind fossil reefs, dunes, and volcanic deposits that provide evidence of past Mediterranean climate changes. The Bay of Almería preserves a geological record spanning 200,000 years, offering valuable insights into environmental history and the ongoing processes that continue to shape the landscape today. The geopark hosts diverse ecosystems, with salt flats playing a key role as habitats for waders, ducks, herons, flamingos, and gulls. These wetlands are not only home to resident bird species but also serve as important migratory stopovers for birds travelling between northern Europe and Africa. Along river margins, species such as the Little Plover (Charadrius dubius), Cetti’s warbler (Cettia cetti), and reed warbler (Acrocephalus scirpaceus) nest among the vegetation. Amphibians and reptiles, including the viperine snake (Natrix maura) and the Caspian turtle (Mauremys caspica), also depend on these wetlands, making them crucial watering holes for the region’s vertebrate wildlife.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Cabo de Gata-Níjar UNESCO Global Geopark has a long history of human settlement shaped by its arid climate and coastal environment. The region has preserved a rich cultural heritage through traditional practices such as dry-stone wall construction, recognised by UNESCO as intangible heritage in 2019. These walls have played a crucial role in preventing landslides, creating agricultural terraces, and maximising the use of limited rainfall. Due to the scarcity of fertile soil, ancient settlers devised systems of windmills, water wheels, wells, and cisterns for the extraction and storage of water. These structures, along with coastal defence towers and medieval mining settlements, are key features in the cultural landscape of the geopark. Artisanal fishing remains a significant economic activity in the geopark, with fishermen’s associations such as Pescartes working to preserve traditional knowledge. This practice is largely concentrated in the villages of San Miguel de Cabo de Gata and La Isleta del Moro, where small-scale fisheries continue to operate within the protected marine area. Agriculture has also shaped the landscape, with traditional cortijos (farmhouses) and auxiliary structures such as stables, haystacks, and irrigation systems reflecting centuries of adaptation to the environment. Although many are now abandoned, they remain important cultural testimonies to the region’s agro-silvo-pastoral traditions. The geopark actively promotes sustainable tourism and geotourism initiatives, such as guided tours of historical sites, including the Valley of Prehistory project, which explores the evolution of human settlement in the area over the past 200,000 years. Research and conservation projects, such as the protection of archaeological sites like the Roman salting factory at Torregarcía Beach, further integrate cultural heritage into geopark activities.
Quote: “One of the best territories to under-stand recent climate change processes in Europe”

Introduction EN: The geopark is on the Camino de Santiago route, on the way to Santiago de Compostela.Several important archaeological sites, including the Castros de Viladonga, a fortified settlement that dates to the Iron Age, are well worth a visit.
Description: The Courel Mountains, in the quiet northwest corner of Spain, are home to tranquil forests and Galician communities living among the remains of medieval villages. This mountain range, part of the Iberian Massif, is characterised by high peaks and deep river valleys. The geopark includes several notable geosites, such as the Ferreira de Pantón Geological Interpretation Centre, which introduces visitors to the region’s geology; the Cova do Rei Cintolo, a cave system containing some of the oldest rock formations in Galicia; and the Fervenza do Belesar, a prominent waterfall. For researchers and geo-tourists, the mountains provide an ideal setting to observe Earth’s geological history, particularly from the Lower and Middle Palaeozoic era, and to a lesser extent, from the end of the Tertiary and the Quaternary periods. The region is shaped by its rivers which have carved deep valleys and canyons through ongoing erosion. Some of the highest summits in the area also display clear evidence of glacial modelling. The area is rich in vegetation, including a variety of oak, beech, yew, alder, and chestnut trees. Ecologically, it is one of the most diverse regions of the northwest Iberian Peninsula.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The Courel Mountains UNESCO Global Geopark, in Galicia, nested in one of the mountain ranges of the Iberian Massif, bears witness to one of the greatest endeavours of European history, the expansion of the Roman Empire. This territory was once so rich in gold that between the 1st and 2nd centuries AD the Roman Empire had more than one hundred mining sites, a wealth due to the ancient Paleozoic (541–252 million years ago) rocks which the rivers Lor, Louzara, Quiroga, Soldón and Selmo carved into deep valleys and canyons. The geopark is home to a rich cultural heritage that continues to shape the identity of local communities. Many villages retain their traditional architecture, with fine-grained slate—quarried locally since the Neolithic period—used extensively for roofing and construction. The art of dry-stone walling, recognised as intangible cultural heritage by UNESCO, remains a significant feature of the built landscape. Despite ongoing depopulation, the region preserves unique traditions and practices. The local language, Galician, is widely spoken and used in place names, publications, and signage, reinforcing cultural identity. Historic settlements include pre-Roman and Roman castros, as well as ancient villages with distinctive thatched-roof pallozas. Geotourism has become an important means of promoting the region’s geoheritage, biodiversity, and cultural legacy. The geopark works with local geotourism companies to offer hiking routes, visits to ethnographic sites, and guided tours of Roman hillforts and gold mines. The Palaeozoic Village Route highlights traditional dry-stone architecture, connecting geological and cultural heritage. Local product exhibitions and wine tourism initiatives, such as those by Atrium Vitis, showcase the connection between the region’s geodiversity and agricultural practices. With a growing network of interpretive centres and hiking trails, the Courel Mountains UNESCO Global Geopark continues to support sustainable tourism, helping local communities preserve their heritage while fostering economic opportunities.
Quote: “Courel Mountains, a Very Human Geology”

Introduction EN: Explore Mur Castle, a medieval fortress set atop a nearly 900-metre hill, offering panoramic views and rich history, from knightly legends to ancient frescoes.Visit Gerri de la Sal, one of the few places in Catalonia where salt is produced without seawater. Learn how this is possible and discover its historic salt warehouse turned museum.Traverse the Mont-rebei Gorge, Catalonia’s most impressive gorge, with 500-metre limestone cliffs, a river route, and a dramatic rock-carved hiking trail.
Description: Orígens UNESCO Global Geopark is located in the northeast of Spain, on the southern slopes of the Catalan Pyrenees in Catalonia, 200 km from Barcelona. Discover a territory where the last dinosaurs of Europe once roamed. The landscape is defined by east–west-oriented mountain ranges and basins, containing a geological record spanning 550 million years. Fossils of vertebrates, invertebrates, and plants provide insights into the evolution of life in this area, with the geopark featuring the oldest rocks in the Axial Pyrenean zone and preserving Upper Cretaceous outcrops with dinosaur remains. Renowned as a natural laboratory for palaeontology and tectonics, it also boasts significant natural and cultural heritage, including astronomy and archaeological sites. The geopark is home to several internationally significant geological sites, including the Collegats and Mont-rebei Gorges, which reveal the formation of the Pyrenees, and the Abella Anticline Global Geosite. The Ilerdian Stratotype, one of the best-known marine stages in Europe, and the Eocene intertidal deposits in La Baronia provide further insight into the region’s geological history. The Paleogene mammal fossil record at the Claret and Fontllonga geosites adds to the wealth of palaeontological heritage. Conservation of these sites is a priority; signage at key locations ensures that geologists understand the restrictions on sample collection and directs them to contact the geopark’s scientific team for further research collaboration.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Orígens UNESCO Global Geopark actively integrates cultural heritage, traditional practices, and local enterprises into its development strategies. The geopark promotes its rich cultural heritage, which spans from prehistoric cave paintings to modern hydroelectric power stations, through guided tours, interpretative panels, and partnerships with local stakeholders. Two sites—Balma de les Ovelles and La Cova del Tabac—are designated as World Heritage sites for their prehistoric rock art, with access now limited to guided visits to ensure preservation. The economy of this rural area is primarily based on the service sector, though agriculture and livestock farming remain important, accounting for over 10% of employment. The region is known for the planting of vines under the "Costers del Segre" Designation of Origin, and for efforts to recover ancient local breeds such as the Xisqueta sheep. Various initiatives related to sustainable rural development have been implemented for over a decade, including projects that integrate agriculture with sustainable tourism. Educational programmes engage both residents and visitors, ensuring knowledge transfer and community participation. Programmes such as Investigadeu bring research into schools, while initiatives like What is the Geopark? introduce children to geological and cultural heritage through interactive activities, including escape rooms. Geotourism is a key component of the geopark’s sustainable economic development plan. Since 2019, a partnership strategy has been in place to develop geotourism products, train guides, and promote local businesses through programmes such as "Enjoy the Geopark" and the Lleida wine route. These initiatives help strengthen the connection between geological heritage and local enterprises, fostering economic resilience in the region.
Quote: “Discover the origins of this territory where the last dinosaurs of Europe lived”

Introduction EN: The Estación Paleontológica del Valle del Río Fardes is a significant hub for the study and preservation of fossil remains, providing valuable insights into the ancient flora and fauna that once thrived in the region.The Sismitas de Galera are distinctive sedimentary structures formed by seismic activity, offering a glimpse into the powerful forces that have shaped the Earth's crust over millions of years.
Description: Located in the heart of the largest and most extensive steppe plateau in Andalusia, Granada UNESCO Global Geopark represents one of the most ancient elements of the Iberian Peninsula’s landscape, offering a treasure trove of information for researchers studying the Mediterranean basin and its evolutionary processes. The geopark’s landscape has been shaped by the formation of valleys through river erosion over the last half million years, creating a striking geomorphological setting. Between approximately 5 million and 0.5 million years ago, this region lacked an outlet to the sea, leading to the accumulation of Quaternary continental sediments, which hold exceptional palaeontological deposits of vertebrates, including over 150 identified sites from the Early Pleistocene. Mesozoic and Tertiary geological history is also visible in the geopark, showcasing key evolutionary processes of the Iberian Peninsula. Active faults within the region highlight more recent geological deformations of the Betic Range, including the presence of seismites—rare sedimentary structures formed by ancient earthquakes—which are among the best examples known worldwide. One of the notable geosites within the Granada Geopark is the Badlands de Gorafe, particularly the Don Diego Viewpoint. This geosite offers a panoramic view of unique geological formations sculpted by erosion, creating a visually stunning landscape of rugged and intricate patterns.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The geopark is a strong example of the relationship between people and their culture, landscape, and geology. A unique element is the development of original dwellings dug out of the earth, inhabited for centuries. Cave-house architecture has been continuously used for generations. The gullied landscape, composed of soft clays and marls interspersed with limestone and cemented conglomerates, enabled communities to excavate cave dwellings into the valley slopes. These bioclimatic homes maintain a stable temperature year-round, making them a sustainable and resilient form of housing. Today, they contribute to a cave-dwelling landscape of international significance. Traditional trades remain an essential part of local identity. Craftsmanship, closely tied to the region’s geological resources, has been preserved in towns like Guadix and Purullena, where ceramic production is linked to the area's high-quality clay deposits. The craft of esparto grass weaving, once a major industry, is showcased in ecomuseums such as those in Castilléjar and Puebla de Don Fadrique, where visitors can learn about historical trades. The food culture of the geopark is another key aspect of local life. Interpretation centres, such as Trópolis in Valle del Zalabí, hold craft workshops where visitors can participate in cheese-making in caves and bread-making traditions. Local gastronomy highlights Segureño lamb, cold meats, olive oil, and regional wines, reinforcing the connection between food production and the territory’s natural resources.

Titre EN: Lanzarote and Chinijo Islands UNESCO Global Geopark
Introduction EN: Discover stunning beaches such as Playa Blanca and Papagayo, with their pristine sands and crystal-clear waters.Visit the Jameos del Agua, a breathtaking underground cave system transformed into an artistic and cultural space by renowned architect César Manrique.Explore the vibrant town of Teguise, known for its historic charm and Sunday market, where visitors can enjoy local cuisine featuring fresh seafood and traditional Canarian dishes.
Description: Located in the northeast of the Canary Islands and separated by a strip of sea about 100 km from the northwest edge of the African continent, the island of Lanzarote is known as the Island of Volcanoes. Its barren, dark land lends it an aura of science fiction. The island has a morphology with a large central oval and two appendices (north and south), which are called Famara and Los Ajaches, respectively. The Chinijo Archipelago (meaning "small" in reference to its mini-archipelago status) is located north of Lanzarote and comprises La Graciosa (separated by the shallow Río Strait and the only inhabited island), Montaña Clara, Roque del Infierno or del Oeste, Alegranza, and Roque del Este. This archipelago constitutes the largest marine reserve in the European Union, spanning 700 km². The islands emerged approximately 15 million years ago, and since then, there have been periods of eruptions accompanied by erosive stages, culminating in a remarkable landscape teeming with striking contrasts. Among the nearly seventy geosites, the most significant is Timanfaya, home to numerous volcanic structures and one of the largest historic lava fields in the world. This geological wonder was formed during the volcanic eruption that occurred between 1730 and 1736, which lasted for six years. Characterised by fissural and basaltic activity, the eruption not only left a lasting impact on the island's landscape but also contributed to its growth, expanding it by a quarter. Another prominent geosite within the Lanzarote UNESCO Global Geopark is the La Corona Lava Tube, a 7.6 km structure featuring various access points known as "jameos." Unlike other lava tubes around the world, La Corona’s last 1.6 kilometres are submerged, making it the longest submerged volcanic tube on the planet. Exploring this unique geological formation provides visitors with a glimpse into the island's volcanic past and showcases the forces of nature that have shaped the landscape over time. Lanzarote and Chinijo Islands UNESCO Global Geopark is not limited to the island of Lanzarote alone. It encompasses the neighbouring islets and the abrasion platform surrounding them, creating a comprehensive geological showcase. The inclusion of the entire archipelago provides continuity and extends the geodiversity of the geopark, offering visitors a complete understanding of the region’s geological features.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Spanning the entire island of Lanzarote, as well as the neighbouring islets La Graciosa, Montaña Clara, Roque del Este, Roque del Oeste, and Alegranza, collectively known as the "Chinijo Island," Lanzarote and Chinijo Islands UNESCO Global Geopark is a remarkable destination that showcases the geological wonders of the Canary Islands. The geopark reflects a deep connection between its geological landscape and the cultural identity of its communities. Agriculture in the geopark has adapted to extreme environmental conditions, with jable and lapilli farming serving as key traditional dry cultivation methods. These techniques allow farmers to retain soil moisture and prevent erosion, making efficient use of the island’s porous volcanic soils. The geopark promotes the preservation and transmission of this agricultural knowledge through guided interpretation routes led by experts. Additionally, two documentary films have been produced to honour the wisdom of elders who have sustained these practices for generations, with public screenings followed by debates to encourage community engagement. Salt production has long been a fundamental part of the local economy and continues to be a significant cultural practice. The Salinas Bajo el Risco, the oldest saltworks in the Canary Islands, played a critical role in food preservation and trade. However, storms and neglect led to their deterioration. The geopark is actively working on a rehabilitation project to restore these salt flats, ensuring their cultural and economic relevance for future generations.
Quote: “Lanzarote is pure geology, underwater and moon-like landscapes, pristine water, thirsty land, palm-tree oasis, harmony between men and nature.”

Introduction EN: Throughout the geopark, faults and folds leave their mark, appearing in various geosites such as Cancho de las Narices and Apreturas del Almonte, inviting exploration and contemplation.The Constanza Mine stands as a poignant reminder of the geopark's industrial past, once serving as a significant phosphorite mine in Logrosán, now bearing testament to the rich history of human endeavours.
Description: In the southeastern province of Cáceres, the Villuercas Ibores Jara UNESCO Global Geopark spans an area of 2,544 square kilometres, nestled between the basins of the Tajo and Guadiana rivers. At its highest point stands the Risco de La Villuerca, reaching 1,601 metres. From this vantage point, visitors can view mountain ranges, valleys, undulating plains known as rañas, and the town of Guadalupe, home to the Royal Monastery—a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The Villuercas Ibores Jara UNESCO Global Geopark’s geological record spans from the Ediacaran (635 million years ago) to the Silurian (443–419 million years ago), with Neogene and Quaternary deposits marking the more recent chapters. Situated within the fluvial network and Appalachian landscapes of the Iberian Massif, the geopark contains remnants of ancient Ediacaran deposits, characterised by shales and greywackes imprinted with primitive fossils. Most of the geopark’s strata, however, originates from the Ordovician period (485–443 million years ago), preserving structures formed during the Variscan orogeny. Among these features, the Crag of La Villuerca is both a geological itinerary and a geosite, offering panoramic views of the characteristic Appalachian relief. It is a site of geological, palaeontological, educational, and touristic value, providing insight into the formation of the supercontinent Pangea. The Cave of Castañar de Ibor, though small in size, contains an exceptional diversity of speleothems. Visits are by reservation only to ensure conservation. Cabañas Castle, another notable site within the geopark, reveals the striking Armorican Quartzite outcrop and offers a view over the Santa Lucía syncline. It reflects the region’s geological heritage and is of significant scientific interest.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: At the heart of the geopark's cultural heritage is the Royal Monastery of Saint Mary of Guadalupe, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1983. The monastery, in excellent restored condition, remains a major religious and cultural landmark, attracting visitors and playing a key role in the valorisation of historical pilgrimage routes within the geopark. Cultural sites are incorporated into hiking routes, bringing visibility to locations such as the historical Logrosán Phosphorite Mine and Berzocana’s Chalcolithic shelters with rock paintings. The geopark also protects intangible heritage, which includes legends, traditional music, folk dance, and historical celebrations deeply rooted in local culture. One of the most significant traditions is the Folk Dances of Villuercas-Ibores-Jara, which have been performed for generations and remain a key element of local festivals and celebrations. Additionally, the geopark safeguards oral traditions and legends, such as the stories of Silvan and Roldán, mythical characters tied to the geological landscape and history of the region. Sustainable tourism plays a key role in supporting local businesses and raising awareness of geological and cultural heritage. The Visitor Centre in Cañamero serves as a hub for tourism, while additional thematic centres, such as the historic Cañamero Phosphorite Mine, the Fossil Interpretative Route in Navaterrina, and the Carnaval of Souls Interpretative Centre in Villar del Pedroso, enrich visitor experiences by integrating scientific knowledge with cultural storytelling. A recent project in the geopark has restored the access road leading to Villuercas Peak, the highest point in the geopark at 1,601 metres. Recognising its significance for geotourism and geological heritage, the initiative improved the 11 km ascent, creating scenic viewpoints and interpretive stops along the route. Visitors can now explore key geological highlights, including Vendotaenid fossils from the Ediacaran period, the Rheic Ocean Outcrop, and the Appalachian Viewpoint, a prime location for understanding the geopark’s geomorphology. Since its reopening, Villuercas Peak has become the most visited site in the geopark, with geotourism companies offering guided tours that enhance public appreciation of its exceptional geological heritage.
Quote: “Landscapes that treasure a memory of hundreds of millions of years”

Introduction EN: The Puumala Art Path combines art and geology with eight checkpoints that reveal the geological stories behind landscape paintings.The Saimaa Geopark Visitor Centre, located in Imatra’s Culturehouse Virta, offers extensive information on the geology and developmental history of the Saimaa region.
Description: Saimaa UNESCO Global Geopark preserves nearly two billion years of Earth’s history. The region’s bedrock formed around 1.9 billion years ago, when granites and other igneous rocks crystallised deep within the Earth’s crust. These ancient rapakivi granites, now exposed on the shores and at the bottom of Lake Saimaa, reflect the area’s long geological evolution. The most recent and visible geological transformations took place during the last Ice Age. As glaciers advanced and retreated, they carved out a complex basin that now holds Lake Saimaa and its surrounding water systems. One of the most striking glacial formations is the Salpausselkä ridge system—a vast terminal moraine formed between 12,000 and 10,400 years ago. Stretching nearly 500 kilometres and reaching up to 80 metres in height, the ridges helped shape the region’s lake system by trapping meltwater, creating the distinctive waterlogged landscape seen today. Lake Saimaa is the dominant natural feature of the geopark. Covering approximately 1,377 square kilometres, it is the fourth largest natural freshwater lake in Europe and one of the largest in the world. The lake’s labyrinthine basin contains 13,710 islands and more shoreline per square kilometre than anywhere else in the world—about 14,500 kilometres in total. In some areas, the lake is so clean that locals still drink directly from its waters. Where the lake gives way to land, it is bordered by pristine taiga forest, home to pine, spruce and larch trees that display brilliant colours during ruska, the vibrant autumn transition. The Saimaa ringed seal, one of the few freshwater seals in the world, lives in these waters. Isolated since the last glacial period, the species has evolved into a distinct subspecies. With only around 430 seals remaining, it is one of the most endangered seals globally and the focus of national conservation efforts.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The shores of Lake Saimaa have attracted human settlement for thousands of years. One of the most remarkable archaeological sites in the region is Astuvansalmi, where 65 rock paintings depicting human and animal figures, handprints, and hunting scenes date back to 3000–2500 BC. This is the largest known collection of rock paintings in Northern Europe and offers insight into the early interaction between people and their environment. Intangible heritage is present in the region’s music, dance, handicrafts, and food traditions. There are notable cultural differences between the Savonian north and Karelian south of the geopark, visible in dialect, cuisine, and customs. Both Savonian and Karelian dialects and traditions are recognised and valued by local communities. Lake Saimaa itself has played a central role in shaping local traditions. The Nordic clinker boat building tradition, recognised on the UNESCO List of Intangible Cultural Heritage, is one example of Saimaa’s importance as a waterway over millennia. Finland’s sauna culture—also listed as Intangible Cultural Heritage—remain widely practiced, with tens of thousands of saunas still in use along the lake’s shores.

Introduction EN: Explore the “Tour des Pierres Dorées,” a major hiking route across the Beaujolais UNESCO Global Geopark, with 12 marked circuits leading to key geosites.Experience the release of “Beaujolais nouveau,” a vin de primeur sold the same year it is harvested. Celebrated on the third Thursday of November, it is marked by festivals across the country and globally.
Description: Beaujolais UNESCO Global Geopark is located in the Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes region in southeastern France. The Beaujolais is renowned worldwide for its wines and the territory benefits from an exceptional geological diversity that has been shaped over nearly 500 million years. Three types of topographical relief characterise the region: the Saône River plain at the eastern border, the gentle slopes where vines grow, interrupted by wood-covered valleys, and the mountains of Beaujolais extending throughout the west and reaching heights of over 1,000 meters at the regions borders. Located on the eastern edge of the Massif Central and in direct view of the Alps, the geopark enjoys a privileged geographical location in the heart of Europe and has a rich and complex geology. The igneous crystalline and metamorphic basement offers a comprehensive history of the evolution of the Hercynian orogenic belt, a series of mountain ranges developed during the Late Paleozoic era (350 to 290 million years ago) as a result of the collision between the supercontinents Gondwana and Euramerica. This period of the geological history of the Beaujolais is a remarkable testament of the geological processes that took place in the deep roots of the high mountain chain, which is of key importance to global paleogeographic history. The secondary sedimentary series cover a timespan of nearly 80 million years. Benefiting from a wide range of geological formations, the Beaujolais region has been the subject of numerous scientific studies, having addressed all major scientific topics of both fundamental and applied geology. The physical geography has led to the establishment of specific natural environments, such as moors, pastures and woods on acid or calcareous soils, bogs, altitude wetlands and peri-fluvial grasslands that are inhabited by a number of unique flora and fauna species.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The Beaujolais UNESCO Global Geopark is deeply shaped by its natural resources and cultural heritage, which continue to support local livelihoods and identity. The region’s plains and small valleys are well-suited to agriculture, most notably the production of Beaujolais wine. This wine, made for centuries from a single grape variety—Gamay—is closely tied to the region’s distinctive geological soils and remains central to its economy and international reputation. Mining also played a historical role in local development. At Chessy-les-Mines, copper was extracted from the Middle Ages until 1875. The site became internationally recognised for its azurite, known locally as “chessylite.” This deep-blue copper mineral is the type locality for azurite, where the mineral was first scientifically described. The region’s architecture and built heritage reflect its geology. Local stone varieties, shaped over hundreds of millions of years, were used in the construction of castles, churches, and traditional villages. These “villages of character” highlight the integration of natural and cultural heritage, while sites such as Mont Brouilly provide panoramic views and a sustainable setting to explore the region’s geology, history, and viticulture. Today, the geopark promotes ecotourism based on its landscapes, geology, and regional products. From forest paths to vineyard trails, the territory invites visitors to explore a region where local traditions, natural beauty, and geological heritage are closely intertwined. One of the most distinctive cultural traditions in the geopark is the annual celebration of “les conscrits.” Originating during the Second Empire, the tradition has evolved into a local commemoration of past military service. Each year, residents born in years ending in the same digit as the current year organise festivities that include parades, banquets, and church services.
Quote: “An identity sprung from the rocks that shape the natural and human landscape”

Introduction EN: The ancient Roman ruins of Oppède-le-Vieux and the medieval fortress of Buoux provide a glimpse into the region’s rich past.The Abbaye de Sénanque, a serene Cistercian monastery surrounded by lavender fields, offers a tranquil and spiritual retreat.The hilltop village of Bonnieux offers panoramic views of the surrounding countryside, while the village of Lourmarin captivates visitors with its Renaissance castle and vibrant arts scene.
Description: Southeast France’s Provence region is known for its diverse landscapes, from the Southern Alps to the Camargue plains. Among rolling vineyards, olive groves and lavender fields, the Luberon UNESCO Global Geopark showcases the geodiversity of the area. The geopark is renowned for its fossiliferous deposits from the Oligocene period (33.9 to 23 million years ago), offering well-preserved animal and plant fossils. Thin platy limestone layers act as a window to the past, preserving species such as fish, leaves, insects, frogs, birds and tortoises. Other sites feature fossil bones of primitive mammals and footprints of rhinoceros, hyenas, goats, and birds, providing valuable insights into the region’s ancient biodiversity. The protected Ochre Massif stands out for its cliffs and gullies in hues ranging from dark red to golden yellow. The grey marl hills near Apt present another unusual geological formation, marking the stratotype of the Aptian stage, dated to 120 million years ago. Scientific studies and excavations are regularly carried out in the geopark in partnership with universities.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The exploitation of mineral resources (ochres, lignites, clays and limestones) has deeply marked the region and is attested by the presence of quarries and factories. The natural landscape, local architecture and human activities have shaped a strong regional culture and identity as can be seen in the dry-stone huts known as ‘bories’ and walls which are so typical of the park. Artisanal craftsmanship is present throughout the area in the form of ceramics, stained glass and wood turning.  There is a wide range of cultural events to be enjoyed throughout the year, in particular, music festivals such as the Festival Durance Luberon and the Luberon Jazz Festival, as well as fairs organised around local products including figs, almonds, wine, cherries, lavender, olive oil and truffles.
Quote: “Footprints and fossil bones of primitive mammals are an important part of Luberon’s geoheritage”

Introduction EN: Visit Antraigues-sur-Volane, a hilltop village in the Monts d’Ardèche, known for its artistic heritage and as the former home of renowned singer Jean Ferrat.Thueyts, in the Ardèche valley, offers a glimpse into the past with its mediaeval castle, stone houses, and volcanic landscapes.Follow the Partage des eaux trail, a 100 km open-air art route where artists, designers and landscape architects have created poetic works along the watershed divide between the Atlantic and the Mediterranean.
Description: The Monts d’Ardèche UNESCO Global Geopark lies on the south-eastern edge of France’s Massif Central, covering over 2,200 km² of medium-high mountains. Its landscapes range from chestnut-covered slopes to Mediterranean hillsides with vineyards and olive groves, shaped by a long geological history and diverse climatic influences. The geopark features a geological record spanning more than 500 million years and is marked by both ancient and recent volcanic activity. Volcanic formations in the region date from 6.6 million to just 47,000 years ago, forming a dense concentration of volcanic landforms rarely found elsewhere in Europe. Among the most striking are the volcanoes of Jaujac, Thueyts, and Aizac, as well as the overlapping Souilhol and Ray-Pic lava flows that stretch across 20 kilometres. Strombolian and phreatomagmatic eruptions have shaped the landscape into basalt columns, craters, and lava formations, some resembling organ pipes. These features—combined with fossil footprints, volcanic domes like the Suc de Mont Gerbier de Jonc, and dramatic gorges—reveal the intensity and variety of the region’s geological past.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: In the southern part of the geopark, near the Pont d’Arc, the Chauvet-Pont d’Arc cave stands as a key cultural landmark. Sealed for around 20,000 years until its discovery in 1994, the cave was designated a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2014. Dating back approximately 32,000 years, it contains over 1,000 remarkably preserved images of animals and human figures, including depictions of mammoths, bears, cave lions, and rhinos. With its vast gallery space, human footprints, and thousands of prehistoric remains, the site represents the earliest known large-scale artistic event in human history. Today, traditional agriculture is vital to the local economy and landscape. Centuries of adaptation are reflected in terraced fields, béalières (irrigation channels), and chestnut groves, the latter forming a cultural and economic emblem of the region. Since 2013, efforts have been underway to restore these groves. Pastoralism is supported through a Territorial Pastoral Plan that promotes collective land use and sustainable grazing. Agri-environmental and climate programmes have also helped over 160 farmers adopt practices that protect biodiversity, water quality, and ecological balance across 10,000 hectares. Organic farming is expanding steadily, reinforcing the connection between environmental stewardship and rural development.
Quote: “Wide open spaces, breathtaking panoramas, picturesque villages nestling at the foot of volcanic hills, gorges, rushing streams and torrents”

Introduction EN: Explore Holyhead’s geological trail from the Fish Dock to Breakwater Quarry, where ancient rocks meet historic stone-built structures across the town.Walk the 200 km Anglesey Coastal Footpath, giving access to 90% of the island’s geological highlights through varied landscapes and geotrails.Visit Porth Amlwch, a former copper shipping hub set in a fault-formed harbour, linked to the globally significant geology of Parys Mountain.
Description: Covering the entirety of the Isle of Anglesey in north-west Wales, GeoMôn UNESCO Global Geopark showcases over a billion years of Earth history. The island’s diverse geology includes rocks from four eras and twelve geological periods, creating an exceptional concentration of geological features within a compact area. The geopark’s coastal landscape reveals volcanic deposits from ancient plate boundaries, metamorphic rocks from deep subduction zones, and extensive glacial deposits from the last Ice Age. These varied formations have produced a striking coastline of sandy beaches, rocky coves, and dramatic cliffs. Anglesey is one of the few places in the world where rocks formed at every type of tectonic plate boundary can be observed. Of particular international significance are the Precambrian blueschists of southern Anglesey and the stromatolitic limestones of the north, which contain the oldest known fossils in England and Wales. Parys Mountain in the north of the island was once the world’s most important copper mine, and the complex folds and faults of South Stack offer clear evidence of Cambrian tectonic activity. With more than 100 rock types exposed in fault-bounded coastal slices, the island serves as a natural archive of environmental and climate change over geological time, offering unique insights into the processes that have shaped our planet.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The human landscape of GeoMôn is shaped by its underlying geology. Local building stones influence architectural styles, while soils determine patterns of farming and forestry. The island bears traces of long human occupation, with archaeological evidence showing settlement since the Mesolithic period around 7,000 years ago, copper mining in the Bronze Age, and later the construction of Beaumaris Castle, considered the best-designed Edwardian castle in Britain. The rocks that shape the land have also helped shape the culture and language of the island’s communities. Renowned local artist Sir Kyffin Williams R.A., a founding member of the geopark, and his great-uncle Sir Andrew Ramsay, known as the “father of Welsh geology,” are among many figures who have drawn inspiration from the landscape. Today, local artists, photographers, and craftspeople continue to thrive in this environment. Visitors to the geopark find a wealth of natural and cultural experiences. The 200 km Anglesey Coastal Footpath offers a journey around the entire island, linking geological sites with historical landmarks. The route includes Beaumaris Castle and the National Trust’s Plas Newydd, and provides access to sandy beaches, rocky headlands, and cliffs that support activities such as walking, bird watching, climbing, coasteering, kite surfing, and swimming. Geotrails along the coast and in towns like Beaumaris, guide visitors through the many rock types used in local architecture, from castles to churches and homes.
Quote: “200 km coastal path with GeoMôn's guidebook gives access to 90% of the island’s diverse geological highlights”

Titre EN: Mourne Gullion Strangford UNESCO Global Geopark
Introduction EN: Take a fishing trip on Strangford Lough, renowned for its salmon, sea trout, and pollock, or try your luck from the shore at one of many scenic spots throughout the geopark.Explore Murlough National Nature Reserve with 6,000-year-old sand dunes, over twenty-two species of butterflies, and boardwalks through wildflower-rich landscapes.Follow the Gullion Geological Trail around Slieve Gullion, where a 60-million-year-old volcanic ring dyke forms a unique geological feature of international scientific significance.
Description: Mourne Gullion Strangford UNESCO Global Geopark’s landscape records over 400 million years of geological history. The closing of the Iapetus Ocean and the later opening of the North Atlantic triggered extensive volcanic activity, with magma forming both beneath and on the Earth’s surface. These events created the varied rocks and geological structures seen across the region today. The land was further shaped during the last Ice Age, particularly between 27,000 and 23,000 years ago, when glaciers carved U-shaped valleys, transported rock, and left behind distinctive landforms such as drumlins. This glacial legacy is visible in features like Carlingford Lough and the drowned glacial landscape of Strangford Lough—the largest sea inlet in the British Isles. The geopark spans three upland areas: the Dromara Hills, the Mourne Mountains, and Slieve Gullion with its notable ring dyke. The highest peak is Slieve Donard, standing at 850 metres. Fertile glacial lowlands encircle the uplands, creating a compact region where mountainous, lowland, and coastal glacial features coexist.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The Mourne Gullion Strangford UNESCO Global Geopark reflects deep-rooted connections between people and landscape, shaped by more than 7,000 years of human presence. Since the Mesolithic period, communities have built Neolithic cairns, Iron Age hillforts, and participated in maritime and agricultural economies. The area is rich in mythology, including tales of Fionn Mac Cumhaill and Cúchulainn, and contains important early Christian sites such as St. Patrick’s first church. Glacially-enriched soils support widespread agriculture, while the granite mountains facilitated a long history of quarrying. Sheep farming remains common in the uplands. Coastal areas have supported fishing, seaweed harvesting, and trade, with Warrenpoint continuing as a working port. Today, agriculture, manufacturing, and public sector employment underpin the local economy. The geopark supports sustainable tourism through its scenic and cultural appeal, underpinned by strong transport links. Its range of habitats—from upland bogs to coastal wetlands—also makes it an important area for biodiversity and environmental stewardship.

Introduction EN: Ski down the slopes of the Chelmos mountains in winter, where snow-covered peaks and forested trails offer a spectacular alpine setting.Visit the extraordinary Cave of the Lakes near Kastria, of almost two kilometres in depth and 85m in height. Explore a remarkable underground world shaped by tectonic uplift and groundwater flow.Walk or take the historic Odontos Rack Railway through the Vouraikos Gorge, passing dramatic cliffs, tunnels and stone bridges.
Description: Connected to mainland Greece by the Isthmus of Corinth—a narrow strip of land named after the ancient Greek word for “neck”—the Peloponnese is a large peninsula in southern Greece with a deep geological history. Long before its renowned mythology and establishment of ancient cities such as Olympia, Sparta and Corinth, this region was shaped by powerful geological forces. The geological history of Chelmos-Vouraikos UNESCO Global Geopark begins 485 million years ago, in the Ordovician period, when the area’s limestones were deposited at the bottom of a warm, shallow sea. These layers were later uplifted during the Alpine Orogeny, as the African plate moved northward and collided with the Eurasian plate, giving rise to the mountains of the region. The Chelmos mountains today reach nearly 2,400 metres above sea level, a result of this prolonged tectonic activity. From the Chelmos mountains, the Vouraikos river descends to the Gulf of Corinth, carving through red conglomerates and limestone strata. The resulting Vouraikos Gorge is a striking example of fluvial and tectonic interaction. Among the most iconic geological features of the geopark is the Styx Waters, located within a 200-metre-deep gorge. Here, water percolates slowly through limestone, creating an active karst system.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The Chelmos Vouraikos UNESCO Global Geopark includes several protected sites of cultural and archaeological importance, such as the ancient city of Feneos, the archaeological site of Lousoi, and traditional buildings like that of the Petmezas family.  Mythological heritage is deeply rooted in the area, with sites such as the waters of Styx—linked to the underworld in ancient Greek mythology—and the Vouraikos River, named after the figure Voura, loved by Hercules. These stories are preserved and shared through initiatives and publications in the geopark.   The region’s intangible heritage is equally significant, with residents maintaining traditional practices in architecture, cuisine, and music. The cultivation of Corinthian raisins, officially recognised as part of Greece’s National Intangible Cultural Heritage, continues across the Achaea Prefecture, reflecting the enduring agricultural knowledge of the region.
Quote: “According to mythology, Achilles was invulnerable as, just born, his mother Thetis plunged him into the waters of the Styx. However, his ankle wasn’t exposed to water. There, later, Paris will find the opportunity to kill him with an arrow”

Introduction EN: Observe diverse bird species in the wetland habitats of Lesvos, including the unique wetland complex of the Kalloni Gulf, an important site for migratory and resident birds.Explore key cultural landmarks such as the medieval Castle of Mytilene, the ancient Roman Aqueduct of Moria, and the ancient theatre of Mytilene.Visit the Petrified Forest of Lesvos, where volcanic activity 20 million years ago preserved entire trees in life position—offering an exceptional glimpse into a Miocene ecosystem.
Description: Lesvos Island UNESCO Global Geopark covers the entirety of the island of Lesvos, located in the northeastern Aegean Sea. The island’s geological structure reflects a complex history, including metamorphic rocks, ophiolitic sequences, Miocene volcanic formations, and Neogene marine and lacustrine deposits. These formations have shaped a diverse landscape of caves, karst systems, fault-controlled landforms, waterfalls and coastal features. The Petrified Forest of Lesvos is one of the geopark’s most significant sites. Around 20 million years ago, intense volcanic activity buried a subtropical forest under ash and pyroclastic flows. Heavy rainfall triggered mudflows that preserved entire trees in life position, with trunks reaching up to 20 metres in length and root systems extending seven metres. Fossilised remains include not only trunks, but also branches, fruits, and leaves—offering an exceptional record of a Miocene ecosystem. Lesvos also holds important palaeontological findings, including the oldest known land mammal in Greece, Prodeinotherium bavaricum, dating to 19 million years ago. Across the island, volcanic craters, thermal springs, and tectonic features provide further evidence of its dynamic geological evolution.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The Lesvos Island UNESCO Global Geopark has a rich cultural heritage, reflected in the architecture and historical continuity of settlements across the island, from prehistoric sites to castles, monasteries, mosques, and traditional villages. Many buildings were constructed using local materials. These include watermills, olive presses, stone bridges, and farm structures, some of which are now repurposed as museums or visitor sites, forming part of the geopark’s tourism routes. Lesvos is known for its literary and artistic legacy as the birthplace of figures such as the poetess Sappho and the philosopher Theophrastus. Today, seasonal festivals celebrate the island’s rich intangible heritage—including music, dance and culinary practices. Agriculture remains central to the island’s economy, particularly olive oil production, livestock farming, and fishing. Distilleries also play a role, especially in the production of ouzo. The geopark collaborates closely with women’s agrotourism cooperatives, key partners in promoting local products and traditional food. The annual agrotourism festival supports these efforts and creates opportunities for small enterprises.
Quote: “The ancient trees of Lesvos were submerged in a sea of volcanic material in an eruption in the Northern Aegean 20 million years ago”

Introduction EN: Explore the erosion-sculpted formations of the Agioi Pantes gorge, where Miocene-era wind and water shaped yellow-white rocks rich in marine fossils such as bivalves and sea urchins.Experience the Sitia Singing Dance at local village festivals, where traditional music, lyricism, and movement reflect the region’s unique cultural heritage.Discover traces of Bronze Age port cities and sacred sites in eastern Crete, including urban centres like Palekastro and mountaintop shrines at Petsofas and Modi.
Description: Sitia UNESCO Global Geopark is located on the easternmost edge of Crete. It is predominantly mountainous, with the Zakros Mountains shaping the interior and a lace-like coastline defining the shoreline. The region is geologically significant for its extensive sedimentary formations and fossil-bearing deposits, offering insight into the island’s deep geological past. The geopark is particularly known for its abundant Pleistocene mammal fossil sites, including the discovery of three Deinotherium giganteum fossils—elephant-like creatures that once roamed the region. Along the coastal zone, remains of other large mammals such as deer, hippos, and elephants have also been found. Neogene sediments contain a rich record of marine fossils, while older strata preserve plant remnants dating back to the Carboniferous period. The landscape is marked by a well-developed karst system formed in the region’s limestone bedrock. More than 170 caves and numerous gorges have been documented, creating one of the most extensive speleological areas in Crete. These subterranean environments support scientific research in speleology, biospeleology, and related fields, making the geopark a valuable site for the study of karst processes and underground biodiversity. Palaeo-shorelines around the Zakros area further enrich the geological record, providing evidence of ancient sea levels and climatic changes over time.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Sitia UNESCO Global Geopark places strong emphasis on the interconnection between geological heritage and local identity. Intangible cultural heritage remains a living part of daily life, shaped by traditions passed down through generations. One of the most prominent expressions is the Erotokritos tradition—a poetic form rooted in Cretan literature—celebrated each year through the “Kornaria” cultural events. Local dances, particularly the Sitia Singing Dance, continue to be performed in village festivals, accompanied by traditional music and cuisine. These events strengthen community bonds and engage younger generations in the region’s cultural continuity. Traditional craftsmanship such as textiles, ceramics, and bell making is actively supported through cultural associations. Culinary practices, too, are closely tied to the local landscape, with olive oil playing a central role. Cultural heritage is also visible in the region’s archaeological sites, ranging from Neolithic dwellings to Minoan-era settlements and classical temples. These sites offer insight into the long-standing relationship between natural resources and human settlement, and several are connected to the geopark’s trail network. To support geotourism and education, the geopark has developed infrastructure including the Natural History Museum of Zakros and the Speleological Centre in Karydi. They serve as key platforms for engaging local communities and visitors in the values of sustainable development, heritage conservation and environmental education.
Quote: “The courses of humans and land, in eastern Crete, intertwine and complement each other.”

Introduction EN: Hike parts of the world-famous Epirus Trail that crosses from Mount Grammos to the Tzoumerka mountain range.Hike up Mount Tymphe to discover its stunning alpine lake, Drakolimni, or Dragon Lake. According to local legend, the lake's depression was formed during battles between dragons who hurled boulders at each other.Visit the Beloi Viewpoint for breathtaking views of the Vikos Gorge, recognised by the Guinness Book of Records as the world's deepest, relative to its width.
Description: Coinciding almost in its entirety with a national park of the same name, the Vikos–Aoos UNESCO Global Geopark is dominated by the high mountains of the Northern Pindos, including Mt. Smolikas, Mt. Tymphe, Mt. Trapezitsa and Mt. Nemertsika, among others. This range, an extension of the Dinaric Alps, is known colloquially as the ‘spine of Greece.’ The geopark is characterised by high rugged relief and a dramatic landscape. Standing at 2,497 m, Mount Tymphe’s naked promontory was uplifted by the collision between the African and Eurasian tectonic plates. It’s a remarkable sight, particularly when viewed from Dragon Lake, or Drakolimni, an erosional depression formed by the action of glaciers, and fed by waters flowing from the territory’s karst system. Local folk tales attribute the lake’s formation to skirmishes between dragons that fought, throwing large stones and boulders at one another.   On the southern slopes of Mount Tymphe, and inscribed in the Guiness Book of Records as the world's deepest gorge relative to its width, Vikos Gorge is truly remarkable. It stretches approximately 32 km in length, with a depth ranging from 120 m to 1350 m, and a width varying from 2500 m at its outlet to just a few meters at its narrowest point. Covering 120 million years of the Earth’s history from its bottom to the top, the gorge was formed by the powerful action of glaciers and the Voidomatis River. Along the course of the river, there are several ancient stone bridges, such as Plakida, Kokkorou and Gefiri Misiou. These bridges can be admired along the 370 km Epirus Trail, which runs from Mount Grammos to the Tzoumerka mountain range.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The Vikos-Aoos UNESCO Global Geopark plays a vital role in sustaining local communities by actively preserving and promoting their cultural and intangible heritage. The region is renowned for its traditional stone houses, arched bridges and narrow paths - some dating back to the 14th century. The structures found in the Konitsa and Zagori regions are famous for having been built and maintained by a travelling group of tradespeople from the Mastorochoria villages who used to travel around together, building houses during the summer season. The Rizario Handicraft Center actively preserves traditional crafts such as weaving, embroidery and dried flower arranging. Through apprenticeships and practical training, it empowers young women by fostering local craftsmanship and providing opportunities for casual employment with the foundation.  Heritage initiatives, such as the conservation of drystone wall constructions and the recognition of transhumance (seasonal livestock migration), showcase the region's vibrant living traditions. Collaborative efforts, including the Interreg Greece-Italy project and UNESCO intangible heritage groups, ensure these practices are well-documented, celebrated, and passed down to future generations. Local communities further honour these traditions through summer festivals, featuring practices like polyphonic singing—songs with interwoven independent melodies—and traditional mourning songs, known as moirologia.
Quote: “Wonderful gorges, rock towers, rivers, stone bridges, traditional architecture and thermal baths”

Introduction EN: Visit the famous Stiniva Beach, a secluded cove enclosed by steep limestone cliffs on the island of Vis.Explore the volcanic island of Jabuka and the extinct volcano Mount Hum, rising to 587 metres.Follow geotrails that showcase defensive forts, religious sites, dry-stone walls, and the former Neptune fish factory.
Description: A two-hour ferry journey from Split through the Adriatic Sea is all it takes to reach Vis, the farthest inhabited island off the Croatian mainland. The small island of nearly 90 square kilometres is a well-kept secret and home to some of the most beautiful beaches in Croatia. The most famous, Stiniva Beach—a small cove hidden by dramatic white limestone cliffs—is a true natural wonder. Vis Archipelago UNESCO Global Geopark is formed by Vis, the largest island, and the surrounding islands of Biševo, Sveti Andrija, Brusnik, Jabuka, and Palagruža. Some of the islands are composed of Mesozoic limestone and dolomite, formed over millions of years from the accumulation of marine sediments on the ocean floor, then situated along the tropics within the western Tethys Sea on a small drifting continent called the Adriatic Plate, or Adria. Tectonic movements folded and uplifted the islands, which—together with millennia of flowing water—created a fascinating karstic landscape of sea cliffs, sinkholes, underground rivers, and caves, such as the Blue Cave on the island of Biševo. The area also features volcanic structures, including Jabuka and the extinct Mount Hum on Vis, which rises to an elevation of 587 metres.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Inhabited since the Neolithic and held by the Liburnian tribes as early as the 10th century BCE, the island was later governed by the Republic of Venice, the Napoleonic Kingdom of Italy, and the Austrian Empire. It was ceded to the Kingdom of Yugoslavia in 1920 and became the headquarters of the Yugoslav Partisan movement during the Second World War. This layered heritage is reflected in towns such as Komiža and Vis, known for their traditional architecture, colourful buildings, and narrow cobblestone streets. The local economy is supported by vineyards and the fishing industry. The most visited sites on Vis include the Blue Cave (Modra špilja) and the Monk Seal Cave (Medvidina špilja). Before the sudden rise in sea level around 12,000 years ago, these islands were much larger and extended more than 20 miles. In this area, known as Mala Palagruža, archaeologists have discovered flint quarry sites believed to have been used by the island’s first prehistoric inhabitants up to 8,000 years ago. Other elements of cultural heritage are highlighted through the geopark’s geotrails. These include defensive structures such as the Komuna fortress in Komiža, former industrial buildings like the Neptune fish processing factory, religious sites such as the Church of Holy Mary and Saint Sylvester Church, as well as the extensive dry-stone walls that characterise the landscape. The gajeta falkuša is a traditional historical fishing boat from Komiža that can be visited. The geopark supports its preservation through cultural and festive events. Related traditions—such as navigation and fishing practices—are promoted in collaboration with researchers from the University of Split. The Chakavian dialect of Vis is recognised as intangible cultural heritage. As the oldest Slavic dialect of the Eastern Adriatic, it is notable for preserving archaic Slavic forms and for maintaining the Lingua Franca lexicon historically used across the maritime and fishing communities of the Mediterranean. Today, this dialect is under threat and there are dedicated efforts to research and preserve it.
Quote: “One of the last Paradise Oases in the Mediterranean”

Titre EN: Burren and Cliffs of Moher UNESCO Global Geopark
Introduction EN: The geopark is on the route of the 2,500 km Wild Atlantic Way, one of the longest defined coastal routes in the world, winding along the Irish coastline.The Cliffs of Moher Visitor Centre, a subterranean building, has won numerous awards, including Best Public/Cultural Building at the 2007 Royal Institute of Architects of Ireland awards.
Description: While the Cliffs of Moher have appeared in global popular culture, few realise that these dramatic cliffs and fissures are not computer-generated—they are a striking geological formation with a history spanning hundreds of millions of years. In the sixth Harry Potter film, Harry and Dumbledore stand atop a dark, wave-battered sea stack, dwarfed by a towering stone wall. This cinematic location is part of the 14-kilometre Cliffs of Moher in County Clare, Ireland. Rising over 150 metres above the Atlantic Ocean, the cliffs are composed of shale and sandstone, deposited in a shallow tropical sea between 323 and 298 million years ago, during the time of the supercontinent Pangea. Today, the cliffs are an internationally important bird habitat, hosting up to 30,000 nesting pairs of over 20 species, including Atlantic Puffins, Guillemots, and Razorbills. Atop the cliffs lies the Burren, a world-class example of a glacio-karst landscape. Formed during the Last Ice Age, the Burren was shaped by glaciers that stripped away soil and weak rock, exposing limestone surfaces that were later eroded by water to form the characteristic limestone pavement. This extensive terrain is among the best-preserved and most accessible karst landscapes in Europe. The geopark is also home to two notable show caves. In Doolin Cave, visitors can see a 7.3-metre stalactite—the largest known in the northern hemisphere. Nearby, Aillwee Cave, discovered in the 1940s, provides further insight into the region’s geological evolution.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The Burren and Cliffs of Moher UNESCO Global Geopark is committed to empowering local communities through skills development, sustainable tourism, and heritage conservation. The GeoparkLIFE project equips local stakeholders with knowledge and tools to conserve natural and cultural resources. Programmes such as Adopt a Hedgerow train local businesses in conservation practices, helping them manage litter and invasive species while protecting biodiversity. Partnerships with local tourism providers are key. Initiatives like Meitheal encourage businesses to support farmers by maintaining walking trails. The Burren Food Trail highlights local gastronomy through chef-led restaurants, producers, and farmers’ markets. Celebratory events like the Burren Food Fayre and the Winterage Festival promote food heritage and seasonal traditions. The geopark supports community-led heritage efforts. For example, the restoration of An Cabhail Mhór, a 17th-century building, trained local groups in conservation methods. Similarly, Ballyvaughan Tidy Towns serves as a biodiversity management model for rural and semi-urban areas. In Lisdoonvarna, the geopark has collaborated with Lisdoonvarna Fáilte to revive historic community assets, including the Victorian Spa Wells Complex and the Pavilion Town Hall. By supporting feasibility studies and development plans, the geopark helps ensure that heritage restoration contributes to sustainable tourism and long-term community benefit.
Quote: “Glacially-smoothed karst limestone hills contrast with dramatic sea cliffs that tower over the majestic Atlantic coast”

Introduction EN: Learn about Golden Bućka, catfish hunting in the traditional way in Tekija.The Visitor Centre in Donji Milanovac has exhibits on geodiversity, biodiversity, and cultural and historical landmarks.The fortress "Golubački grad" near Golubac is a cultural monument and museum showcasing the medieval period of the Lower Danube region and Serbia.
Description: For those visiting eastern Serbia, the Đerdap National Park, stretching along one of the meanders of the Danube River from the 14th-century Golubac Fortress to the dam near Novi Sip, is a mandatory stop. This natural area is home to thousands of plant species, such as the Turkish hazel—a relic from the Tertiary—and provides habitat for predators such as the wolf and the lynx. Together with parts of the Miroč and Kučaj mountain massifs, it forms the Djerdap UNESCO Global Geopark. The region is defined by the Đerdap Gorge, which separates Serbia from neighbouring Romania. The gorge, one of the most dramatic landscapes in Europe, forms the valley in which the Danube flows through the Southern Carpathians, between the Pannonian Plain to the west and the Dacian Plain to the east. At over 100 km long, it is the longest breakthrough-type gorge in Europe. The best views are from the peaks Veliki Štrbac and Mali Štrbac in the Miroč mountains. With a geological history spanning more than 600 million years, most of the geopark’s geosites are dedicated to representative rock exposures and karst landforms, including caves, natural arches, karst springs, waterfalls, and scenic viewpoints. One of the most striking examples is the Prerast limestone arch, which forms a natural bridge. The region is also notable for hosting the earliest known evidence of European copper mining and metallurgy, dating back to the 5th millennium BCE, at the Rudna Glava archaeological site.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Djerdap UNESCO Global Geopark is exceptionally rich in cultural heritage. The archaeological site of Lepenski Vir, one of the oldest known settlements in southeast Europe, dates back 8,000 years and represents a significant part of Danube civilisation. Additionally, Rudna Glava holds evidence of the earliest metal mining in the region, dating back 5,000 years. The cultural landscapes have been shaped by the traditions of Serbs, Vlachs, Romanians, Swabians, Hungarians, and Turks. The family patron saint’s day (slava) and the traditional dance kolo are recognised on UNESCO’s Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. Other customs are actively maintained and celebrated by local communities. The annual event “Let’s Keep Bagpipes and Old Dances from Oblivion,” held in the village of Rudna Glava, celebrates the bagpipe tradition. Flute playing remains a living practice through folklore troupes and festivals across the geopark. Saint George’s Day, widely celebrated among local communities, is deeply connected to seasonal cycles and traditional beliefs. At the Kazan Cult event, experts discuss approaches to preserving intangible heritage, ensuring that traditional practices are safeguarded and adapted to contemporary cultural expressions. Djerdap Geopark experts have documented elements of Vlach heritage, including Vlach embroidery (shtampuvit), traditional dances and songs, oral traditions, and local myths and legends. These efforts contribute to the conservation and promotion of intangible heritage, strengthening the identity and cultural diversity of the region.

Introduction EN: Explore the Sculpture Trail starting in Nova Palma, a 10 km route featuring stunning sandstone sculptures every kilometre, ending at the Sculpture Garden with over 500 carvings and forest trails.Visit Caminhos de Ivorá for an authentic eco-tourism experience, combining scenic trails, local crafts, and opportunities to connect with the natural beauty of the region.Discover Serra do Segredo Municipal Park, where geo-trails and conservation initiatives offer climbers, hikers, and students a chance to engage with the region's geological heritage.
Description: The Quarta Colônia UNESCO Global Geopark is a living testament to Earth's ancient history, offering visitors the chance to explore one of the most significant palaeontological landscapes in the world. This territory, located in the southern portion of the Paraná Basin, contains sedimentary rocks deposited between 233 and 225 million years ago during the Triassic Period. These rocks preserve remarkable fossils that chronicle a pivotal moment in the history of life on Earth: the rise of the dinosaurs. Species such as Buriolestes schultzi, Bagualosaurus agudoensis, and Macrocollum itaquii—all discovered exclusively in the Quarta Colônia—highlight the region’s unmatched contributions to our understanding of this evolutionary transition. The palaeontological value of the Quarta Colônia is further enhanced by its unique geological context within the Paraná Basin. This intracratonic basin offers a continuous record of depositional environments from the Early Triassic to the Early Cretaceous. Fossil assemblages found here, including species like Procolophon trigoniceps, connect this region to globally significant sites such as Africa’s Karoo Basin, underscoring its importance in understanding the tectonic and biological evolution of southwestern Gondwana. Beyond its palaeontological riches, the Quarta Colônia is celebrated for its breathtaking landscape heritage. Sandstone-basalt escarpments, adorned with fragments of the lush Atlantic Forest, frame a network of deep valleys shaped by thousands of years of erosion. This hydrographic network has created a mosaic of waterfalls, river beaches, and navigable rivers, offering visitors a blend of natural beauty and geological wonder.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Located in the south of Brazil, at the transition between the Pampa and Atlantic Forest biomes, the Quarta Colônia UNESCO Global Geopark boasts one of the richest cultural diversities in the central part of Rio Grande do Sul, reflecting Italian, German, Portuguese, Quilombola, Indigenous, and missionary heritage. These cultural influences are celebrated through gastronomy, music, dance, and crafts, which continue to thrive across the territory. The geopark's integration with the Mata Atlântica Biosphere Reserve, designated by UNESCO in 1991, highlights its commitment to preserving both cultural and ecological heritage. The agricultural economy, supported by family-based industries, remains a vital element of local livelihoods, with municipalities like Restinga Seca and São João do Polêsine showcasing strong connections to their rural roots. Recent initiatives have emphasised sustainable development through community-based tourism and the promotion of local products, such as handmade knives, artisanal food, and thematic crafts like mountable dinosaur models. Youth entrepreneurship has played a transformative role in revitalising the region’s economy. Businesses like Caminhos de Ivorá and Agudo Ecoturismo have embraced tourism, creating new opportunities for local engagement while preserving the natural and cultural landscapes. Events such as the Recanto Maestro tourist complex, with its emphasis on hospitality, gastronomy, and historical trails, further reinforce the geopark’s mission to sustain and celebrate the unique identity of this remarkable territory.

Titre EN: Rocca di Cerere UNESCO Global Geopark
Introduction EN: Follow in the footsteps of the German writer by taking Goethe's Way, stretching from the Capodarso bridge over the Imera to the ancient Fondaco della Cuba on the Dittaino River.Visit the Villa Romana del Casale, a UNESCO World Heritage Site renowned for its remarkably preserved mosaics, offering a glimpse into the luxurious rural lifestyle of ancient Rome.Explore the Floristella Grottacalda Mining Park, one of Southern Italy’s key industrial heritage sites, preserving the memory of the region’s sulphur mining legacy.
Description: Right at the centre of Sicily, the Valley of Enna was once believed to be the domain of Ceres—the goddess of agriculture, grain crops, fertility, and motherly relationships—who watched over her land from the limestone monolith known as the Rocca di Cerere (the Rock of Ceres). Centred around the city of Enna, the Rocca di Cerere UNESCO Global Geopark takes its name from this deity. According to Roman mythology, she lived in the surrounding valleys with her daughter Persephone, who was abducted by Hades to the underworld and returned every spring—symbolising the renewal of nature. The region is characterised by gently rounded peaks that culminate in Mount Altesina, the highest of the Erei Mountains at 1,200 metres above sea level. Torrential rivers have carved gorges into the limestone, forming features such as the Cateratta del Serieri and the Cateratta di Capodarso. The area was once one of the world’s leading centres of sulphur mining and home to the Pasquasia mine, a major global producer of kainite—a hydrated potassium and magnesium salt. This mineral is a geological remnant of the Messinian Salinity Crisis, a 600,000-year period during which reduced inflow from the Atlantic to the Mediterranean, due to tectonic uplift and sea-level changes, led to extreme evaporation and massive salt deposition, dropping Mediterranean sea levels by about 1.5 km.
