Today, this mining heritage can be explored at the Floristella Grottacalda Mining Park, named after two sulphur mines active from the late 18th century to the mid-1980s. Established in 1991, it is one of Southern Italy’s most significant sites of industrial archaeology, preserving machinery, transport systems, smelting infrastructure, and the ruins of miners’ quarters and the infirmary.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The geopark is also home to important cultural heritage from antiquity. Among its most notable sites are the ancient polis of Morgantina—hellenised in the 5th century BCE—and the UNESCO World Heritage Site 'Villa Romana del Casale.' The latter is one of the most luxurious rural villas of the Roman Empire, with exceptionally well-preserved mosaics considered the finest in situ in the Roman world. Agriculture, traditional crafts, and local festivals continue to shape the region’s identity. Renowned local products include olive oil, almonds, black chickpeas, and ancient grains such as Timilia, praised by Goethe for its resilience and quality. The F.lli D’Angelo farm, a member of the Oro Rosso Cooperative of Sicily, is dedicated to producing saffron—one of the world’s most prized spices. By carefully harvesting the delicate red threads of the saffron flower, the family combines precision farming with artisanal cheese-making in their historic dairy, even offering saffron-infused dairy products to visitors. The geopark also hosts centres that engage with natural and cultural heritage while responding to contemporary challenges. The Ecomuseum of Leonforte celebrates the region’s “Water Theatre” and its geological context. Meanwhile, the new visitor centre in Assoro—Borgo della Cultura del Sulfur—acts as an information hub, archaeological museum, art gallery, and homage to the region’s mining past.
Quote: “Gypsum, Sulphur and Myth”

Introduction EN: Embark on New Zealand’s longest and most varied scenic cycle trail, the Alps 2 Ocean Cycle Trail, offering a fully sustainable, zero-carbon way to explore the district. Marvel at the iconic Moeraki Boulders, spherical formations over 60 million years old, scattered along Koekohe Beach.Visit the remarkable Ōamaru Blue Penguin Colony to observe these 30 cm-tall blue penguins returning to shore at dusk, or explore their nesting area during the day while learning about related conservation efforts.
Description: New Zealand’s first UNESCO Global Geopark lies on the east coast of the Te Waipounamu (South Island), extending from the Waitaki Valley to the base of the Southern Alps. The landscapes, rivers and tides of this geopark have enormous cultural significance for the local Indigenous people, the Ngāi Tahu whānui. The geopark serves as testament to Earth's dynamic history and cultural richness, offering a window into the evolution of Zealandia, the Earth's eighth continent, or Te Riu-a-Māui in Māori. The geopark provides evidence of the formation of Zealandia, which broke away from the ancient supercontinent of Gondwana around 80 million years ago. The continent then became submerged under the ocean for millions of years before tectonic forces thrust New Zealand above the waves and the country’s current mountain-building phase began. Today, about 94% of Zealandia remains submerged, stretching from east of New Zealand all the way north to New Caledonia. The Waitaki Whitestone UNESCO Global Geopark includes an abundance of unique geological and cultural features. The Te Kaihīnaki, also known as the Moeraki Boulders, are remarkable spherical rocks that hold immense cultural and geological significance. In Kāi Tahu traditions, the boulders are the round food baskets and hue (gourds) that were washed ashore from the Araiteuru waka, a voyaging canoe that capsized nearby during its return journey from Hawaiki. The coastline, Te Tai-o-Araiteuru, honours this waka, whose remnants became integral to the landscape and oral histories of Te Waipounamu. Geologically, the boulders formed over millions of years within mudstone, as calcite from groundwater cemented around shell fragments or pebbles, gradually forming the distinctive spherical shapes. Subsequent erosion of the softer mudstone has revealed the boulders, with their calcite-filled cracks. offering a glimpse into ancient natural processes. Visitors to Te Kaihīnaki are reminded to respect the surrounding environment, which is a habitat for rare species like yellow-eyed penguins (hoiho) and New Zealand sea lions (rāpoka). Another striking feature of the geopark are the Elephant Rocks, where dramatic karst limestone formations rise from a prehistoric seabed. These unique rocks, sculpted by millions of years of uplift and erosion, create an otherworldly landscape that has been used as a filming location for its surreal beauty. The limestone's shapes and textures are a testament to the powerful geological forces that shaped this region.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Shaped by volcanoes and glaciers, the Waitaki district is bordered by the Waitaki River, which served as an early super-highway for New Zealand’s first people, the Māori. Along its banks, limestone caves and overhangs offered shelter and a canvas for charcoal and red ochre drawings, preserved at sites like Takiroa and Maerewhenua. These artworks provide a glimpse into the lives of the first travellers in the area, portraying bird, animal life, human figures, and early observations of European settlers. In the 19th century, European settlers turned to the region’s abundant limestone, known locally as "whitestone," to construct buildings in the absence of trees. Today, these historic structures define the character of Ōamaru, home to the most complete collection of Victorian-era buildings in the Southern Hemisphere. The Victorian Precinct, lovingly restored by the Ōamaru Whitestone Civic Trust, is now a vibrant community hub filled with artisans, artists, and craftspeople. Visitors can explore Whitestone City and take part in walking tours to immerse themselves in the region’s heritage, culture, and geology. The geopark supports local food and wine producers, fostering an emerging "geogastronomy" scene that connects visitors with the region’s unique flavours. Agriculture remains the dominant business sector, but tourism is a growing contributor to the local economy, driven by the geopark’s rich cultural and natural attractions. Through its focus on sustainability, the geopark also promotes values deeply rooted in the community, following four key Māori principles. Kaitiakitanga emphasises guardianship of natural, cultural, and environmental resources for future generations. Manaakitanga fosters care, hospitality, and generosity toward visitors and locals alike. Whanaungatanga strengthens relationships through shared experiences and collaboration, creating a sense of belonging. Finally, Whakaute underscores respect for individuals, cultures, and the environment, ensuring that all interactions honour the region's heritage and diversity.

Titre EN: Sesia Val Grande UNESCO Global Geopark
Introduction EN: Discover Candoglia’s pink marble quarries, the source of the iconic stone used in the Duomo of Milan.Hike along Cimalegna’s geological trail, a circular route with panels detailing the geological history, key outcrops, and soils of the Alps.Visit the remnants of the Sesia Supervolcano, where exposed crustal sections reveal the magmatic roots of a 280-million-year-old super eruption.
Description: Nestled within the Sesia-Lanzo Zone—a tectonic area marked by high-grade metamorphic rocks and granitic intrusions—the Sesia Val Grande UNESCO Global Geopark offers a rare opportunity to explore Pleistocene geomorphology shaped by glacial retreat and human settlements dating back to the Palaeolithic. The geopark unites two neighbouring territories, the Val Grande and the Sesia Valley, which share both geological and cultural heritage. Extending from the Po Valley to the peaks of the Alps, the geopark exemplifies the power of geological processes and the endurance of human presence. It is the highest and steepest geopark in Europe, with elevation ranging from Lake Maggiore at 190 m to the Gnifetti Peak at 4,554 m within just 60 km. At its core lies the Monte Rosa massif, rising to 4,634 m, which provides a dramatic backdrop to one of the most captivating environments in the Western Alps. This area includes the Parco Naturale dell’Alta Valsesia—Europe’s highest natural park—and is historically inhabited by the Walser population. The traditional Walser buildings and cultural practices reflect their resilience and adaptation to alpine life since the 13th century. The geopark presents a world-class section of continental crust, revealing rocks from the deep, middle, and upper crust. These formations offer insights into the Alpine Orogeny—resulting from the collision of the African and European plates over the past 100 million years. One of its most remarkable features is the Sesia Supervolcano, which erupted around 280 million years ago, forming a massive caldera now partially covered by Po Plain sediments. This supervolcano, with a caldera over 15 km in diameter and an eruptive volume exceeding 300 km³, ranks as a true “super eruption” and exposes a rare cross-section of its underlying magmatic plumbing system.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The historical and cultural heritage of the geopark is reflected in its stone. The renowned pink marble of Candoglia, quarried in the Ossola Valley, has been used since the 14th century in the construction of Milan’s cathedral. The soft talc-bearing serpentinite, known locally as pietra ollare or laugera, was traditionally carved to make pots and other tools, leaving visible archaeological traces across the region. The geopark captures the complexity and richness of the region’s geological and cultural evolution. It invites visitors to explore the interaction between deep Earth processes, climatic shifts, and the development of human civilisation over time. Traditional dry stone walling—recognised in 2018 on UNESCO’s Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity—continues to shape the region’s landscapes. Used in terracing, construction, and agriculture, the technique reflects a sustainable relationship between people and stone over centuries. With over one million visitors each year, the geopark draws people to its snow-capped peaks and tranquil alpine lakes. Seasonal guided tours and geological walks offered by official guides deepen public understanding of the area’s significance. In partnership with the Sesia Val Grande Tourism Association, local producers and stakeholders integrate agri-food, handicrafts, and geo-experiences into the tourism offer. This collaboration supports sustainable tourism, safeguards local livelihoods, and protects the region’s natural and cultural assets.
Quote: “Where rocks turn into culture”

Introduction EN: Hike the award-winning Mullerthal Trail, a 112 km network of well-marked paths that wind through deep gorges, forests, and sandstone rock formations.Discover the impressive rock formations of Noumerleeën, where weathering has created narrow crevices, overhangs, and natural passageways through Luxembourg Sandstone.
Description: Situated at the north-eastern rim of the Paris Basin, the Mëllerdall UNESCO Global Geopark lies within the Trier-Luxembourg Basin, a synclinal structure of Triassic and Lower Jurassic sediments. This region presents an outstanding example of sedimentology and geomorphology, with many outcrops and landforms that illustrate the dynamic geological evolution of the landscape, particularly during the Cenozoic era. At the heart of the syncline is the Luxembourg Sandstone Formation, dating from the Lower Liassic period. This thick sequence of porous sandstone has given rise to one of the most remarkable sandstone landscapes in Western Europe. Steep cliffs, narrow gorges, cuesta escarpments, triangular caves, and sculpted rock formations such as those seen in the Noumerleeën and Wollefsschlucht illustrate the effects of long-term weathering and erosion processes. These geomorphological features are not only visually striking but also scientifically significant, providing insights into sediment deposition, tectonic activity, and surface processes over millions of years. The Luxembourg Sandstone also plays a crucial role in the region’s hydrology. Its high porosity and permeability allow for long-term water storage and filtration, contributing to a near self-sufficient supply of drinking water for the surrounding communities. Springs such as the Salzwaasserquell are directly linked to the area's geological characteristics. Beyond its geological value, the region’s biodiversity and cultural history are intimately connected to its geology. The cliffs and rock faces serve as habitats for protected species of lichens, mosses, and ferns. Archaeological discoveries, traditional uses of local materials, and botanical features also reflect this deep interrelationship. Luxembourg Sandstone was commonly used as a building material, visible today in churches, castles, and paving stones throughout the region.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The Natur- & Geopark Mëllerdall is a vibrant region where natural beauty, cultural heritage, and community life are deeply intertwined. Known for its iconic traditional orchard meadows (Bongerten), the region is home to hundreds of fruit varieties, expansive forests, and a unique flora of ferns and mosses. With 42% of its land designated as Natura 2000 areas, the park serves as a haven for biodiversity and a model for sustainable living. A cornerstone of community engagement is the annual Mount vum Bongert (Month of the Orchard), held each October. This month-long celebration highlights the vital role of the Bongerten in the region’s identity. Local restaurants prepare themed menus inspired by orchard produce, and families take part in apple-picking, juice-pressing workshops, and events like the Fruit Varieties Drive-In. These activities, organised in partnership with the Office Régional du Tourisme – Région Mullerthal – Petite Suisse Luxembourgeoise (ORT-MPSL), Leader Region Mëllerdall, Administration de la nature et des forêts (ANF), and Mëllerdaller Produzenten asbl, bring the community together to celebrate the ecological and cultural value of the orchards. The region’s commitment to preserving its heritage extends beyond the Bongerten. Castles such as Beaufort and Larochette, Echternach Abbey, and remnants of early industries like ironworking and textiles speak to a rich historical legacy. This is complemented by the intangible world cultural heritage of the Hopping Procession of Echternach and archaeological traces of the “oldest Luxembourgers,” making Mëllerdall a place where history and tradition remain alive.

Introduction EN: The Hünenweg / Hondsrugpad is an award-winning long-distance hiking trail of 325 kilometres long. The hiking trail connects the geoparks, De Hondsrug in the Netherlands and TERRA.Vita in Germany, and is considered among the most beautiful cross-border hiking trails in Europe.Visit Van Gogh’s House in Nieuw-Amsterdam, where the renowned artist lived and worked in the winter of 1883. Step into his preserved room, featuring his original bed and paint palette, and experience the authentic atmosphere of the era.The Nabershof is a traditional Saxon-style farmhouse, built in 1681. The oldest farmhouse in Emmen is a State Monument and is owned by the Drenthe cultural-historic society ’t Volk van Grada.
Description: Scarred by the force of moving glaciers during the Saalian Ice Age, the territory of the De Hondsrug UNESCO Global Geopark is a relic from a time when Neanderthals hunted mammoths in the vast plains and local folklore tales speak of twin giants who robbed travellers.  In the northern part of the Netherlands, extending from Groningen to the fortified town of Coevorden, the Hondsrug is the most prominent landscape feature. This 70 km long glacial till ridge made of sand and clay is unique in Europe and, in some locations, reaches 3 km wide. The Hondsrug UNESCO Global Geopark, however, extends beyond the Hondsrug and features several other parallel ridges separated from each other by stream valleys. These ‘megaflutes,’ as they are also known, were shaped during the Saalian Ice Age about 150,000 years ago, when an ice mass from the North Sea region bulldozed over today’s Drenthe and Groningen. The pressure of the ice and the force of the melt water left behind this pattern of parallel ridges and depressions. Stream valleys such as the Hunze and the Drentsche Aa later re-shaped the lower areas.  The presence of the glaciers has strongly influenced the way human settlements developed in the region. On the Ballooërveld, north of Balloo, the landscape is formed by white sand, boulders and gravel brought here by the glaciers, and several collapsed pingos, curious conical structures formed in permafrost environments. Due to the availability of raw materials, it was here that the first settlers built their homes, raised their cattle and even buried their dead. Spread over the Ballooërveld, dozens of burial mounds or tumuli have been found, and archaeologists believe the area was used as burial grounds for an uninterrupted period of at least 3,000 years. Clearly visible across the Ballooërveld from Gasterensche Diep to Rolde are the grooves made by the horse wagons that crossed this area in past centuries. At that time, the church tower of Rolde, in the distance, acted as a beacon in an endless sea of heathland. After the last ice age about 10 thousand years ago, the climate slowly warmed and became wetter. Sphagnum moss began to grow in the stagnant waters of the broad valleys leading to the formation of vast areas of peat bogs. To the east of the Hondsrug, between the Hunze and the Eems rivers, the enormous Bourtange peat bog, thought to have once spread over an area of more than 3,000 square kilometres, was formed. The layer of peat became so thick that it grew up high against the sides of the Hondsrug and in some places, such as on the edge of the Bargerveen, the peat covered the Hondsrug completely.  The Bargerveen is the only large area of the Bourtange peat bog still surviving in the Kingdom of the Netherlands. It is now a nature reserve of more than 2,000 hectares. Sphagnum moss still grows here in small pools known as ‘meerstallen’.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The cultural landscape of the geopark is celebrated through its museums, historical landmarks and traditions. Notable among these is the Museum farm “De Nabershof,” which showcases the deep connection between the geological framework of the region and the evolution of agriculture. This museum, a product of local volunteer efforts, houses interactive exhibitions that explore the agricultural revolution and features an 18th-century country house, providing visitors with a glimpse into historical rural life. The geopark also promotes local traditions, such as weaving and blacksmithing, through craft workshops like “The Homestead” in Dalen, which emphasise sustainable use of resources. Community involvement extends to the development of geotourism, as seen in Oud Aalden, where residents actively participate in cultural and natural heritage projects, from guiding tours to crafting traditional art and recipes. Sustainability is a core principle of the geopark. Cooperative initiatives, such as the Landwikel Goense farmshop, support local farmers while promoting environmentally responsible practices. The intangible heritage of the region is closely tied to its legends and traditional practices. Stories of giants and Neolithic tombs, such as the Hunebeds, are woven into the fabric of the territory’s identity. The geopark has integrated these narratives into its eight storylines, complemented by engaging videos and educational materials that bring the past to life. The geopark’s natural heritage is equally significant, with efforts focused on preserving its biodiversity and ecological systems. Areas like the Bargerveen peatlands serve as exemplary models for biodiversity restoration, showcasing the impact of sustainable water management practices. The preservation of medicinal plants, unique geological formations, and peatlands not only contributes to the environment but also offers opportunities for education and tourism, creating a strong connection between natural heritage and community livelihoods.
Quote: “For thousands of years people shaped a landscape that is of all ages”

Introduction EN: Climb Pico Island’s Mountain, the tallest peak in Portugal at 2,351 meters, offering breathtaking panoramic views of the Azores archipelago.Experience Cozido das Furnas, a traditional Portuguese dish, slow-cooked underground by harnessing the natural geothermal heat of the Furnas Valley, providing a unique culinary experience that blends tradition with the forces of nature.Embark on a whale and dolphin watching tour, where you can observe a variety of marine species in the pristine waters surrounding the Azores.
Description: Between the American and European continents and sitting atop the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, the Azores Islands are a true jewel of the Atlantic. This volcanic archipelago with majestic mountains and enchanting dark beaches forms a unique ecosystem that endangered marine species call home.  A Portuguese autonomous region scattered across 600 km in the North Atlantic Ocean, the nine islands that form the Azores archipelago are an enchanting destination that has been captivating nature lovers for decades. Each of the islands, ranging in size from 17 to almost 750 square kilometres, is a small paradise painted in a thousand shades of green and brown and positioned at the convergence of the North American, Eurasian, and African lithospheric plates. A position that justifies why the archipelago has been experiencing episodes of intense volcanism for the past 36 million years, the most recent in 1957 when the Capelinhos Volcano, in Faial Island, burst into activity. The nearby Costado da Nau, a deeply eroded fossil sea cliff, provides a unique window into the eruptive sequence of Capelinhos.  To this day, the Azores showcase secondary manifestations of volcanic activity, such as thermal springs, fumaroles, and diffuse gas emissions and are home to 16 polygenetic volcanoes, most of which show calderas where deep blue lakes have formed. The Furnas Volcano Caldera, on São Miguel Island, is one of those and renowned for its summit calderas. The older caldera, dates back to around 34,000 years and is the crown jewel of the island. The area offers a diverse range of geodiversity, including a volcanic lake, domes, tuff rings, and a rich hydrothermal system. In the ocean the Mid-Atlantic Ridge and Hydrothermal Fields stretch for approximately 120 km east of Flores and Corvo islands. These are fascinating deep-sea hydrothermal fields, including Lucky Strike and Menez Gwen, offering captivating insights into underwater volcanic activity.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: With nearly six centuries of continuous human presence, the Azores have earned a significant place in the history of Portugal and the Atlantic, from their role as a crucial stopover for exploratory voyages during the Age of Discoveries to their strategic importance as allied bases during the two World Wars. Bathed in a mild and humid climate the islands have long been renowned for their agricultural activity. Faced with small patches of fertile land, the ingenuity of the Azorean people has throughout the centuries, transformed the landscape into a mesmerising patchwork of terraced fields and sturdy stonewalls, meticulously crafted from local basalt. In the fajãs, small, flat portions of land, typically fertile and cultivable located by the sea Azoreans not only managed to produce all the necessary sustenance but also established the sole tea plantation in Europe, a venture that began in 1820. Today, the islands are also known for their aged cheese and rare wine.  The Azores' rich traditions are reflected in their craftsmanship and local delicacies. The Pottery Tradition Centre in Chałupki stands as a testament to the region’s artisanal heritage, offering educational workshops and preserving age-old techniques. Meanwhile, the islands’ unique gastronomy blends traditional methods with modern sustainability practices. The Azores UNESCO Global Geopark offers a diverse range of educational activities aimed at fostering awareness and appreciation for the region's unique geological and cultural heritage. Hands-on activities such as "Create Your Own Seismograph," "Mould Your Own Fossils," and "JellyVolcano – an Effusive Eruption" allow children and visitors to explore scientific concepts in an interactive way. The geopark’s educational agenda extends to critical environmental topics such as climate change, waste management, and biodiversity conservation, with coastal clean-ups and removal of invasive flora sessions integrating practical actions with classroom learning.
Quote: “Azorean volcanoes are an eruption of flavours, smells and experiences!”

Introduction EN: Visit thermal water springs in the region, including the Termas de Monfortinho and Termas da Fadagosa.Try "Bica de Azeite," a flatbread made with wheat and olive oil, derived from the Hebrew "pita" bread.Discover the pedrado, a traditional form of pottery from Nisa, decorated with inlaid milky quartz and crafted using carefully selected local raw materials.
Description: Just 12 km after entering Portugal from Spain, the Tagus River—the longest river on the Iberian Peninsula—meets the imposing quartzite ridge of the Tallhadas Mountain. Forced to change course, the river turns nearly 90 degrees and flows north for less than 4 km before exploiting a weakness in the rock to cut through the quartzite barrier near the riverside village of Vila Velha de Ródão. This dramatic passage, known as the Portas do Rodão, gives the impression—especially to those viewing it from the riverbanks—that the Tejo is born from the rocks here, rather than over 600 km upstream in Spain. Naturtejo UNESCO Global Geopark is the largest in continental Portugal and contains geological heritage spanning more than 600 million years. At the Penha Garcia Ichnological Park, 36 different trace fossils provide insight into life on the ocean floor 460 million years ago and the ecological changes associated with the Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event—one of the major periods in the evolution of life on Earth. Monsanto is a village perched on a granite inselberg that rises 350 metres above the surrounding plains. For centuries, its 360-degree views made it a strategic stronghold, leading the Knights Templar to construct a keep at its summit. The village’s streets and houses are built around enormous granite boulders that seem to defy gravity. This distinctive landscape has drawn attention from filmmakers, including for House of the Dragon, a recent spin-off of the Game of Thrones series, which used Monsanto as a filming location.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Rooted in tradition and committed to sustainability, Naturtejo UNESCO Global Geopark is a territory where agriculture—including the production of olive oil, cheese, and meat—and forestry continue to thrive. At the same time, the geopark works to safeguard its geological heritage while promoting tourism and regional development to support a vibrant and sustainable future for local communities. The geopark places strong emphasis on cultural heritage, with 71 protected monuments and more than 2,000 archaeological sites catalogued in the national heritage inventory. Among these are significant locations such as the Conhal do Arneiro Roman gold mine, megalithic structures dating back over 7,500 years, and Bronze and Iron Age burial mounds, all accessible to visitors. The Tagus Valley Rock Art Complex is one of Europe’s most important collections of post-Palaeolithic art, featuring over 20,000 engravings spread across 40 km along both banks of the Tagus River. These engravings, created mainly through perforation, date from 20,000 BC to the late Bronze Age and depict geometric, anthropomorphic, and zoomorphic forms. Cultural events and festivals are an integral part of community life. Supported by the geopark, annual celebrations such as the Templar Penha Garcia Festival, the Arts and Walking Festival in Alpalhão, and the Olive Oil and Smoked Sausages Festival highlight local traditions and promote the region’s cultural and gastronomic heritage.
Quote: “Share a moment of deep Time”

Introduction EN: The cultural and natural heritage is evident in the landscape; archaeological sites, 16th-century colonial churches and convents, as well as extensive areas of natural vegetation, blend with the geology and landforms that create unique landscapes.Explore the Ñu-Un Yucu interpretative trail in Santa María Tiltepec to witness the region’s incredible biodiversity, featuring dense oak and pine forests, vibrant orchids and diverse bird species.Experience the world-famous flavours of Oaxacan cuisine, rooted in Indigenous traditions, featuring unique dishes made with insects, worms and other natural ingredients.
Description: The Mixteca Alta UNESCO Global Geopark is situated in one of the most geologically complex regions of Mexico, at the boundary of two tectonostratigraphic terrains. Its geological foundation includes Precambrian and Paleozoic metamorphic rocks, as well as plutonic formations that form the basement complex. These are overlain by Mesozoic and Cenozoic rocks, volcanic flows, and continental sediments. This diverse geological setting reveals key features of the region’s Earth heritage, including plutonic and tectonic structures such as dikes, sills, and faults, as well as outcrops shaped by spheroidal weathering. The geopark lies within the Sierra Madre del Sur physiographic province, a mountainous landscape shaped by prolonged tectonic activity and volcanism, bordered to the north by the Mexican Volcanic Belt. Sites such as Las Conchas and La Laguna are valued for both geological and cultural significance. At La Laguna, for example, a geological sinkhole formed by water erosion is the focus of active conservation, with access restricted to protect visitor safety and preserve the site.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Mixteca Alta owes its name to the Mixteca civilization, which flourished between the 2nd century BCE and the 15th century CE, and ended at the beginning of the 16th century CE with the arrival of the Spanish conquistadores.  The region's landscape has been shaped by agricultural practices that intentionally induced erosion, a relationship explored through several of the geopark’s geosites. These include gullies, badlands, mass wasting features, lamabordos, and palaeosols. Developed by Mixtec farmers, lamabordos are stone walls designed to capture water and sediment, creating fertile terraces for crops. Still in use today, this technique, dating back 3,400–3,500 years, represents a cultural shift toward sedentary agriculture. During the Postclassic period (circa 1000–1520 CE), this agricultural innovation supported a population of up to 50,000 inhabitants across 111 sites. Today, the population is mainly Indigenous, including groups such as the Chinantecos, Mixes, Mazatecos, Zapotecos, and, mainly, Mixtecos, who are deeply involved in the management of the geopark. Indigenous communities play a central role in preserving both biodiversity and living cultural traditions. Nineteen geotrails have been designed to enable people to visit geosites and other sites of interest. Visitors are guided along these geotrails by local people, who teach them about the geological heritage and its relationship with ecological, historical, archaeological and cultural heritage.
Quote: “Erosion, culture and geoheritage”

Titre EN: Colca y Volcanes de Andagua UNESCO Global Geopark
Introduction EN: The region’s gastronomy with its traditional jallpa is a journey in time to the way Indigenous populations survived the harshness of the region.Throughout the geopark there are traditional and mystical festivities such as: payments to the Pachamama, planting and harvesting water and Catholic masses that are accompanied by dances and bullfights.
Description: Cutting the Colca y Volcanes de Andagua UNESCO Global Geopark in an East-West direction, the Colca Canyon reaches depths of more than 3,400m – twice as deep as the Grand Canyon - making it one of the deepest in the world. It is home to the majestic Andean condor that can be seen exhibiting its two-metre wingspan, gliding close to the canyon’s walls. The diversity of the landscape is impressive and for the most adventurous, hiking the multiple paths that go from the terraced farmlands on the rim to the bottom of this impressive fissure, is a must. Surrounding the canyon, the area is known as the Valley of Andagua, a vast stretch of volcanic landforms where 25 volcanic cones, lava domes and lava flows can be observed like nowhere else. These are testimony to millennia of eruptions that have formed lava flows, dense pumice clouds and lahars from melting icecaps that have threatened the populations in the vicinity since the dawn of ages. However, our planet’s history has always been a dichotomy between creation and destruction, and the volcanoes of Andagua have also provided the building materials for one of the most outstanding cities in the world, Arequipa, the White City, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Arequipa is the region’s most important urban centre and the second most populated city in Peru. Founded in 1540 within a valley previously cultivated by pre-Hispanic societies, the city sits at the base of Mount Misti an active imponent volcano. Formed by 49 original blocks of the Spanish layout and 24 blocks from the colonial period and the 19th century, the city is characterised by its predominantly white or pink volcanic rock (sillar) constructions that lend it a unique charm shaped by both natural phenomena and historical circumstances. The convergence of pre-existing Indigenous communities, the Spanish conquest and subsequent evangelisation, the awe-inspiring natural surroundings, and the recurrent earthquakes all contribute to an intricate identity. This city stands as a testament to the resilience of its inhabitants against the forces of nature and the unwavering spirit of diverse cultures in times of adversity.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: In llama land, with the Andes volcanoes as a backdrop and home to one of the deepest canyons in the world, the Colca y Volcanes de Andagua UNESCO Global Geopark is part of the ancestral home of the Huancarama, Coporaque, Sibayo, and Cabanaconde Indigenous peoples. Its geological features are deeply intertwined with the cultural identity of its inhabitants, who revere the mountains as sacred spirits known as "Apus." These Apus are believed to protect and provide for the people, forming a millenary religious system that views the land as a sacred space. Mining, particularly of gold and silver, has historically been a cornerstone of the region's economy. Some of these mines have been active since ancient times, providing livelihoods for generations. Today, funds generated from tourism are increasingly allocated to environmental and cultural conservation efforts, ensuring the preservation of this unique landscape for future generations. Cultural sustainability is also prioritised, with the preservation and promotion of traditions that reflect the profound connection between people and their geological heritage. The Andean Sanctuary Museum in Arequipa showcases this legacy through the famous Mt. Ampato Maiden, also known as the "Juanita mummy," discovered in 1995. Her remarkably preserved remains, found in ceremonial robes at the summit of Mount Ampato (6,715 m), provide invaluable insights into the region's genetic, cultural, and religious history. The living heritage of local communities is further expressed through handicrafts, music, and Andean cuisine, which form an integral part of the visitor experience.

Introduction EN: Visit Kinuseo Falls, a 60-metre waterfall, taller than Niagara and surrounded by remote wilderness.Hike the Monkman Pass Memorial Trail, a six-day route through untouched mountains and waterfalls named after fur trader Alexander Monkman.Take the Shipyards-Titanic and Boulder Gardens route through alpine wildflower meadows and towering rock columns to formations that resemble life-sized petrified ships, shaped by the collapse of the Babcock Mountain slopes.
Description: On the eastern edge of the Rocky Mountains—the largest mountain system in North America, stretching 4,800 km from Canada to New Mexico—the Tumbler Ridge UNESCO Global Geopark is a remote and wild mountainous region of breathtaking views. The geopark has a long and complex geological history. Its rocks bear witness to ancient glaciations during the existence of the supercontinent Rodinia (1.1 billion to 633 million years ago); the deposition of carbonate sediments in warm, shallow waters where sponges, corals and crinoids lived (525 to 252 million years ago); the rise and fall of dinosaurs during the Jurassic and Cretaceous periods (173 to 66 million years ago), when the region consisted of swampy coastal plains and river deltas where extensive coal deposits were forming; multiple mountain-building events, including the formation of the Rocky Mountains (80 to 55 million years ago); and finally, a recent ice age that covered the region in thousands of metres of ice, shaping the topography of the geopark, deepening valleys and steepening mountain slopes. The crown jewel of the geopark is Kinuseo Falls, a majestic waterfall located 65 km from Tumbler Ridge in Monkman Provincial Park. The 60-metre cascade—slightly taller than Niagara Falls—is also a departure point for those exploring the region via the Monkman Pass Memorial Trail, a six-day, 63-km wilderness route through untouched mountains. The trail includes the breathtaking Monkman Cascades, a series of ten waterfalls named after Alexander Monkman, a fur trader based in the Peace River Country who discovered Monkman Pass.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Tumbler Ridge UNESCO Global Geopark is situated on the traditional and ancestral territories of the Tse'khene, Dunne-za, Saulteau, and Nêhiyawak (Cree) First Nations. Archaeological sites across the geopark reflect the long-standing presence, culture, and knowledge of Indigenous communities in the region. Hunting, fishing, and trapping remain important cultural and subsistence practices, governed by regulations that support sustainable harvesting and wildlife population monitoring. Traditional activities such as meat smoking—particularly of fish and red meat—and ice fishing on nearby lakes continue to be part of everyday life. Tourism activities such as hiking, nature observation, and wildlife spotting offer opportunities to experience the region’s diverse alpine and subalpine ecosystems. The geopark is home to moose, black and grizzly bears, mountain caribou, goats, marmots, and mountain lions, and serves as a migratory route for Golden Eagles. Natural features such as Bergeron Falls—the tallest accessible waterfall in northern British Columbia—also attract winter visitors, including ice climbers.
Quote: “World Class trackways and fossils form the cornerstone of Tumbler Ridge UNESCO Global Geopark”

Titre EN: Enshi Grand Canyon-Tenglongdong Cave UNESCO Global Geopark
Introduction EN: Explore the spectacular Tenglongdong Cave system, shaped by tectonic uplift and home to multi-level karst chambers.Experience Tujia, Miao and Dong ethnic heritage through traditional dances, stilted houses, festivals and folk music.Visit Jiantianba village to see China’s largest Late Permian sponge fossil reefs and a growing rural geotourism route.
Description: Enshi Grand Canyon–Tenglongdong Cave UNESCO Global Geopark lies in the southwest of Hubei Province and is renowned for its world-class erosion and dissolution landscapes. The geopark's geological features span exposed strata from the Cambrian to the Cretaceous periods (approximately 539 to 66 million years ago), with the most extensive formations found in the Permian and Triassic carbonate rocks. These rocks form the foundation of a spectacular karst landscape —defined by steep cliffs, deep gorges, disappearing rivers, and vast cave systems—deeply dissected by the Qingjiang River. Stepwise tectonic uplift linked to the collision of the Indian and Eurasian plates gradually raised the region, forming multiple planation surfaces. This process gave rise to iconic landforms such as the Enshi Grand Canyon and the multi-level Tenglongdong Cave system, recognised for their scientific, educational and aesthetic value. The Yunlonghe Gorge area, located at the boundary between the Permian and Triassic periods, preserves evidence of large-scale volcanic activity connected to the Permian–Triassic mass extinction. The geopark is a biodiversity hotspot, with forest cover reaching 67.3% across its 450 km². It supports over 4,000 plant species and 500 species of terrestrial vertebrates, including numerous nationally protected flora and fauna.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Beyond the geopark’s geological splendour, the rich cultural heritage of the Tujia, Miao and Dong ethnic minority groups lies at the heart of the territory. Visitors can experience traditional architecture, folk songs, dances, and festivals, which enrich their understanding of the region's cultural fabric. The area is home to rich intangible heritage including woodcarving, opera, brocade weaving and the Tujia “hand-waving” dance. Performances such as the large-scale “Dragon Boat Tune” allow local communities to share their traditions while generating income through tourism. In this way, the geopark strengthens cultural identity while supporting livelihoods. Education is a core priority. The geopark runs environmental outreach through the “six entries” approach—bringing geoscience into parks, scenic areas, schools, homes, and local communities. Local schools such as Mufu Middle School and Mazhe Primary School host dedicated geology showrooms and hands-on activities, encouraging students to learn about the region’s unique landforms and how to protect them. Interpretation plays a key role in connecting visitors and residents with their landscape. The geopark has constructed 11 science corridors and installed over 350 boards explaining geological, ecological and cultural features. Each area showcases its own strengths—Mazhe is known for geological hazards, Jiantianba for sponge fossil reefs, and Tuanbao for karst sinkholes. Geological showrooms are being developed to highlight these local identities.

Introduction EN: Visit the Peitian Roundhouses to experience living Hakka heritage in traditional cobbled villages.Watch a performance of Western Fujian Han Opera or join in the Longyan Spring Lantern Dance.Visit the rich forest of the Meihuashan Mountain, home to endemic animal and plant species, including the Panthera tigris amoyensis (South China tiger) and the rare Taxus chinensis var. Mairei (Chinese Yew).
Description: Longyan UNESCO Global Geopark offers a geological record of tectonic evolution in southeast China spanning more than 300 million years. Located on the southeastern margin of the South China Plate, the region preserves a continuous sequence of geological strata from the Neoproterozoic to the Cenozoic, capturing key episodes in South China’s transition from continental collision to oceanic subduction. The geopark’s geological heritage includes several sites of international significance. The Meihuashan granitic complex—formed between 430 and 95 million years ago—covers over 1,000 km² and illustrates the multi-phase granite magmatism of the region. The Guanzhaishan red bed basin, formed in the Late Cretaceous, is the foundation for the Danxia landforms that define the area’s dramatic red cliffs and layered rock formations. Volcanic features such as the Nanshanding Mesozoic caldera represent early signs of the Paleo-Pacific Plate’s subduction, while the Zijinshan copper–gold deposit is globally unique—recognised as the first high-sulphur epithermal ore deposit of its kind in the circum-Pacific volcanic-magmatic belt. Today, a preserved section of the mine wall serves as a public geosite. The park also showcases textbook examples of Danxia landform evolution, from youthful peaks to old eroded surfaces, including rare monocline peaks and rock wall clusters. This range makes Longyan a valuable site for geoscientific research and education. In addition to its geological richness, the geopark is home to the densest natural forests in West Fujian. Meihuashan Mountain—locally known as the “Mother Mountain of Fujian Province”—reaches a forest coverage rate of 95.4%. It supports high biodiversity, including the critically endangered South China tiger (Panthera tigris amoyensis) and the rare Chinese yew (Taxus chinensis var. mairei).
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Longyan is the birthplace of Hakka culture, a distinctive community that migrated from central China and settled in this region over 800 years ago. Many Hakka people still live in traditional villages and continue to practise their customs, fostering strong intergenerational ties. In some villages, residents provide meals and support to elders over the age of 80—an enduring example of communal care and solidarity. Hakka architecture is one of the most visible expressions of this cultural heritage. The Peitian Landscape Roundhouses, arranged along cobbled streets, showcase the compact, defensive design typical of Hakka settlements. These buildings are both preserved and inhabited, with tourism offering new opportunities to celebrate and sustain the traditional way of life. Longyan is known as “the jewel of Hakka folk culture”, with nearly 20 cultural practices passed down through generations. Six have been recognised as National Intangible Cultural Heritage, including Western Fujian Han Opera, Hakka “Shi Fan” music, the Art of Tulou Architecture, and traditional woodblock printing. Local festivals such as the Spring Lantern Celebration and the Longyan Pick-Tea Lantern Dance remain vibrant public events. Unique traditions continue today. “You Da Long” is a communal dragon dance performed in large formations, while “Zou Gu Shi” sees residents dress in traditional clothing for a street carnival. Puppet shows, folk music, and local opera performances all contribute to a living cultural landscape.

Introduction EN: See Tianchi Lake, the largest and highest volcanic crater lake in northeast Asia, surrounded by 16 dramatic peaks.Explore Manchu cultural heritage such as traditional paper cutting and sacred forest rituals.Discover rare alpine ecosystems across Changbaishan’s volcanic slopes, from red pine forests to tundra flora above 2,100 metres.
Description: Located in southeast Jilin Province, Mount Changbaishan UNESCO Global Geopark is a remarkable natural record of volcanism. The geopark spans the junction between the northeast margin of the North China Plate and the Pacific volcanic orogenic belt, an area marked by strong magmatic activity across multiple geological eras. Mount Changbaishan is one of the best-preserved composite volcanoes in northeast Asia, formed through repeated volcanic episodes from the Quaternary period. The most significant of these—the so-called ‘millennium eruption’ about 1,000 years ago—was one of the largest explosive eruptions in modern history. This Plinian-type eruption produced extensive pyroclastic deposits, now considered a geological site of international importance. Volcanic activity in the region dates back to the Archean and Proterozoic, with phases of magma intrusion, island-arc volcanism, and lithospheric thinning all contributing to the area's complex geology. These processes have created diverse rock types, multi-phase volcanic cones, and layered pyroclastic gorges. At the summit of Mount Changbaishan lies Tianchi Lake, the largest and highest crater lake in northeast Asia. Surrounded by 16 peaks, the lake occupies a classic caldera formed by past eruptions. Water began to accumulate tens of thousands of years ago following the Tianwenfeng eruption and re-filled after the millennium eruption. With its scientific value and stunning scenery, Tianchi Lake is both a key research site and a major visitor attraction.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Mount Changbaishan UNESCO Global Geopark works closely with local communities to promote sustainable tourism, restore ecosystems, and protect cultural heritage. Most recently, efforts have focused on rehabilitating the freshwater ecosystem at the source of the Songhuajiang River—an important environmental project carried out in collaboration with residents. The geopark is considered the birthplace of the Manchu ethnic group, who trace their lineage to the Nϋzhen people of the Jin Dynasty. Mount Changbaishan was historically revered as sacred land, and remnants of that spiritual tradition remain. Key archaeological sites include the Changbaishan Shrine in Baoma Village—built by the imperial family during the Jin Dynasty—and the Bagua Temple near Tianchi Lake, once dedicated to the god of the mountain. Intangible heritage is also deeply rooted in daily life. Manchu paper cutting, made with locally produced rough paper, depicts rituals, beliefs, and customs such as weddings, funerals, and worship. This intricate craft was inscribed on China’s national intangible cultural heritage list in 2008 and recognised globally in 2009. Traditional forest work songs—once sung by loggers to coordinate rhythm and effort while hauling timber—are now endangered but remain a symbol of collective identity. Similarly, the local custom of wild ginseng collection continues to reflect values of ecological respect, traditional knowledge, and careful stewardship of the forest environment.

Titre EN: Impact Crater Lake – Lappajärvi UNESCO Global Geopark
Introduction EN: Touch real impact-altered rocks and micro-diamonds formed 78 million years ago at Europe’s largest confirmed meteorite crater lake.Experience local heritage through the region’s 32 museums, including the Nelimarkki Art Museum and the Villa Vainola folk museum.Discover living traditions such as Finnish Baseball, log rolling championships, and folk music performances.
Description: Impact Crater Lake – Lappajärvi UNESCO Global Geopark is located in South Ostrobothnia, in western Finland. Its centrepiece is the Lappajärvi Impact Crater Lake, the largest confirmed impact crater lake in Europe. Formed 78 million years ago by a meteorite collision, it represents one of the youngest and most extensively studied impact structures in the world, with nearly 200 international scientific publications contributing to its understanding. The territory preserves the geological legacy of this rare event and invites visitors to engage with it directly. At various sites, visitors can touch the impact-altered rocks, including diamonds formed under the extreme pressure of the collision. Interactive exhibits offer virtual reality experiences, including journeys into the asteroid belt to witness the moment of impact. Among the most notable geological features in the geopark is Pyhävuori in Alajärvi, home to the prominent Uhrikivi, or “Sacrifice Rock.” Standing approximately five metres high and eight metres wide, it offers dramatic views and insight into the area’s diverse geology.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Impact Crater Lake – Lappajärvi UNESCO Global Geopark works closely with its local communities to promote sustainable development, cultural continuity, and economic wellbeing. Local natural resources are used in everyday life, with fish and products from the crater lake used in school meals. Cultural heritage plays a central role in community life. Institutions such as the Nelimarkki Art Museum and the Regional Art Museum of Southern Ostrobothnia host exhibitions, educational programmes, and artist residencies. The Villa Vainola folk museum offers visitors a vivid snapshot of traditional rural life. Traditional skills and practices such as forestry and log rolling remain part of local identity. The national log rolling championships are held in the area, demonstrating historic techniques for transporting timber along rivers and lakes. Intangible heritage is celebrated through narrative songs, folk costumes, and traditional dance. Local music, such as tanhu, and outdoor summer theatre continue to animate rural spaces. Events like dance hall performances and theatre on small stages help keep local traditions alive. Folk costumes with roots in the 18th and 19th centuries are still worn at events like those held at Villa Vainola. The Meteor Centre brings together geology, education, and community outreach. It features engaging displays, a study base for school groups, and a 12-minute immersive VR journey into the asteroid belt.

Introduction EN: Walk through traditional agricultural landscapes shaped by centuries-old dry-stone wall construction, still practised today.Explore Biokovo Mountain, part of the Dinaric Alps, with over 400 pits and caves and the third-highest peak in Croatia, St George Peak.Taste the traditional čupter grape must cake.
Description: The Biokovo-Imotski Lakes UNESCO Global Geopark is situated in central Dalmatia. It sits at a unique intersection of Mediterranean and Central European landscapes and cultures. At the heart of the geopark lies Biokovo Mountain, part of the Dinaric Alps, featuring the third-highest peak in Croatia—St George Peak—rising to 1,762 metres above sea level. This high karst mountain is a geological marvel, housing more than 400 pits and caves and characterised by a central high plateau with striking polygonal karst formations. The geopark’s natural wonders include the Red Lake, the deepest karst lake in Europe, formed from the collapse of a massive doline (sinkhole). The Blue Lake, another striking feature, is considered one of Croatia’s most beautiful karst lakes. Both the Red and Blue Lakes are designated as some of the world’s most remarkable natural phenomena, reflecting the region’s exceptional geomorphology and high-karst setting.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The Biokovo-Imotski Lakes UNESCO Global Geopark is situated in central Dalmatia, at the meeting point of Mediterranean and Central European landscapes and cultures. Local communities across this karst region have developed livelihoods and traditions shaped by the area’s unique geology and climate. The Vrljika River winds through the fertile Imotski Region, providing vital freshwater sources and supporting agriculture. Known locally as the ‘source of sustenance’, it has enabled generations of farming communities to thrive. Vineyards and gardens are widespread, and watermills such as the historic complex at Perinuša illustrate the long-standing use of natural resources for economic activity. Cultural heritage is preserved at hundreds of recorded sites across the geopark area, particularly archaeological sites and medieval heritage. Among these are prehistoric fortifications, Roman and Greek architecture, and medieval monasteries. The region is also known for stećak tombstones—unique medieval monuments recognised as UNESCO World Heritage. These are found in several locations in and around the geopark, including sites near Cista Velika, Zagvozd, and Župa Biokovska. Intangible heritage is also a defining part of the region’s identity. The art of dry-stone wall construction, a practice dating back to prehistoric times, remains a dominant feature of the landscape. Other traditions include the kantanje sung laments and the preparation of the Makarana cake and čupter grape must cakes, practices passed down through generations.

Introduction EN: Explore Peirópolis Geosite, home to Brazil's highest concentration of dinosaur eggs and vertebrate fossils, featuring attractions like the Dinosaur Museum and the L.I. Price Paleontology Research Center.Visit Serra da Galga Geosite, an internationally significant excavation site with new infrastructure planned for tourists and school visits.Celebrate Dinosaur Week in September with hands-on excavation activities, workshops, and guided geosite tours.
Description: Nestled within Brazil’s Cerrado biome, the Uberaba UNESCO Global Geopark stands as a testament to Earth's geological and palaeontological history. The Serra da Galga and Serra Geral formations feature prominently, their basalt flows chronicling volcanic episodes that paved the way for the breakup of the Gondwana supercontinent and the emergence of the South Atlantic Ocean. These flows cap the Botucatu Formation, a significant geological layer that houses the Guarani Aquifer—one of the largest freshwater reserves in the world. The geology of the Uberaba region also includes sedimentary sequences from the Bauru Basin, formed during the Upper Cretaceous period. These sequences, such as the Uberaba and Marília formations, showcase depositional environments that alternated between river plains, interbedded fluvial systems, and shallow lagoons, creating ideal conditions for fossil preservation. Notable lithological features include fine-grained sandstones interspersed with silty deposits and conglomerate layers, which serve as a record of ancient ecosystems and climatic fluctuations. The Serra da Galga Formation, in particular, stands out for its fossiliferous abundance and diverse palaeontological discoveries, including ichnofossils of invertebrates and megafauna remains. The geopark’s title, “Land of the Giants,” reflects its rich palaeontological heritage. Over 10,000 fossils from the Late Cretaceous period have been recovered. Highlights include the Uberabatitan ribeiroi, a colossal dinosaur measuring 27 metres in length and 10 metres in height, alongside fossils of crocodyliforms, turtles, and other prehistoric species. These discoveries are concentrated in formations like Serra da Galga, which represent some of the last chapters of the non-avian dinosaur era. The region’s palaeontological wealth even extends into urban areas, with fossils discovered in construction sites across the city. Peirópolis Geosite, a hub for vertebrate palaeontology, lies at the heart of these discoveries. Known for its extensive dinosaur egg findings and vertebrate fossils, this geosite is home to the Dinosaur Museum and the L.I. Price Palaeontology Research Center.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The Uberaba UNESCO Global Geopark seamlessly integrates its scientific heritage with community-driven initiatives to foster sustainability and inclusivity. Zebu cattle farming, a pioneering practice introduced by local farmers in the late 19th century, is a cornerstone of the region's agricultural identity. This initiative revolutionised the Brazilian livestock market, positioning Uberaba as a global leader in sustainable cattle breeding. Compared to traditional methods, Zebu cattle farming produces significantly lower CO₂ emissions, addressing critical global sustainability challenges. The annual EXPOZEBU, now in its 89th edition, highlights the breed’s contributions to sustainable animal protein production and showcases advancements in science, culture, and technology. Geotourism plays a pivotal role in uplifting local communities. Peirópolis, the geopark’s cultural and scientific heart, exemplifies this through initiatives like the Casa do Turista, where local artisans sell handicrafts, homemade sweets, and other regional goods. This vibrant hub of geotourism directly supports residents’ livelihoods while preserving cultural traditions. Similarly, the revitalisation of the historic Peirópolis Railway Station into a Cultural and Scientific Complex has transformed it into a centre of palaeontological excellence, attracting visitors and fostering economic resilience. Community-focused projects further enhance inclusivity and sustainability. The “Sewing a Better Future” initiative trains women in geoproduct crafting, providing vocational skills and creating sustainable income streams. Educational programmes, such as the Teacher Training Course for the Uberaba Geopark, engage educators in geoscience and heritage education, reaching over 40,000 students and fostering a deeper connection to the region’s heritage.

Introduction EN: Explore the famous “Great Wall of Dinosaur Fossil,” an 18-kilometre stretch of fossil-bearing rock layers dating back approximately 170 million years.Witness one of the world’s deepest sinkholes, plunging to a depth of 335 metres.Visit Zhangfei Temple, originally built during the Three Kingdoms period to honour General Zhang Fei, known for its distinctive calligraphy, sculptures and harmonious integration with mountain and river landscapes.
Description: Yunyang UNESCO Global Geopark, located in Chongqing Municipality in southwest China, features low to medium mountains and distinctive hilly landforms. Its geological history spans nearly 260 million years, recording the disappearance of an inland sea and the formation of a terrestrial environment that followed. The geopark is best known for its dinosaur-rich fossil deposits, most notably the ‘Great Wall of Dinosaur Fossils’—an 18 km stretch of sedimentary rock laid down between 175 and 161 million years ago. This sequence contains thousands of fossils, including plesiosaurs, crocodilyiforms, turtles, ray-finned fishes, and early amphibians. In one spectacular outcrop measuring 150 metres wide and 6–10 metres high, approximately 5,000 dinosaur fossils are exposed. These finds are globally significant as they fill a critical knowledge gap in understanding dinosaur evolution during the Middle Jurassic, especially the early part of the period. Yunyang is also characterised by dramatic karst landscapes formed through the interaction of limestone formation, tectonic deformation, and long-term dissolution in a humid climate. These processes have created a variety of features including sinkholes, canyons, caves, funnels, and stone columns. Among them, one sinkhole measures 335 metres deep, ranking fifth in the world and offering valuable insights into karst processes and formation.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Yunyang UNESCO Global Geopark has a rich cultural history spanning over 2,300 years, with temples, traditional villages and fortresses strategically positioned along the Yangtze River. The geopark is home to the Tujia ethnic group, who have sustained distinctive traditions including root carving, brocade weaving and waving dances. To ensure these traditions thrive, the geopark works with local communities to support the production and sale of handicrafts, while local schools have incorporated lessons that teach these traditions to younger generations. Events such as the Tujia Daughters' Meeting and cultural art exchanges provide local communities with opportunities to share their heritage and engage in the geopark’s development. The geopark’s museums and multiple tourist information centres—located in key scenic areas—offer visitors access to science education materials, guide services and interpretive tools. Yunyang also promotes geotourism and local development through the “Born in Yunyang” brand, which actively supports agricultural products such as citrus, black fungus, chrysanthemum, honey, tea and Yunyang beef.

Introduction EN: Explore Seboro Village, home to two iconic geosites—Lava Bantal and Lincak Merah—featuring volcanic rock formations and vividly coloured layers that date back 80 million years.Learn about community-led turtle conservation efforts at Jogosimo, Tambak Mulyo, and Lembu Purwo Beach, where eggs are safeguarded from poaching and nurtured in secure hatching areas.Engage with the rich cultural tapestry of Kebumen, shaped by diverse historical influences and expressed through local crafts, traditional cuisine, language, and customs.
Description: Kebumen UNESCO Global Geopark offers a remarkable record of Earth’s geological past, showcasing the oldest rock formations on the island of Java. A key feature is the Karangsambung site, a natural laboratory of oceanic and continental margin rocks that illustrate plate tectonic theory—showing how an ancient ocean floor was pushed up to the surface. These rocks document the subduction of the Indo-Australian plate beneath the Eurasian plate between 119 and 55 million years ago, a process that formed metamorphic rocks and exposed deep-sea materials. Between 55 and 25 million years ago, sedimentary rocks were deposited in tectonic basins, followed by volcanic activity between 25 and 16 million years ago. A subsequent pause in volcanism, combined with rising sea levels, led to the formation of fossil-rich limestone layers, while renewed volcanic activity from 10 to 2 million years ago left a distinct sequence of volcanic ash and limestone. These geological episodes have created a diverse and dynamic landscape, featuring ancient marine fossils, dramatic limestone karsts, underground rivers, and dozens of cave systems shaped by erosion and karstification.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The cultural richness of Kebumen UNESCO Global Geopark is deeply rooted in Javanese traditions, crafts, and cuisine, shaped over centuries by the region’s geological features. Settlement patterns and agricultural practices have long been influenced by proximity to rivers and groundwater sources, while spiritual and cultural expressions reflect this strong connection between geology and community life—from the Megalithic era to the Hindu-Buddhist and Islamic periods. One key example of environmental stewardship is the turtle conservation initiative at Jogosimo, Tambak Mulyo, and Lembu Purwo beaches. Here, eggs once threatened by hunting are now carefully relocated to secure hatching sites, protecting endangered species and raising awareness of conservation issues. Traditional crafts also play an important role in sustaining local identity and livelihoods. In Wonorejo Village, the Jiemat geopark programme teaches schoolchildren how to weave Pandanus leaves—used for generations to make bags, mats, and sandals—preserving this local wisdom. In Grenggeng Village, the Kebumen Youth Forum strengthens this heritage by supporting pandanus crafters with training in digital marketing, linking ancestral knowledge with new opportunities.
Quote:
Pandanus weaving has existed since our ancestors’ time. Our hope is that pandanus weaving, as part of Kebumen’s cultural heritage, becomes known around the world while benefitting our community.
— Bu Eko, Pandanus Craftsman, Kebumen UNESCO Global Geopark

Introduction EN: Learn about Sasirangan fabric, a key part of the Banjar Tribe’s identity, with each motif reflecting cultural heritage dating back to 1335.Visit the Sewangi Traditional Shipyard on Sewangi Island, an historic boatbuilding centre where visitors can observe traditional wooden ship construction and learn about the region’s riverine heritage.Take in the panoramic views from Matang Kaladan, where Jurassic-era metamorphic rocks rise above Lake Riam Kanan, offering striking geological features and stories deeply rooted in local legend and cultural memory.
Description: Meratus UNESCO Global Geopark offers a fascinating geological record of complex tectonic evolution beginning in the Jurassic period, 201 to 145 million years ago. The geopark is home to the oldest and most complete ophiolite sequence in Indonesia—rare seafloor rocks that were uplifted onto land between 137 and 110 million years ago due to tectonic plate collisions. This makes Meratus a key site for understanding subduction-related geological processes. Subsequent tectonic activity uplifted marine limestones deposited between 36 and 16 million years ago, forming dramatic karst landforms and extensive cave systems. The dynamic geological history has shaped a varied landscape of mountains, valleys, rivers, waterfalls and lakes, ranging from lowlands to peaks reaching 1,900 metres above sea level. The area also contains alluvial deposits formed over the past one million years that are rich in diamonds, supporting traditional artisanal mining. This geological diversity has fostered rich biodiversity, including orchid species such as moon orchids and sugarcane orchids. The Bekantan long-nosed monkey, once endangered, is now the mascot of South Kalimantan Province. The geopark has supported mangrove restoration efforts that are critical to the species’ survival, contributing to a gradual recovery of the population.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Meratus UNESCO Global Geopark is home to two main Indigenous groups, the Banjar and Dayak tribes, who continue to uphold their distinct ways of life. The Banjar people have traditionally relied on rivers for transport and trade. The Floating Market of Lok Baintan, where goods are exchanged from small boats known as jukung, is one of the region’s best-known cultural landmarks. The Dayak Meratus tribe draw on forest knowledge and bamboo resources, with traditional techniques such as Balanting Paring—a method of bamboo rafting used for transport. Cultural heritage is well recognised and actively passed on through festivals, education, and community events. The Sasirangan fabric is a cornerstone of Banjar identity, dating back to 1335, with each colour and motif carrying symbolic meaning. Traditional Banjar houses and shipyard sites are also protected as intangible heritage. The Meratus Great Culture Carnival, the Meratus Geopark Run, and floating market festivals are among the public events that highlight the region’s cultural richness and attract visitors.

Introduction EN: Hike to Lake Chon, a vast caldera lake formed by a major eruption in 946 A.D., and explore volcanic features such as lava towers, hot springs, and mushroom-shaped rocks along Mt. Paektu’s summit rim.Experience geothermal activity at Rimyongsu Falls, where magma-heated groundwater cascades from volcanic rock, and unwind in nearby hot springs surrounded by alpine landscapes.Discover food traditions based on potato starch, shaped by the community’s adaptation to a cold, mountainous climate.
Description: Mt Paektu UNESCO Global Geopark is marked by a fascinating geological legacy, with spectacular landscapes shaped by volcanic eruptions and glacial erosion. It is the first UNESCO Global Geopark to be nominated in the country. Mt Paektu sits at the heart of the geopark and is a key site for understanding volcanic activity. It was the location of one of the largest eruptions in recorded history – the Millennium Eruption in around 1000 CE – which spread volcanic ash as far as Japan and created extraordinary geological features, including Lake Chon, a striking caldera lake that sits at 2,190 metres above sea level. The aftermath of the eruption is vividly preserved in the landscape. Hot springs, carbonised trees and rising magma channels in the Janggun Peak laccolith offer a rare glimpse into different stages of volcanic eruptions. Today, geophysical research continues to monitor Mt Paektu’s volcanic zone where magma chambers and gaseous emissions hint at ongoing activity. The geopark extends across 1,326 square kilometres in Samjiyon County, Ryanggang Province, and is geographically divided by the Paektu mountain range. Its volcanic landscape includes both explosive and effusive eruption features, shaped by multiple eruptions of varying chemical composition over time. Glacial landforms such as cirques, moraine hills and outwash plains further contribute to the diversity of its topography. The site demonstrates a dynamic interplay of geological processes and remains under scientific observation due to its potential for future volcanic activity.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: For centuries, Mt Paektu has been celebrated as an ancestral mountain, a symbol of dignity with deep spiritual and cultural significance. This reverence is reflected in centuries of poetry and travel writings, including works such as Pounjib (1533), Chongguyongon (1727) and Kwangokjib (1895). At the foot of Janggun Peak, a stone relic known as “Ryongsinbigak” was unearthed—believed to symbolise the Dragon God who protects Lake Chon. The inscription reflects early 20th-century beliefs in the sacredness of the lake and its protective role. The area is also home to enduring traditions such as the “Arirang” folk song, and food customs centred on potato starch—a reflection of the community’s adaptation to the region’s cold, mountainous climate, where temperatures average -0.6°C annually and can fall as low as -19.8°C in January. The practice of making potato starch, along with related traditions such as producing frozen potato noodles, fresh kimchi, and cultivating medicinal herbs, has been formally recognised as intangible heritage through cooperation with the Samjiyon City National Heritage Conservation Office. The geopark promotes sustainable tourism by developing guided routes to volcanic landmarks and improving accessibility through infrastructure such as cable cars, hiking trails, and planned rail links. Seasonal activities, winter festivals, and year-round geotourism initiatives help sustain the local economy, while residents play an active role in preserving and sharing traditional knowledge.

Introduction EN: Trace the geological history of Jukdosan Yukgyedo, where layers of sandstone and pebbles reveal how this once-isolated island merged with the mainland through sedimentary processes.Visit the Yangnam Columnar Joints to see rare horizontal fan-shaped lava formations, and try the locally inspired “Columnar Joint Bread” created by a Gyeongju baker to celebrate the site’s geological heritage.Explore the Seokguram Grotto and Bulguksa Temple UNESCO World Heritage sites, where ancient Buddhist art meets the region’s granite landscape.
Description: Gyeongbuk Donghaean UNESCO Global Geopark, located along the southeastern coast of Korea, presents a striking combination of mountain peaks, coastal cliffs, limestone caves and ancient volcanic formations. The area records more than two billion years of Earth history, including ancient rocks that help explain the geological evolution of the Korean Peninsula in the broader context of East Asia. A diverse range of granites and sedimentary rocks reveal episodes of continental collision, subduction, and the opening of new seas, along with fossil evidence that illustrates environmental change and biological evolution over time. Among the geopark’s highlights is Seongryugul Limestone Cave, stretching 870 metres and adorned with stalagmites that preserve valuable records of ancient sea levels and marine environments. The Yangnam Columnar Joints—horizontal fan and radial shaped formations created by cooling lava—are one of the most celebrated features in the geopark. Since the geopark’s establishment, awareness of their significance has grown, and local communities now play an active role in their protection. This renewed sense of pride is reflected in initiatives like the creation of “Yangnam Columnar Joint Bread” by Gyeongju baker Lee Chang-woon. Using regional ingredients such as glutinous barley, walnuts, and squid ink, the bread mirrors the joints’ dark colour and textured form. It was the first local product to be officially recognised by the geopark and has become a symbol of how geological heritage and community identity can come together.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The region is also rich in cultural heritage. Gyeongju, the ancient capital of the Silla Kingdom, is home to the Seokguram Grotto and Bulguksa Temple UNESCO World Heritage site. The grotto enshrines a monumental statue of the Sakyamuni Buddha carved from white granite, looking out to sea, and is widely regarded as a masterpiece of East Asian Buddhist art. The geopark promotes eco-tourism and environmental awareness through a variety of activities, including hiking, sightseeing, and “Plogging” days, where participants clean up litter while learning about conservation. In one initiative, elementary school students became “GeoRangers” for the day, exploring the east coast of the geopark and completing hands-on missions focused on protecting natural heritage. The “East Coast Geo-walk” programme also brings together residents from diverse backgrounds to strengthen community ties and share knowledge through guided walks and conservation efforts.

Introduction EN: Explore one of Europe’s richest prehistoric landscapes in Costa Quebrada, where Paleolithic tools and world-renowned cave paintings offer insight into the lives and worldviews of early human species.Discover the limestone caves of Cantabria, shaped by water over millennia and home to specialised underground life forms such as bats, crustaceans and adapted fish species.Visit Tremeo Well, a rare stratified lagoon ecosystem that supports unique aquatic plants and animals, and attracts diverse bird and mammal species to its freshwater habitat.
Description: Costa Quebrada UNESCO Global Geopark, located along the rugged Cantabrian coast in northern Spain, offers an extraordinary opportunity to explore the forces of nature that shape Earth’s landscape. Over the last 120 million years, tectonic movements have pushed mountains up from the seabed, forming highlands that have been sculpted by wind and water into the coastline we see today. The region's geological history is shaped by ancient layers of sedimentary rocks deposited in shallow seas and river deltas, with evidence of changing sea levels and the shifting position of the coastline. The cliffs and beaches of Costa Quebrada reveal an exceptional variety of rock types and structures. As waves erode the coast, different landforms are created depending on the hardness and tilt of each rock layer—producing dramatic coves, capes, islets, and arches. Some beaches now found high above sea level are “raised beaches,” formed when the land was uplifted during mountain-building events between 55 and 5 million years ago. The area also contains salt domes formed around 240 million years ago in evaporating seas, and fossils such as crabs preserved in pyrite—sometimes called “fool’s gold.” Inland, the landscape is shaped by the dissolution of limestone into sinkholes and underground caves, some of which were used by early humans and are now protected as World Heritage sites. These features make Costa Quebrada a living classroom for understanding how Earth’s surface evolves over time.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The geopark is home to a vibrant cultural heritage, where community-driven initiatives celebrate the region’s traditions and history. Susana Pacheco, founder of the tourism experiences company NansaNatural, leads guided walks in Cueto, a neighbourhood of Santander, that explore the landscape’s geological features, biological diversity, and agricultural history. Her project introduces visitors to the traditional art of dry-stone wall building—locally known as morios—which has been recognised by UNESCO as Intangible Cultural Heritage. These structures once supported extensive vineyards and are now part of a collaborative effort to recover, restore, and promote the cultural landscape through tourism and local engagement. Winemaking is a centuries-old tradition in the region.
