One current initiative led by agricultural engineer and winemaker Pablo Oria, in partnership with the European University of the Atlantic and the Costa Quebrada Geopark, is focused on identifying and reviving native grape varieties. The aim is to preserve the area’s distinct wine heritage and, in time, produce wines using local grapes that have long formed part of the region’s productive and social fabric.
Quote: Who would have thought that the places I walked as a child would one day become the heart of the geo-ecotourism I now lead with residents and visitors in the Costa Quebrada UNESCO Global Geopark — Susana Pacheco, Manager of NansaNatural

Titre EN: The Fjord Coast UNESCO Global Geopark
Introduction EN: Learn about and participate in the revival of ancient traditions in Hardbakke, where the community sustains coastal heathlands through Old Norse sheep grazing and controlled burning, preserving biodiversity and cultural heritage.Walk to Brurastakken on Atløyna, a coastal landmark known as “Norway’s most beautiful fold,” attracting geologists worldwide and once used by sailors for navigation.Hike, bike or kayak where the Sognefjord – the world’s second-deepest fjord – meets the Atlantic, and take in spectacular views from coastal mountain peaks near Hyllestad.
Description: At the westernmost point of Norway, where the majestic Sognefjord meets the rough Northern Sea, the Fjord Coast UNESCO Global Geopark offers an extraordinary landscape of islands, fjords, cascading waterfalls and the lowest-lying glacier in Scandinavia. The geopark is home to the ancient Caledonian mountain range, formed between 425 and 395 million years ago, and showcases exceptional geological exposures, including remnants of oceanic crust and volcanic complexes. Few places in the world offer a better opportunity to study the rise and fall of a gigantic mountain range within such a limited area. The geology of the geopark includes ancient continental crust, island-arc volcanics, and deep oceanic material that was pushed to the surface during tectonic collisions—making it one of the finest analogues to a Himalayan-style mountain belt. These features are concentrated in an unusually compact area, providing unique insight into mountain-building processes. Over millions of years, recurring ice ages have carved and reshaped the landscape, with the most recent glaciation ending around 10,000 years ago. The vertical difference between the fjord floor and nearby peaks, such as Blægja at 1,304 metres, reaches over 2,500 metres, exemplifying the dramatic topography created by both tectonic uplift and glacial erosion.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The region’s geological history, combined with its abundant natural resources, paved the way for early human settlements along the coast, as people were drawn to the rich fishing grounds while glaciers still covered inland areas. These settlers quickly developed sustainable practices to manage the unique coastal heathlands. Today, local residents have revived the 5,000-year-old tradition of Old Norse sheep grazing and controlled heather burning, through a volunteer-led initiative that brings people together of all generations and backgrounds. Old Norse sheep grazing plays a crucial role in maintaining the heathlands, preventing the spread of taller shrubs, and allowing rare species to thrive, including birds and insects. In a blend of tradition and innovation, the younger generation of sheep herders is incorporating GPS-controlled fence technology to guide the sheep, enhancing land management while preserving ancient grazing methods. The park’s Viking heritage is also a source of strong local identity. The region was home to notable historical figures, such as Ingólf Arnarson from Rivedal, who brought Viking traditions to Iceland in the mid-800s. In 1066, Norway’s largest Viking fleet assembled at Utvær, the westernmost point of the country and now part of the geopark. Led by King Harald Hardrada, this fleet sailed to England, where the Battle of Stamford Bridge marked the decline of the Viking era. Youth involvement is a core priority of the geopark. Through the “Youth Communication” project, young people are trained to share their natural and cultural heritage in innovative ways. The geopark is also part of a wider UNESCO network in Vestland County, which is working to establish a UNESCO Trail linking all UNESCO-designated sites in the region.

Introduction EN: Explore the impressive crater of the Sumaco volcano at Laguna Guagua Sumaco, where weathered pyroclastic deposits and calm, crystalline waters offer rich geological insight and a haven for birdwatchers.Visit the AMUKISHMI women's association in Puerto Misahuallí, where Kichwa cultural traditions are shared through workshops, crafts, and the welcoming drink of yucca chicha.Follow the Cacao and Chocolate Route in Napo, linking birdwatching, ecotourism and cultural events with the region’s fine aroma cacao and Amazonian chocolate-making traditions.
Description: Napo Sumaco UNESCO Global Geopark is located in the heart of Ecuador’s Amazon Basin, where the Andes meet the Amazon plains. The geopark records over 170 million years of geological history, spanning the Jurassic, Cretaceous, Paleogene, Neogene and Quaternary periods. The landscape features irregular slopes, mesas, plateaus, valleys and terraces, with Sumaco Volcano rising to 3,830 metres above sea level as its highest point. Sumaco Volcano is the geopark’s most prominent geological feature. It is potentially active and stands out from other volcanoes in northern Ecuador due to its rare alkaline composition, with volcanic rocks such as phonolites, basanites and feldspathoid tephrites. This makes it a key site for exploring how geological diversity is linked to biological diversity. The geopark also contains important karst formations, where scientists study cave deposits (speleothems) to reconstruct past climate changes. With more than 6,000 plant species and many rare and endemic animals, the area is recognised as one of Ecuador’s biodiversity hotspots. Its unique geological setting continues to attract scientific research and geotourism.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Local communities play an active role in protecting and maintaining the geopark’s geological sites, carrying forward the Indigenous Kichwa concepts of minga and turkana. Pacha Mama (Mother Earth) is central to the Amazon Kichwa people's value system, preserved as valuable ancestral knowledge that connects geodiversity, biodiversity and culture. Many geosites can only be accessed with the guidance of local residents, ensuring respectful land use while providing opportunities for local communities.  In the early stages of the geopark’s development, researchers from Ikiam University turned to local residents for their knowledge of the landscape. This collaboration led to the creation of the Pushak Runas Guides—Pushak Runakuna meaning “guides with knowledge” in Kichwa—who received training in geology, cave science, and conservation. With support from the Ministry of Tourism and the geopark team, many guides gained national certification, and today they operate independently as a self-managed group. Through their own tour operator, GeoPushak Travel, they now lead visits to geosites and continue training future guides, strengthening local participation in geotourism. Several other key community groups contribute to the geopark’s activities. The Yachak Awakkuna collective specialises in traditional crafts such as ceramics, natural pigment painting, fibre art, and handmade costume jewellery featuring seeds and mullos, which are key elements of Amazonian attire. The Mikusha Kawsari Gastronomic Group highlights the importance of the Amazonian agroecological chakra system, showcasing its role in food production and natural medicine, while also bringing a gourmet twist to traditional Amazonian dishes.
Quote: Thanks to the support of the Ikiam university and the geopark, I’ve been able to take many training courses—water rescue, wilderness rescue, even courses in mycology and enology. Through all of this, I’ve come to understand what it means to work in tourism — Marcelo Bedoya, Director of Pushak Runakunas Guides

Introduction EN: Mt. Siguniang UNESCO Global Geopark is situated on the eastern edge of the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, featuring an alpine terrain with distinct vertical climate zones.
Description: The geopark is known for its complex tectonics, including folds, flysch deposits, and towering granite peaks. Significant geological formations such as the “Xikang-type” folds, “Xikang Group” flysch, offer key insights into continental collision. Traversed primarily by the Fubian, Wori and Xiaojinchuan Rivers, the region exhibits a dendritic drainage pattern in the upper Yangtze basin. These landforms record the uplift processes of the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, with dramatic alpine landscapes and numerous peaks towering over 5,000 metres.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The region is a key settlement for Jiarong Tibetan communities. The Tibetan language and associated cultural practices continue to be central to community identity and intergenerational knowledge transmission, and every year the Mt. Siguniang Pilgrimage Festival is held, paying homage to the legend that four girls transformed into mountain peaks. The region’s distinctive folding structures and tectonic context are of global scientific significance, while the region’s pastoralism, architecture, and cultural practices reflect long-standing relationships with and adaptation to high-altitude environments. Environmentally friendly tourism connects outsiders with the spectacular scenery in a way that supports sustainable local development and gives visitors a chance to experience traditional Tibetan dance, cuisine, and art, reflecting the practical knowledge and practices of the people developed over generations in the region.

Introduction EN: The Manantiales Serranos UNESCO Global Geopark is located in southeast Uruguay, in the Department of Lavalleja. The region presents a rich geological history, with more than 80% of the territory composed of metamorphic and igneous rocks that record significant tectonic activity.
Description: Over 28 distinct lithologies and valuable mineral deposits testify to the formation and breakup of ancient supercontinents such as Rodinia and Gondwana. Geological records document the opening of the Atlantic Ocean during the Mesozoic, which led to the separation of South America and Africa, followed by tectonic processes of uplift, erosion, non-deposition, and sedimentation accompanied by climate change.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Community is at the heart of the aptly-named ‘Manantiales Serranos’ (‘Mountain Springs’ in English), which was even named through a community-driven process to reflect the area’s hilly landscape and abundant water sources. The region is home to the headwaters of the Santa Lucía River, Uruguay’s third-largest basin, which supplies drinking water to 60% of the population and supports much of the country's industry. Its main urban centers include Minas, Solís de Mataojo, and the tourist village of Villa Serrana, which swells from 300 residents to 10,000 during peak seasons. Surrounding rural communities often bear names linked to local geological features. The region’s economy is based on agriculture, livestock, mining, water use, and tourism, fostering a culture strongly connected to natural resources and committed to environmental conservation.

Introduction EN: Explore geological, biological, and cultural heritage at the Geopark Museum and Huangshan Museum through exhibitions, videos, and educational tools.Hike three main trails in the park: Yungu to Beihai, Wenquan to Ciguangge, and Houtouyan to Diaoqiaoan.Visit a site recognised as both a World Heritage Site and Biosphere Reserve for its outstanding natural and cultural value.
Description: Huangshan UNESCO Global Geopark, located in East China’s Anhui Province, presents one of the world’s most striking Mesozoic granite landscapes. Elevations within the geopark range from 500 to 1,864 metres, forming part of the broader Southeast Hilly Area of China. The region’s geological heritage centres on the Huangshan granite landform, which is globally recognised as a natural granite museum. The mountain’s geological story begins in the Late Jurassic period, around 140 million years ago, when hot magma intruded through the Earth’s crust and slowly crystallised beneath the surface. This created the massive granitic bodies that define the area today. Around 65 million years ago, tectonic forces caused these intrusive rocks to uplift. Over millions of years, the overlying material was stripped away by erosion, exposing the granite and revealing a network of intersecting joints. These processes were critical in shaping the Huangshan landscape, allowing the formation of dramatic landforms such as domes, cones, crests, columns and box-like shapes across the valleys radiating from the main massif. The landscape continued to evolve, reaching its current form around 1.75 million years ago. Differences in mineral composition, crystallisation, and resistance to weathering contributed to the diverse and picturesque topography seen today. Geomorphologically, the area is an important site for studying granite formation processes and is considered a reference site for understanding granite morphology worldwide. Huangshan is also notable for its possible glacial history. While the presence of Quaternary glaciers in the region remains a subject of scientific debate, the hypothesis of past glaciation continues to attract geologists and adds further intrigue to the site’s geological evolution. Known for its iconic “Three Wonders of Nature” – spectacularly shaped rocks, peculiarly contorted pines, and sea-like clouds – the geopark integrates geological heritage with a broader natural and cultural landscape. These features, combined with the area’s scientific importance and aesthetic value, make Huangshan a key site for geoscientific research, conservation and education.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Huangshan UNESCO Global Geopark has long been embedded in Chinese culture and collective memory. According to legend, many turns around the sun ago, Emperor Huang journeyed to the enigmatic Yi Mountain with his entourage, in pursuit of immortality. Amid the mist-shrouded peaks, they refined herbal remedies and embraced a spiritual existence. Their dedication culminated in the creation of an elixir of immortality. In 747 AD, Tang Dynasty Emperor Li Longji, a devout follower of Taoism, renamed the site “Mount Huangshan” in tribute to the forefather of Chinese civilisation. The geopark is home to three nationally recognised intangible cultural heritage elements: Huangshan Maofeng green tea production, Taiping Houkui tea processing techniques, and Hui Opera. Tangkou ham curing, recognised at the provincial level, is also preserved. Institutional measures ensure the safeguarding and transmission of these traditions, including the establishment of legal frameworks and identification systems for local knowledge holders. The cultural influence of the geopark extends to the visual arts. The unique landforms and dramatic scenery have inspired the ‘Huangshan school’ of painting, which has had a lasting impact on Chinese landscape painting. In this way, the geological landscape continues to shape art and cultural expression. Educational routes have been developed in collaboration with tourism agencies to support school visits. Partnerships with academic institutions such as the China University of Geosciences and the Chinese Academy of Geological Sciences have led to the establishment of several research bases, with results informing both education and park management.
Quote: “Rock, cloud and sculpted pine combine to form a unique landscape that has shaped art and culture”

Introduction EN: Azilal is a buzzing city with traditional Moroccan architecture and food, and is home to the impressive Azilal Museum. Each year the Aït Hdiddu tribes hold an engagement festival where young men and women can meet. It is considered one of the most beautiful and unique gatherings in Morocco. Visit the amazing Mastfrane Cathedral, an imposing sandstone formation rising 300 m above the Assif n’zou Ahançal valley.
Description: East of Marrakesh, the M’Goun UNESCO Global Geopark sits in the central High Atlas Mountains, enjoying a mild climate year-round. In the green valley of Asif Mellulen lie the enchanting lakes of Isli and Tislit.According to local lore, the lakes were formed from the tears of star-crossed lovers—two young people from enemy Berber tribes, divided by a long-standing feud. Forbidden to be together, they fled to the mountains on a moonlit night; as they looked back at their village, knowing their love was doomed, their tears flowed down the mountainside, forming the two lakes. In despair, they exchanged vows and drowned in their own tears. Shamed by the tragedy, the elders of the feuding families ended their quarrels and vowed to allow future generations the freedom to choose their life partners. On the margins of these lakes, the Aït Hdiddou tribes host a yearly moussem engagement festival, where young men and women gather to meet. This event is considered one of the most beautiful and culturally significant gatherings in Morocco. Moroccan and Italian research suggests that the lakes were formed by the impact of a meteorite. Geologically, the geopark bears witness to over 200 million years of Earth’s history, with significant stages of its evolution occurring during the Jurassic period, about 180 million years ago. The region is renowned for its dinosaur footprints, including those of Megalosauripus, a bipedal dinosaur found in the Iouaridene synclinal, and the feathered Dromaeosauridae discovered in the Ait Blal geosite. The territory's geological history is deeply tied to the evolution of the central High Atlas, beginning in the Triassic period, 250 million years ago. Its NE-SW intra-continental chain was shaped by the structural reversal of a Jurassic basin during the collision of the African and European plates. The region is also abundant in minerals such as copper, zinc, barite, iron, basalt, limestone, and dolomitic Triassic red clays. Among the most iconic natural landmarks of the M’Goun Geopark are the awe-inspiring Mastfrane Cathedral, a 300-meter-high sandstone cliff towering over the Assif n'ou Ahançal valley, and the stunning D'Ouzoud Waterfalls on the El-Abid River, showcasing the area's remarkable geological and natural heritage.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The M’Goun UNESCO Global Geopark is home to diverse and resilient communities that have lived for centuries in the rugged landscape of the High Atlas Mountains. Farming forms the backbone of the local economy, with over 40 cooperatives engaged in saffron cultivation, grown on terraced slopes, and others producing olive oil, almonds and sesame.  The communities in the geopark are deeply invested in preserving biodiversity. The region’s vast knowledge of medicinal plants, with over 80 species growing naturally in the area, has been passed down through generations. Many of these plants are cultivated locally, combining conservation with practical benefits for the community. The geopark works alongside local residents, authorities and associations to promote sustainable practices that align with traditional knowledge while supporting biodiversity conservation and poverty alleviation. The territory is rich in cultural heritage, including kasbahs, granaries, irrigation systems, and terraced slopes, all testament to the ingenuity of local communities in adapting to their environment. Rock engravings, weaving, pottery and other crafts continue to enrich the cultural identity of these communities, creating a tangible connection to their past.
Quote: “Valleys, natural curiosities, fossilised footprints, engravings and authentic Berber villages”

Introduction EN: Engaresero, near Lake Natron, reveals footprints of modern humans dating back 5,000 to 19,000 years, offering a glimpse into our ancient past.The geopark has four discovery routes: the North, South, Caldera, and Oldonyo Lengai Routes.
Description: From the towering rainforest giants on the eastern flanks of the volcanic highlands to the sweeping savannahs of the Serengeti plains, 90% of the Ngorongoro-Lengai UNESCO Global Geopark serves as a sanctuary for an extraordinary array of wildlife. It is home to the highest density of mammalian predators in Africa, including lions, leopards, and cheetahs. Prey species such as zebras, Thomson’s and Grant’s gazelles, and over a million wildebeest support this ecosystem. Between July and November, these species form part of one of the world’s most remarkable natural events: the Great Migration. The geopark also hosts more than 500 species of birds. Flamingos wade in the alkaline lakes, ostriches roam the savannah, and lilac-breasted rollers add bursts of colour to the landscape. Beneath the surface lies the geological engine that has shaped the region. Located in the eastern branch of the East African Rift System, the landscape reflects more than 20 million years of crustal extension. Towering fault scarps mark the terrain, and the Ngorongoro Volcanic Highlands—a complex of basaltic volcanoes—may once have rivalled Mount Kilimanjaro in scale. At its centre is the Ngorongoro Crater, the world’s largest inactive, intact, and unfilled volcanic caldera. Although major volcanic activity has ceased, one volcano remains active. Oldoinyo Lengai, meaning “Mountain of God” in the Maasai language, is a sacred site and an active stratovolcano standing at 2,962 metres. It is the only known volcano in the world to erupt natrocarbonatite lava, which is low in silica and erupts at a relatively low temperature of around 510 °C. As a result, the lava appears black in sunlight rather than glowing red like typical lava flows.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The Ngorongoro-Lengai UNESCO Global Geopark is a living landscape where geology, biodiversity, and human cultures have coexisted for millennia. It is home to four distinct Indigenous communities—the Maasai, Hadzabe, Datoga, and Iraqw—each with unique traditions, livelihoods, and knowledge systems deeply rooted in the natural environment. The Maasai, the most prominent group in the region, are semi-nomadic pastoralists whose livelihoods revolve around cattle herding. Their sustainable grazing practices have long shaped the region’s grasslands, maintaining a delicate balance between livestock and biodiversity conservation. The Datoga, also pastoralists, are skilled blacksmiths, crafting tools and jewellery from recycled metals—an ancient practice that continues to sustain local trade. The Iraqw people engage in terraced farming on the slopes of the Ngorongoro Highlands, using advanced agricultural techniques that help prevent soil erosion and maintain the fertility of volcanic soils. The Hadzabe, one of the last hunter-gatherer groups in Africa, have preserved their traditional way of life, relying on foraging and hunting, demonstrating an unparalleled understanding of the region’s ecosystems. The communities express their cultural identities through music, dance, and oral storytelling. The Maasai are renowned for their ceremonial dances, the Hadzabe for their hunting songs, and the Datoga for their metalwork rituals—all of which contribute to the rich intangible heritage of the geopark. This dynamic cultural landscape, shaped by its geological setting, continues to evolve while maintaining a strong connection to traditions passed down through generations.
Quote: “An extra-ordinary volcano, extra-ordinary paleoanthropological sites and extra-ordinary wildlife”

Introduction EN: The region is also known as the birthplace of Zen Buddhism and is home to the 1,500-year-old Sanzu Temple, which remains open to visitors.In the southern part of the geopark, Doumu village preserves a 6,000-year-old pottery tradition. Local artisans continue to use the same dragon kiln as their ancestors.
Description: Nested in Qianshan County, Anhui Province, Tianzhushan UNESCO Global Geopark takes its name from Tianzhushan Mountain, the “Heavenly Pillar” – a giant granite block rising above the clouds, surrounded by lush green forests. The mountain is also known as Mount Wan, a reference to the ancient fiefdom of the same name – Wan State – one of many vassal states that contended for power during the Spring and Autumn Period of the Zhou Dynasty (1046–256 BCE). Cut across by the Qian and Wan Shui rivers, which meander through the mountains towards the Yangtze River plain, the geopark features more than twenty caves and waterfalls in its lower elevations. It covers 413,000 hectares of evergreen subtropical forest and includes significant areas of paddy fields. With some imagination, the light grey granites of Tianzhushan UNESCO Global Geopark appear to resemble animals and human forms. Visitors may spot a rooster in the “Flying-from-Afar Peaks,” a parrot leaning its head toward the clouds, a toad and a slug. Others see a grandchild whispering to a grandmother, or the five fingers of an open stone hand pointing skyward. These shapes are formed by the way granite responds to weathering agents, either fracturing or shedding layers like an onion. For geologists, these 800 million-year-old rocks reveal valuable insights into Earth’s history. During the Triassic Period (around 240 million years ago), the region was part of a subduction zone that pushed older rocks deep into the mantle. There, they were subjected to extreme pressure and temperature, transforming into what geologists classify as ultra-high-pressure metamorphic rocks. These rocks were later brought back to the surface by the same tectonic forces that once buried them. Their presence records the full cycle of plate collision, subduction, and uplift, and they are internationally recognised for their scientific significance.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: In the southern part of the geopark, Doumu village is the home of an ancient pottery culture dating back 6,000 years. To this day, local artisans use the same dragon kiln as their ancestors, continuing a tradition rooted in the region’s distinctive red clay-rich rocks. This material has supported generations of craftsmanship and cultural continuity. The same geological formations that enabled this enduring pottery heritage have also preserved numerous vertebrate fossils from the Paleogene (66–23 million years ago), many of which exhibit characteristics unique to Asia. The geopark’s cultural heritage dates back to the reign of Emperor Xian, the last emperor of the Eastern Han Dynasty (189–220 CE), a period often regarded as a golden age in Chinese history. The region is also associated with the Qiao Sisters, figures featured in the 14th-century historical novel Romance of the Three Kingdoms, which recounts the division of China into the Cao Wei, Shu Han, and Eastern Wu dynasties. Tianzhushan UNESCO Global Geopark integrates geological heritage with education, environmental protection, and sustainable livelihoods. Educational activities serve tourists, geological professionals, residents, and students through outdoor interpretation, a geo-museum, science communication materials, documentaries, seminars, and field exploration. The geopark prioritises geo-environmental protection, supports green industries such as geotourism, ecological agriculture, and forestry, and enforces strict environmental standards. It also promotes local culture, supports the development of cultural industries, and raises awareness of environmental stewardship to support the long-term sustainability of the local economy and society.
Quote: “At the origin of Asian mammals”

Introduction EN: Enjoy a hike on the Jade Belt Road. Alternatively, visitors can walk or cycle on the Erhai Ecological Corridor.Explore the popular science and cultural stories of Cangshan and Erhai Lake at the Geopark Museum and the Erhai Museum.
Description: The rugged nature of Mount Cangshan Geopark, with deep valleys, cliffs, and canyons, has given form to multiple ecosystems—tropical and subtropical forests, temperate-boreal forests, as well as savannas and grasslands. These are home to several protected animals, such as the clouded leopard, Hume’s pheasant, the black stork, and the dwarf musk deer. Still, even though one can find remarkable wildlife and landscapes, a small part of the geopark, particularly in the lowlands surrounding Erhai Lake, is also used for agriculture and animal husbandry. Although the Cang Mountains, as they are also known locally, form a relatively short mountain range of about 50 km, they feature 19 peaks, with the tallest being Malong at 4,122 metres. This serrated alpine landscape has developed an immense drainage network, from which thousands of picturesque creeks flow between each of the summits, and waterfalls cascade untroubled through ancient rocks. With a geological evolution spanning around 2,000 million years and strata from four eras between the Proterozoic and the Cenozoic, the region showcases several key relics of tectonic movements that took place during that period. One distinctive feature is the abundance of metamorphic rocks locally known as China Daliyan (China marble). Mount Cangshan is also linked with pivotal geological events and significant geological formations in China, making it a key site for observing China’s Quaternary glaciations. In 1937, H. V. Wissmann, an Austrian scholar, referred to the glacial activity in the area as the “Dali Glacial Period” and considered it representative of the most recent glacial period of the Late Quaternary (2.58 million years ago to the present). This glacial period produced two types of relics: glacial deposits and glaciated landforms. The Chinese Geological Survey has adopted it as China’s reference for both international and domestic glacial comparison, and Mount Cangshan’s glacial relics provide the best sources for studying the China Dali Glacial Period.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Dali was once one of the 14 largest cities in the world and was known as the “Famous Literature State”. The region, where Mount Cangshan is the most prominent geographical feature, has been inhabited for over 5,000 years. Today, its cultural heritage is reflected in the traditions of the different ethnic groups that live in the area, including Bai, Han, Yi and Hui. Situated at the crossroads of the ancient Southern Silk Road and the Ancient Tea Horse Road, the geopark is shaped by a unique multi-ethnic culture. It is home to eight nationally recognised intangible cultural heritage elements, including Raosanling of the Bai, the Sanyue Street Fair, and Bai Tie-dye Craftsmanship. The geopark actively supports the transmission and promotion of intangible heritage. Traditional practices such as Bai Tie-dye Craftsmanship, Xiaguan compressed tea production, and embroidery are used to encourage cultural and creative enterprises. These initiatives aim to integrate local heritage into the economy, support the development of products with distinctive cultural characteristics, and foster sustainable local industries.
Quote: “A sealed book of natural geology that has been written for over 2 billion years by nature”

Introduction EN: Take a hike along the 2 km path to the Ryvarden cultural lighthouse, passing through 1.5 billion-year-old, ice-polished Auge gneiss and enjoying breathtaking views of the Hardangerfjord and volcanic seabed formations.Discover the charm of Espevær Village, a scenic collection of small islets with no cars and a winter population of around 45. Once a bustling hub for 19th-century herring fisheries, it remains a peaceful retreat today.Experience the geological wonder of Skjervika, an early Stone Age quarry for red microcrystalline quartz (jasper), formed by ancient hydrothermal sea floor volcanic activity. Accessible via a scenic path from Berge or by boat.
Description: The geological landscape of Sunnhordland presents a remarkable narrative of Earth's dynamic history, featuring facinating examples of glacial erosion shaped during 30–40 ice ages. At its heart, the Hardangerfjord Fault marks a boundary separating a billion years of geological evolution, illustrating the extraordinary processes that shape continents and societies. The geopark showcases how volcanic systems built continents: at the place where two tectonic plates converge, the compressed plate crumples before being uplifted to form a mountain range in a process known as orogeny. Two of the largest orogenic belts on Earth meet in the geopark. On the south side lie rocks related to a continental volcanic arc (1.5 billion years ago) and, on the north side, lies bedrock from the oceanic crust and an island arc system (500–450 million years ago). Sunnhordland UNESCO Global Geopark vividly demonstrates these processes through the remnants of the ancient Iapetus sea, where tectonic activity created cracks in the oceanic crust, driving volcanic eruptions that built towering volcanoes. These processes formed the oceanic crust and island arc system found on the north side of the Hardangerfjord. Meanwhile, the south side reveals rocks from the ancient Baltica continent, a fragment of Earth's crust dating back 1.6 billion years. The collision of the continents Laurentia and Baltica initiated the formation of the colossal Caledonian Mountains—once reaching heights of 8,000 to 9,000 meters. This collision was a pivotal step in assembling the supercontinent Pangea. Today, the remnants of this immense orogenic event can be seen in Sunnhordland, where the rocks tell the story of an ancient seabed's journey through volcanism, tectonic uplift, and metamorphism. Glacial activity has further sculpted the region. The glacially carved Hardangerfjord stands as one of the world's deepest and most beautiful fjords, flanked by alpine landscapes, fertile moraines, U-shaped valleys, and the iconic Folgefonna glacier. Across the geopark, glacial striations, potholes, and erratic boulders serve as natural archives of the ice ages, preserving evidence of their long, icy journeys.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Sunnhordland’s rich geological resources have played a crucial role in shaping the livelihoods and cultural identity of its inhabitants for thousands of years. Hespriholmen, one of Northern Europe’s oldest continuously operating quarries, provided greenstone for axe production for over 5,700 years, contributing to the region’s early trade networks and tool-making traditions. Today, remnants of this quarry showcase the ingenuity of early communities who recognised and utilised the area's geological wealth. Mining has been an essential part of Sunnhordland's economy, with resources such as pyrite, copper, and soapstone being extracted at various periods. The quarry at Moster Amfi, which once provided marble for construction, has been repurposed into a cultural centre, preserving the geological heritage while serving as a hub for community engagement and tourism. Maritime traditions have been deeply embedded in Sunnhordland’s culture, with the Hardangerfjord serving both as a natural barrier and a vital transportation route. Local shipyards in Rosendal built the legendary Gjøa, the vessel Roald Amundsen, the famous Norwegian Explorer, used to navigate the Northwest Passage from 1903 to 1905, showcasing the region’s expertise in wooden shipbuilding. The enduring tradition of the 'Færing' boat, a design unchanged since the Viking Age, continues to be a symbol of the region's connection to the sea. Sunnhordland has also been a pioneer in sustainable energy. Since 1952, hydropower from Folgefonna has powered local homes and industries, including energy-intensive aluminium production in Husnes, which today boasts one of the lowest carbon footprints in the world. The completion of Norway’s largest wind farm in 2010, with 55 turbines generating 443 GWh annually, further cements the region's role as a leader in renewable energy.

Introduction EN: Observe 30 million years of geological history at Chibidanya, where interlaced sandstone and conglomerate layers reveal changing palaeoclimates and striking red cliffs.Witness the iconic Danxia landforms of Danxiashan, where red sandstone cliffs, sculpted over 140 million years, form spectacular peaks, pillars, and gorges shaped by water and time.
Description: Danxia means “rosy-red clouds,” a name that perfectly describes the multi-layered red sandstones and conglomerates formed by fluvial deposition between 140 and 65 million years ago, and shaped by millions of years of uplift, weathering, and erosion. Northeast of Shaoguan City in Guangdong Province, Danxiashan’s landscape is of exceptional beauty, with spectacular peaks, pillars, cliffs, and imposing gorges through which rivers wind and majestic waterfalls drop dozens of metres. Approximately 140 million years ago, Danxiashan was an intermountain basin within the Nanling Mountains. Over the course of the Cretaceous period, from 140 to 66 million years ago, floods and rivers carried sediments of silt and gravel from the surrounding hills, gradually depositing them in the basin. The hot and humid conditions, coupled with oxidation, transformed these sediments into distinctive red sandstone and gravel formations known geologically as Red Beds. As the land in the region uplifted, water erosion further sculpted the landscape, resulting in the breathtaking red walls and cliffs seen today—known as the Danxia landforms. In Danxiashan UNESCO Global Geopark, visitors can witness the remarkable shapes and formations of the Danxia landscapes, gaining insights into their evolution over the past 140 million years, from their origins in a basin to the majestic mountains they are today.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Alongside its geological significance, Danxiashan UNESCO Global Geopark also holds considerable cultural and archaeological value. It is the discovery site of prehistoric ‘Maba Man,’ who lived in the area around 129,000 years ago. It is also the birthplace of the 4,000-year-old Nian Yu Zhuan culture. According to legend, Emperor Shun (2233–2184 BC) visited the region, played the local Shao Music, and named the mountain Shao Shi. Since then, Danxiashan has been recognised as a renowned scenic site. Hundreds of rock carvings from the Tang and Song Dynasties (1,500 to 1,000 years ago) remain well preserved. Together with ancient villages, temples, and tombs, these cultural elements illustrate the long-standing interaction and harmony between people and the natural environment. The inhabitants of Danxiashan include the Hakkas and Tanka people. Over a thousand years ago, the Hakkas migrated from the north and settled in the small plain near the Jinjiang River at the mountain’s foothills. They formed more than 70 ancient villages, with each family bearing a distinct surname such as Li, Zhang, Wu, Zhou, Liu, and others. Agriculture was their primary livelihood. Surrounding Danxiashan, a wealth of intangible cultural heritage continues to be preserved and practiced, including the Yuejiege (Songs of Sister Yue), the vibrant Incense Dragon Dance, the Tea-leaf Picking Opera, Danxia ormosia hand-knitting, Baimao Tea from Renhua County, and the traditional rice wine of Shitang Town.
Quote: “The name Danxia means rosy red clouds and perfectly describes the appearance of this geological wonder”

Introduction EN: Experience the Salauat Yiyiny Festival, an internationally recognised folklore event celebrating Bashkir traditions. Activities include a yurt competition, kuresh wrestling, horse races, and performances by ethnic groups from around the world.Relax at the Karatau Recreation Centre, a community-run retreat on the banks of the Yuruzan River. Enjoy fishing for local species, a wood-fired sauna, and peaceful picnic areas, all supporting sustainable tourism in the geopark.Ski at Berkut Ski Resort, with three slopes for skiers and snowboarders, a tubing run, and cross-country trails through scenic forest landscapes.
Description: Spread across the rocky ridges and deep gorges of the Yangan-Tan Range, and covered by vibrant forests of conifers and a wide variety of deciduous trees—home to bears, wolves, lynx, and deer—Yangan-Tau UNESCO Global Geopark, located in the southern part of the Ural Mountains in the Russian Federation, is a remote and wild landscape. Key geosites include Mount Bolshoy Iremel, the highest peak in the Yangan-Tau Range, offering spectacular views of the surrounding terrain; the Taganai Plateau, known for its caves, canyons, and waterfalls; and the Pechishchora River Canyon. The region’s relief consists primarily of a hillocky plain. In the east and south, elevations reach 400–450 metres with rugged topography, while in the west and north, the land flattens and descends to around 190–300 metres. Hills and ridges follow a north–south orientation, aligned with the strike of the main tectonic structures. A defining geological feature of the geopark is Yangantau Mountain—meaning “Burning Mountain” in Bashkir—which exhibits unique thermal anomalies. Temperatures of up to 380 °C have been recorded at a depth of 90 metres, despite the absence of magmatic activity. This phenomenon has both geological and medical significance, with steam and gas emissions used in balneological treatments. The site is listed in the Global Register of the Earth's Geological Heritage under the ProGEO programme.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The region has a long history of human settlement, with archaeological evidence dating back to the Stone Age. Today, the local economy is largely based on farming, mining, and processing industries. The area is rich in natural resources, including deposits of bauxite, limestone, sand-gravel mixtures, cement clays, and silica sand, and has historically been an important source of gold, copper, and iron. Agricultural production focuses on winter rye, spring wheat, oats, barley, and potatoes, along with meat and dairy cattle, horse breeding, and pig farming. The folk craft of borteovoi beekeeping is one of the oldest living cultural traditions in the region and remains actively practised in the Republic of Bashkortostan. This ancient method involves keeping bees in natural and artificial tree hollows—a technique once widespread across Eastern and Central Europe, now preserved almost exclusively in this area. The geopark’s location at the meeting point of Europe and Asia creates ideal conditions for linden forests, which sustain this beekeeping tradition. As part of sustainable tourism efforts, horse-riding routes include visits to traditional bortey sites, where visitors can sample bortey honey and other beekeeping products. Future plans aim to develop dedicated honey tourism experiences, linking the preservation of intangible heritage with local economic development.

Introduction EN: The Royal Hunt Museum (Hunneberg) – an experience centre that explores the royal moose, the nature of the mountains, captivating cultural history, and royal hunting traditions.The region offers outstanding hiking trails such as the Kinnekulleleden – around the table mountain Kinnekulle and through lush deciduous forests and flower-rich pastures.
Description: In west Sweden, between the country’s two largest lakes—Vänern, the third largest in Europe, and Vättern—Platåbergens UNESCO Global Geopark presents a unique landscape of 15 flat-topped table mountains (platåbergen in Swedish). These mountains were shaped by the force of ice and water during the last Ice Age, approximately 115,000 years ago, and rise above the surrounding Västgöta Plain, a landscape of shallow floodplain lakes, undulating ridges, and well-preserved cultural heritage. The geological history of the geopark spans 1.7 billion years, capturing significant events in Earth’s evolution. The region preserves evidence of the Paleoproterozoic and Neoproterozoic orogenies (1,650–950 million years ago), followed by the formation of the sub-Cambrian peneplain (600–550 million years ago)—a flat rock surface that represents the remains of an ancient mountain range. This peneplain, visible in only a few places worldwide, forms the geological foundation of the geopark. The table mountains of Platåbergens were built by layers of Cambrian to Lower Silurian sedimentary rocks (540–400 million years ago), which sit atop the peneplain. Their striking flat-topped formations result from differential erosion, where resistant dolerite sills (300 million years old) protected the underlying rock from glacial and weathering processes. These mountains, along with Quaternary Ice Age deposits, are of international geological significance. Beyond their geological importance, the diverse ecosystems of the geopark support rich biodiversity, including large mammals such as moose, red deer, and fallow deer. The forests, wetlands, and rocky outcrops host a variety of birds of prey, dancing cranes, orchids, and deep spruce forests, contributing to the region’s ecological value. The landscape of Platåbergens transforms throughout the seasons. In winter, the northern lights can sometimes be seen from the flat rock surface of the peneplain at Nordkroken near Vargön. In spring, the region bursts into life with the blossoming cherry trees on Härad, adding a spectacular contrast to the rugged geology of the table mountains.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The Platåbergens UNESCO Global Geopark is deeply intertwined with human history, from early Neolithic settlements to the industrial age. The region’s geology has shaped both the landscape and livelihoods of its inhabitants. The fertile plains of Västgöta, enriched by glacial and limestone-derived soils, have made it one of Sweden’s most productive agricultural areas. For millennia, people have farmed these lands, cultivating crops and raising livestock. Today, this legacy continues, with local producers offering high-quality ingredients and food products, many of which can be experienced through farm shops and local markets. Human presence in the region dates back over 5,000 years, with one of the most significant concentrations of megalithic tombs in northern Europe. The Falbygden area holds around 250 passage tombs from the Funnelbeaker culture (5300–4700 BCE), scattered across the limestone plateaux. These ancient burial sites highlight the long-standing human connection to the land, with ongoing efforts to establish a dedicated megalithic centre to further study and preserve this heritage. The area is also home to one of Sweden’s most important Viking-era discoveries. At Varnhem, on the western slopes of Billingen, the remains of the first known stone church in Sweden were excavated, revealing that Christian Vikings had settled here by the early 11th century. The influential landowner Kata, who commissioned the church, was buried in an elaborate grave with a runestone, marking an important shift in Swedish history. Today, the geopark continues to support local communities through sustainable tourism and cultural initiatives. Historical sites such as Ekehagen’s ancient village allow visitors to experience Sweden’s early history in an open-air setting. Local businesses, from food producers to nature tourism operators, benefit from the growing interest in the region’s natural and cultural heritage. By promoting sustainable land use and conservation, the Platåbergens UNESCO Global Geopark ensures that its landscapes, resources, and traditions remain a foundation for both present and future generations.

Introduction EN: Visit the Mingsha Mountain region to see multicoloured dunes and the sacred Crescent Moon Spring, a site of geological and cultural significance.Experience local traditions through events like the Buddha Bathing Festival and the desert Dragon Boat Festival, which connect Dunhuang’s natural landscape with deep-rooted cultural heritage.
Description: Approximately 1.95 billion years ago, the area surrounding Dunhuang geopark was submerged beneath the vast expanse of an ancient ocean. Over the course of millennia, tremendous tectonic forces and relentless erosion shaped the geopark into the remarkable landscape we witness today. The park's formation predominantly occurred during the Quaternary period, characterised by subsidence, piedmont floods, river deposits, and local lacustrine formations. Continuous uplift, along with the persistent action of erosion, sculpted the land, eventually transforming it into an arid region dominated by the stunning Yardang landform and the captivating Gobi Desert. When embarking on a journey through this geopark, visitors are presented with a multitude of geological marvels. While each site offers its own unique allure, two aspects stand out as must-see attractions—the Yardang landform and the majestic Mingsha Mountain region. Unlike other Yardang landforms, the Yardang bodies in Dunhuang exhibit a remarkable variation in orientation within a relatively small area. A thorough exploration and study of these landforms proves instrumental in understanding the intricacies of arid landscapes, the evolution of paleogeography and paleoclimate, and the formation of distinctive wind-eroded features. The renowned Mingsha Mountain region holds its own allure, captivating visitors with its mesmerising sand dunes. Folklore has it that "the sand mountain will not move for thousands of years, and the clear spring on the sand mountain will not dry up for ten thousand years." Mingsha Mountain’s sands, adorned with five distinct colours and intricate compositions, hold great significance for researchers studying the material composition and origins of these majestic dunes. Amidst this natural marvel lies the sacred Crescent Moon Spring, once believed to be a holy water basin associated with a long-lost temple, obliterated by an evil warlock who failed to damage this revered relic.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: As one delves into the rich tapestry of Dunhuang geopark, it becomes evident that its geological wonders are inextricably intertwined with its profound cultural heritage. Legends and tales narrate the park's historical significance and contribute to the vibrant tapestry of festivals and cultural events that animate its landscapes. One such event is the annual Buddha Bathing Festival, held on the eighth day of the fourth lunar month. During this celebration, residents flock to the Mogao Grottoes, paying homage to the Buddha in a ritual bathing ceremony. This solemn occasion serves as a poignant reminder of the deep spiritual connection between the park’s natural wonders and the local community. Equally captivating is the Dragon Boat Festival, held on the fifth day of the fifth lunar month, where a unique desert dragon boat race takes place within the enchanting confines of Mingsha Mountain. This festival weaves together the vibrant threads of tradition, folklore, and the natural grandeur of the geopark, creating an immersive experience that delights both locals and visitors. Furthermore, Dunhuang geopark stands as a testament to its historical role as a vital waypoint along the ancient Silk Road. Its location along this fabled trade route played a crucial role in connecting civilisations, facilitating cultural exchanges, and fostering economic prosperity.
Quote: “Land of yardangs: rock protuberance shaped by wind erosion”

Introduction EN: Visit the Neixiang Local Magistrate’s Office, considered the best-preserved magistrate’s office from China’s feudal era, with over 280 buildings across 2,000 square metres.Explore the Great Wall Ruin Site of Chu State, known as the “father of the Great Wall”, built during the Chunqiu period and among the earliest Great Wall structures in China.
Description: Located in the hinterland of the Funiushan Mountain Range, Funiushan UNESCO Global Geopark derives its name from the prominent Mt. Funiushan. The mountain's name has multiple interpretations, one of which suggests it resembles a sleeping bull when viewed from above, as described in the Henan Annal during the Sui and Tang dynasties. The grandeur of Funiushan is characterised by its vast expanse, steep peaks, and narrow ridges, with jagged summits reaching altitudes of over 1,500 metres. The geopark preserves a wide range of geoheritage, including palaeontological relics such as a dinosaur fossil group from the Cretaceous period, granite landscapes, karst landforms, and distinctive pond and pool waterscapes. Among the most important geosites is the Sanlimiao Dinosaur Egg Fossil Locality, situated in Xixia County, where a significant number of dinosaur egg fossils have been unearthed. This site is a key component of the global Cretaceous dinosaur record and holds immense scientific value for research into palaeobiology, the evolution and extinction of Cretaceous dinosaurs, and broader geological questions related to cataclysmic events. The Shangnan–Danfeng Fracture Belt serves as a structural suture zone between the North China Plate and the Yangtze Plate. It marks the boundary fracture that once divided ancient China into its southern and northern regions and is of major importance for understanding the tectonic evolution of the North China Plate and the Qinling orogenic belt. Another remarkable site is the Jiguan (Cockscomb) Cave Scenic Area, a natural limestone formation with a distinctive ladder-like pattern dating back approximately 534 to 438 million years. The cave itself formed between 1.8 and 0.13 million years ago. Extending 5,600 metres in length and with a vertical drop of 138 metres, Jiguan Cave features spectacular underground water formations, including subsurface rivers, ponds, pools, splashes, and drops. These have given rise to non-gravitational water travertine deposits, with stalactite landforms in various shapes such as stone pillars, stalagmites, stone shields, stone curtains, crystal needles, and stone flowers. Revered as "the No.1 Cave in north China", it serves as a key site for cave observation and research.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Funiushan UNESCO Global Geopark lies within the culturally rich cities of Nanyang and Luoyang, whose long histories have shaped the heritage of the region. The geopark is home to a range of significant cultural sites, including the Neixiang Local Magistrate’s Office, the Great Wall Ruin Site of Chu State, and the Laojunshan Laozi Cultural Buildings, as well as temples and memorial sites such as Fan Li Memorial Site, Yi Yin Temple, Zhang Liang Temple, and Yuhuang Pavilion. The geopark also preserves diverse forms of intangible cultural heritage. It holds one world intangible heritage element—Beating the Spring Ox in the 24 Solar Terms—and four nationally recognised traditions: Xiping folk songs, Zhenping jade carving, Wanbang, and pyrography - the art of decorating wood or other materials with burn marks. Local craftsmanship is promoted through cooperation with Nanyang pyrography workshops to produce cultural and creative products featuring elements of the geopark. In parallel, Funiushan UNESCO Global Geopark actively supports environmental education and community engagement through school partnerships and outreach initiatives. These programmes introduce young people to the region’s biodiversity, karst landscapes, and cultural heritage.
Quote: “Thirteen different types of fossil dinosaur eggs have been discovered and are on display, including two very rare specimens”

Introduction EN: Visit the Tin Hau Temples at Kat O and Leung Shuen Wan, important cultural landmarks and historic buildings.Explore the Hip Tin Temple, a site of great religious and cultural significance.Discover the Lai Chi Wo rural revitalization project, recognised for sustainable development in the 2020 UNESCO Asia-Pacific Awards for Cultural Heritage Conservation.
Description: Hong Kong UNESCO Global Geopark boasts a diverse landscape, including low-elevation flatlands along the coast and picturesque islands adorned with cliffs that gracefully meet the sea. It is a place where nature and human heritage seamlessly intertwine, offering visitors a multifaceted experience. With a geological record spanning more than 370 million years, from the Devonian to the Paleogene, and a diversity of ancient environments that over time changed from a large river delta flowing into a shallow sea, to a territory of lava-spewing volcanoes, and finally a tropical lagoon, Hong Kong UNESCO Global Geopark bears witness to a planet in constant change. One of the most impressive geological formations of the geopark, and part of the First 100 IUGS Geological Heritage Sites, is the rhyolitic columnar rock formation found in the High Island Reservoir in Sai Kung East Country Park. Unlike other hexagonal rock columns found around the world—usually composed of dark-grey basalt with low silica content—the High Island Formation is made of light-coloured rhyolitic volcanic rock that is rich in silica. The formation comprises a huge number of columns, which are large, well-preserved and widely distributed, making it a globally rare and iconic geological wonder. Visitors can hike and observe these rhyolitic rock columns up close on the High Island Geo Trail along the East Dam, or take a boat tour for a panoramic view from afar. Tung Ping Chau is a picturesque island with the youngest rock formation in Hong Kong, consisting of shale, a fine-grained sedimentary rock. Aside from the shale formation, which is well exposed along the island’s coast, visitors can observe a wide range of sedimentary features and coastal erosion landforms. The roughly 6-km-long Ping Chau Country Trail winds around the island’s coastline, allowing hikers to visit many significant geosites. On Sharp Island, there are large boulders mostly composed of rhyolite and granite (quartz monzonite). These granite boulders exhibit extraordinary cracks and resemble Hong Kong’s iconic snack, the pineapple bun. Appropriately, they have been named the Pineapple Bun Rocks. There is also a tombolo that emerges at low tide, allowing visitors to walk across it to the small island of Kiu Tau and climb to its highest point. From there, visitors can enjoy panoramic views of the tombolo, the Sai Kung Inner Sea, and the Clearwater Bay Peninsula.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Due to its unique proximity to Hong Kong’s renowned financial centre, the Hong Kong UNESCO Global Geopark is a one-of-a-kind “Geopark in the City,” just a one-hour bus or car ride away. A visit to the Hong Kong Geopark offers encounters with protected wildlife thriving among a wide range of geological features. Beyond its geological significance, the geopark is rich in cultural traditions and history. Local communities, including Hakka villagers and fishing families, maintain distinctive customs, festivals, and ways of life. These traditions form a vibrant tapestry of intangible heritage, reflected in architectural styles, seasonal celebrations, traditional songs, and healing practices. Coastal residents maintain a deep spiritual connection with the sea, expressed in rituals that honour sea gods and goddesses. On the island of Kat O, believed to be blessed with a “dragon vein,” residents celebrate the Da Jiu Festival to nourish this sacred energy through community gatherings and offerings. Several sites within the geopark have received international recognition for cultural heritage conservation. The Hung Shing Temple on Kau Sai Chau received the Outstanding Project Award at the 2000 UNESCO Asia-Pacific Awards for Cultural Heritage Conservation, while St. Joseph's Chapel on Yim Tin Tsai was honoured with the Award of Merit in 2005. These restored sites reflect the ongoing commitment of local communities to preserving their cultural heritage.
Quote: “A city Geopark with rare acidic columns, diverse coastal landforms and a wide range of sedimentary rocks”

Introduction EN: Taste local specialities including pineapple, coffee, red sugar, and black beans, all grown in the geopark region.Explore local crafts such as litchi wood carvings and scented rosewood chains traditionally worn as ornaments.Visit Rongtang village and its 72 lava tube caves, an 800-year-old stone village explored with local guides and connected to traditional legends and practices.
Description: Leiqiong UNESCO Global Geopark is located in southern China, straddling the Qiongzhou Strait. The geology of the area is defined by the Leiqiong Rift Volcanic Belt, and 78 geosites—mostly volcanic—document its complex formation history. Over 100 volcanoes are densely distributed across the geopark, with 38 protected volcanic structures. These include nearly all known volcanic types formed through basaltic and phreatomagmatic eruptions. Particularly notable are the numerous maar craters—broad, low-relief volcanic depressions formed when rising magma interacts explosively with groundwater. Several sea cliffs in the geopark also originated from maar-type explosions. These features represent a highly complete and well-preserved collection of Quaternary volcanoes, and the site is regarded as one of the most significant Quaternary basaltic volcanic regions in China. Among the geopark’s most prominent geological features is Huguangyan Maar Lake, where the first Chinese research on maar lakes was conducted. It remains an important reference site for international cooperation, particularly between Chinese and German scientists. Leiqiong UNESCO Global Geopark also contains a wide variety of lava structures and volcanic landforms, including different types of lava flows and tunnels. These form a natural exhibition of basaltic volcanism and contribute to the park’s scientific and educational value. The geopark is also situated in an ecological transition zone with a high diversity of flora and fauna. Volcanic processes have created fertile red soils that support dense tropical forest, in contrast to the surrounding blue sea and silver beaches. These geological and ecological elements combine to form a dynamic landscape where natural processes and biodiversity coexist.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Leiqiong UNESCO Global Geopark has a long and rich historical and cultural background. The region includes significant cultural heritage sites such as Lengyan Temple, built during the Sui Dynasty (581–618 AD), and the Leizu Ancestral Hall (642 AD). It is also connected to the Ancient Maritime Silk Route, which linked China to overseas countries through trade, communication, and cultural exchange. Across the geopark, more than 20 old villages preserve traditional architectural styles, including stone houses, walls, gates, towers, temples, and basalt-paved passageways. These sites reflect the region’s long-standing interaction between human settlement and volcanic landscapes. Longmen Village, located within what is locally known as the “pineapple sea,” is an example of an active community embedded in the geopark. The village maintains a strong cultural identity based on pineapple cultivation, introduced in the 17th century. The village also reflects how agricultural practices have adapted over time to volcanic soils and economic change. The geopark spans both Haikou City and Zhanjiang City—important coastal cultural centres—where human activity has long coexisted with volcanic features. In Mt. Ma’an Scenic Area near Haikou, visitors can walk along well-developed paths to observe lava flows, tropical forests, and volcanic cones. The area includes science centres and restaurants that serve local cuisine prepared with meat and vegetables grown in the fertile volcanic soil.
Quote: “Maar craters were formed when groundwater came into contact with lava and exploded”

Introduction EN: Discover the Dashiwei tiankeng cluster, featuring 35 spectacular collapsed dolines along the Bailang underground river, including one over 600 metres wide and 613 metres deep.Explore the Sanmenhai karst windows, a unique group of surface openings in the Poxin resurgence area connected to an underground cave river system.
Description: Leye-Fengshan Geopark, nestled between the Yunnan-Guizhou Plateau and the Guangxi Basin, holds a remarkable tapestry of natural wonders within its expansive borders. Rising to its pinnacle, Gaodaping Mount stands tall at an awe-inspiring height of 1,982 metres, while the Liangwanhe River gracefully meanders through its lowest point at 412 metres. Here, the stage is set for a captivating journey into the heart of geological marvels and cultural treasures. Karst formations dominate the landscape of Leye-Fengshan Geopark, displaying their grandeur in various captivating forms such as dolines, karst canyons, poljes, underground rivers, and karst springs—each inviting exploration into hidden realms. Countless caves, adorned with magnificent chambers, beckon adventurous visitors. Unveiling the geological history of the region, the park’s heritage traces back to the Cambrian era over 500 million years ago, as expressed through a diverse array of sedimentary rocks. Amidst this geological spectacle, three captivating wonders demand attention. The Dashiwei tiankeng cluster astounds with its 35 collapsed dolines, nestled along the midstream of the Bailang underground river. Among them, the most spectacular spans a staggering 600 metres and plunges 613 metres into the Earth's depths. The Sanmenhai karst windows, a group of karst features scattered across the Poxin resurgence area, form a mesmerizing ensemble. These intricate landforms are shaped by the convergence of six formations and harmonise with the serenity of an underground cave river. Adding to the geological diversity, Luomeidong Cave reveals its splendour across two levels. The upper level, dry and serene, showcases a captivating array of lotus rimstone formations in various shapes and sizes. The "king of lotus rimstones" commands particular attention with its colossal 9.3-metre diameter.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Leye-Fengshan UNESCO Global Geopark spans the counties of Leye and Fengshan and is home to 11 Indigenous communities, with the Zhuang ethnic group making up more than half of the local population. The region combines agricultural livelihoods with significant efforts to conserve biodiversity, and large areas of the park continue to support protected species of plants and animals. The geopark has actively worked to transition to more sustainable economic practices. Traditional agricultural production—previously based on rice, corn, sweet potato, canola, and sugarcane—has been transformed toward organic crops including walnut, chestnut, aniseed, kiwifruit, tea, and Roxburgh rose. These are promoted for their higher market value, contributing to increased income for local farmers. Six art processing enterprises and eight agricultural product enterprises operate within the geopark, supporting local employment. Local craftsmanship includes weaving methods from the Zhuang community, and many products are distributed through commercial platforms to reach wider markets. Tourism has become an increasingly important economic activity. The geopark features 39 scenic routes, offering hiking, cycling, and boat tours that allow visitors to experience the geological and cultural landscape firsthand. The area is also known for geotourism events and sports-based tourism. Activities such as the China Rock Climbing League Contest, Leye Hiking Contest, Leye Outdoor Sports Cross-Country Challenge, and the Chinese-Foreign Cave Expedition take place annually. Education is a key focus of the geopark’s work. The Leye Rock Climbing School runs a monthly “Journey to the Hidden Earth” programme for students. Cultural and promotional events—such as the 3rd March Festival and the Bulong Song Festival—celebrate local traditions and are also used to strengthen cooperation with sister geoparks including Danxiashan, Yandangshan, Zhangjiajie, and Lushan.
Quote: “The territory of caves and of the world’s longest natural bridge”

Introduction EN: The Traditional Torch Festival is one of the most important and splendid festivals in southwestern China.The Naigu (or ‘black’) Stone Forest in the north of the geopark features dark-coloured dolomitic limestone.Changhu Lake, surrounded by green hills, is a natural karst lake where traditional festivals are held, and also makes for a good picnic spot.
Description: Literally “stone forest”, Shillin Geopark got its name from the region’s distinctive karstic landform part of the Yunnan karst plateau.  The Major Stone Forest is deemed the quintessential stone forest worldwide.  In Shilin, visitors will also enjoy beautiful views of rivers, lakes, and green trees. Many of the plant and animal species living in the park are protected. The area’s geological history traces back to the late Palaeozoic era. Shilin’s bedrock consists primarily of Devonian, Carboniferous, and Permian shallow marine carbonate deposits. These sediments, originally laid down in an ancient sea, were later uplifted and subjected to long-term weathering and dissolution processes. This resulted in one of the world’s most complete and varied expressions of karst development, characterised by striking limestone formations in the shape of pillars, swords, mushrooms, and towers. The Major Stone Forest, one of the park’s most iconic sites, displays dense clusters of stone pillars rising 20–50 metres high, creating a forest-like appearance on the horizon. These geomorphological features are not only scientifically significant, offering insight into karst evolution over multiple stages, but also hold substantial aesthetic and cultural value.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The Indigenous Sani People of the Yi ethnic group have lived in the Shilin UNESCO Global Geopark for more than 2,000 years. Their culture is closely tied to the karst landscape, with stories such as the widely celebrated epic Ashima reflecting this connection. Geological sites across the geopark are interpreted in relation to this legend, and the Ashima Intangible Culture Exhibition Hall—housed within the Geopark Museum—plays an important role in presenting Yi traditions. The geopark supports the preservation and transmission of Yi intangible cultural heritage through partnerships with the local tourism bureau, cultural museum, and intangible cultural heritage protection centre. Intangible cultural heritage elements include Yi embroidery, dance, music, language, wrestling, religious customs, and the Traditional Torch Festival—southwestern China’s most significant Yi celebration, held according to the lunar calendar.
Quote: “Shilin delights visitors with its fantastic karst formations while educating them about fundamental geology”

Introduction EN: Experience the vibrant village life of Chanxinju, where homestays, workshops and a vegetarian restaurant offer a model for sustainable tourism.Marvel at the quartzite cliffs of Shaoshi Mountain, folded by the Zhongyue Movement and a key site for understanding regional tectonics.Visit the iconic Shaolin Temple, a traditional Buddhist site and birthplace of Shaolin Kung Fu, still active under the guidance of Abbot Shi Yongxin.
Description: Songshan UNESCO Global Geopark stretches east–west across the mountains and ridges of Ma An, Five Fo, Dan Yang, Shaoshi, and Taishi. These striking hills rise straight up, each seemingly higher than the one before, making for a grand setting. It consists of five scenic areas – Mount Taishi, Mount Shaoshi, Mount Wufo, Mount Wuzhi, and Shicong River – revealing 3.6 billion years of geologic history in a region described by geologists as “Five-Era-in-One” for its continuous and clearly exposed stratigraphic sequence. The geopark preserves rock layers from the Archean, Proterozoic, Paleozoic, Mesozoic and Cenozoic eras, and provides one of the best places to study the evolution of the Earth’s crust. It is also internationally significant for recording three major Precambrian tectonic movements – the Songyang Movement (around 2.5 billion years ago), the Zhongyue Movement (around 1.85 billion years ago), and the Shaolin Movement (around 0.8 billion years ago) – which created the angular unconformity interfaces visible today, especially in Shaoshi Mountain.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The area surrounding Songshan UNESCO Global Geopark is home to an exceptional concentration of cultural heritage, including ten temple monasteries, five shrines, five palaces, three Taoist temples, four Buddhist convents, and more than 270 pagodas. Mount Songshan itself represents a confluence of Buddhist, Taoist, Confucian, wushu, and folk cultures. In 2010, UNESCO inscribed the “Historic Monuments of Dengfeng in ‘The Centre of Heaven and Earth’” as a World Cultural Heritage site. This includes eleven historical structures across eight locations, among them Shaolin Temple, the Three Han Que Gates, Zhongyue Temple, Songyue Temple Pagoda, Huishan Temple, and Songyang Academy. In addition to the World Heritage sites, the geopark contains nationally recognised cultural heritage sites, such as the Shaolin Temple Pagoda Forest and the Astronomical Observatory. These cultural sites are not only preserved but actively integrated into the geopark’s educational and visitor programming. On site, visitors can engage with traditional practices such as calligraphy and the making of prayer beads, as well as attend performances including the Zen music festival, which showcases the area’s intangible heritage.
Quote: “Geological and cultural heritage together in an ancient landscape”

Introduction EN: Make sure not to miss the traditional Nuo Dance, dating back to the Shang Dynasty 3,000 years ago, and performed as an exorcism ritual.Follow the hiking route through Zhaixia Grand Canyon to the historic Jingui Temple.Explore the cycling and walking trail that runs from Jixi Village to Luozhu Rock.
Description: Taining UNESCO Global Geopark is located in the northwest of Fujian Province, on the southeastern side of the mid-Wuyi Mountains. The landscape consists of mountains, hills and basins, with elevation decreasing from northwest to southeast. Baishiding, the highest peak in the area at 1,858 metres, is one of the tallest granitic peaks in southeastern China. The geopark preserves a wide range of landforms shaped by different geological substrates: steep volcanic mountains, low and hilly Danxia landforms, and gently undulating metamorphic and red-bed landscapes. The geopark’s geological heritage records five major tectonic stages and spans sedimentary, volcanic, intrusive and metamorphic rocks. It developed on the Wuyi mountain range, situated along the Cathaysian block, and has remained on the active tectonic margin of the West Pacific since the Late Triassic, approximately 200 million years ago. Volcanic activity and magma intrusions have occurred multiple times, and several types of geological basins—coal-bearing, oil-bearing, double-peak volcanic, and red-bed—overlap across the territory. The Shaowu–Heyuan Fault is the main structural feature. Taining is especially renowned for its Danxia landforms, formed from Cretaceous red beds, and granite egg-shaped formations. The ancient planation surface, deep-incised meandering canyons, early-stage peak clusters, and striking red cliffs offer high scientific and aesthetic value. Key geosites include Hongshi Mountain, Zhaixia Grand Canyon, and the Golden Lake area. Features such as the Shangqing Stream meander, Shiwang Grand Canyon, Danxia caves, and stone pillars provide insight into the region’s complex geological evolution.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Taining UNESCO Global Geopark supports sustainable rural development by integrating geotourism with local livelihoods. In recent years, six geovillages have been established, each with distinct characteristics that reflect both geological and cultural identity. These villages are now key components of the geopark’s visitor routes, offering residents new economic opportunities through tourism. Shuiji Village, once a low-income farming community, is a notable example—local farmers now lead tourism activities, generating income while strengthening ties to their land. The geopark also plays a significant role in preserving and promoting intangible cultural heritage. Efforts include the protection of traditional practices such as the Taining Meilin Opera, recognised at national level, alongside other locally valued forms of cultural expression. These are sustained through community partnerships, public events, and educational outreach, helping to maintain cultural continuity across generations. Geoscience education is a core part of the geopark’s mission. Programmes are tailored to different age groups, from schoolchildren to young docents, and include outdoor learning activities and student-led science communication. In parallel, the geopark contributes to risk preparedness and climate resilience. It supports public awareness of geo-hazards through early warning systems, and runs regular education campaigns on forest fire and typhoon prevention across key sites within the territory.
Quote: “Taining offers a wealth of geological and cultural sites to visitors”

Introduction EN: Fans of hiking and climbing shouldn’t miss the Taishan climbing route from Daimiao to Yuhuangding.Experience the dramatic relief and neotectonic landforms of Mount Taishan, including scenic features like Caishixi Stream and Zuixin Garden.
Description: Taishan UNESCO Global Geopark, located in the midwest of Shandong Province, occupies a key position at the eastern edge of the North China Plain. The geopark lies to the north of Qufu, the hometown of Confucius, and east of the Yellow River. Mount Taishan rises prominently from a group of surrounding mountains, offering striking geological formations and extensive scientific value. This ancient land has witnessed dynamic and violent geological events dating back approximately 2.8 billion years. The park contains rich and diverse geoheritage, long recognised by national and international geologists. The Taishan Group-Complex includes basic igneous rocks such as komatiite and multiple phases of Precambrian intrusive rocks formed between 2.73 and 1.8 billion years ago. These provide key insights into Archean–Proterozoic geology, including the formation of granite–greenstone belts and the broader geodynamic processes involved in the evolution of Earth’s early continental crust in East China. A complete and well-preserved Cambrian stratigraphic section, located in Zhangxia County within the geopark, allows researchers and visitors alike to explore more than 50 million years of early palaeontological history. The sequence contains abundant trilobite fossils and other Cambrian fauna, aiding scientific understanding of regional and international age correlations for the Cambrian Period. The influence of more recent neotectonic activity is also visible across the landscape, contributing to the dramatic relief of Mount Taishan and shaping its distinct landforms. Among the notable features within the geopark are Caishixi Stream, a 5-kilometre-long scenic waterway, and Zuixin Garden, both of which provide further opportunities to engage with the area’s geological and geomorphological evolution.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Taishan UNESCO Global Geopark has a cultural history spanning over 5,000 years and is home to numerous historic and cultural sites, including the Dai Temple and Azure Clouds Temple.
