The geopark also features an integrated museum where visitors can explore the region’s natural and cultural heritage, and learn about the importance of safeguarding its aesthetic, ecological, and scientific values. Taishan UNESCO Global Geopark places protection at the core of its development strategy. Its natural landscapes, geological heritage, and ecosystems are subject to strict conservation measures. Tourism activities are managed within the limits of environmental capacity to ensure long-term sustainability. Drawing on its unique geological features, including the rare komatiite and the Taishan Group-Complex, the geopark supports Tai’an City in achieving balanced environmental, cultural, and economic development. Through activities such as sightseeing, scientific research, ecotourism, and cultural tourism, the geopark creates employment opportunities, raises local living standards, and promotes community wellbeing. This integrated approach ensures that geoheritage is protected while contributing to the sustainable development of the local economy and society.
Quote: “Zuixin stone and barrel-shaped structure, Popular Bridge quartz diorite, Fan cliff, Three large faults, Summit stone”

Introduction EN: The region is also known for traditional festivals such as Inti Raymi, a religious ceremony from the Inca Empire in honour of the god Inti (Quechua for "sun"), the most venerated Inca deity, celebrating the winter solstice.Relax in hot springs heated by the region’s volcanic systems, popular with visitors.
Description: Travelling from Quito to Ibarra, the largest city in the Imbabura UNESCO Global Geopark, one will inevitably circle around the Imbabura volcano. This inactive stratovolcano, rising to 4,621 metres above sea level, dominates the landscape with its rock crest towering above San Pablo Lake. While nearby Cayambe reaches 5,790 metres, making Imbabura seem modest in comparison, its steep, water-carved slopes and imposing presence remain striking. Although it has been dormant for around 7,500 years, Imbabura is not considered extinct. The geopark spans the western foothills of the Cordillera Real and Cordillera Occidental and is home to twelve other volcanoes. Some, like Chachimbiro and Cuicocha, are potentially active. Others, such as Pilavo, Parulo, Yanahurcu de Piñan, Pulumbura, Cotacachi, Cubilche, Cushnirumi, Cusin, Fuya-Fuya and Mojanda, are dormant or extinct. This volcanic terrain provides habitats for the Andean bear—the only bear species native to South America—and the Andean condor, one of the world’s largest flying birds. The geology of the Imbabura UNESCO Global Geopark reflects the formation of the Andes, the world’s longest continental mountain range, stretching 8,900 kilometres through seven countries. The Andes began forming during the Triassic period (252–201 million years ago), when the oceanic Nazca Plate began subducting beneath the South American Plate. This process generated both uplift, creating mountains, and volcanic activity through magma formation. In Imbabura, volcanic activity has been ongoing for over 60 million years. The volcanoes are the key geoheritage of the geopark, many of which can be explored on foot. The Gorki Campusano Trail, a 14.5-kilometre route, follows the rim of the Cuicocha volcanic caldera—a three-kilometre-wide lake at 3,256 metres altitude. Cuicocha takes its name from the Kichwa Indigenous language, meaning “Guinea Pig Lake”.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The Imbabura UNESCO Global Geopark is the ancestral territory of Kichwa Indigenous peoples, including the Cayambi, Otavalo, Zuleta, and Natabuela communities. It is also home to Afro-Ecuadorian peoples, as well as Montuvio and Awa communities, creating a multicultural territory where diverse traditions and identities coexist. The Andean volcanoes of the region, including Imbabura, are deeply embedded in Indigenous worldviews and are seen both as spiritual presences and as the source of fertile soils. These soils support traditional agriculture, including maize, beans and sugarcane—staple crops cultivated for generations. The volcanic terrain has also given rise to the cloud forests of the northern Andes, which reach altitudes of up to 3,000 metres and contribute to the region’s biodiversity and food systems. Volcanic activity also provides opportunities for sustainable development. The hydrothermal systems of the region are being explored for geothermal energy, with drilling in Chachimbiro reaching depths of 2,000 metres and capturing temperatures over 200°C. These geothermal resources offer a renewable energy source while nearby hot springs support local tourism. Traditional knowledge, crafts and gastronomy continue to play an important role in community life and livelihoods. Many entrepreneurs produce and sell handicrafts—such as pottery, embroidery, and wool or wood-based items—using techniques passed down through generations. Local cuisine, based on fresh produce, includes distinctive preparations of pancakes, meats and ice cream. Through such practices, culture is maintained as a living, evolving element of daily life and economic activity.
Quote: “Imbabura: land of lakes and volcanoes, inter-cultural heritage, legends, and more”

Introduction EN: Visit Parangireng Beach to explore pillow lava formations and fossilized foraminifera, unique geological features that reveal the region’s volcanic and marine history.Discover the Bondowoso Coffee site, where coffee plantations coexist with diverse flora and fauna, including rare butterflies like Papilio memnon and Papilio polytes, and shade plants like Suren Toona sureni, and Cinnamomum zeylanicum.
Description: Ijen UNESCO Global Geopark is characterised by a high concentration of volcanic cones, craters, and lava flows, showcasing the complex geological processes that have shaped the region over millions of years. The most prominent attraction within the geopark is Ijen volcano and its crater lake, which is famous for being the most acidic lake in the world, and its otherworldly blue fire phenomenon—a rare sight attributed to the reaction between sulphur and oxygen. While most volcanoes produce red or orange fire, the high sulfur concentrations and temperatures exceeding 360°C in Ijen Crater create a unique environment for the formation of blue fire. This phenomenon is observable only during night-time due to the intensity of sunlight obscuring the visibility of the blue flames. Ijen is one of the most active volcanoes in the Ijen caldera system. Approximately 22 post-caldera volcanic cones were generated inside and on the rim of the caldera. This volcanic activity rises above the limestone basements and tertiary volcanic rock which can be found forming the old hills 50 km south of Ijen. The geopark overlaps with the Belambangan Biosphere Reserve, designated by UNESCO in 2016.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The communities of Ijen maintain a deep connection to their cultural heritage, which is upheld and celebrated through various traditions and ceremonies including the Gandrung Dance of Banyuwangi, performed to the accompaniment of traditional Javanese-Balinese musical instruments. Annual events like the Gandrung Sewu Festival and the Banyuwangi Ethno Carnival not only highlight these rich traditions but also contribute to the local economy by drawing visitors from across Indonesia and beyond. The geopark has made concerted efforts to bridge the communication gap between visitors and local communities. By providing trainings for local guides, the geopark ensures that visitors experience an authentic connection to the region's heritage.  The geopark supports schools of all levels with the teaching of Earth sciences and sustainable living. Its “School Goes to Geopark” programme facilitates student and public visits to various sites within the geopark for hands-on learning. The Geopark Corner initiative supports schools in setting up small information centres, creating outdoor learning spaces within a controlled environment.

Introduction EN: Don’t miss the Holy Water Festival. Unique to Wudalianchi, this vibrant celebration is recognised as part of China’s National Intangible Cultural Heritage.Hike the scenic plank road. This long, wide trail winds around the lakes of Wudalianchi, stretching from the lava plateau to Laoheishan Volcano.
Description: Wudalianchi UNESCO Global Geopark is located in the middle-north part of Heilongjiang Province, China, approximately 380 km from Harbin, the provincial capital, and 230 km from the Russian Federation border city of Blagoveshchensk. Its name means “five connected lakes,” a reference to the lava-dammed lakes that define the landscape — and the local economy, thanks to the region’s commercial mineral water industry. The geopark is internationally renowned for its exceptional volcanic landforms, shaped by eruptions that occurred across different geological periods. Fourteen volcanoes — both ancient and relatively recent, including two that erupted in the 18th century — rise dramatically above the otherwise flat terrain. These include rare features such as driblet cones: miniature lava formations created by droplets of lava projected from gas vents. More than 1,500 such cones have been documented in the park, falling into four distinct types: cone-shaped, tower-shaped, mound-shaped, and corolla-shaped. In addition to its Quaternary volcanic landscapes, the geopark preserves rich geoheritage from the Cambrian and Cretaceous periods, offering an outstanding cross-section of geological time. Its unique combination of undisturbed volcanoes, expansive lava plateaus, mineral-rich springs, and well-preserved geomorphology has earned Wudalianchi the reputation of a “Natural Volcano Museum” and a “Living Textbook on Volcanoes” among geologists.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Wudalianchi UNESCO Global Geopark is home to several Indigenous communities, including the Manchu, Daur, Ewenki, and Oroqen peoples, each with deep-rooted cultural ties to the region. The Daur people, believed by some historians to descend from the Khitan of the Liao Dynasty, maintain distinctive cultural practices, including traditional garments such as the “Hashmi” leather robe worn by men and embroidered gowns worn by women. Daur bridal dress styles are uniquely ornate, differing from the Phoenix coronas of the Han tradition, and are rich with ethnic symbolism. The Oroqen, historically known as “the People in the Forest,” preserve a hunting-based culture deeply connected to nature. Their traditional clothing is made from roe deer skin, including coats and vividly lifelike head caps shaped and sewn to resemble roe deer, using roe deer tendons and fur. These garments, decorated with motifs such as “bow cut” or “cloud roll,” are both functional and symbolic, designed for warmth and camouflage. Similarly, the Ewenki people, whose name means “People Living in the Mountains,” have long relied on leather garments and reindeer for winter travel, referring to their animals as the “Boats of the Forest.” Cultural storytelling and spiritual practices are vital to the region’s intangible heritage. One of Wudalianchi’s most distinctive cultural traditions is the Holy Water Festival, a National Intangible Cultural Heritage event. According to local legend, the festival began after a Daur hunter was led by a deer to a healing spring at the foot of Yaoquan Volcano. The spring’s waters were said to cure ailments and were attributed to the intervention of the Holy Water Goddess. Today, the festival—held annually during the Dragon Boat Festival—draws together multiple ethnic groups. Families gather to bathe in and celebrate around the springs with bonfires, food, and traditional songs. Before leaving, they tie red silk to tree branches to symbolise health and protection for the coming year. Wudalianchi’s commitment to education and public engagement is exemplified by its Global Geopark Museum, located in the heart of the park, covering topics from global volcanism and ecology to the cultural heritage of the region. Designed for hands-on, inquiry-based learning, the museum also includes research labs, a specimen collection, and a 3D cinema.
Quote: “A Natural Volcano Museum with every volcanic landscape that one expects to find”

Introduction EN: Visitors should not miss the Yumushan Rock Paintings, the Heiyao Cave Traditional Steel Furnaces, the Gaoche Domed Tents, the Machangtan Battle Site, and the Kanglong Temple.Make sure to listen to Yugur folk songs and discover unique oral literature.
Description: Zhangye UNESCO Global Geopark, located in the northwest of China and known for its colourful hills, centres on Sunan County—the only Yugur autonomous county in China. In the heart of the Qilian Mountains, the region boasts a diverse range of mesmerizing landforms that showcase its geological evolution. In the Nine Springs area, centrally incised mountainous terrains dominate the landscape, captivating visitors with their awe-inspiring beauty. Journeying to the eastern region of Sunan County Town, one is greeted by mid to low mountainous terrains shaped by structural erosion, resulting in enchanting vistas like the vibrant Colourful Hills and mesmerizing Danxia landscapes. Zhangye lies within a transitional zone between the Qilian Caledonian fold belt and the Alxa block, shaped by complex geological processes over hundreds of millions of years. This has given rise to a wide range of geological features, including Danxia formations, structural landforms, erosion-formed gorges, and the internationally significant Nine Springs ophiolite suite—an Early Palaeozoic collision zone between the North China and Qaidam plates. The site has long drawn international geological interest, serving as a field stop for the 30th International Geological Congress in 1996 and for joint field research by the Australian-China Tectonics and Earth Resources Centre in 2018. The Colourful Hills, shaped by tectonic uplift into striking monocline peaks, and the Binggou Danxia, with its window-lattice and palace-style landforms, provide vivid examples of arid-region Danxia topography. Along the Heihe River, the second largest inland river in northwest China, steep gorges and erosion-formed landforms further enrich the region’s geological diversity and contribute to its value as a natural classroom for geoscience education.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Zhangye UNESCO Global Geopark is home to fifteen ethnic groups, including Yugurs, Tibetans, Mongols, Huis, Manchus, Dongxiangs and Bonans. With 56.5% of the local population belonging to minority groups, and the core area located in Sunan County—the only Yugur autonomous county in China—the geopark reflects a rich cultural and linguistic diversity. Zhangye is an important site along the ancient Silk Road. Cultural heritage sites within the geopark include Yumushan rock paintings, Heiyao Cave Traditional Steel Furnaces, Gaoche domed tents and yurts, the Machangtan Battle Site, and Kanglong Temple. Intangible cultural heritage is also a defining feature of the geopark. Three practices—Yugur folk songs, costumes, and weddings—are inscribed on China’s national intangible cultural heritage list. Additional practices, including leather carving, are recognised at the provincial and municipal levels. Whether on foot, horseback, or camelback, there are countless ways to immerse oneself in the wonders of Zhangye Geopark. For a truly unique perspective, helicopter and hot-air balloon rides offer a bird's-eye view of the park, allowing to marvel at its geological marvels from above.

Introduction EN: Explore traditional Batak houses, centuries-old wooden structures, adorned with intricate Gorga carvings in symbolic colours, feature unique architectural elements like "bara" lower rooms for pet cages and cone-shaped roofs.Experience the beauty of the Eden Park botanical garden featuring endemic Toba plants such as andaliman, a key spice in Batak cuisine, Toba orchids, and pitcher plants.
Description: The Toba Caldera UNESCO Global Geopark, located in North Sumatra, Indonesia, has a unique landscape shaped by one of Earth’s most powerful eruptions. Approximately 75,000 years ago, the Toba Caldera experienced a super-eruption, considered one of the most powerful volcanic events in Earth's history. This eruption is estimated to have been a thousand times stronger than the 1980 eruption of Mount St. Helens in the United States. It released vast amounts of ash and gases that spread across South Asia, causing significant climate cooling and widespread ecological devastation. Although earlier theories suggested this event led to the near extinction of the human species through a "genetic bottleneck," these theories have since been dismissed. Nevertheless, the eruption left behind a barren landscape where few plants or animals survived. Today, the Toba Caldera hosts Lake Toba, the world’s largest volcanic crater lake, spanning 1,100 km². Surrounded by lush Sumatran forests, the lake also features Samosir Island, located at its centre. The caldera’s steep walls form watersheds, and the lake's surface lies at 904 meters above sea level, with a maximum depth of 505 meters. The surrounding terrain includes undulating hills, mountains, and plains, creating a varied and dramatic landscape. Lake Toba is not only a geological wonder but also a vital ecological and cultural site. It provides habitats for diverse flora and fauna while sustaining local communities like the Batak people, who have lived in harmony with the area's natural resources for generations.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The Toba Caldera UNESCO Global Geopark is home to the Batak Toba people, whose culture and traditions are deeply rooted in the region’s history and environment. Their traditional wooden houses, known as “rumah adat,” are built using wooden planks with walls shaped like a boat hull and supported by sturdy pillars set on stone foundations without cement. This architectural style reflects the community’s deep understanding of their environment, as the region is prone to tectonic activity, earthquakes and flooding. The front of a traditional Batak house is adorned with Gorga, intricate carvings in white, red, and black—each carrying its own symbolic meaning.  The Batak culture is vibrant and diverse, marked by skilled handicrafts and traditional festivals like the Sigale-gale festival, where wooden puppets are used to tell stories and entertain. One of their most iconic crafts is ulos, a handwoven cloth made in vibrant red, black, and white hues, often adorned with gold or silver thread. Ulos is integral to traditional ceremonies, gifted at important moments such as weddings and births, and even worn for protective purposes during labour. Though some varieties, such as Ulos Raja and Ulos Sibolang, are no longer produced, ulos remains a significant cultural symbol and is now crafted into modern items like bags and tablecloths. The region’s rich biodiversity supports these traditions: Salaon (Indigofera tinctoria) and Sona (Pterocarpus indicus) plants provide blue and red dyes for ulos-making, while Kemiri trees (candlenuts) are an essential spice in Batak cuisine.

Introduction EN: Walk along a 650-meter trail through the serene Kuale Granite Mangrove Forest, home to at least six mangrove species and rich geological history dating back 145 million years.Explore the Nam Salu Open Pit at Gunung Kik Karak, one of Southeast Asia’s oldest tin mines, where visitors can see remnants of historic tin-processing technologies and some of the island’s oldest exposed rocks.
Description: The Belitong UNESCO Global Geopark, located off the east coast of Sumatra, Indonesia, is a remarkable landscape shaped by tectonic activity and rich geological diversity. The region's formation was influenced by the convergence of the Eurasian and Indo-Australian tectonic plates, which led to the creation of the Barisan Mountains and Belitung Island. Today, the geopark spans land and sea, including 241 surrounding islands, which feature thriving marine ecosystems of coral reefs, mangrove forests and seagrass beds. One of the most striking features of Belitong is its tor granite landscape, where massive, light-coloured granite boulders, with minimal jointing, rise dramatically from the crystal-clear waters. These formations are found in the northwestern coastal plains and nearby small islands, creating breathtaking scenery and offering opportunities for exploration by boat. The island is also home to the Nam Salu primary tin deposit, one of Southeast Asia’s most significant geological sites. Visitors can explore open ramp sites showcasing some of the oldest exposed rocks on Belitung Island, offering insights into ancient geological phenomena through fossils, minerals and rock structures. Rare tektites —natural glass formed by meteorite impacts— of international geological importance have also been discovered here, forming part of the Australian Strewnfield and accounting for 18–19% of the world’s known tektite distribution. Belitong’s biological diversity is equally remarkable, exemplified by the Belitong Tarsier (Cephalopachus bancanus saltator), an endemic species found in the island’s dry shrublands and secondary forests, known for its large eyes adapted for night vision and its long hind legs. These ecosystems, although sustained by nutrient-poor soils derived from granite weathering, also support diverse flora and fauna, making Belitong an important site for ecological and biogeographical studies.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Belitong’s vibrant communities reflect a deep connection to their environment and a long history of adaptation and sustainability. As a hub of maritime trade, Belitong's waters played a crucial role in the maritime silk route from the 7th to the 13th century, linking the Tang Dynasty in China with the Abbasid Dynasty in the Middle East. Ships crossing the Gaspar Strait and Karimata Strait bypassed Palembang, the capital of the Sriwijaya Empire, on their way to Java. Shipwrecks from the 9th to the 20th centuries, scattered across these waters, provide tangible evidence of this dynamic trade history, with many artifacts preserved in the Tanjungpandan Museum. This maritime legacy continues today, as fishing remains a vital livelihood for coastal communities. Traditional kater boats, designed for nearshore fishing with minimal environmental impact, reflect a harmony between human activity and nature, enabling sustainable fishing practices. Unique traditions such as Nirok Nanggok, guided by village shamans, align fish harvesting with ecological cycles, protecting marine ecosystems. Cultural rituals like the Muang Jong ceremony, where a replica boat is offered to the sea for safety and abundance, and Maras Taun, a celebration of gratitude for agricultural prosperity, highlight the community's enduring connection to nature. Both rituals have been recognised as Intangible National Heritage by Indonesia’s Ministry of Culture and Education. Local beliefs further demonstrate a commitment to environmental sustainability. Small forests known as “Hutan Watas” or “Dinding Kampong” serve as natural dividers between villages, while “Tali Utan” protects riverbanks, preserving groundwater reserves and preventing erosion. In rural areas, agriculture plays a central role, with crops like white pepper, coconut, and oil palm.

Introduction EN: Visit Low’s Gully, the deepest and longest canyon on Mount Kinabalu, formed by glacial erosion and later shaped by rivers.Explore the traditional crafts of the Kadazandusun, Bajau, Dusun, and Rungus communities, including weaving, embroidery and decorative objects.Discover the unique flavours of Kadazandusun traditional cuisine, featuring dishes like purple rice, turmeric-cooked chicken, and salted egg paired with side dishes such as hinava (a raw fish salad), tuhau (wild ginger), sliced young papaya fruit, and bambangan (a wild mango).
Description: Mount Kinabalu, the highest peak between the Himalayas and New Guinea, dominates the Kinabalu UNESCO Global Geopark in the State of Sabah, at the northern tip of Borneo. Rising over 4,000 meters above sea level, it has attracted explorers for over a century and offers an outstanding mountainous landscape at its peak, shaped by glacial processes during the last Ice Age. The geopark boasts exceptional geodiversity, including the youngest granitoid intrusion in Southeast Asia (7–8 million years old) and an ophiolite sequence representing ancient oceanic crust (130 million years old) from the subducted Proto-South China Sea lithosphere. Ultramafic rocks, typically found in the Earth’s mantle, are exposed here and date back billions of years, contributing to unique landforms such as the Poring Hot Springs and the folded and faulted sedimentary rocks of the Ranau-Tambunan area. A highlight is the Sungai Baliojong River gorge in Tandek, Kota Marudu, where tightly folded red chert layers (130 million years old) rest on pillow basalt, providing a rare glimpse into the ancient oceanic crust. Along the summit trail from Laban Rata to Low’s Peak, visitors can observe the Hornblende Granite, distinguished by fine-grained hornblende minerals within the Kinabalu pluton. The geopark is home to numerous endemic species, including 90 orchids found only on Mount Kinabalu and the crimson-headed partridge, a bird unique to this region. Kinabalu Park, inscribed as a World Heritage site in 2000, covers about 16% of the geopark’s total area.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The Kinabalu UNESCO Global Geopark is a significant site for geological research and education, offering visitors a unique opportunity to explore the geological history of Southeast Asia. Its distinctive position for the biota of Southeast Asia also enhances the site's ecological importance, making it a vital location for both scientific discovery and biodiversity conservation. Beyond its scientific and ecological values, the geopark emphasises the empowerment and active participation of local and Indigenous communities in its management and conservation efforts. Through initiatives that foster sustainable tourism, community-based entrepreneurship, and the preservation of natural and cultural heritage, the geopark has delivered significant economic and social benefits to its residents. Kampung Luanti, a village community within the geopark, serves as a prime example, promoting a traditional river management practice where locals sustainably manage fish populations. This Tagal system not only preserves natural ecosystems but also incorporates eco-tourism activities, offering visitors an engaging way to learn about conservation while providing economic opportunities for the community. Similarly, community-based entrepreneurship in other areas, such as homestays in Bundu Tuhan and small cafes in Kampung Kiau, has enabled residents to secure livelihoods while maintaining their natural and cultural heritage. The geopark celebrates the rich heritage and cultures of its Indigenous communities. Traditional crafts—such as weaving, embroidery, and the creation of decorative objects—are preserved as important expressions of material culture and are also integral to tourism. The Sumazau, a traditional folk dance of the Kadazandusun, is a lively celebration of the region's intangible heritage. Performed during festivals, it reflects the community's deep spiritual connections and cultural identity, showcasing traditions that have been passed down through generations.

Introduction EN: Explore the Zhijindong Cave Geological Museum, which presents local biodiversity research and conservation efforts.Visit eco-parks and garden landscapes where native species like gingko and wild mushrooms are integrated into limestone peak settings.
Description: Zhijindong Cave UNESCO Global Geopark is located in the west of the Guizhou Plateau, covering parts of Zhijin County and Qianxi County in Bijie City, Guizhou Province. It is composed of three scenic areas—Zhijindong Cave, Qijiehe River, and Dongfenghu Lake—each corresponding to distinct karst geomorphic units. Intense tectonic uplift during the Triassic period (251 to 201 million years ago) gradually created the inland plateau. Since then, successive phases of crustal movement and water flow have shaped a range of surface and underground karst landscapes. These include caves, gorges, natural bridges, and sinkholes—features that stand out globally for their geological significance and beauty. Zhijindong Cave, the main geosite of the geopark, developed within Triassic limestone formations over 300 metres thick. The cave exemplifies subsurface karst systems and forms part of a broader sequence of karst evolution across the geopark. From the subsurface formations of Zhijindong Cave to the surface karst of Dongfenghu Lake, the region provides a systematic record of geomorphological development on the Guizhou Plateau. The geopark spans seven geological periods, from the Sinian to the Quaternary, and is legally protected. Conservation measures for Zhijindong Cave include real-time air quality monitoring and restrictions on visitor numbers to protect sensitive formations such as stalactites and stalagmites. Additional efforts focus on preserving groundwater systems and restoring degraded forests to maintain the integrity of the cave’s hydrology and air system.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Zhijindong Cave UNESCO Global Geopark reflects the cultural diversity of Guizhou Province, home to 23 ethnic groups including Han, Miao, Yi, Hui, and Buyei communities. Nearly half of Zhijin’s population belongs to minority groups, contributing to a wide range of tangible and intangible heritage expressions. Cultural heritage is preserved in the form of ancient architecture and traditional village structures, including large family complexes and houses made of mixed mud and straw. A newly designated cultural area, the Zhijin Ancient Architectural Complex, comprises 25 historical buildings such as the Temple of the God of Wealth, Wenchang Pavilion, and Feng Xi College. Recognised in 2006 as a national key cultural relic protection unit, it is considered a unique example of this ancient architecture in China. The geopark’s intangible heritage is actively practised and passed on across generations. Regionally recognised traditions include Miao batik from Caiqun in Guanzhai, Zhijin grit ceramics, Shixing shooting crossbow, the Nuo Opera of the Chuanqing people, and traditional Miao hairstyles and musical practices. These are celebrated during local festivals such as the Miao Flower Dance Festival, the Yi Torch Festival, and ceremonies linked to Zhuanqing beliefs. Culinary heritage, rooted in Miao and Yi food cultures, is promoted through local restaurants using regional produce. A dedicated centre trains women in traditional crafts and provides employment, while cultural performances and guided tours further support local livelihoods.
Quote: “Karst wonderland”

Introduction EN: Wander through the Troodos National Forest Park and take one of the geopark's 84 hiking trails.Marvel at the rare sight of an exposed fragment of an oceanic tectonic plate.Discover an ancient heritage of lost empires in the Byzantine chapels and monasteries.
Description: The history of Troodos, the rugged mountain chain in the south of Cyprus, is both violent and gripping. Stretching for about 90 km and hosting an outstanding Mediterranean forest, rich with countless endemic species and contrasting with the rust-coloured surroundings typical of limestone regions, the range is what geologists call an ophiolite—a fragment of oceanic crust and the underlying upper mantle that has been thrusted (obducted) on to the edge of continental plates. The Troodos Ophiolite Complex, as it is known, was formed due to the convergence between the African and Arabian tectonic plates with the Eurasian plate approximately 92 to 82 million years ago (Upper Cretaceous). It is considered the most stratigraphically complete, best exposed, and best-preserved ophiolite sequence in the world. Troodos UNESCO Global Geopark features 38 geosites that display this geological wonder in all its splendour. The Troodos Ophiolite’s importance is such that since the 1960s, 120 PhD dissertations, 60 Master’s theses, and thousands of research papers have delved into the intricacies of its formation, structure, evolution, and mineralisation—and, more importantly, into the features that help us understand oceanic crust and sea-floor spreading. Through the 84 hiking trails set by the geopark, places like the Lower Pillow Lavas in the Maroullena River, the veins of Mandari Ridge (Teisia tis Madaris), and the scenic view of the Arakapas Valley help visitors engage with this complex region.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Cyprus, the third-largest island in the Mediterranean, lies at the crossroads of European and Asian cultures and histories. Its cultural significance is reflected in literature and mythology—from Shakespeare’s Othello, which contrasts Venice with the dangers of Cyprus, to ancient Greek myths that describe the island as the birthplace of Aphrodite, emerging from the sea near Paphos. The cultural heritage of Troodos is as rich as its geological significance. The region is home to one of the largest concentrations of churches and monasteries from the former Byzantine Empire. A group of ten churches, dating from the 11th to the 17th centuries and decorated with elaborate murals, is inscribed on UNESCO’s World Heritage List. In the hills and valleys of Troodos, several villages retain their medieval character. One example is the village of Fikardou, located on the eastern slopes of the mountain. The region is also known for producing koumandaria, regarded as the oldest wine in the Mediterranean, with continuous production over centuries. Local wineries welcome visitors, who can also sample traditional sweet delicacies such as soutzouko, palouze, kiofteri, and pastellaki.
Quote: “Oceanic whispers on high altitude”

Introduction EN: Visitors to Balicasag Island, part of the Bohol Marine Triangle, can explore world-class snorkelling and diving spots, encountering its fringing reef and diverse marine life, including dolphins, whale sharks, and sea turtles.Hinagdanan Cave, located in Panglao Island, features an impressive pool of brackish water and striking stalactites and stalagmites formed through limestone deposition. The cave, once used as a wartime hideout, is now a popular site for tourism, research, and exploration.Discover the iconic Chocolate Hills, a remarkable cone-karst landscape with 1,268 conical hills ranging from 30 to 400 meters in height.
Description: Bohol Island, the Philippines' first UNESCO Global Geopark, is located in the heart of the Visayas island group. Its geological story unfolds over 150 million years, with tectonic forces continuously shaping and elevating the island from the ocean depths to create a dynamic landscape rich in geological diversity.   The island’s geological framework is built upon a “half-horst” structure, featuring elevated marine terraces in the southwest, formed by tectonic movements over the past 1.8 million years. Bohol’s physiographic diversity ranges from gently undulating northern landscapes to higher hills in the east, while the southern region is marked by narrow coastal plains and east-west trending mountain ranges. In the west, a plateau-like interior is flanked by broader coastal plains.   The rocks that make up Bohol span from the Late Jurassic to the Pleistocene period. Among the oldest formations is the Alicia Schist, whose colour varies from light green to light grey depending on its mineral composition. The island’s geological history also includes the emplacement of the Bohol Ophiolite during the Early Cretaceous period, followed by the Ubay Formation, comprising andesite, basalt, gabbro, and diabase interbedded with sandstone and mudstone, dating back to the Eocene. Subsequent volcanic activity in the Late Eocene to Oligocene gave rise to the Jagna and Jetafe Andesite, while the Neogene period saw the development of extensive limestone formations, including the Wahig, Carmen, Sierra Bullones, and Maribojoc formations.   Two of Bohol’s most significant geosites are the world-renowned Chocolate Hills and the uplifted marine terraces of Maribojoc. The Chocolate Hills, a stunning cone-karst landscape of 1,268 conical hills with elevations ranging from 30 to 400 meters, formed during the Plio-Pleistocene period through limestone uplift and subsequent weathering. Declared a National Geological Monument in 1988, the Chocolate Hills continue to attract thousands of visitors annually, supporting the local tourism industry.   The Maribojoc uplifted marine terrace is a testament to the island’s dynamic geological processes. The result of a 7.2 magnitude earthquake in 2013, this coastal feature showcases an extensive marine platform uplifted by 1.5 meters, with the shoreline shifting approximately 50 meters seaward, exposing 4 meters of previously submerged coral reef. This site provides a unique example of natural biological succession, as once-submerged marine ecosystems have transformed into thriving terrestrial habitats within just a few years.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Main industries in the geopark include agriculture, aquaculture and tourism. Agriculture is the primary source of income, with rice, coconut, and corn as key crops that support local communities. Aquaculture and fisheries provide additional livelihoods, particularly in coastal areas. Tourism is rapidly growing, driven by the island’s natural beauty, unique geological features, and rich cultural heritage. Fishery and aquaculture also play an essential role in sustaining coastal populations, offering both sustenance and economic opportunities.   Tourism in Bohol has seen a significant rise, positioning the island as a premier eco-cultural destination. With its white sand beaches, renowned diving spots, unique geological formations, rich biodiversity, and deep-rooted cultural heritage, tourism serves as a major economic driver. The traditions and culture of the island's people reflect their long-standing adaptation to the natural environment, showcasing a living heritage passed down through generations.   One of the unique aspects of Bohol’s cultural fabric is the Eskaya Tribe, an Indigenous community residing in the southeastern part of the island. Their distinct language, which has no known connection to any other language, and their rich cultural heritage are protected under the Indigenous Peoples Rights Act of 1997. The Eskaya Tribe has been involved in the process of developing the geopark, ensuring that their heritage is preserved and celebrated. Efforts are being made to sustain and promote their traditions through educational programs and cultural initiatives.   The Banacon Island Mangrove Forest in Getafe stands as a testament to local community efforts in environmental sustainability. Covering 425 hectares, it is the largest man-made mangrove plantation in Asia, with 410 hectares thriving in tidal flat areas. Initially established as a response to deforestation in the 1950s, the mangrove forest has provided vital protection for marine biodiversity and sustained livelihoods through fishing and eco-tourism. The nutrient-rich waters surrounding the mangroves serve as breeding grounds for fish, seahorses, shrimps, and crabs, contributing to both food security and economic growth. Hundreds of families now benefit from the mangrove plantation, which has become a popular tourist destination with walking trails offering visitors an immersive experience in the natural landscape.

Introduction EN: Explore the vast Kiamaki Wildlife Refuge, home to species including the Armenian mouflon - Ovis orientalis gmelini - and golden eagles - Aquila chrysaetos - along with scenic rivers such as the Kharvana and Dastjerd, stunning waterfalls like Asiab-Kharabeh, and diverse tree species including willow - Salix - and walnut - Juglans regia.Experience the vibrant Ashiq Music Festival, a cherished tradition during Nowruz holidays in March, showcasing poetic melodies inspired by the region’s rich natural and cultural heritage.
Description: Aras UNESCO Global Geopark is situated in the northwest of Iran. The Aras River forms the northern boundary of the geopark, serving as the dividing line between Iran, Armenia and Azerbaijan. Within the geopark’s region, there are three designated protected areas. Conservation efforts are significantly influenced by the area's rich wildlife and the presence of endangered species such as the Caucasian black grouse, red deer, Armenian mouflon, and leopard. Within Aras geopark, four lithological provinces can be identified. The western cliffs and highlands consist of Late Paleozoic and Early Mesozoic carbonate rocks. In the central areas, Cretaceous and Eocene sandstone, shale, and marl beds with prevalent flysch facies dominate. Towards the east, intrusive igneous rocks, primarily granitic in nature, are present. In the southern and central parts of the area, dacitic volcanic and sub-volcanic rocks can be found. The Alli-Bashi geosite within the geopark holds exceptional international geological significance. It provides a rare opportunity for geoscientists to study uninterrupted successions of carbonate to claystone-dominated facies, rich in fossils, at the Permian–Triassic boundary. In addition to Alli-Bashi, the geopark includes approximately 30 other geosites.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Aras UNESCO Global Geopark is home to several important cultural landmarks. These include the UNESCO World Heritage site of Saint Stepanos Monastery, which reflects the region's historical and religious significance. Other national monuments include the Khajeh-Nazar Caravanserai, the Historical Bath, the Duzal Historical Tower, the Zia-ol-Molk Bridge, and the Choopan Church—each representing key elements of the region’s cultural heritage. The geopark also preserves vibrant intangible heritage traditions. Celebrations such as the Chaharshanbe Suri ceremony, held on the last Wednesday of the year, involve jumping over fires for purification, sharing sweets, and performing the traditional “Hanging Shawl” ritual. During Yalda Night, the longest night of the year, families gather to tell stories and myths, and enjoy seasonal fruits—customs that reflect a deep connection to community and nature. Aras geopark engages actively with communities through a variety of educational programmes. These include student-targeted materials such as information leaflets and themed playing cards that promote environmental awareness. Public workshops support women’s empowerment by teaching skills for creating geoproducts and sustainable businesses, including soap making and casting in Oshtobin village, and Varni bead-weaving in Shoja village. A dedicated geoeducation course for Indigenous youth prepares future tourism guides with knowledge of geology, ecotourism, and cultural heritage—fostering both educational growth and local economic development.

Introduction EN: Dive into the hot spring waters of Aso’s onsen in Uchinomaki, Jigoku, Tarutama, and the mountain resorts of the Oguni-go area.Drive through the vast grasslands on the Milk Road. Between mid-February and March, it’s noyaki season, when local communities undertake controlled burnings.Take the Mt. Kishima trail route starting from the Aso Volcano Museum. At the top, enjoy a spectacular view of the northern part of the Aso caldera, with the Nakadake volcano still fuming in the background.
Description: While larger calderas exist elsewhere in the world, the 25 by 18 kilometre caldera of Mount Aso remains a striking feature—not because of its size, but because of what human communities have built within it: thousands of hectares of cultivated land, a large city (Aso), and several other towns and villages, all connected by railway and road networks. Some 70,000 people live here, not only undisturbed by the presence of Japan’s largest active volcano but seemingly thankful for it. The reason becomes clear when viewing the area from the Daikanbo viewpoint: the land is extraordinarily fertile, and water is abundant. Having erupted four times between 90,000 and 270,000 years ago, Mount Aso is what geologists refer to as a somma volcano: a caldera filled or partially filled by a new volcanic cone—Nakadake—formed during the most recent eruption and still visibly steaming today. That eruption, the largest of the four, left behind a vast pyroclastic plateau, with ash reaching as far as Yamaguchi Prefecture, 160 km away. Descending from the Nakadake crater, the sight of the Komekuza cone is almost surreal. The scoria cone, created around 3,000 years ago, is perfectly shaped. Behind it lie hundreds of cultivated fields and the jagged rim of the caldera—an ideal photo opportunity.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The Aso UNESCO Global Geopark is a significant centre for preserving cultural and intangible heritage, closely linked to the traditions and daily lives of its communities. Aso Shrine is a key landmark, dedicated to the deity Takeiwatatsu-no-mikoto. It symbolises the deep spiritual and historical roots of the region. Though severely damaged in the 2016 Kumamoto earthquakes, the shrine is undergoing reconstruction and remains a cornerstone of local identity and devotion. Rituals and festivals connected to the shrine—particularly those celebrating agriculture—express the community’s gratitude for harvests and their hopes for protection from natural hazards. Several of these events are designated National Important Intangible Properties, reflecting the continuity of agricultural life and spiritual practice in the region. The geopark also supports historical and cultural education through its museums and visitor centres. The Aso Volcano Museum and related institutions share the story of how people have coexisted with the dynamic environment of the caldera for centuries. Agriculture and livestock remain central to the local economy, supported by traditional practices. Among these is the centuries-old tradition of noyaki, the controlled burning of grasslands. This technique helps maintain cultural landscapes, supports biodiversity, and sustains agriculture—demonstrating the deep-rooted connection between human activity and environmental stewardship in the region.
Quote: “Vast grassland, rich bio-diversity and unique human culture based on the volcano are its symbolic features”

Introduction EN: The Hidaka Yabakei, a breathtaking 7-km stretch of cliffs where Mt. Apoi plunges into the Pacific, marks the ancient collision site of the Eurasian and North American Plates, with the Hidaka Main Thrust boundary still visible today.The historic Samani Mountain Path, built 200 years ago to navigate the cliffs along National Route 336 (Golden Road), is now a picturesque footpath offering stunning coastal views.
Description: The Hidaka Mountains, stretching 150 km across southern Hokkaido, form the rugged backbone of Japan's northernmost island. Rising to peaks between 1,500 and 2,000 metres, this mountain range is a testament to the immense geological forces that have shaped the landscape over millions of years. At its southwestern edge lies the remarkable Mt. Apoi UNESCO Global Geopark, located in the coastal town of Samani. While much of the geopark’s 92% forestland consists of hilly terrain with Cretaceous period formations and coastal intrusive rock monoliths, it is Mt. Apoi itself, standing at 810 metres, that commands global attention for its geological significance. Mt. Apoi is formed of peridotite, a rare, dense rock from the Earth’s mantle. This unique feature stems from a tectonic collision 13 million years ago between the Eurasian and North American plates. The immense pressure of this collision forced part of the Earth's mantle—normally deep below the crust—to rise to the surface, creating the Horoman peridotite complex, of which Mt. Apoi is the centrepiece. These mantle-derived rocks offer a rare glimpse into the inaccessible depths of our planet, providing invaluable insights into Earth’s internal processes. Beyond its mantle rocks, Mt. Apoi UNESCO Global Geopark also reveals the story of plate collisions and other geological marvels, such as oddly shaped masses of cooled magma and rocks transported from distant southern seas. This diverse geological narrative, combined with cultural ties and striking natural beauty, makes Mt. Apoi a unique and globally significant site for understanding Earth’s history and cultural continuity.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The Mt. Apoi UNESCO Global Geopark holds deep cultural and spiritual significance for the Ainu people, whose ancestral connection to the land is reflected in the mountain’s name, “Apoi,” derived from their language. The geopark acts not only as a geological treasure but also as a vital bridge for preserving and sharing the Ainu’s rich heritage. Through partnerships with the Samani Ainu Association, the geopark ensures that Ainu traditions—including dances, songs, and rituals—are celebrated and passed down to future generations. Education and community engagement are central to the geopark’s mission of fostering a strong sense of local identity. In 2010, the geopark Promotion Council launched the Hometown Geo-workshop, a lecture series designed to help residents connect with their heritage by exploring the region’s geological, ecological, and cultural resources. These efforts have also attracted researchers and students. In 2013 alone, 344 researchers and university students from 30 institutions visited the geopark, underscoring its international role as a hub for scientific exploration. Cultural preservation is woven into the fabric of daily life in Samani, with vibrant seasonal festivals such as the Wasuke Jizo Festival and the Apoi Fire Festival bringing the community together to honour their history and the natural world. Food traditions like iizushi—a fermented salmon and vegetable dish—further emphasise the deep connection between local customs and the surrounding environment. Trail maintenance initiatives by the Mt. Apoi Fan Club help ensure continued access to the area’s unique and spectacular landscapes.
Quote: “A story of gifts from deep inside the Earth connecting land and people together”

Introduction EN: Visit Shiramine Village near Mt. Hakusan to experience traditional architecture and crafts, including Ushikubi Pongee, a soft and durable silk fabric made from unique twin silk cocoons. Discover Oguchi Dekumawashi Puppetry, a rare and captivating art performed on waist-high stages, passed down through generations in the snowy mountain regions.Celebrate the Mikawa Okaeri Festival, where vibrant floats and mikoshi bring local traditions to life, honouring the historic Kitamaebune trading ships.
Description: Located in central Japan, the Hakusan Tedorigawa UNESCO Global Geopark follows the Tedori River from Mount Hakusan down to the sea, recording approximately 300 million years of Earth history. Part of the geopark overlaps with the Mount Hakusan Biosphere Reserve, designated by UNESCO in 1980. The region includes rocks formed by continental collisions and strata containing dinosaur fossils that accumulated in rivers and lakes at a time when Japan was still part of the Eurasian continent. Volcanic deposits from about 15 million years ago mark the rifting that separated Japan from the continent, as tectonic plates pulled it eastward. More recent volcanic layers originate from the still-active Mount Hakusan, one of Japan’s ‘Three Holy Mountains.’ Rising 2,702 metres above sea level, it records some of the highest levels of snowfall in the world for a mountain so close to the Equator. This heavy snow drives a water and erosion cycle that continues to shape the landscape. The geopark encompasses a significant concentration of early Cretaceous fossils from the Tetori Group, a geological layer spread across the Tedori River Basin and much of the Hokuriku region, including Fukui, Ishikawa, Toyama, and Gifu Prefectures. The Kuwajima Fossil Bluff within the geopark contains one of the most complete exposures of the Tetori Group. This site provides a unique opportunity to observe the processes of sedimentation and fossilisation. The formation of sedimentary rocks through erosion, transport, and deposition is clearly visible, offering a valuable context for understanding Earth’s geological history.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The Hakusan Tedorigawa UNESCO Global Geopark supports sustainable community development through education, cultural preservation, and local collaboration. Partnerships with schools and organisations such as the Hakusan-roku Bunamori Nature School foster environmental awareness through monthly activities involving elementary schools, community centres, and colleges. Cultural heritage in the geopark is closely tied to its varied topography and historical evolution. Shiramine Village, designated as a National Important Preservation District for Groups of Historic Buildings, exemplifies architectural resilience in a snowy mountain setting. Its temples, shrines, and Ushikubi Pongee silk production reflect deep adaptation to the natural environment. The geopark also preserves and promotes intangible cultural heritage. Oguchi Dekumawashi Puppetry is a traditional art form passed down through generations. The Mikawa Okaeri Festival celebrates the maritime heritage of the Kitamaebune trade routes. Hinoki-zaiku Cypress Weaving, with over 400 years of history, continues to produce fine crafts such as vases, decorations, and jewellery, linking natural resources to cultural identity. Geotourism further strengthens local communities by showcasing natural and historical sites. The Torigoe and Futoge Castle Ruins tell stories of regional conflict and resilience, while the Yokoe-no-Sho Estate offers a glimpse into the Nara–Heian period. Visitors can also explore Shirayama Hime Shrine, dedicated to the deity of Mt. Hakusan, deepening understanding of the region’s religious significance.

Introduction EN: Explore Manjanggul Cave, one of the longest lava tubes in the world. Stretching over 7 kilometres, it was formed by lava flows from Hallasan, the island’s largest volcano.Visit Seongeup Folk Village to see traditional thatched-roof houses, stone walls, and cultural artefacts that reflect Jeju’s heritage.
Description: Jeju Island UNESCO Global Geopark, located at the southernmost tip of the Korean Peninsula, is a volcanic island in the centre of northeast Asia. The island enjoys a mild climate, with clean air maintained by land and sea breezes and temperatures that rarely fall below zero due to the influence of the warm Kuroshio Current. As the youngest volcanic island in Korea, Jeju preserves a wide range of volcanic landforms, including lava tubes, small volcanic cones, and shield volcanoes. Its landscapes range from the alpine forests of Mount Hallasan to vibrant coral ecosystems beneath the sea. The geopark is a Quaternary shield volcanic island with a generally gentle topography and an elliptical shape, located off the Republic of Korea’s southern coast. Formed by volcanic activity between approximately 2 million years ago and historic times, the island is composed largely of basaltic to trachytic lava flows. Jeju features diverse volcanic landforms, including Mount Hallasan at its centre and around 360 volcanic cones scattered across the island. Below the surface, numerous hydromagmatic volcanoes—such as tuff rings and tuff cones—can be found, along with volcanoclastic sedimentary deposits resulting from explosive hydrovolcanic activity. One of the most iconic geological features of the geopark is Seongsan Ilchulbong Peak, also known as "Sunrise Peak" for its east-facing position ideal for watching the sunrise. This volcanic cone rises 182 metres above sea level and offers panoramic views of the surrounding landscape. A well-maintained hiking trail allows visitors to reach the summit in approximately 30 to 40 minutes.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Jeju UNESCO Global Geopark preserves and promotes the island’s rich cultural heritage. Traditional batdam (stone walls) continue to support sustainable land management and local farming practices. Other protected cultural sites—including prehistoric settlements and dol-hareubang, the island’s iconic stone sculptures—contribute to community identity and continuity. The haenyeo of Jeju, a community of women divers who harvest shellfish up to 10 metres underwater without oxygen masks, represent a unique and enduring cultural tradition. Some divers continue this work into their 80s, spending up to seven hours a day in the water for as many as 90 days each year. Their distinctive verbal resurfacing signal is recognised by UNESCO as Intangible Cultural Heritage. Jeju’s ecotourism programme contributes to the local economy by linking nature, culture, and community infrastructure. Forest trails at Seonheul Gotjawal and Gyorae Samdasoo attract visitors while promoting biodiversity conservation and offering guided interpretation by local residents. A notable success story is the revitalisation of a small branch school, which—due to population growth driven by sustainable tourism—was upgraded to a regular elementary school in 2021. In addition to being a UNESCO Global Geopark, Jeju Island is also designated as a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve and a World Heritage site.
Quote: “UNESCO’s triple crown of Jeju Island”

Titre EN: Harz - Braunschweiger Land - Ostfalen UNESCO Global Geopark
Introduction EN: Follow the Harz Border Trail along the former Iron Curtain, where patrol paths have become part of Europe’s “Green Belt.” The trail crosses an area once divided for over 40 years, where the UNESCO Global Geopark now serves as an instrument for overcoming the legacy of separation.Discover the Schöningen Spears, the oldest complete wooden weapons in the world, dating back over 300,000 years and providing exceptional evidence of early human hunting strategies and technological skill.Witness forest ecosystems and raised bogs preserved since the Last Ice Age in Harz National Park, home to wild cats, lynx, and the black stork.
Description: The Harz - Braunschweiger Land - Ostfalen UNESCO Global Geopark is Germany’s largest geopark, stretching from the industrial city of Wolfsburg in the north to the medieval town of Allstedt in the south. Its central geological feature is the Harz Mountains, a low-altitude range composed of Palaeozoic sediments and magmatic rocks. The Brocken, with its highest peak at 1,142 metres, is notable for its plateau summit and subalpine climate, with an average annual temperature of 2.9°C and persistent snow cover for much of the year. The surrounding area is part of the Harz National Park, which conserves forest ecosystems and raised bogs dating back to the Last Ice Age, as well as habitats for species such as the lynx, wild cat, and black stork. The geopark encompasses a geological record extending from the Silurian period to the Last Ice Age, covering approximately 400 million years. The Braunschweiger Land and Ostfalen areas to the north are characterised by fossil-rich Mesozoic and Cenozoic sediments, shaped by salt tectonics that led to the formation of diverse mineral resources such as iron ore, brown coal, salt, and oil. One of the most renowned geological areas within the geopark is the so-called "Classic Square Mile of Geology" near Goslar, where the abrupt contact between Variscan basement and Mesozoic cover rock is visible in numerous reference outcrops. This juxtaposition between the Harz Mountains and the surrounding foreland exemplifies the exceptional geological diversity of the geopark.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The Harz Mountains region is one of Germany’s most renowned tourist destinations, with the Brocken peak serving as a major attraction. Beyond its geological significance, the Brocken holds cultural importance as the site of the world’s first television tower, constructed in 1936 to broadcast the Berlin Summer Olympics, and later used for Cold War surveillance operations. Referenced in Goethe’s Faust, the summit today hosts the Brockenhaus museum and a botanical garden, while the historic Brocken Railway, operated year-round by steam locomotive, connects visitors to this emblematic peak. The region’s mining heritage, particularly in the Upper Harz, dates back to the Bronze Age and reached its peak between the 16th and mid-19th centuries. During this time, silver, lead, and copper mining contributed significantly to the wealth and influence of the Hanover and Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel royal families. This legacy is preserved at various sites across the geopark, including the Knesebeckschacht and Upper Harz Mining Museums, the Lange Wand mine, the Kaiser Wilhelm and Ottiliae shafts, and the Oker Region Industrial Landscape. Cultural traditions continue to play a central role in the region’s identity. Walpurgis Night, celebrated in over 20 towns across the Harz Mountains on 30 April, has roots in pre-Christian spring rituals once dedicated to the Germanic god Wodan. Today, the celebration includes costumes, bonfires and community gatherings. The region is also known for its vibrant Christmas markets, with towns such as Goslar, Quedlinburg, and Nordhausen hosting events that showcase regional crafts, local foods and winter customs, supporting local livelihoods and attracting visitors year after year.
Quote: “Uplift area at the Northern Rim of the Harz Mountains”

Introduction EN: Explore the newly developed Tula Cave geosite, where a limestone cave opens into a pristine sinkhole with a unique, independent ecosystem, home to newly identified endemic species. Discover the traditional Nora Dance, a UNESCO-recognised element of Thailand’s intangible cultural heritage, performed alongside local songs in Satun.
Description: Satun UNESCO Global Geopark, located in the southern province of Thailand, is a site of extraordinary geological significance, spanning two national parks and a wildlife sanctuary. The region is widely recognised as the “Land of Palaeozoic Fossils,” home to an unparalleled diversity of fossil species dating back over 500 million years. The geopark contains an extensive and continuous sequence of marine sedimentary rocks from the Cambrian to the Permian period, making it a key location for understanding Earth’s early evolutionary history. The geopark's fossil-rich landscapes provide crucial insights into past life forms, with discoveries including trilobites, brachiopods, stromatolites, conodonts, graptolites, tentaculites, and nautiloids. Cambrian trilobites found on Tarutao Island are the oldest recorded in the Thai-Malay Peninsula. The presence of volcanic ash layers interbedded with trilobite fossils allows for absolute dating of the Late Cambrian biostratigraphy, reinforcing the international geological importance of the site. A significant amount of evidence supports the theory that Shan-Thai was once part of the peri-Gondwana terrane, a crucial aspect in reconstructing Earth's ancient paleogeography. Among the most striking geological features of the geopark is Prasat Hin Panyod, a breathtaking pinnacle karst formation. This geosite is characterised by dramatic limestone towers, sea caves, and a hidden lagoon, accessible only by kayak, offering visitors an immersive journey through one of Thailand’s most spectacular geological formations. The continuous formation of karst landscapes, including notable sites such as Talu Cave, showcases the ongoing geological processes shaping the region. Beyond its fossil heritage, Khao Noi in Lal-Ngu District is an internationally recognised geosite where a stratigraphic boundary marks the transition from Ordovician to Silurian rock formations, providing vital evidence for global geological time boundaries. Additionally, Molae Bay in Mueang Satun District holds the distinction of preserving the oldest fossils in Thailand, dating to the Late Cambrian.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Satun UNESCO Global Geopark is home to a diverse population, and the geopark has played a significant role in fostering strong collaborations between local communities, governmental bodies, and conservation efforts—particularly following the discovery of its extensive fossil records in 2007. One of its key initiatives has been the promotion of geotourism, which has provided economic benefits through job creation, new income streams, and investment in infrastructure. Events such as the Satun Fossil Festival and other cultural fairs provide platforms for local artisans and businesses to showcase traditional crafts, food, and products. Satun’s rich intangible cultural heritage includes distinctive traditions such as the Pe-Bo ceremony, a ritual of praying to spirits, and the Loi Rue (boat floating) festival of the Urak Lawoi people, which reflects their deep connection to the sea. Tangible cultural landmarks like Tarutao Island and the historic town of Su-Ngai U-Poh further highlight the region’s historical significance.
Quote: “A peaceful place with renowned natural beauty”

Titre EN: Non nuoc Cao Bang UNESCO Global Geopark
Introduction EN: Visit the Magic Water Mine in Lung Sang hamlet, where a local legend tells of three sisters who protected hidden treasure by raising floodwaters to seal the cave.Discover the traditional paper-making craft of the Nung An people in Dia Tren Hamlet, where May Sla tree bark is transformed into votive paper using age-old techniques passed down through generations.Visit the Lung Luong rock chrysanthemum site, where 260-million-year-old ammonite fossils in layered limestone reveal the region’s ancient marine origins and help geologists date rock formations.
Description: Located around 300 km from Hanoi, Non Nuoc Cao Bang UNESCO Global Geopark is characterised by both natural diversity and cultural richness, home to eight Indigenous groups. The geopark showcases an exceptional geological heritage, with limestone sequences displaying a complete tropical karst evolution cycle. This includes classic landforms such as caves with speleothems, underground and surface rivers, and the Ban Gioc Waterfall—one of the world’s largest waterfalls situated on an international border. The Thang Hen lake system, comprising 36 interconnected natural lakes, is another key feature, offering insights into karst hydrology and presenting a tranquil landscape shaped by geological processes. The geopark is also home to rare and endangered species, including the Eastern black crested gibbon, which inhabits the forested limestone mountains.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Non Nuoc Cao Bang UNESCO Global Geopark reflects a long history of human occupation and cultural continuity. The region is known for its vibrant cultural traditions, including festivals, traditional crafts, and folk arts maintained by its eight ethnic groups. It is considered a ‘Holy Land’, with archaeological evidence showing human presence over 20,000 years ago. It was once the capital of various feudal dynasties and later became a centre of revolutionary activity in Viet Nam’s modern history. The geological heritage and biodiversity have strongly influenced local culture, shaping traditional cuisines, costumes, rituals, and daily life. The traditional paper-making craft of the Nung An people in Dia Tren Hamlet, transforms May Sla tree bark into votive paper using age-old techniques passed down through generations. Cultural identity and natural heritage come together to form a foundation for sustainable tourism, as local communities offer visitors meaningful engagement with both Earth history and living traditions.
Quote: “Frontier province and one of the cradles of pre-historic people”

Introduction EN: The geopark contains a particularly high concentration of archaeological features, some dating back to Neolithic times. The Burren Forest in west Cavan offers striking examples of prehistoric tombs.Discover the 2,600-hectare Lough Navar Forest, a paradise for walkers, anglers, and outdoor enthusiasts. A scenic 10km drive offers one of the best views in Ireland, with diverse trails through bogs, woodlands and open water.Embark on the Scarplands Cycle Trail, starting in Belcoo and ending in Lough Navar Forest. With panoramic views over Lough Erne, 60km of rugged terrain, and shorter options like the 21km Aghanaglack Loop, it's ideal for biking enthusiasts seeking adventure.
Description: Cuilcagh Lakelands UNESCO Global Geopark is the world’s first UNESCO Global Geopark to cross an international border. Located in the northwestern corner of the island of Ireland, it spans County Fermanagh in Northern Ireland and County Cavan in the Republic of Ireland. The landscape reflects a glaciated history, with extensive uplands smoothed by successive ice sheets and broad U-shaped valleys leading down to lowlands dotted with lakes formed in glacial hollows. Swarms of drumlins form rounded, egg-shaped hills throughout the region. The uplands are characterised by forest, blanket bog, and karst terrain, where limestone has been sculpted by rainfall into significant cave systems—most notably the world-famous Cuilcagh Lakelands caves. These caves, widely regarded as a world-class natural attraction, contain stream passages formed by three rivers that sink underground on the slopes of Cuilcagh Mountain. Visitors can explore this subterranean environment via guided tours, beginning with a boat ride along an underground river and continuing on foot past formations of stalactites, stalagmites and flowstones. While the oldest rocks in the geopark date back 895 million years to the Precambrian and consist mainly of metamorphosed sedimentary rocks, the dominant geology consists of marine and deltaic sedimentary rocks—including limestones, mudstones, shales, and sandstones—from the Lower and Upper Carboniferous period (340 to 320 million years ago). These sequences are best viewed in the upland regions, where dramatic cliffs, escarpments, and caves expose the layers. Palaeogene intrusive igneous dykes, formed around 65 million years ago, are also present. More recent Quaternary deposits, starting from 1.8 million years ago, include glacial material such as drumlins and moraines, while extensive peat bogs have developed since the last glaciation about 15,000 years ago.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Cuilcagh Lakelands UNESCO Global Geopark celebrates a near-continuous human presence spanning more than 10,000 years, shaped by and deeply connected to the landscape. Communities have long depended on the land’s resources, fostering a strong cultural and ecological relationship that the geopark continues to support through engagement and collaboration. Initiatives such as the Digital Poetry Map, created during the COVID-19 pandemic, showcase this connection through contributions from local poets, schoolchildren, and ambassadors inspired by the geopark’s geoheritage. The geopark’s network of Guides, Ambassadors, and Heritage Champions further strengthens these ties by helping local residents and visitors explore and interpret the natural and cultural heritage of the area, while also advancing sustainable tourism and community-based development. Education is a core priority. The geopark offers hands-on, curriculum-aligned learning experiences in its "Outdoor Classrooms," where students of all ages engage with topics such as geology and biodiversity through interactive workshops, including poetry sessions and minibeast hunts. These programmes foster a lifelong appreciation for the environment and the region’s unique heritage.
Quote: “A natural underworld of rivers, waterfalls, and winding passages”

Introduction EN: Within the territory, there are four colles castelleres, groups that create human towers at almost all the local festivities.The geopark features a unique heritage related to the art of dry-stone construction paired with the culture of wine, the Denomination of Origin "Pla de Bages."In 2003, the Salt Mountain Cultural Park was established, providing a captivating insight into the significance of this natural wonder.
Description: The remarkable tale of Central Catalonia UNESCO Global Geopark unfolds approximately 41 to 37 million years ago, in the midst of the Eocene epoch. At that time, this region lay submerged beneath vast waters, stretching from the present-day Balearic Islands to the northeastern reaches of the Iberian Peninsula. Within this expanse, rivers deposited sequence upon sequence of sediments. However, the relentless forces of tectonic activity shaped the landscape, giving rise to the majestic Pyrenees. These dramatic transformations caused the once-thriving sea to retreat, ultimately transforming it into an expansive salt lake. Gradually, this ancient body of water succumbed to evaporation, leaving behind a rich tapestry of sediments that now bear witness to the birth and demise of an ancient sea. Once at the depths of that sea stood Montserrat’s imposing massif which, resembling a saw-shaped wonder, dominates the geopark, captivating the gaze from every vantage point. Its remarkable conglomerate-built geomorphology adds to its allure, forming a distinctive silhouette that has fascinated not only local Catalans but also renowned modernist authors and architects worldwide. Figures like Santiago Rusiñol, Ramon Casas, and, according to tradition, Antoni Gaudí found inspiration in the deep wells, vast chambers, and awe-inspiring speleothems within the caves. One of the most remarkable legacies is the Cardona Salt Mountain. The Salina Valley of Cardona, known for its abundant salt reserves and the discovery of potash in the early 1900s, has been a vital part of the region's identity since Neolithic times. In 2003, the Salt Mountain Cultural Park was established, providing a captivating insight into the significance of this natural wonder. This unique salt formation, resembling a mountain of pure salt that continues to grow with each extraction, stands as a testament to the Earth's geological processes throughout the ages. Beneath the surface lie the magnificent El Toll Caves, subterranean wonders formed within calcareous rocks deposited as an ancient coral reef 38 million years ago. Known as the "Palace of the Fauna of the Quaternary" (Palau de la Fauna del Quaternari,) these caves are not only a geological marvel but also a crucial paleontological site. Archaeological excavations have uncovered remnants of human presence from the Middle Paleolithic to the Bronze Age, offering a fascinating glimpse into our ancestors' lives. Paleontologists have made significant discoveries, including important Neanderthal remains, within these historic depths.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The cultural heritage of the geopark is deeply connected to the region’s history, with Romanesque and medieval sites such as the Santa Maria Monastery at L’Estany, the Castle of Castellbell, the Castle of Mura, the Castle of Súria, the Salipota Tower, and the Castle of Talamanca, all designated as Cultural Assets of National Interest. Additionally, elements of industrial archaeology, particularly related to the textile and mining industries, reflect the historical economic activities of the area. Local communities maintain and promote their heritage which includes wine vats, dry-stone constructions, along with churches and lime kilns, which contribute to the traditional landscape and economy. Intangible heritage plays a significant role in sustaining local traditions. The art of dry-stone walling is closely linked to viticulture, with ongoing collaborations between the geopark, the DO Pla de Bages, and the Natural Park of Sant Llorenç del Munt i l’Obac to safeguard this practice. The human towers (castells) tradition, upheld by four colles castelleres in the region, remains a key feature of local festivals and community life. Additionally, the geopark promotes the Mediterranean diet, which has been recognised by UNESCO for its cultural significance in food production, preparation, and shared consumption.
Quote: “Amazing geology, mining heritage and landscape, together with millennia of human presence”

Introduction EN: Visit the Red House Glass Cone, one of the UK’s last surviving glassmaking cones, now a visitor centre showcasing the region’s glassmaking heritage.Explore Bumble Hole and Warrens Hall, a historic coal mining landscape and active canal junction central to the Black Country’s industrial past.Discover Park Lime Pits, a former limestone quarry now transformed into a local nature reserve with clear pools and species-rich grasslands.
Description: The Black Country UNESCO Global Geopark, located between Birmingham and Wolverhampton, presents a unique urban landscape shaped by 428 million years of geological history. The area is internationally recognised for its exceptionally well-preserved fossils and rich deposits of coal, ironstone, fireclay, and limestone—natural resources that fuelled discovery and invention, placing the region at the heart of the Industrial Revolution. The rocks of the Black Country record major environmental changes over deep time and include Europe’s thickest coal seam (12 metres), interbedded with other economically important layers. Fossil reef structures preserved in life position and the world’s best-preserved fossil spider highlight the scientific value of the area. The trilobite species Calymene, known locally as the ‘Dudley Bug’, has strong cultural ties and appeared as the mascot of the limestone miners and on the town of Dudley’s coat of arms. The geopark encompasses a wide range of geosites, including disused mines and quarries, canals, nature reserves, museums, open-air attractions, and historic buildings. It connects the geology beneath our feet with the cultural and industrial heritage that continues to shape the landscape above.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: At the height of the Industrial Revolution, American Consul Elihu Burritt described the Black Country as a land “black by day and red by night”, shaped by intensive coal mining. Despite its dark industrial past, the region became a centre of experimentation and innovation, closely linked to the development of geology. It was here that the oldest geological map (Metallum Martis, 1665) was produced, and the earliest seismograph recording was made (Milne-Shaw, 1913). The area’s geodiversity supported a variety of landscapes and habitats, as well as vast natural resources, enabling the emergence of the world’s first large-scale industrial region. It became a cradle of technological innovation, with major contributions from figures such as Abraham Darby, known as the “Father of the Industrial Revolution”, and Sir Roderick Murchison, who defined the Silurian Period. The world’s first powerful steam engine—the Newcomen engine—was developed in the Black Country, revolutionising mining. To support industry, the region also constructed a dense network of canals, including the world’s oldest navigable canal tunnel. Today, the legacy of this industrial past is visible in the landscape and continues to be expressed through the traditions, dialect, and cultural practices of local communities. The geopark welcomes nearly 32 million visitors each year, many of whom walk the Monarch’s Way, a historic route linked to King Charles II’s escape after the English Civil War.
