Introduction EN: Discover an important concentration of Megalithic monuments, with remnants of Celtic fortifications atop each Lora, including the fourth largest Celtic fortification in Europe at Ulaña Lora.Visit the Cañón de la Horadada for scenic hiking trails overlooking limestone gorges carved by the Pisuerga River.
Description: Located at the southwestern edge of the Basque-Cantabrian Basin, Las Loras UNESCO Global Geopark offers a unique geological experience. Visitors can witness the effects of the opening of the Atlantic Ocean, discover remnants of Mesozoic fauna and flora, observe the grand marine transgression of the Upper Cretaceous, and explore the stages of deformation during the Alpine Orogeny. Two notable natural monuments within the geopark are Las Tuerces and Covalagua. These sites showcase the final stages of karst evolution, often referred to as rock cities or enchanted towns. They exemplify the karst ruinform landscape, featuring doline fields and other remarkable karstic elements. The morphology of the area is controlled by the different hardness of the Mesozoic substrate materials, as well as by the geological structures of the sedimentary rock layers. In this sense, the limestones and dolomites are the competent materials compared to the loams and sands, which erode more easily. This generates the development of large and deep canyons excavated by the current river network. The transitional location of the geopark, halfway between the Castilian Plateau and the Cantabrian Mountain Range, gives the region a wide range of environments and biodiversity, with both Euro-Siberian sites and Mediterranean sites. Limestone cliffs and significant high-altitude moorlands alternate with gorges and deep valleys sunk by the existing river system. Palaeontology and geomorphology are other highlights of the geological heritage of the territory. There are many important palaeontological sites such as Upper Jurassic floral macrofossils, skeletal remains of a Camptosaurus, and also important Upper Cretaceous rudist and coral colonies. The Mesozoic moorlands, known as Loras, define the landscape of the region and serve as a unifying element for the geopark, connecting geology, landscape, and cultural characteristics and setting the region apart from neighbouring areas. The presence of several castros (forts), almost one for each Lora, gives coherence and cohesion to Las Loras UNESCO Global Geopark.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The communities within the Las Loras UNESCO Global Geopark rely primarily on arable and livestock farming as their main sources of livelihood, maintaining traditional agricultural practices that have shaped the landscape for generations. In Aguilar de Campoo, the biscuit industry plays a significant role in the local economy, contributing to employment and regional production. The oil industry is also present in the territory, with the only onshore oil field in the Iberian Peninsula located in Ayoluengo. Cultural heritage is deeply rooted in the region. The geopark boasts the highest concentration of Romanesque churches in Spain, with over 100—many of which are maintained through local restoration initiatives. The Monastery of Santa María la Real, managed by a foundation in collaboration with the geopark, serves as a centre for conservation, interpretation, and promotion of the area's historical and architectural legacy. The restoration of San Lorenzo Mártir Church in Fuentes de Valdepero, led by the Manapites Association, reflects community efforts to preserve heritage while fostering cultural engagement. The geopark also supports intangible cultural heritage, with dry-stone walling and manual bell ringing recognised by UNESCO for their historical and cultural significance. Local festivals, music, dances, and traditions—such as Mascaritos y Zamarrones—continue to be actively promoted through community initiatives and regional tourism efforts, strengthening cultural identity and sustaining traditional knowledge.
Quote: “The Loras, high altitude moorlands, topped with impressive forts”

Introduction EN: Visit the enchanting Spring of the Pitarque River, one of the geopark's remarkable natural wonders.Explore 13 historical villages designated as "National Monuments" for their Middle Age castles and traditional country houses known as "masadas."
Description: Nestled within the Spanish western Iberian Range and formed during the Alpine Orogeny, some areas of Maestrazgo UNESCO Global Geopark are characterised by a large and varied number of Mesozoic (220–65 million years ago) stratigraphic formations, deposited when an embayment of a warm sea periodically covered this area. During periods of sea ingress, the seabed became a thriving habitat for corals and various invertebrate creatures. However, as the tides receded, rivers took their turn, depositing layers of sandy sediments on to the seabed. This alternating cycle of marine colonisation and river sedimentation created a dynamic environment within the geopark, leaving behind a remarkable geological record which was later shaped by the formation and folding of the Pyrenees. This makes Maestrazgo UNESCO Global Geopark an exceptional laboratory for exploring the geological evolution of the Iberian Plate during the Mesozoic and Tertiary periods. Some of the geopark’s highlights include the mesmerising Grutas de Cristal (Crystal Caves) in Molinos—a network of chambers adorned with stalactites and stalagmites—and the towering limestone formations known as the Órganos de Montoro, reaching over 200 metres in height. The small village of Aliaga, 50 km northeast of Teruel, is another geological hotspot. Lying at the nodal point of two geological folds that follow one another, the geological structures can be clearly observed in the Guadalope River valley, which cuts deep into them. An educational path with eleven interpretive points explains these geological processes. The village also features a Mining Interpretation Centre that tells the story of past coal mining, used to generate electricity until 1982. Maestrazgo UNESCO Global Geopark also has an important palaeontological heritage, which has been used to accurately reconstruct palaeoenvironments that existed millions of years ago in this area. Focusing exclusively on dinosaurs, there are 76 catalogued palaeontological sites, including one at Galve—a small village with a significant collection of fossils, several footprints, and life-size reconstructions of the most representative specimens.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: During the medieval era, the region—then part of the Kingdom of Aragón—was governed by a military order called the maestres, who named it “Maestrazgo”, from which the geopark takes its name. Maestrazgo UNESCO Global Geopark is deeply connected to its cultural heritage, with over 600 documented archaeological sites highlighting centuries of human settlement and activity. The rock art of the Mediterranean Basin on the Iberian Peninsula, inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List, includes exceptional prehistoric paintings depicting the way of life during a key phase of human development. The built heritage of the geopark reflects its long history of human habitation, including monasteries, churches, castles, and structures linked to traditional industries. A notable example is the Piquer Tower, the only preserved fortified farmhouse in the Somontano region of Teruel. The geopark has played a key role in drafting restoration plans for this unique structure. Another significant feature is the network of ice houses and cold vaults, which showcases historic methods of ice storage and trade. Intangible heritage is an integral part of life in the geopark, encompassing traditional festivals, music, and rituals. The Tamboradas drum-playing rituals take place annually during Easter Week, with coordinated drum performances resonating across villages along the Tambor and Bombo Route. Seasonal traditions such as the Fiestas de Invierno (Winter Parties), including Hogueras, Mochigangas, and Sanantonadas, are supported by the geopark and reflect the region’s deep-rooted folklore and communal celebrations. The Romerías (pilgrimages) to hermitages, accompanied by traditional music and customs, are a vital part of local identity and were the subject of a publication in 2021. Another key cultural event is the Poplar Tree Festival, celebrated in Berge and Cuevas de Almudén to honour the role of poplar tree culture in Aragonese traditions.

Titre EN: Sierra Morena de Sevilla UNESCO Global Geopark
Introduction EN: The “Beja-Acebuches” amphibolites, interpreted as the remains of an ancient ocean floor and a suture between tectonic plates, are a rare occurrence.Located in the geographical centre of the park, Cazalla de la Sierra is one of the most famous towns in this northern part of the province of Seville.Constantina is a stunning small village that is well worth the visit.
Description: Like a balcony overlooking the vast and fertile plains of Andalusia, the Sierra Morena de Sevilla UNESCO Global Geopark stretches across the gentle mountains of the western Sierra Morena, north of Seville. The landscape is shaped by ancient Mediterranean forest, with towering holm and cork oaks forming a distinctive natural environment. The geopark reveals over 1 billion years of Earth’s history through its undulating terrain—ranging from carbonates and quartzite to eroded plutonic rocks and expansive valleys filled with more recent sediments. Several canyons and river gorges cut through the landscape, and numerous geosites offer insights into the region’s geological evolution. One of the most notable is the Cerro del Hierro Natural Monument, a palaeo-karst landscape formed 520 million years ago in a tropical marine environment that once hosted archaeocyathids and cyanobacteria. In the Valle Syncline, sedimentary layers document the Lower Palaeozoic, when marine fauna thrived around the supercontinent Gondwana. The area preserves a complete fossil record spanning from the Ordovician to the Devonian period. Another exceptional palaeontological site is found in Constantina, where Lower Cambrian jellyfish imprints are preserved. Ninety large discoidal imprints are etched into a single surface, providing a rare glimpse into the marine life of this ancient period.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Sierra Merena de Sevilla UNESCO Global Geopark actively supports local communities by preserving cultural heritage, promoting sustainable tourism, and fostering economic opportunities linked to geodiversity and traditional practices. The geopark plays a key role in safeguarding the intangible heritage of the region, which includes Holy Week processions, religious pilgrimages, woodworking, saddlery, liquor production, and traditional crafts such as charcoal making, embroidery, and song and dance. Collaboration with cultural associations and volunteers has enhanced the visibility of historical routes like the Camino Real del Azogue (Royal Mercury Path), which was crucial for mercury transport during the 16th to 18th centuries. Interpretation materials and guided activities inform visitors of the region’s mining history, contributing to local engagement and tourism. Additionally, the geopark is linked to historical trade routes such as the Vía de la Plata, a Roman consular road that facilitated commerce and cultural exchange. By promoting this network of historical paths, the geopark connects communities and fosters economic opportunities tied to heritage tourism. Key heritage sites such as the Mina de Cerro del Hierro, the Necropolis of La Traviesa, and the Roman quarries of Los Covachos highlight the intersection of geology, history and local traditions.
Quote: “700-million-year story”

Introduction EN: The Mycological Garden "La Trufa", the first of its kind in Europe, combines research, an interpretation centre, and a garden featuring eight recreated Andalusian ecosystems where mushrooms are cultivated.The Santa Rita Visitor Centre is the main reception point of the geopark, offering general information and featuring a stratigraphical column made of natural rocks and a giant ammonite sculpture.
Description: In the heart of Andalucía, approximately 80 km south of Córdoba, lies the region of La Subbética, an area of notable natural and geological interest in the central part of the Betic Mountain Range. Here lies the Sierras Subbéticas UNESCO Global Geopark. Limestone and dolostone formations dominate the higher terrains of the geopark, creating a landscape marked by significant karst features. These include poljes, dolines, and karrens, as well as the recent formation of a ponor—a sinkhole that provides access to a network of around 900 caves and abysses. Among these is the Sima de Cabra, a vertical shaft located near the village of Cabra. With a depth of 131 metres, it is recognised as a distinctive cave and geosite of historical and geological importance. The first documented descent took place in 1683, when a quarry worker was lowered into the chasm as part of a murder investigation. He successfully retrieved a body from the bottom, in what is considered one of the earliest recorded cave rescues. In 1841, two teachers from Cabra High School undertook a scientific exploration of the cave and documented their observations. This expedition predates the work of Édouard-Alfred Martel, who is widely credited with founding modern speleology. Today, access to the Sima de Cabra is restricted to professional speleologists in order to ensure the site’s preservation.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Traversing the low and midlands of the Sierras Subbéticas UNESCO Global Geopark means passing through extensive olive groves—evidence of the region's main economic activity: olive oil production. Olive farming, particularly in the hilly landscapes of the geopark, is increasingly practised as ecological agriculture, ensuring sustainability for future generations. The region’s extra virgin olive oil has been recognised as among the best in the world since 2013, earning numerous international awards. The town of Cabra holds a unique place in literary history. Miguel de Cervantes, the renowned author of Don Quixote, spent five years of his childhood in Cabra and referenced the town’s well-known sinkhole in three of his works, including Don Quixote. This connection to Spain’s literary heritage reflects the deep cultural layers present within the geopark. Traditional cultural expressions remain vibrant throughout the geopark. Flamenco, born in Andalusia and designated UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2010, continues to thrive in the region, with Peñas Flamencas (flamenco clubs) present in many villages and the annual Zambra Flamenco Festival in Rute. The region also preserves a distinct local musical tradition, the Mochileros de Gaena, celebrated in a dedicated museum in Gaena (Cabra). Education and sustainable tourism play a key role in community development. The geopark has implemented school programmes such as the "Geodiversity and Geological Heritage of Sierras Subbéticas" didactic unit, aimed at secondary students. Other educational projects include the Book of Strata, documenting the region’s geological evolution, and the Benches of Time in Doña Mencía, which incorporate geological storytelling into public spaces.
Quote: “Sierras Subbéticas, the Kingdom of Ammonites”

Introduction EN: Hike the over 1,000 km of well-maintained trails that offer breathtaking views, accompanied by the ever-present sound of flowing water from melting ice.Visit the Ordesa y Monte Perdido National Park, a spectacular ensemble of four valleys: Ordesa, Añisclo, Escuaín and Pineta.
Description: The Sobrarbe-Pirineos UNESCO Global Geopark, encompassing the entire Sobrarbe region in northern Spain’s Huesca province, is a striking geological and ecological sanctuary where the forces of nature have sculpted the landscape over half a billion years. The geopark’s diverse topography, ranging from the El Grado reservoir at 475 metres to the Llardana peak at 3,375 metres, hosts a unique blend of Mediterranean and high-mountain climates, fostering a remarkable variety of ecosystems. The geopark is structured into four main geomorphological units, each bearing witness to major geological events. The axial zone of the Pyrenees preserves the area’s oldest rocks, dating back 500 million years, while the Inner Sierras, dominated by Monte Perdido, represent the largest limestone massif in Europe, with summits exceeding 3,000 metres. The dramatic collision of tectonic plates and the disappearance of the Tertiary Sea played a fundamental role in shaping these landscapes, leaving behind vast sequences of Cambrian to Quaternary rocks. This geological evolution is still visible today, from ancient Variscan metamorphic rocks to the more recent Pyrenean orogeny, which gave rise to the imposing mountain chain. The geodiversity of Sobrarbe-Pirineos is exceptional, shaped not only by mountain-building processes but also by glacial, periglacial, karst, and fluvial activity. The last Ice Age left a profound imprint, with active glaciers such as those of Monte Perdido, Marboré, and Llardana continuing their slow retreat. The karst landscape, particularly abundant in the region, features fluviokarstic ravines, deep limestone gorges, and hidden cave systems formed by underground water erosion. Rivers like the Cinca and Ara have carved their way through the mountains, forming terraced deposits that align with ancient glacial moraines, offering invaluable insights into past climatic conditions. Landslides and mass movements, still active today, further contribute to the region’s dynamic geology.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The local communities of the Sobrarbe-Pirineos UNESCO Global Geopark have a deep appreciation for their landscapes, and education plays a key role in the geopark’s approach. Activities include geological itineraries for primary and secondary schools, an intensive geological heritage course for university students, and an annual seminar open to the general public. A training course for geological heritage guides has also been established to generate new employment opportunities and strengthen local businesses. The geopark is home to many heritage sites. Notable among them is the Pirineos-Monte Perdido UNESCO World Heritage Site, recognised for its cultural landscape and historical transhumance practices. Additionally, the Camino de Santiago European Cultural Route passes through Sobrarbe, linking the geopark to one of the most important pilgrimage routes in Europe. Intangible heritage is also well preserved, with several traditions officially recognised by UNESCO. The Pyrenean Summer Solstice Fires and the Falleta de San Juan de Plan are both designated as UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage. The region is also known for its dry-stone constructions, recently added to the UNESCO Intangible Heritage list; the Mallata Project focuses on restoring traditional dry-stone buildings and preserving transhumance practices. Other significant traditions include the Navatas descent of the River Cinca—an Aragonese Activity of Touristic Interest—and the conservation of folk legends tied to the region’s geological heritage, including ancient tales of Silvan and Roldan.
Quote: “The formation of the Pyrenees”

Introduction EN: The Isterinkoski rapids in the Poikajoki River fall nearly thirty metres and span millions of years in the geological record.Visit Lake Oulujärvi, the fourth largest lake in Finland, covering almost 900 km².Local museums, such as Lamminaho Farm and the Kalevala village of Ahmas, preserve traditional ways of life and support educational activities focused on sustainability.
Description: Just 200 km south of the Arctic Circle, between the cities of Oulu and Kajaani, Rokua UNESCO Global Geopark tells the story of a landscape shaped over billions of years by tectonic activity and glaciation. The geopark lies within one of the oldest and most stable parts of the Earth’s continental crust, composed of Archean granite and gneiss formed up to 3.6 billion years ago. These ancient rocks are visible at geosites such as Kilonniemi. Although the area has experienced multiple phases of mountain building and glaciation, it was the last Ice Age—ending around 10,000 years ago—that left the most visible imprint. Features such as drumlins, moraines, esker ridges and kettle holes define the landscape. The geopark forms a geological corridor following the Rokua esker field, extending in a northwest–southeast direction. Glacial activity over millennia ground the bedrock into fine sand. As the glaciers retreated, winds carried this sand inland, forming extensive dune fields. Today, these dunes are covered with vegetation that supports a wide range of plant and animal species. Viewed from the air, the dunes appear as long ripples across the terrain.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Rokua UNESCO Global Geopark reflects the strong relationship between local communities and the region’s arctic nature, traditions and history. In winter, visitors can experience a snow-covered landscape shaped by the Ice Age, where frozen lakes and forests offer a glimpse into past ways of life. The Geopark School concept, launched in 2015, integrates geodiversity, sustainability, and heritage into education. In Muhos, a secondary school, upper secondary school, and adult education centre form a shared “Geopark Campus.” Students participate in field trips, expert-led lessons, and international exchanges. The school buildings themselves reflect local geology through natural colours, recycled materials, and public art created by students. This place-based approach to learning is now being adopted in other geoparks across Europe. The region’s intangible heritage is rooted in local folktales and oral traditions, especially those linked to the Oulujoki River and stories of giants, some of which are tied to the Finnish national epic, the Kalevala. Villages within the geopark were home to the poets whose verses were collected during the compilation of the Kalevala in the 19th century. These tales were used to explain landscape features and are still preserved in place names today. Rokua UNESCO Global Geopark supports this heritage through publications, exhibitions and locally produced crafts inspired by these stories. Human settlement in the area dates back approximately 9,000 years, shortly after Lake Oulujärvi separated from the Ancylus Lake stage of the Baltic Sea. Archaeological remains of early dwellings—particularly around Säräisniemi village—include the oldest ceramics found in the geopark, known as Säräisniemi ceramics.
Quote: “Tells the story of the last Ice age and the story of people who followed the retreating ice”

Introduction EN: Visit Susiluola (Wolf Cave), the oldest archaeological site in the geopark.The medieval road of Kyrönkankaantie is one of the best-preserved medieval roads in Finland.The region is home to vast wildlife, typical of the boreal coniferous forest, including bears, lynx and wolves. The elk population is high and more recently, a population of Finnish Forest Reindeer has been reintroduced to the area.
Description: Located in southern Finland, 268 km north of Helsinki, Lauhanvuori–Hämeenkangas UNESCO Global Geopark spans a landscape shaped by dramatic geological change—from ancient mountain ranges to mires and sandy plains. Its gently undulating terrain, covered by boreal forests, raised bogs and sparse human settlement, bears the marks of tectonic forces and glacial retreat. The geopark traces a journey beginning 1.9 billion years ago, when tectonic collisions formed a mountain range, now worn down by erosion and reshaped by Ice Age glaciers and the retreating waters of the Baltic Sea. Kivijata, a sandstone boulder field formed from an ancient beach, is one of the geopark’s most striking sites. Originally a sandstone cliff, it collapsed under erosion and was later shaped by glacial and marine activity. Today, a 4.6 km hiking trail allows visitors to explore this unique landscape. Nearby, the Aumakivi corestone is a rounded granite tor, seemingly placed in the forest like a giant stone egg. Its origin—possibly through freeze–thaw cycles or groundwater weathering—remains a point of scientific discussion. The Hämeenkangas ridge, a sandy esker in the southern part of the geopark, features kettle holes, fossil dunes, and paleo-shorelines. Natural springs emerge from its edges, including the culturally significant Jämijärvi's Uhrilähde (Sacrifice Spring) and Kylmänmyllynlähde (Cold Mill Spring), highlighting the ongoing interaction between geology, water and human history.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Lauhanvuori–Hämeenkangas UNESCO Global Geopark is home to rich cultural and intangible heritage shaped by thousands of years of human presence and interaction with the landscape. Archaeological remains such as the Myllyluoma tepee—inhabited between 6000 and 6500 BC when the area was part of the shoreline of the ancient Lake Ancylus—highlight early settlement in the region. The Susiluola cave has drawn national and international attention for its evidence of possible Neanderthal habitation during the Eemian interglacial period. It remains the only known site with such traces later covered by a continental ice sheet. Today, the site is protected under the Finnish Antiquities Act and managed in cooperation with national and provincial heritage authorities. Cultural heritage is actively promoted through exhibitions, educational programmes, and guided tours. Intangible heritage is also a strong focus. Traditional practices such as tar burning and the brewing of sahti—a traditional beer—remain part of local identity. Spelit, a traditional folk music and dance festival, celebrates the musical heritage of southern Ostrobothnia each summer, and includes the the Finnish championships for harmonica and mandolin players.

Titre EN: Causses de Quercy UNESCO Global Geopark
Introduction EN: The Camino de Santiago, known in English as the St. James Way, crosses the geopark from Gréalou to Flaujac-Poujols.The region is renowned for its megaliths, with over 400 early human constructions. The Dolmen of Pierre Martine, on the hills above Livernon, is the largest, measuring 7.10 metres long and 2.30 metres wide, with support slabs over 5 metres long, weighing 22 tonnes.The dry-stone constructions known as 'caselles,' built without mortar, date from the 19th century and are still preserved today.
Description: The geological heritage of the Causses du Quercy UNESCO Global Geopark reflects the long interplay between tectonic uplift and water erosion. These forces have shaped a distinctive limestone landscape of cliffs, sinkholes, dry valleys, caves and chasms. It is a region where the slow processes of Earth’s history are clearly visible in its karst formations. The best-known of these is the Gouffre de Padirac, a 75-metre-deep sinkhole accessible by lift, where visitors can travel by boat along underground galleries filled with turquoise water. The Cloup d'Aural, another key karst feature, is a collapsed cave filled with phosphate-rich clay. This rare geological phenomenon preserved thousands of fossils and was mined for phosphate in the 19th century. It is now recognised internationally as a site of geological and palaeontological importance. Covering 186,000 hectares in the south of France, at the northern end of the Occitanie/Pyrénées-Méditerranée region, the geopark lies between the low plains of the Aquitaine Basin and the mountains of the Massif Central. Its limestone plateaus—known as causses—rise as arid expanses with networks of dry valleys. In contrast, their depths conceal complex underground water systems that have carved caves and nourished green corridors, home to 26 bat species. Tectonic activity and the constant action of water have also shaped dramatic surface features: cliffs and canyons, where patches of oak woodland grow and villages cling to rocky outcrops. Rocamadour, a historic pilgrimage site built against a limestone cliff, and Saint-Cirq-Lapopie, perched above the Lot River, are among the most striking examples. The geopark's remote setting, with low population density and minimal light pollution, also makes it one of the best places in France to observe the night sky. The area between Rocamadour and the Célé Valley is known as the “Black Triangle of Quercy”—the darkest zone in mainland France—where visitors can see the Milky Way in exceptional clarity.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Causses du Quercy UNESCO Global Geopark takes its name from both its geological and cultural heritage: the causses, or limestone plateaus, and Quercy, the historic territory of the Cadurques Gallic people. The relationship between humans and stone defines the region, where limestone has shaped the identity and landscape for millennia. This connection is visible throughout the built environment—every dry-stone wall, shelter, or house reflects the use of local limestone. Generations have adapted to the karstic terrain by carving basins to retain water, clearing dolines and dry valleys for cultivation, and using caves for shelter, ritual, or artistic expression. Some of the oldest archaeological evidence in the region dates back 400,000 years, with uses ranging from hunting traps and pigment sources to phosphatic clays mined in the 19th century. The region is also home to Pech Merle, one of the few prehistoric painted caves in France still open to the public. With over two kilometres of galleries on two levels, it showcases paintings nearly 29,000 years old and remains accessible to a wide range of visitors. Today, the geopark is a rural territory with an economy based on agriculture, crafts and tourism. The geopark works to support sustainable tourism that benefits the entire region. Its “open-air museum” approach encourages visitors to experience the landscape in situ through an extensive network of discovery routes. The Via Causs’mos, a 20 km artistic and interpretive itinerary, invites visitors to explore the limestone plateaus of Gramat, Saint-Chels and Limogne, highlighting the natural environment and traditional built heritage of the valleys.
Quote: “If stones could speak…”

Introduction EN: Try butterfly watching in Digne-les-Bains.Enjoy the amazing view from the Vélodrome d’Esclangon or the Pénitent des Mées.Hike the ‘La Routo’ trail that connects the Camargue and Crau plains in lower Provence to Piedmont’s Alpine valleys.
Description: Located on the south-western flank of the Alpine Arc, the Haute-Provence UNESCO Global Geopark preserves an exceptional 300-million-year geological record. Studied over generations by European geologists, it continues to serve as an open-air classroom for universities and research institutions. The region’s textbook outcrops provide clear evidence of the geodynamic processes that shape the Earth's surface, from the continental break-up between the Triassic and Jurassic periods (approximately 251 to 152 million years ago) to the glacial cycles of the Quaternary (beginning around 2 million years ago and continuing to the present). Several geosites are of international significance. These include the ammonite slab at Digne-les-Bains, where over 1,500 ammonites—some measuring up to 70 cm in diameter—are fossilised in a 320 m² limestone surface; the Vélodrome d’Esclangon, a natural amphitheatre revealing a nearly continuous 15-million-year sequence of sand, clay, and pebble deposits deformed by tectonic forces and later exposed by erosion; and the 185-million-year-old Ichthyosaurus fossil at La Robine, which led to the creation of Europe’s first site museum dedicated to the protection of a palaeontological specimen.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: For millennia, the rugged landscape of the Haute-Provence UNESCO Global Geopark provided strategic protection. The hilltop village of Thoard and the Citadel of Sisteron, built into vertical limestone strata, are enduring examples. At the Pierre-Écrite site, a 5th-century Roman inscription by Claudius Postumus Dardanus describes the foundation of Théopolis—a spiritual centre fortified against barbarian threats. The limestone cliffs that characterise the geopark support unique biodiversity, including wallcreepers, thuriferous junipers—relicts from the last Ice Age—and a variety of aromatic plants such as thyme, rosemary, and sage. Local traditions tied to this biodiversity remain strong. Seasonal festivals held in July and August, including the “Corso de la Lavande” and the “Foire de la Lavande” in Digne-les-Bains, celebrate the lavender harvest and its essential oil, a key ingredient in regional perfume and cosmetic production.
Quote: “300 million-year old rocks reveal their secrets in Haute Provence”

Titre EN: Massif des Bauges UNESCO Global Geopark
Introduction EN: Local wine producers have long been aware that the quality and originality of their wines is due to the region’s underlying geological conditions, which not only define the soil type but also the topography, and therefore influence climate. The Vin de Savoie, as it is known, holds the appellation d'origine contrôlée label (AOC) that identifies it as unique.To go with the wine, the Tome des Bauges is a semi-hard cheese made from unpasteurised milk from cows that feed exclusively on grass, giving an earthy aroma.Visit one of the three astronomy-inspired centres in Curienne, Aillon-le-Jeune, and Le Châtelard ito explore the stars through sculptures, a planetarium, interactive games, poetry, and a giant stargazing hammock.
Description: Just a few kilometres from Mont Blanc, the limestone crests of the Massif des Bauges form over 200 km² of karstified surface, supplying water to France’s two largest natural lakes: Lake Bourget and Lake Annecy. Located in the northern French Alps, the geopark rises as a preserved natural area from the surrounding urbanised valleys, forming a sequence of folded limestone crests aligned southwest to northeast and reaching altitudes above 2,200 metres. The stratigraphic record of the geopark spans from the Upper Jurassic (around 163.5 million years ago) to the Lower Cretaceous (113 million years ago). Though geologically brief, this period saw the formation of exceptional alpine structures such as the Arclusaz Syncline—a perched syncline clearly visible from the Isère flood plain. The folded V-shaped rock structure is accessible via mountain trails through the Vallon des Bellevaux, offering both scientific value and scenic views. The region’s karst system plays a central role in its geological and hydrological identity. It feeds Lake Annecy—formed by glacial activity around 18,000 years ago—through rivers, streams, and an extensive subterranean network. This system has given rise to significant geosites such as the Prérouge karst spring, the Pissieu Waterfall, and the Chéran Gorges, which are spanned by the 19th-century Abîme Suspension Bridge.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Local communities in the Massif des Bauges UNESCO Global Geopark play an active role in maintaining a tradition of nature-based tourism, managing mountain chalets and supporting access to hiking trails throughout the year. Agriculture and forestry remain key economic sectors, and the geopark works closely with local producers to support sustainable practices and promote products linked to the territory, including cheeses, honey, wine, and aromatic plants. Several of these, such as “Tome des Bauges” and “Vins de Savoie,” hold official designations of origin. Some producers offer guided visits that connect local geology and landscape with wine production, illustrating the link between soils, exposure and taste. In recent years, the geopark has led innovative work on night-time light pollution, implementing measures to preserve the quality of the night sky and studying the effects of artificial light on biodiversity. They have produced practical toolkits for local municipalities.  Three astronomy-themed sites have been created in Curienne, Aillon-le-Jeune, and Le Châtelard; developed with local artisans and astronomy clubs, these sites offer installations such as a planetarium, sculptures, interactive games, an audio guide, and a stargazing hammock. The initiative has successfully engaged schools and families, strengthening community involvement in the conservation of local biodiversity, strongly impacted by light pollution.
Quote: “More than 200 km² of karstified surface to supply water to the two largest natural lakes in France””

Introduction EN: Visit Fort Point at the stunning natural harbour, Trinity Harbour and conjure up a history of defence against invaders.Bird Island Puffin Site is a perfect spot to observe seals, dolphins, and seabirds including black guillemots, kittiwake, terns, and murres.The popular Haootia walking trail is where scientists discovered one of the world’s oldest complex animal fossils.
Description: Covering 280 km of rugged coastline full of remarkable views, caves, arches and sea stacks, the area is dominated by an assemblage of Neoproterozoic rocks (1,000 to 538 million years ago), offering a unique opportunity to observe, study, and celebrate one of the most significant transitions in Earth’s history: the Ediacaran Period, which marks the first appearance of widespread multicellular fauna. The Catalina Dome comprises deep-marine siliciclastics containing Bouma-type turbidites. It is upon the laterally extensive bedding planes that the exceptionally preserved remains of rangeomorph and other Ediacaran fossil forms are found. Often preserved beneath volcanic ash beds, the Catalina Dome fossil assemblage contains over 20 different taxa, and offers a globally significant opportunity for studies into the taphonomic, taxonomic, ecological, environmental, and stratigraphic contexts of the rise of large, complex life. The glaciated landscape of Bonavista Island in Newfoundland offers extraordinary geology both inland and along its coastline. Rock layers exposed along the shoreline record a dramatic transition in Earth history, from approximately 575 to about 525 million years ago (Ediacaran to early Cambrian periods). One must-see site is the Spillars Cove shoreline, which offers stunning views of a rugged coastline created by thousands of years of exposure to natural elements. Spillars Cove is a spectacular rocky bay, lying between Spillars Point to the east and Cape Bonavista to the west. This geosite has special significance, marking the boundary between the two geological halves of the Bonavista Peninsula. The Spillars Cove–English Harbour Fault Zone divides the Ediacaran fossil-containing rocks of the St. John’s Basin in the east from the rocks of the Bonavista Basin in the west.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Known to Europeans since 1497 when the Italian explorer Giovanni Caboto first arrived on this ‘new-found land’, the region is the ancestral home of the now-extinct Beothuk People. Legend has it that upon arrival, Caboto exclaimed "Oh che buona vista!"—forever coining the name of Bonavista Bay and the peninsula on which the Discovery UNESCO Global Geopark extends. The Discovery UNESCO Global Geopark respectfully acknowledges its territory as part of the ancestral homelands of the Indigenous Peoples of the region. Historical and archaeological records document the Beothuk People who lived throughout the northeast coast of Newfoundland, particularly around Notre Dame Bay and Bonavista Bay. The Beothuk had a distinct language and culture closely tied to land and sea resources. Early European explorers most likely encountered Indigenous communities in this region. The Bonavista Peninsula’s economic development has historically been based on the fishing industry. Today, community life continues to be shaped by strong links to land and sea, as well as a growing cultural and tourism economy. Internationally recognised hiking trails, boat tours, kayaking, museums, galleries, theatres, restaurants, tea rooms, shops, and accommodations contribute to the local economy. Many structures of architectural and historical significance have been preserved, including churches, lighthouses, fishing wharves, and stone root cellars. Examples include the Coaker Foundation and Ryan Premises National Historic Site, as well as restored village buildingsNear the Coaker Foundation, the geopark has supported the creation of an Art House, which is managed by young people in collaboration with the municipality.

Introduction EN: Herberts Quarry is a training ground for university students in geological mapping and research on alkaline pollution effects in Devonian and Carboniferous rocks.Cribarth, a striking ridge in the Swansea Valley, contains nationally and internationally important sedimentary and tectonic records of the Variscan Orogeny.Garn Goch and Pen-y-Crug are Iron Age hillforts linked to the Celtic Silures tribe, whose name inspired the Silurian period in geological history.
Description: Echoing ancient tales and dating back to a time when Norman French invaders reserved this upland realm for hunting in the 11th century, Fforest Fawr UNESCO Global Geopark is a landscape where nature and history intertwine. Visitors are taken on a geological journey spanning over 470 million years. Within the limestone terrain, swallow holes and sinks—like portals to the underworld—are found in greater abundance than anywhere else in the British Isles. In Waterfall Country, the rivers Nedd, Mellte, and Hepste meander through deep, forested gorges carved into the rock over millennia. The diverse soils, derived from a long sequence of marine and terrestrial strata, support an exceptional range of flora and fauna across the geopark. Karstification of the Carboniferous Limestone has given rise to extensive doline fields and some of the UK’s longest and deepest cave systems. Between 28,000 and 11,700 years ago, glacial activity sculpted the landscape, shaping the upland and lowland features seen today. These natural features are closely tied to human stories: myths and legends such as Culhwch ac Olwen and the tale of the Twrch Trwyth—considered the first record of Arthurian romance—are rooted in the local landscape. Stone circles, hillforts, Roman remains, medieval castles, and ancient churches form part of the region’s enduring cultural heritage.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Fforest Fawr is defined by the close relationship between its geology, natural environment, and the cultural and industrial heritage of Wales. Nearly 11,000 years of human activity have shaped a cultural landscape where ancient monuments sit alongside the remains of 200 years of industrial exploitation. Abandoned quarries, brickworks, limekilns, and fragments of historical transport infrastructure are now integrated into the landscape, bearing witness to a period when the area's geological resources supported metal production in South Wales. Since the early 20th century, the area’s geological, archaeological, industrial, and intangible heritage has served as an outdoor laboratory for research and education. The geopark supports both formal and informal learning, from schools and universities to amateur societies and the general public. It also plays an active role in supporting the local economy, using the landscape and its geological assets as a foundation for sustainable growth. Engagement with local businesses is fostered through initiatives such as the Geopark Ambassador Scheme, orientation days, and contributions to the Brecon Beacons National Park Ambassador Scheme.
Quote: “Ordovician to Carboniferous rock record, glaciated landscape, industrial archaeology”

Introduction EN: Neolithic dolmens, Iron Age forts, pre-Christian inscribed stones, ruined medieval churches, and a spectacular castle owned by the local community await discovery.The Geological Garden in Bunmahon is a good starting point to understand the geological history of the area.
Description: Named after the extensive copper mining that took place here in the 19th century, the Copper Coast UNESCO Global Geopark stretches some 25 km along the southeast coast of Ireland, bounded to the north by the Comeragh Mountains. Once covered in ice, it is now an idyllic rural area and an outdoor geology museum with a heritage that reflects its evolution over the last 460 million years. The region is a relatively flat glacial outwash plain, largely covered by glacial till and bog, with occasional but spectacular erratic boulders. The coast features numerous sandy and rocky coves with sea stacks, arches, and blowholes. Sedimentary and volcanic rocks, fossil-rich limestones, and columnar jointed rhyolites are exposed along the spectacular cliffs. The Copper Coast boasts extraordinary geological features tied to its position along the ancient Iapetus Suture, a significant tectonic boundary that once stretched from Newfoundland to Norway. This area provides exceptional exposure of mafic sequences, volcanic rocks, and intrusives that document the region’s dynamic geological history. During the 19th century, the region’s copper mines, formed along structurally controlled veins, played a key role in global copper production, further intertwining human heritage with geological significance. Additionally, the Copper Coast offers insights into the southern extent of the last Ice Age, showcasing the interplay of glacial and marine processes, including sheet ice, glaciers, and sea ice. The region’s striking sea cliffs and bays have been celebrated by geologists, with Sir Archibald Geikie, a prominent Scottish geologist and key figure in the development of modern geology, describing them as “perhaps the most wonderful series of volcanic vents within the British Isles.” This globally significant landscape highlights the intersection of geological evolution, mining heritage, and natural beauty, making it an unparalleled window into Earth’s history.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The Copper Coast UNESCO Global Geopark offers educational programmes designed to engage learners of all ages with the region’s rich geological heritage. Covering topics such as rocks and minerals, landforms, biodiversity, and Earth history, these initiatives foster hands-on, meaningful learning experiences. Children visiting the geopark can enjoy interactive activities such as “Jumping near the Seismometer,” which demonstrates the principles of seismology, “How old is the planet?”, or attend presentations like “Children of the mines”. They can also explore geology through demonstrations of fossils, rock types, and the Plate Tectonic Jigsaw Model, which simplifies complex geological processes into a fun, educational puzzle. The Copper Coast UNESCO Global Geopark is rich in intangible cultural heritage, preserving traditions that connect the community with its history and identity. The area celebrates traditional Irish music, regularly performed in local pubs and community halls, and hurling, a sport recognised on UNESCO’s Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. The ongoing practice of thatching, carried out to a high standard, has helped preserve many of the region’s historic thatched cottages. Stories of shipwrecks, piracy, and smuggling along the coast add a unique maritime element to the heritage. Additionally, beekeeping is widely practised, with the East Waterford Beekeepers Association offering training at the Dunhill Ecopark. These traditions are promoted through exhibitions and events, ensuring their continued vitality for future generations.
Quote: “The Copper Coast tells the amazing story of the formation of Ireland”

Titre EN: North Pennines AONB UNESCO Global Geopark
Introduction EN: A sanctuary for breeding wading birds, the geopark is the most important area in the English uplands for these iconic species.The North Pennines contains 27% of England’s blanket bog—an essential carbon store that plays a key role in capturing and storing carbon dioxide.The Pennine Way National Trail, a 435 km long-distance walking route, passes through the geopark from the northwest to the south.
Description: The North Pennines UNESCO Global Geopark presents an exceptional geological story spanning over 500 million years. From its origins in the ancient Iapetus Ocean to its dramatic shaping by the last Ice Age, the landscape reflects a dynamic Earth history. The geopark is internationally significant for its mineral wealth, particularly the North Pennine Orefield, which is renowned for its world-class mineral assemblages and mining legacy. Layers of Carboniferous limestone, shale, and sandstone form terraced hillsides, supplying material for the area's characteristic dry-stone walls and traditional buildings. The Great Whin Sill, a 295-million-year-old igneous intrusion, is a key geological feature, creating striking cliffs and waterfalls and serving as a prominent geosite. Glacial activity during the last glaciation smoothed the terrain, depositing a range of glacial features and sediments. Cutting through the rock layers are mineral veins rich in lead ore and other minerals, which supported centuries of mining. This industrial heritage has left behind extensive ruins and spoil heaps, now colonised by specialised vegetation. The post-glacial development of extensive peatlands on the uplands adds further geological and ecological significance, making it one of England’s most important peatland resources.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The North Pennines AONB UNESCO Global Geopark uses its geological heritage as a foundation for community engagement, education, and sustainable tourism. The relationship between geology, biodiversity, and human activity is explored through a wide range of initiatives, including festivals, public events, educational programmes in and out of schools, evening classes, and an extensive network of walking and cycling trails, supported by an electric bike network. Painted by J.M.W. Turner and written about by W.H. Auden and Charles Dickens, the area’s cultural associations complement its strong geological identity and reinforce its sense of place as the wild heart of the north of England. One notable initiative is the North Pennines Young Archaeologists’ Club, open to young people aged 8 to 16. The club meets monthly and offers opportunities for participants to uncover hidden stories from the region’s lead and silver mining past. Through hands-on archaeological activities, members investigate historic sites and artefacts, supporting intergenerational learning and a deeper connection to local heritage.
Quote: “Visitors can discover the world class lead mining heritage of the North Pennines”

Titre EN: North West Highlands UNESCO Global Geopark
Introduction EN: The steep limestone cliffs of Stronchrubie and Knockan certainly command attention.Crafted by glaciation and rainfall, underground water systems and caves such as Ben More Assynt’s unique formations—protected as Sites of Special Scientific Interest—entice speleologists with their enchanting subterranean world.The Bone Caves tell an extraordinary story, preserving the remains of long-extinct Scottish creatures within their ancient chambers.
Description: The North West Highlands UNESCO Global Geopark presents a geological record spanning two-thirds of Earth’s history. The western coast is shaped by the Lewisian gneiss, a suite of metamorphic rocks ranging from 3 to 1.7 billion years old, forming a landscape of gentle hills and inselbergs. These are overlain by Torridonian sandstone and capped by hard quartzites, with preserved stromatolites offering some of the earliest evidence of life in Europe. The Moine Thrust, a major geological feature running 190 km from Loch Eriboll to the Isle of Skye, records a dramatic episode of crustal upheaval around 400 million years ago, when the continents of Laurentia and Baltica collided, closing the Iapetus Ocean. This event gave rise to the ‘Highlands Controversy’, a scientific debate that challenged existing geological theories and ultimately contributed to the understanding of thrust faulting. The region’s geology includes outstanding geosites such as the Old Man of Stoer and the Ben More Assynt caves, where formations shaped by glaciation, erosion, and tectonic movement are visible in the landscape. These features make the geopark a key site for understanding Earth’s ancient past and the development of geological science.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The North West Highlands UNESCO Global Geopark preserves and communicates a cultural landscape shaped by centuries of human struggle and adaptation. The Highland Clearances are recorded in the remains of stone walls, fences, and abandoned crofts. These sites, including those near Loch Inchard, show how small-scale farmers once lived from the land—fishing in lochs, cultivating fields, and using common grazing lands. Today, the geopark supports sustainable development through conservation, education, and geotourism. Tourism, particularly focused on the landscape and wildlife, is now the main industry in the region. Many residents are also employed in the public sector or in traditional livelihoods such as crofting, aquaculture, and fishing. Protected sites such as the Ben More Assynt caves attract visitors interested in subterranean environments, while features like the Bone Caves support education and scientific interest through the remains of long-extinct species.
Quote: “A fascinating story can be read in the landscape of North West Highlands”

Introduction EN: Visit the Eshaness Lighthouse, a beacon of history and a gateway to breathtaking panoramic vistas.Walk across the tombolo to St Ninian’s Isle, home to one of the most spectacular beaches in the region.Explore the dramatic Eshaness Cliffs, where ancient volcanic activity and relentless Atlantic waves have sculpted one of Britain’s most impressive coastal landscapes.
Description: The Shetland UNESCO Global Geopark spans more than 500 million years of Earth’s history, offering a rare opportunity to observe a compact vertical section through ancient oceanic crust. The islands contain some of the best exposures of a volcano’s flank in the United Kingdom and feature one of Europe’s most prominent tectonic faults. The Shetland landscape has undergone extensive geological transformation, from tropical seas and volcanic activity to deserts, glacial ice ages, and ancient river systems. Visitors can explore this dynamic evolution by traversing oceanic crust, extinct volcano remnants, and shifting sand dunes—all within a single day. Sites such as the Eshaness Cliffs provide striking geological exposures and reveal the power of coastal erosion shaped by the North Atlantic. These cliffs, along with the surrounding terrain, demonstrate the interplay between geological processes and biodiversity, making the geopark a valuable site for education, conservation, and scientific research. The islands also host some of the earliest geological evidence of tectonic activity in Europe, offering valuable insights into the formation and movement of continents.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Tourism focused on landscape, wildlife, and heritage plays a vital role in the local economy of the Shetland Islands, complementing traditional livelihoods such as crofting, fishing, and aquaculture. The richness of the geology and geomorphology underpins the natural habitats and cultural heritage that shape life across the archipelago. From early settlement patterns that made use of fertile soils to the development of distinctive drystone building techniques in a treeless environment, geology has directly influenced human activity. The Shetland UNESCO Global Geopark contributes to community wellbeing by connecting residents and visitors to this deep relationship between people and place. Interpretation of key sites such as the Broch of Clickimin and the Jarlshof Prehistoric and Norse Settlement highlights thousands of years of occupation, from the arrival of the first settlers nearly 6,000 years ago to the Viking and Norse presence between the 8th and 15th centuries. More recently, Shetland’s geological location contributed to its role in the global energy industry with the development of the North Sea oilfields.
Quote: “Shetland's Volcano, active 395 million years ago, now forms one of the world's highest energy coast-lines at Eshaness”

Introduction EN: Witness the northern lights between September and March.Visit the Icelandic Lava Show in the town of Vík, an exhibition where lava from the 1918 Katla eruption is re-melted and flows into the exhibition room.Hike the Fimmvörðuháls trail from Skógar to Þórsmörk and between the Eyjafjallajökull volcano and the Mýrdalsjökull ice cap.
Description: Many of us have dreamt of setting foot on the Moon or Mars, yet only 12 humans have ever walked on another planet. There is, however, a place where you can explore landscapes that feel truly otherworldly: the Katla UNESCO Global Geopark. Although difficult for non-Icelanders to pronounce, Eyjafjallajökull is arguably one of the world’s most famous volcanoes—not for particularly spectacular eruptions, but for its 2010 eruption that grounded air travel, leaving thousands stranded in airports. However, it is its neighbouring volcano, Katla, capped by the Mýrdalsjökull ice sheet, that claims the title of one of Iceland's most dangerous and active volcanoes. With over 20 eruptions since Iceland’s settlement in the 9th century, Katla is a fitting (and more easily pronounceable) name for the geopark that sprawls across its slopes and dark valleys. Here, a dramatic palette of blacks and browns is softened by velvety green moss that blankets cooled lava flows, creating scenery worthy of fairytales. The Skaftáreldahraun geosite, where moss carpets dozens of square kilometres of pāhoehoe lavas, is particularly mesmerising. Despite being a relatively small country, Iceland is home to 30 different volcanic systems that have given rise to hundreds of volcanoes. While many, such as Helgafell, are now dormant, others like Katla, Eyjafjallajökull, and Hekla, located within the Katla UNESCO Global Geopark, remain active. This extraordinary volcanic landscape, responsible for roughly a third of the global lava output, is shaped by Iceland's unique position atop the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. This tectonic boundary, which separates the North American and Eurasian plates, is the world’s longest mountain range. At its axis, a deep rift valley allows magma from the mantle to emerge, reaching the sea floor, driving the plates apart at an average rate of 2.5 cm per year. The geopark is home to two of Iceland's most significant basaltic flood lava eruptions in recorded history. The Laki eruption (1783–1784) created the 27 km-long Lakagígar fissure, consisting of 130 massive craters, while the Eldgjá eruption (circa 938 AD) formed a stunning 50 km-long gorge, into which the Ófærufoss waterfall flows. These colossal eruptions were so impactful that they disrupted climate patterns from Europe to China. Along the coast, Reynisfjara’s dark sand beach, renowned for its striking columnar basalt formations, and the Dyrhólaey viewpoint, with panoramic vistas over its arched peninsula, are must-visit landmarks.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Located on Iceland’s south coast, Katla UNESCO Global Geopark is a hub for both traditional livelihoods and local enterprise. While agriculture has historically been the cornerstone, tourism has grown substantially, bringing new opportunities to the region. Local initiatives showcase the region's commitment to sustainability and innovation. For example, the Geo Schools project collaborates with primary schools to deliver geo-education, improving outdoor teaching skills and materials. Enterprises like the Katla Woolen Knitting Factory produce high-quality wool products using Icelandic wool, combining traditional techniques with modern craftsmanship. Similarly, Æsa's Jams, a local GEOfood-certified business, uses ingredients grown on volcanic soils to create syrups and jams. Citizen science plays an important role in connecting residents and visitors with environmental monitoring. Schoolchildren from Víkurskóli participate in regular beach profiling at Víkurfjara beach, collecting data on coastal erosion and learning research techniques such as GPS mapping, drone photography and sediment analysis. Visitors can also take part in citizen science expeditions, contributing to glacier monitoring and landscape change research across Mýrdalsjökull and nearby outlets. These initiatives enhance local understanding of climate and geological processes while providing valuable data to scientific research.
Quote: “The eruptions of Eldgjá in 934 and Laki in 1783 produced two of the biggest lava flows on Earth during the Holocene”

Introduction EN: Discover the first identified ophiolites—sections of ancient seafloor uplifted above sea level—which played a key role in shaping the revolutionary scientific theory of plate tectonics.In August, several villages hold colourful and lively traditional festivals.During winter, enjoy skiing at the Vasilitsa National Ski Center.
Description: In West Macedonia, between the towering Pindus Mountains to the west and the lower Vourinos-Vounassa range to the east, the Grevena-Kozani UNESCO Global Geopark feels like a place where time moves at its own unhurried pace. In this predominantly rural region of northern Greece, annual harvests are still celebrated, cattle grazes peacefully on the plains, and brown bears roam the primeval forests—home to some of the oldest trees in Europe. The geology of the region is complex, tracing back to a long-lost ocean that existed throughout much of the Mesozoic Era. This ancient ocean once lapped the shores of the supercontinent Pangea, stretching from what is now the western Mediterranean to eastern Asia. First described by Austrian geologist Eduard Suess, the ocean was appropriately named after the Greek mythological figure, Tethys, daughter of Uranus and Gaia, wife of Oceanus, and mother of all Earth's waters. Due to the forces of plate tectonics, a fragment of oceanic floor from this lost ocean was preserved. The Vourinos Ophiolite, first identified by Jan Brunn in the 1930s, is a sequence of rocks formed at the bottom of the Tethys Ocean and emplaced on the older European continental block. It was the first ophiolite ever recognised. Initially identified by Brunn and later studied by other geologists in the 1960s, these rocks were found to resemble those formed in spreading ridges—a groundbreaking discovery that gave strength to the theory of plate tectonics, that was still in discussion at the time. This unique rock formation is prominently visible along a roadcut leading to the Zavorda Monastery, a stunning Byzantine structure perched atop a cliff, offering panoramic views. Another captivating feature, the Rainbow Rocks, consists of highly folded sedimentary layers dating back 247–237 million years.  The geopark is also famous for its cataclysmic canyons, such as the Portitsa Gorge, a narrow 300 m deep gorge thought to have been formed in just a few thousands of years when glacial meltwaters accumulated in an upstream lake. The lake eventually overflowed, rushing through a fracture in the rocks and carving the immense chasm. At the entrance to the gorge stands a beautifully crafted 18th-century stone bridge.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The human history of this region is intimately linked with its geological history, as its terrain and resources influenced the livelihoods and folklore of the West Macedonian people from the Paleolithic to the present day.  In West Macedonia, dragon legends and the oral traditions of the Vlach people vividly connect the landscape to folklore. Glacial lakes are said to be filled with the tears of mourning mythical beasts, scattered boulders are seen as remnants of their battles, and the region’s long stone ridges, such as Baltses, are believed to be defeated dragons lying on their bellies having being slain by Hercules or St. George. Hellenistic and Byzantine archaeological sites, antique stone bridges, and traditional mountain villages highlight the region’s unique blend of natural and cultural significance. Its combination of stunning landforms, primeval forests, ancient woodlands, unspoiled biodiversity, and rich cultural heritage—shaped by its unique and rare geodiversity—offers an unparalleled geotourism experience.

Introduction EN: The House of the Pannonian Sea is a recently renovated visitor centre in Velika that features one of Papuk’s most interesting geological stories, that of the long-gone Pannonian Sea.The Geo Info Centre in Voćin is the perfect starting point for getting to know the Papuk UNESCO Global Geopark through a multimedia and interactive exhibition.Explore over 200 km of marked hiking trails in Papuk, supported by a long mountaineering tradition, six hiking shelters, and an active network of 24 mountaineering association.
Description: A two-and-a-half-hour drive from Zagreb takes visitors through the Sava River floodplain to Papuk UNESCO Global Geopark. The region of Slavonia is a fertile lowland that was once submerged beneath the Pannonian Sea, a shallow ancient lake that existed from about 10 million to 1 million years ago. This inland sea, part of the larger Paratethys system, formed when tectonic uplift of the Carpathian Mountains during the Miocene period (approximately 23 to 5 million years ago) isolated it from the ocean. Remnants of former islands in the Pannonian Sea are now the Pannonian Island Mountains, scattered across modern-day Croatia, Hungary, and Serbia. Among these is the Papuk Mountain—at 953 metres, the highest peak in Slavonia and the central feature of the geopark. Covered in dense beech and oak forest, Papuk is home to several endemic species that evolved in isolation when the mountain was once an island. The geopark preserves a geological record spanning more than 600 million years. In addition to an exceptional variety of ancient metamorphic and igneous rocks, the region features karst formations such as caves and sinkholes and fossil-rich sites like the Gornji Vrhovci geosite, which provides insight into life in the Pannonian Sea. Of particular significance are volcanic geosites such as Rupnica, a striking example of Late Cretaceous volcanism (around 100 to 66 million years ago). Its columnar basalt formations—created during the final collision of the African and Eurasian tectonic plates—make it the first designated geological monument in Croatia, protected since 1948.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Situated on the eastern edge of the Hallstatt cultural zone—the dominant cultural tradition of Western and Central Europe in the Late Bronze Age—the geopark contains the important archaeological site of Kaptol-Gradci. This site includes a hillfort and necropolis with approximately 25 tumuli uncovered to date. Among the burial objects discovered are rare examples of Greek-Illyrian and Corinthian helmets, marking the northernmost findings of their kind in Europe. One of the most unspoiled regions in Europe, Papuk is a haven for hikers and cyclists. The Papuk Long-Distance Trail spans 45 kilometres along the main ridge and serves as the central route where many other trails intersect or end. The surrounding villages of Velika, Kutjevo, and Jankovac serve as key access points and hubs for visitors exploring the region on foot or by bike.
Quote: “At first glance, the pillars at Rupnica appear made by man, yet they are the work of a cooling volcano”

Introduction EN: The Lake Cave, which extends for 13 km below the city of Tapolca, allows visitors to paddle the waters of an underground lake.The geopark boasts several Romanic and Gothic churches and defensive fortresses such as those of Veszprém and Palota. Whole streets of stone buildings with arched porches and stone castle fences have been preserved such as those of Magyarpolány, Vöröstó and Szigliget.Visit the curious ‘seas of stones’ around the Káli Basin.
Description: Lake Balaton, in the Bakony-Balaton UNESCO Global Geopark in western Hungary, has been a magnet for visitors since the late 19th century, for its rolling hills and Mediterranean atmosphere. Despite its well-established tourism industry, the lake and its surrounding Bakony Mountains, Balaton Uplands, and Keszthely Mountains offer plenty of hidden treasures to explore. The largest lake in central Europe at 77 kilometres long, Lake Balaton is relatively young, formed around 5,000 years ago when erosion broke down ridges that once separated smaller lakes. The surrounding region showcases a rich geological history, with rocks dating from the Ordovician period (485–419 million years ago) to the Quaternary period (2.5 million years ago to the present). This diverse landscape, shaped by sedimentary, volcanic and erosional processes, supports ecosystems ranging from marshlands and agricultural plains to broad-leaved forests, particularly in the higher elevations of the Bakony range. In the Upper Balaton region, the Káli Basin is one of the area’s crown jewels. Its landscape is dotted with large, silicified sandstone boulders, and charming villages like Salföld, Balatonhenye, and Monoszló which are well worth exploring. Near Monoszló, on the northern slope of the Hegyestű butte, decades of quarrying have uncovered the interior of an ancient volcano, revealing striking columnar basalt formations. Across the geopark, approximately 50 volcanoes were active between 8 and 2.3 million years ago, shaping the region’s isolated mounds and contributing to its fertile soils. The geopark’s geoheritage extends beyond its volcanic landscape, featuring a mosaic of 172 different rock formations, with karstified limestones playing an important role. The Lake Cave and the Tapolca Visitor Centre are outstanding demonstrations of the power of water over millions of years. This 12-kilometre-long thermal water maze lies directly beneath the town of Tapolca, offering visitors the chance to journey through its crystal-clear waters in small boats which appear to float in the void.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The Bakony–Balaton UNESCO Global Geopark provides a rich geotourism offering with a strong emphasis on interpretation and education. Seven visitor sites, ten nature trails and caving tours offer ways to discover the geopark’s geological heritage. Educational initiatives are central to the geopark’s mission. Since 2008, the annual ‘Bakony–Balaton Geopark Contest’ has engaged students from the region, fostering a deep connection to geological heritage. The geopark’s fertile volcanic soils, combined with the mild climate and humidity from Lake Balaton, create ideal conditions for viticulture (winegrowing). The region is home to six distinct wine districts, each with distinct flavours and characteristics.  Cultural heritage in the geopark dates back to the 10th century, with Romanesque and Gothic churches in Litér, Szentkirályszabadja, Vörösberény, and Nagyvázsony, alongside monasteries in Tihany, Bakonybél, Monostorapáti, Zirc, Nagyvázsony, and Salföld. Defensive fortresses such as those in Veszprém and Palota further enrich the region’s historical significance. Adding to this rich heritage, many of the geopark’s villages feature dry-stone architecture, a construction style almost unique in the Carpathian Basin, where wood and earth walls are typically used. Streets of stone buildings with arched porches and stone castle fences, preserved in places like Magyarpolány, Vöröstó, and Szigliget, offer visitors a glimpse into this unique architectural tradition.
Quote: “A geological–geomorphological mosaic”

Introduction EN: The Apuan Alps are characterised by their towering peaks, reaching elevations of over 2,000 m. Monte Pisanino, the highest in the range, offers breathtaking panoramic views.The area is renowned for its rich marble deposits quarried for centuries.The Alps are home to a network of caves, including Grotta del Vento and Antro del Corchia, where stalactites, stalagmites, and underground rivers can be explored.
Description: Famed for the beauty of its white marble, quarried since Etrurian times (8th–3rd centuries BCE) and used by Renaissance artists such as Donatello and Michelangelo, the Apuan Alps (Alpi Apuane) form a rugged mountain range in Tuscany, Italy. Part of the northern Apennines, the area is known for hiking, rock climbing, scenic drives and picturesque towns. Located in north-western Tuscany, the Apuan Alps are a geological complex known worldwide for their marble, deep karst cavities, and extensive cave systems. The geopark covers the entire territory of the Apuan Alps Regional Park and includes high mountain slopes such as Monte Pisanino (1,947 m), down to the lower valleys of the Frigido River near Massa. More than 250 geosites testify to the outstanding geodiversity of the geopark. Outstanding geosites include the Corchia Underground System and the Equi Terme Park, which integrate tourist attractions such as quicksilver mines, underground quarries, museums, speleological trails, palaeontological sites, and thermal springs. The Apuan Alps host 19 of Italy’s 50 deepest caves and 8 of its 50 longest karst cavities. The geopark holds national records: Abisso Paolo Roversi (Paolo Roversi Abyss) has the greatest height difference (1,350 m), and Antro del Corchia is the longest karst complex in Italy (approximately 53 km). So far, over a thousand karst caves have been identified. Tourist-accessible caves include Grotta del Vento, Antro del Corchia, and Buca di Equi. Exploring these caves offers a rare opportunity to experience the underground landscape while supporting its protection.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The Apuan region is widely recognised for its historical and cultural significance in ornamental stone quarrying, especially marble. Extraction began with the Etrurian populations in the 6th century BCE, making it the longest-running quarrying activity in the world. During the Roman Empire, Apuan marble, known as Lunense marble, was widely used in sculptures and as a construction material for monuments across the Western provinces. In the Renaissance period, demand surged, drawing artists such as Michelangelo to extract the prized white marble. The region’s quarrying heritage, technical expertise, and the fame of its stone have shaped its identity. The legacy is visible in surviving blocks, artefacts, and remnants of ancient quarries that still mark the landscape. Despite modern challenges, the Apuan Alps remain a symbol of the enduring connection between human craftsmanship and geological resources. The Apuan Alps Park Authority runs an annual educational programme titled Tra ambiente e tradizione: conoscere, sapere e fare (Between Environment and Tradition: Knowledge, Skills, and Actions), for primary and secondary schools both within and beyond the protected area. The initiative combines classroom learning with guided excursions led by the geopark's tour guides, offering students an immersive introduction to the region’s geological and cultural heritage. Activities include programmes such as Alla scoperta dei geositi apuani (Discovering Apuan Geosites) and Vivere il Parco (Living the Park), focusing on landscapes, biodiversity, and geodiversity. The programme also features a creative competition, Il Parco nel quaderno (The Park in the Exercise Book), which invites students to create stories, drawings, or poems inspired by the Park.
Quote: “The most beautiful marble mountains of the world.”

Introduction EN: The town of Sassello, with its medieval architecture and narrow cobblestone streets, exudes a timeless charm.The Abbey of Tiglieto, a medieval monastery nestled in a tranquil valley, stands as a testament to the region's religious heritage.
Description: Located between the low-altitude Beigua Mountains and the Mediterranean Sea, the Beigua UNESCO Global Geopark in Liguria, just west of Genova, is home to a unique geological heritage. It preserves a fragment of oceanic lithosphere from the Jurassic Period (201.3 to 145 million years ago), when the Tethys Ocean covered the region. The lherzolites of Lago dei Gulli and the metamorphic gabbros and serpentinites found along the path between Varazze and Cogoleto are just two examples of rocks that once formed the ocean floor. The geopark also offers insight into the peculiar landforms shaped at the southern edge of Ice Age glaciers—such as the Laione blockstreams and the Pratorotondo blockfields—as well as evidence of past sea level fluctuations visible on the marine terraces of Varazze and in the striking canyons of Val Gargassa. Beigua is one of Liguria’s richest areas for biodiversity and is home to three Special Areas of Conservation (SAC) and a Special Protection Area (SPA) designated under European Union conservation directives. The geopark supports a wide range of wildlife, including over 80 bird species such as the short-toed eagle, golden eagle, and eagle owl. Wolves inhabit its remote areas, and whales can occasionally be observed off the coastal cliffs. Endemic plant species such as Viola bertolonii and Asplenium cuneifolium thrive in the park, alongside species like the Montpellier snake and Alpine newt. The Deiva, Lerone, and Tiglieto State Regional Forests within the park are also home to Ligurian Apennine wildlife, including wild boar, roe deer, and fallow deer.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The Beigua UNESCO Global Geopark offers a wide range of geotourism opportunities, inviting visitors to explore its diverse landscapes and cultural heritage. With trails through the Ligurian Apennines, the park provides an outdoor haven for sports enthusiasts and nature lovers. Visitors can enjoy birdwatching, cycling routes, and hiking itineraries while learning about the area’s geology and biodiversity. Visitor centres, historical heritage sites, and museums further showcase the region’s artistic and cultural legacy. The geopark plays a vital role in supporting local communities by promoting traditional products, crafts, and industries rooted in the region’s natural and cultural heritage. The park’s “Naturally Tasty” label highlights fresh and processed products from the Beigua area—such as cheeses, sausages, baked goods, and preserves—that reflect both biodiversity and culinary tradition. Local specialities include the famous amaretti of Sassello (traditional almond-based cookies), crumiri of Masone (a type of shortbread biscuit), locally processed meats, berries, chestnuts, mushrooms, fruit jams, and a variety of honeys. Special initiatives also support beekeeping, including the "Mieli dei Parchi della Liguria" contest celebrating regional honey varieties. Traditional crafts are equally important in shaping local identity. In Campo Ligure, the ancient art of filigree continues, with artisans creating intricate gold and silver designs showcased in the town’s Filigree Museum. In Masone, cutlery heritage is preserved through the Masunin, a traditional knife with a handcrafted wooden handle originally designed for forestry and agricultural work. Through these initiatives, the geopark fosters sustainable development, preserves local traditions, and enhances the livelihoods of its communities.
Quote: “Discovering Earth Heritage, enjoying nature and local traditions”

Titre EN: Cilento, Vallo di Diano e Alburni UNESCO Global Geopark
