Introduction EN: Don’t miss the villages of Agropoli, with its stunning beaches and medieval hilltop castle; Camerota, known for its pristine coves and natural beauty; and Teggiano, a perfectly preserved medieval town rich in history and cultural festivals.Explore the coast with Capo Palinuro, renowned for its dramatic cliffs and sea caves; Pozzallo Beach, a secluded paradise with crystal-clear waters; and the Santa Maria di Castellabate Marine Protected Area, celebrated for its rich marine biodiversity and pristine snorkelling spots.
Description: In southern Italy, the Cilento, Vallo di Diano and Alburni UNESCO Global Geopark combines the Mediterranean character of its sun-drenched beaches and pastel-coloured fishing villages with the rugged interior of its limestone massifs. Two hours south of Salerno, the Cilento, Vallo di Diano and Alburni National Park is a region of contrasts. In the north stands Mount Alburni, where medieval villages sit on the edge of massive limestone cliffs overlooking vast forests. Central features include Mount Cervati and Mount Gelbison, while Mount Bulgheria to the south and Mount Stella to the west open toward the Tyrrhenian Sea and the picturesque villages nestled in small bays. This varied morphology, part of the second-largest national park in Italy, supports a unique natural and cultural heritage. It holds three UNESCO designations: UNESCO Global Geopark, UNESCO Biosphere Reserve, and World Heritage Site. Integrated into the UNESCO World Network of Biosphere Reserves since 1997, the designation helps to protect this predominantly rural area, where more than 70% of the territory is covered by Mediterranean forest. It is home to several threatened European species, including the otter, the Apennine wolf, and the Italian roe deer, alongside dozens of rare plants such as Primula palinuri. Part of the Southern Apennines fold-and-thrust belt—formed between the Late Cretaceous (145–66 million years ago) and the Pleistocene (2.58–0.0117 million years ago)—the geopark is known for its karstic features and numerous caves. These include Cala and Serratura near Marina di Camerota, as well as Castelcivita-Ausino, Pertosa, Polla, Sassano, and Vallicelli in the interior mountainous zone. The geopark is also home to a unique example of an underground river in the karstic area of Mount Pannello. Here, the Bussento River plunges into a ponor—a natural opening in the rock face—only to resurface 2 km downstream near the village of Morigerati on the opposite side of the mountain.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: With evidence of human occupation dating back 250,000 years, Cilento has hosted Neolithic farmers, Bronze and Iron Age societies, Etruscans, Greek colonists, Lucanians, and, eventually, the Roman Empire. The region’s cultural landscape is of immense value. Its World Heritage Site designation includes sanctuaries and settlements in the mountains, the two major archaeological sites of Paestum and Velia, and the Certosa di Padula—the largest Carthusian monastery in Italy. In Teggiano, visitors can follow the Itinerary of the 13 Churches, featuring works by artists such as Tino da Camaino and Andrea da Salerno. This medieval citadel, part of the UNESCO World Heritage designation, also reflects its political and military past through sites like the Sanseverino Castle and the Roman Oppidum layout. The complex of SS. Pietà, with its frescoed cloister and historic stone well, is another important site. In Ascea, the archaeological site of Velia tells the story of an ancient city founded in the 6th century BCE by Phocaean settlers. Velia became both a commercial hub and a centre of philosophical thought, home to the Eleatic School led by Parmenides and Zeno. Visitors can explore the well-preserved Porta Rosa, the theatre, and the Ionic temple, set against the natural beauty of the Tyrrhenian coast. Together, Teggiano and Velia exemplify the region’s rich blend of art, history, and cultural legacy. The geopark’s environmental education programme engages schools each year to raise awareness about biodiversity, geodiversity, and sustainable development. Through excursions, themed learning modules, and direct experiences in the landscape, young people gain a deeper appreciation for their environment. The park also runs a dedicated Award for Students, supporting visits to geosites and museums to strengthen youth engagement with this remarkable UNESCO Global Geopark.
Quote: “The Geopark constitutes a real living landscape that plays an active role in contemporary society”

Titre EN: Cliffs of Fundy UNESCO Global Geopark
Introduction EN: Learn about copper and semi-precious stone deposits, including agate and amethyst, found in the basalt cliffs of Cape D’Or, formed by ancient lava flows.Taste local dulse, a hand-harvested dried seaweed unique to the Bay of Fundy, with flavour that varies depending on where it was picked.Visit the Fundy Geological Museum to see some of the oldest dinosaur bones in Canada and learn about the ancient creatures that once lived in the region.
Description: When talking about the Cliffs of Fundy UNESCO Global Geopark, located on the north shore of the Bay of Fundy in Nova Scotia, one aspect stands out for its dramatic impact on the landscape: the Bay of Fundy tides. The geopark’s shores experience the highest tides in the world, with tidal differences reaching an astonishing 16 metres. These tides have a characteristic oscillation where water sloshes back and forth. The Bay’s funnel shape, 16,000 km² area, and depths of up to 200 metres align closely with the Atlantic Ocean’s tidal period of about 12 to 13 hours. This near-perfect synchrony creates a powerful tidal resonance, amplifying the tidal range and shaping the region’s rugged appearance. Alongside other erosion agents, these tides have carved cliffs that expose remarkable geological features, including the Cobequid Fault—an ancient fault zone that recorded both the assembly and breakup of the supercontinent Pangea. Around 300 million years ago, during the formation of Pangea, long-lost continents collided, driven by tectonic forces that still move Earth’s plates today. The Cobequid Fault, active at the time and comparable to the modern San Andreas Fault, marked this collision zone. It was reactivated more than 100 million years later, when Pangea began to break apart. At that time, the region lay near the equator and experienced a dry, warm climate. As Pangea fragmented at the end of the Triassic Period (around 200 million years ago), massive volcanic eruptions released lava and gases—including carbon dioxide, sulphur, and methane—that triggered global climate changes. These changes led to the extinction of about 76 percent of marine and terrestrial species, opening the way for dinosaurs to dominate for the next 135 million years. This event is well preserved in the basalt islands and headlands of the Cliffs of Fundy, particularly the Old Wife at Five Islands Provincial Park. This internationally significant geosite is one of the world’s clearest examples of the massive volcanic activity that preceded the rise of the dinosaurs. Here, contrasting bright red sandstones emerge through dark alluvial fans from the overlying basalt, offering one of the most striking views in the geopark.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The Cliffs of Fundy are part of the ancestral and unceded territory of the Mi'kmaq people. Present-day communities live just outside the geopark. Within the geopark, the Mi'kmawey Debert Geosite represents the oldest known human settlement in eastern North America, dating to between 11,000 and 14,000 years BP. The Mi'kmawey hold a rich tradition of timeless stories, including that of Kluskap, a powerful mystical being credited with creating landscape features across Quebec, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, and Cape Breton Island. Kluskap created turtles, crabs, and leeches, removed the noses of porcupines and toads, and gave beavers their distinctive tails. One day, annoyed by a mischievous rodent that kept building dams threatening the Mi’kmawey’s lands, Kluskap flung huge sods of earth toward it, forming the Five Islands—a group of five basaltic islands in the Bay of Fundy. Trail systems in Cape Chignecto Provincial Park are both exceptional and challenging, though the breathtaking views of geosites along the Watsonville Trail are highly accessible. Trails are also well developed in the Kenomee Wilderness Area and at Five Islands Provincial Park.

Titre EN: Tuscan Mining Park UNESCO Global Geopark
Introduction EN: Visit the museum in Gavorrano, housed in the “riservetta”—a former explosives warehouse—offering a vivid reconstruction of mining life and working conditions.Experience geothermal activity first-hand at the Biancane Geosite, where hot hydrothermal fluids, sulphur vents, and mud pools shape a unique landscape.Walk the "Via delle Città Etrusche", a 173 km network of trails linking archaeological sites, medieval towns, and ancient Etruscan roads across the Metalliferous Hills.
Description: Exploitation of mineral resources is as old as humanity itself. It was through mining the Earth that our species transitioned from the Stone Age to the Bronze and Iron Ages and eventually powered the furnaces that transformed industrial society. In the Tuscan Mining UNESCO Global Geopark, thousands of years of mining heritage attest to that story—and much more. Known locally as the Parco Nazionale delle Colline Metallifere Grossetane (National Park of the Metalliferous Hills Grossetane), the geopark stretches from the Mediterranean coast of the Gulf of Follonica—once home to the legendary Ilva steelworks—to the wooded interior of Montieri, more than 30 km inland. Between them lie the rolling hills of Tuscany and six municipalities, including Massa Marittima, the region’s most influential centre, enclosed within its medieval walls atop an isolated hill. This extraordinary natural richness was forged over hundreds of millions of years of geological activity. It began with the deposition of Carboniferous (358.9–298.9 million years ago) sediments, originating in vast swamp forests that would later yield coal deposits, including lignite mined in the geopark’s territory. The story continues through the formation of the Apennines and the opening of the Tyrrhenian Sea in the Miocene (23–5.3 million years ago.) As magma rose through the crust, hydrothermal fluids deposited minerals within the rocks—traces of which are still visible at the Biancane Geosite, where high-temperature (approx. 150°C) hydrothermal liquids rise to the surface, forming sulphur vents, mud pools, and a distinctive surrounding flora.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: From Neolithic jasper quarrying at the La Pietra geosite to the industrial-scale mining projects of the 20th century, the Metalliferous Hills have long been a source of metals and materials—copper, iron, aluminium, coal—powering Italy’s development until the 1990s. Etruscans, Romans, and later medieval and Renaissance societies relied on these resources to produce tools, weapons, currency, and the very stones used to build Tuscany’s iconic hill towns. The geothermal energy flowing at the Biancane Geosite has also shaped local livelihoods. Since the 18th century, it has been tapped for boron extraction—a vital industrial element—and is now used to generate electricity that supports local food production, including cheese-making. The site is also home to MUBIA, the Geomuseum of the Biancane, which provides an interactive overview of how Earth’s natural heat and mineral wealth can be harnessed sustainably. The Via delle Città Etrusche is a pioneering initiative redefining slow and sustainable tourism in the Maremma region. This 173 km trail network connects the Etruscan cities of Vetulonia, Roselle, Populonia, and Volterra. By restoring ancient paths and linking archaeological sites, medieval villages, and cultural itineraries such as the Via Clodia and Via Francigena, it offers accessible routes for walkers, cyclists, and horseback riders. The park also thrives as a centre for sustainable agriculture and local innovation. Producers like Saba Formaggi in Cura Nuova are celebrated for their pecorino and caprino cheeses. In collaboration with the University of Pisa, they are developing new pecorino varieties aimed at reducing "bad" cholesterol. This intersection of science, tradition, and high-quality food production exemplifies the geopark’s role in nurturing resilient, sustainable rural communities.
Quote: “The Geopark is one of the most important mining district in Italy. Mining has been carried out for 3,000 years”

Introduction EN: Explore the Marine Terraces of Gambarie, high-altitude beaches formed 1.8 million years ago, shaped by glacial movements and tectonic uplift, reaching 1,350 metres above sea level.Connect with the Aspromonte’s Greek-Calabrian heritage through the ancient Grecanico language, the Museum of Ancient Greek Language in Bova, and vibrant cultural rituals like the Persephone celebration in Gallicianò.Visit the Mammola fossil forest, where fossilised trees provide a rare glimpse into Aspromonte’s prehistoric biodiversity and geological history.
Description: Located on the southern tip of Calabria, Italy, the Aspromonte UNESCO Global Geopark is a mountainous region defined by a complex mix of geological formations, predominantly composed of Paleozoic metamorphic rocks such as schists, gneisses, and marbles, formed between 540 and 250 million years ago. The geopark provides valuable insights into Earth’s history, including the evolution of the Apennine chain and the formation of the Mediterranean Sea. It is home to numerous geological features of scientific and cultural importance, including the San Lorenzo and Gambarie marble quarries, the Amendolea river canyon, the Stilaro river springs, and the Mammola fossil forest. The park also features mixed forests of holm oak, fir, and larch, thriving alongside unique geological formations such as Woodwardia radicans, a rare prehistoric fern. Protected areas—including the southernmost UNESCO World Heritage Beech Forest and multiple Natura 2000 sites—highlight the park’s ecological importance. The park’s rangers play a key role in maintaining these landscapes and ensuring the conservation of natural heritage. Aspromonte’s main geological peculiarity lies in its geodynamic and seismotectonic history. As part of the Calabrian-Peloritani Arc (OCP), this southern peninsular fragment represents a unique segment of the Alpine chain. It detached from regions including Spain, northwest Italy, Sardinia, and Corsica due to the opening of the Ligurian-Piedmontese Basin and the Tyrrhenian Sea. Overridden by the nascent Apennine Chain in the lower Miocene, it forms a rare geological system that is ancient yet still evolving. The region’s geological heritage includes crystalline-metamorphic rocks, plateaux, terraces, landslides, deep gravitational deformations, rivers, waterfalls, and remarkable geomorphological features such as the Rocche and Pietre.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The Aspromonte Geopark celebrates its deep-rooted Greek-Calabrian culture, where the ancient Grecanico language survives among approximately 1,000 speakers. Recognised as a protected minority language under Italian law, the geopark helps preserve this heritage through trilingual signage, the Museum of Ancient Greek Language in Bova, and events such as the Persephone ritual in Gallicianò, accompanied by music, food, and local traditions. Cultural exchanges with Greek-speaking communities in Athens and Macedonia further reinforce this living legacy. The geopark’s diverse geotourism offerings provide experiences for every type of visitor. From panoramic walking routes and serene forests to adventurous activities like canyoning, sport climbing, and canoeing, there is something for everyone. Horse-riding and cultural tours add further depth to the visitor experience. Local food and wine traditions reflect the hospitality and heritage of Aspromonte’s communities, offering flavours deeply connected to the land. Educational initiatives engage children with the geological and cultural wealth of their region, fostering stewardship among younger generations. The geopark also works with universities and research institutions to study key features such as the Montalto Shear Zone, marine terraces, and the Calabrian-Peloritan Orogen. These collaborations promote scientific discovery, environmental education, and the continued transmission of knowledge, ensuring the geopark’s legacy for the future.

Introduction EN: Discover rich Viking history including the oldest trading town in Norway, Kaupang, and the traces of one of the three large Viking ships in Norway (Klåstad skipet).The Norwegian Coastal Trail follows the coastline and is part of the Norwegian Trekking Association's extensive network of trails and ski routes, offering year-round opportunities for exploration and adventure.
Description: The Gea Norvegica UNESCO Global Geopark in southeastern Norway was the first in Scandinavia; it is named after one of the first books describing the geology of the area in 1838. Gea Norvegica means ‘the part of the Earth belonging to Norway.’  This geopark tells a 1.5-billion-year story, from a time when Scandinavia was at the opposite pole to the most recent erosional landforms carved by the ice age glaciers. In between, the long path of the Baltica tectonic plate, where Norway sits, has left traces of mountain chains, tropical seas, intense volcanism, and even continental break-up—an immense geological heritage found in the geopark’s geosites.  Two remarkable sites, Jomfruland and Mølen, stand as testaments to the region’s geological history. Jomfruland, an enchanting island of cobblestone beaches, showcases the remnants of the Younger Dryas Era moraine—the last major abrupt climate change event of the last deglaciation, occurring 12,900–11,700 years ago. Mølen reveals a treasure trove of Iron Age and Viking Age graves and relics. Further into the geopark, the Fen volcanic complex near Ulefoss and the renowned Telemark Canal await discovery. The Fen Volcano, active approximately 580 million years ago, now exists only as remnants along the shores of Lake Norsjø, including the deep parts of the volcano and the system of pipes and conduits that once connected to the magma chamber, as well as various rocks altered by eruptions and deep geological processes. In 1921, renowned Norwegian geologist Waldemar C. Brøgger published a groundbreaking work suggesting that certain rare limestones formed directly in a magma chamber and that their unique chemical composition results from volcanism. One enduring example is the white magmatic rock known as Søvite, named after the local farm Søve. Søvite’s carbonate composition and ease of use made it a favoured material for buildings, including many medieval churches. The Fen area holds special significance as the birthplace of the discovery of carbonatite volcanoes. Consequently, it is considered the world’s key locality for rocks like fenite (named after Fen), søvite, and damtjernite, as well as the geological process known as fenitization. Currently, the only active carbonatite volcano in the world is the Ol Doinyo Lengai in the Ngorongoro Lengai UNESCO Global Geopark.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The Gea Norvegica UNESCO Global Geopark encompasses eight municipalities across two counties that collectively own and manage the geopark, fostering cooperation in education, sustainable development, and cultural preservation. Despite Norway’s strong reliance on geological resources like petroleum,  public knowledge of geological heritage remains limited, making education a core focus of the geopark. Within the geopark, more than 100 schools and numerous kindergartens benefit from teaching materials, lessons, and field trips provided by the geopark staff, including activities that explore key sites like Fen and its volcanic heritage. Students can learn about ancient geological processes, such as those that formed Søvite and rhomb porphyries, or visit sites like Kjærra Fossepark to discover ancient salmon fishing techniques alongside a 90-meter geological timeline. Partnerships with universities and local communities further enhance learning opportunities, fostering deeper understanding and appreciation of the region’s geological and cultural significance.
Quote: “The long and diverse geological history in Scandinavia's first Geopark”

Introduction EN: The Senhora da Mó panoramic geosite is one of the viewpoints of the Arouca geopark, located high above the town of Arouca. At its highest point stands a chapel believed to date back to the 16th century.The celebration in honour of Nossa Senhora da Mó, considered in Arouca as the patroness of the fields, the crops and the animals, and protectress against droughts and thunderstorms, takes place every year on September 7th and 8th.The Geological Interpretative Centre of Canelas (CIGC) displays some of the most impressive specimens of giant trilobites from the Middle Ordovician.
Description: Some 60 km southeast of Porto, in the heart of the Aveiro district in northern Portugal, Arouca is a small but lively town surrounded by verdant deep valleys. Despite is small size, Arouca UNESCO Global Geopark is a true wonder. Here, one can find some of the largest trilobites ever to be found on the geological record, rocks that give birth, one of the longest pedestrian suspension bridges in the world and an incredible network of wooden walkways that winds through the Paiva River gorge – one of the wildest rivers in Europe -  where stunning waterfalls and raging rapids attract hundreds of thrill-seeking visitors every year.  With over 20,000 species and having lived for nearly 300 million years, trilobites, an extinct marine arthropod, are amongst the most successful groups of organisms to have lived on Earth.  At the Arouca UNESCO Global Geopark, their fossils are the largest to have been discovered and the rock formation where they are found is one of the most prolific in the world. The Geological Interpretative Center of Canelas, also known as the Trilobite Museum, provides a window into a past when the continents were gathered in the supercontinent Pangea. Most of the trilobites from Arouca come from the “Canelas Quarry,” a slate quarry that has been in operation since 1820 providing high-quality slate to be used in roofing and wall tiling around the world.  Known by geologists as “nodular granite of Castanheira,” the “Pedras Parideiras” (birthing stones) is a granite outcrop with a very special and rare characteristic: its mineral composition contains an outstanding amount of biotite nodules, small, round and dark spherical structures formed in very specific conditions of magma cooling. Exposed to the elements for millennia, expanding in the scorching summer heat and freezing during the winter months, the nodules break free from the host rock leaving a concave space in their place, a rock birthing a stone. The phenomena, unique in the world, is involved in a fertility myth dating back to the Bronze age. According to legend, Pedras Parideiras have the power to help couples conceive a child. To work, one must sleep with one of the baby stones – a biotite nodule - under the pillow. By the 1990s the myth had spread throughout Portugal and abroad and the birthing stones of Arouca had been almost completely plundered of their baby nodules. The geopark was crucial in protecting this valuable geological heritage.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The region’s archaeological, historical, and mining legacy—including Neolithic graves, Roman and Medieval ruins, the Arouca Monastery, and the abandoned tungsten mines of Regoufe and Rio de Frades—serves as a foundation for educational and tourism programmes that highlight the area's historical significance and attract visitors year-round. Arouca's culinary heritage is deeply rooted in local traditions, with cuisine based on the indigenous cattle breed, Arouquesa beef, and convent pastries that trace their origins back to the 10th-century foundation of the Arouca Monastery. Traditional flavours are celebrated through events such as the Feira das Colheitas (Harvest Festival), which showcases products like chestnuts and mushrooms. Geotourism activities, including rafting, canoeing, canyoning, rock climbing, and the extensive network of walking trails, allow visitors to explore Arouca’s diverse landscapes and geosites while experiencing the region's unique cultural traditions and engaging with the local community.
Quote: “Motherland of the biggest trilobites in the world”

Introduction EN: The Interpretative Centre of Zêzere Glacial Valley is a dedicated hub that provides insights into the rich geological history of the region, emphasising the significance of the glacial valley.The region boasts a collection of significant military monuments, with castles taking centre stage. Among them, the 13th-century Belmonte Castle stands out as a prominent attraction, along with the 12th-century castles of Celorico, Linhares da Beira, Guarda, Avô, and Folgosinho.
Description: In East Central Portugal, amongst massive granite boulders of quirky shapes that defy imagination, Estrela UNESCO Global Geopark is a slow-paced region where sheep still graze the land, followed from afar by lone shepherds and their faithful Estrela Mountain Dogs.  With a geological history of more than 541 million years, the present-day landforms are the result of an intense phase of uplift in the Miocene (23-5 million years ago) which exposed the ancient granites, and which was key for the development of extensive glaciers that carved the landscape into what it is today. During the Last Glacial Maximum, about 20,000 years ago, when the global sea level was more than 120 metres lower than it is today and glaciers occupied nearly 8% of Earth's surface, the region was covered by a glacier with an estimated area of 66 km2. At the time, the 90m-thick ice fed several glacial valleys, of which the Zêzere Valley, an almost perfect U-shaped gorge, was the longest.  Estrela’s impressive naked walls of granite are an almost constant presence throughout the geopark’s trails. These form a network of more than 60 trails that cross the territory, treading together over 1000 km. From the piedmonts and valleys to the summit of Estrela Mountain, visitors can explore the Lagoa Seca moraine fields between the Zêzere and Beijames valleys, the granite columns of Covão do Boi watched over by the 7-metre statue of Our Lady of the Good Star, Patroness of the Shepherds, and panoramic viewpoints such as Mirante do Olho, Varanda dos Carquejais and Miradouro de Piornos.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The Estrela UNESCO Global Geopark boasts an immense and diverse intangible heritage shaped by the historical relationship between humans and nature. Ecological evidence of human activities in Serra da Estrela dates back 7.6 to 5.5 thousand years, primarily in the lower mountainous areas. This long history of human presence has fostered the development of numerous legends, habits, and traditions, enriching the cultural fabric of the region. For centuries, pastoral life played a vital role in the area, alongside activities closely linked to it. Both infield-outfield farming and transhumance—the seasonal migration of livestock between lowland winter pastures and summer mountain grazing grounds—were essential economic activities that contributed to the unique character and culture of Serra da Estrela. For centuries, much of Estrela has been sheep grazing territory, valued for both wool—used to weave traditional burel felt—and milk, which produces Queijo da Serra, a renowned soft cheese made with thistle using traditional methods. Moreover, the industrial heritage associated with textiles, particularly wool, and dairy production is central to understanding the cultural identity of the region and its evolving landscapes. Serra da Estrela is home to over 60 textile factories and industrial complexes, some of which have been transformed into museological spaces that preserve and celebrate this heritage. The region is renowned for its high-quality gastronomy. Key products include the iconic Serra da Estrela cheese, Serra da Estrela lamb, cottage cheese, and goat queijetas.

Introduction EN: Explore the salt-karst caves of Buzău Land, including some of the longest and deepest in the world, where fossils of Ice Age plants and animals have been preserved.Hike one of the geopark’s seven thematic trails to discover its diverse geology, rich biodiversity, and cultural heritage.Visit the 17th-century Berca Fortified Monastery, the only religious fortified structure in the region.
Description: Deep in the heart of Romania lies a land where tales of wounded dragons hidden underground and ogres setting traps for cattle are closely connected to the region’s geological past. The Buzău Land UNESCO Global Geopark is located in one of Europe’s most geodynamically active regions, at the edge of the Southern Carpathians in what geologists call the Carpathian Bend Area. Here, 40 million years of exposed geology—including an uninterrupted record of the past 12 million years—reveal how a living planet and shifting continents formed mountains where oceans once existed. The geology of the geopark is highly complex due to its position at the junction of three landmasses. Its history dates back 100 million years, to the Late Cretaceous period and the northward movement of the African Plate. At that time, the space between the African and European plates was filled with small landmasses and oceans. The continued push of the African Plate caused the formation of the Carpathian mountain chain. This collision, still active today, makes Buzău Land one of the most seismically active regions in Europe. While Buzău Land has no traditional lava-spouting volcanoes, it is home to a distinctive geological phenomenon: mud volcanoes. Easily accessible, these features—including both large and small cones as well as the Boilers of Beciu—are created by the release of gas from an underground hydrocarbon reservoir. Thick grey clay builds conical shapes that bubble with colourful mud. In the Boilers, with over 45 active vents, the eruptions are especially dynamic. Elsewhere, dry gas seepage feeds the Eternal Flames of Buzău Land, where fire appears to rise from the earth. The region is also known for rumanite, a rare type of amber derived from the largest amber deposits in the Carpathians. Buzău Land contains a prolific salt-karst landscape with sinkholes, ravines, salt amphitheatres, canyons, and caves filled with stalactites and stalagmites. To date, 46 salt caves have been documented, including one of the longest and deepest in the world, measuring 1,257 metres in length and 45 metres deep. Many ice-age plants and animals have been preserved as fossils within them.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Buzău Land is a rural region where the economy remains largely based on subsistence agriculture and animal husbandry. More than 55% of the geopark’s territory consists of forests and wild grasslands.  Over 77 habitat types have been recorded in the area, some directly influenced by local geology. These ecosystems are home to all three of Europe’s large carnivores: the grey wolf, brown bear, and Eurasian lynx. Architectural heritage is among the most valuable forms of tangible cultural heritage in the region. Notable examples include the wooden Church of the Assumption of the Virgin Mary in Ivănețu, which preserves 19th-century interior paintings; the fortified Berca Monastery, the only such religious structure in the region, dating from the 17th century; and numerous traditional mansions and cottages such as the Măntescu mansion and Luana’s cottage. Another notable site is the Teutonic Tower in Pârscov, built in the 13th century by the Teutonic Knights as part of a defence system against Tatar invasions. The geopark also preserves rock-hewn dwellings carved into 20–30-million-year-old sandstone by a population from Anatolia in Late Antiquity. These spaces were used as homes and workspaces, and later served as hermitages for Christian monks.

Introduction EN: Fish for trout in the crystal-clear waters of the Idrija River in the Upper Idrijca Landscape Park.Walk Anthony’s Mine Road and visit the interactive Hg Visitors Centre dedicated to mercury. In 2012, the region’s mercury mining heritage was listed as UNESCO World Heritage.Sample Idrijski žlikrofi, a Slovenian dish made from noodle dough with a potato filling.
Description: The Idrija UNESCO Global Geopark is located in the western part of Slovenia, approximately 60 km from Ljubljana, at the junction of the Dinarides and Alps mountain ranges. This geological setting has given rise to exceptional geoheritage, including deep gorges with well-preserved stratigraphic cross sections, notable tectonic features, and diverse mineral and fossil deposits. Watercourses further shape the terrain, contributing to a rich variety of surface features. Tectonic movements that shaped the Idrija UNESCO Global Geopark began in the Anisian (Middle Triassic) and continued throughout the Triassic period. It was during this time that the area’s mercury ore deposits—supporting 500 years of mining and now recognised as a UNESCO World Heritage Site—were formed. Complex tectonic activity interrupted carbonate sedimentation in the Upper Cretaceous, leading to the deposition of flysch in a foreland basin. As a result of this tectonic complexity, most contacts between the Carboniferous to Paleocene–Eocene rock sequences are tectonic in nature. The predominant rock types in the geopark are carbonates and clastic sedimentary rocks dating from the Permian, Triassic, and Cretaceous periods. Volcanic outcrops linked to Ladinian (Middle Triassic) volcanism are also found in the western part of the geopark. During the Miocene, the ongoing collision of the Adriatic microplate with the European plate produced a characteristic thrust structure across the landscape.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The region was sustained for 500 years through mining activity. At Anthony’s Mine Road, the oldest preserved section of the mine remains accessible despite the cessation of exploitation in 1995. Here, visitors can explore the tunnels of what was once the second-largest mercury mine in the world and one of the oldest preserved mine complexes in Europe, inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The site offers insight into the harsh conditions of underground mining and provides a rare opportunity to see naturally occurring mercury spheres embedded in rock formations. The mining complex also features an interactive Visitors Centre dedicated to the history and significance of mercury. Visitors can learn not only about its extraction but also about its applications in science, engineering, and medicine, as well as its presence in daily life. Additionally, the site includes the (Mercury) Hg Smelting Plant, home to the largest rotary furnace for smelting cinnabar ore in the world, demonstrating the industrial scale of mercury production. In 2018, the UNESCO Intergovernmental Committee for the Safeguarding of the Intangible Cultural Heritage inscribed Slovenia’s bobbin lace-making on the UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage List. This traditional craft, which involves crossing and twisting threads wound on wooden bobbins to create intricate lace patterns, has a strong presence across Slovenia, with around 120 associations and groups dedicated to the practice. However, the tradition is particularly rooted in the northwest, especially in Idrija, Cerkno, and Škofja Loka. Idrija hosts both a bobbin lace-making school and the annual Idrija Lace Festival, reinforcing the region’s status as the cradle of Slovenia’s bobbin lace-making tradition. One of the region’s signature dishes is Idrijski žlikrofi, a traditional Slovenian specialty from Idrija. These small dumplings, made from noodle dough with a potato filling, have a distinctive shape and are prepared following a recipe dating back to the mid-19th century. While the precise origins of the dish remain uncertain due to limited historical documentation, it has become an integral part of the region’s cuisine. Idrijski žlikrofi are served as an appetizer, a side dish to meat dishes, or as a standalone meal, often topped with browned breadcrumbs.
Quote: “Home to the second largest mercury mine in the world”

Introduction EN: The Pachuca’s 40m monumental clock tower in Plaza Independencia of Pachuca, built between 1904 and 1910, has machinery identical to Big Ben in London.El Chico National Park, founded in 1898, is one of the oldest protected areas in Mexico.Visit the columnar basalts in Santa María Regla, a breathtaking natural formation discovered by Alexander von Humboldt. These towering basaltic prisms are among the tallest columnar basalts in the world.
Description: Comarca Minera UNESCO Global Geopark is located in the region where the first football match was played in Mexico, and the tallest columnar basalts in the world were discovered by Alexander von Humboldt. The geopark, in the south-central part of Hidalgo state, preserves a long mining history. The geopark’s territory stretches along the Pachuca and Las Navajas mountain ranges, where two magmatic provinces meet. The earlier province is linked to the volcanism of the Sierra Madre Occidental, a mountain range spanning western Mexico and part of the southwestern United States. The latter province is associated with the Transmexican Volcanic Belt, a modern continental volcanic chain that runs east-west across Mexico, formed by the subduction of the Cocos and Rivera oceanic plates beneath the North American continental plate. This intense volcanic history has shaped the landscape and given form to one of the most important mining regions of the world, exploited since the times of the Teotihuacan (100 BCE–650 CE), Toltec (950–1100 CE), and Mexica (1325–1521 CE) cultures who mined obsidian. This volcanic glass was a fundamental material for the pre-Hispanic states of the region, used to produce weapons, tools, jewellery, and other utensils. For the last 40 years, in Cerro de las Navajas, one of the geopark’s geosites and the largest obsidian mine in the world, archaeologists have been studying how these civilizations used this natural material. Although the beauty of obsidian fascinated the Indigenous civilizations, it was two other minerals, more coveted and valuable, that drove the European invasions and made Hidalgo one of the largest mining provinces in the 16th century: gold and, especially, silver.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Indigenous people and local communities play a central role in the stewardship of the territory. A significant portion of the land within the geopark falls under the Ejidos, a system of communal land ownership recognised and protected by national laws in Mexico. These laws ensure that the communities retain the autonomy to make decisions about how their lands are managed, and this is integrated into the geopark management.  The geopark is also a pioneer in Mexico for combining geo-conservation, education, and sustainable community development. It has fostered interdisciplinary collaborations and created opportunities for students and researchers to explore the region’s geological and cultural heritage. The geopark has created a number of innovative programmes such as “Geolandscapes: Art and Science” which provides interpretative routes, and “Geopark for Girls and Boys”, a creative initiative introducing children to Earth Sciences.  The Pachuca-Real del Monte mining district, home to one of the world’s largest silver deposits, experienced a resurgence in the mid-19th century with the arrival of Cornish miners from Cornwall, United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland. Their expertise revitalised mining activities and left a lasting cultural impact on the region, earning it the nickname ‘Little Cornwall.’ The Cornish influence is still evident today in local architecture, traditions, and cuisine, with the paste, a variation of the traditional Cornish pasty, becoming a symbol of cultural fusion celebrated at the Museo del Paste in Mineral del Monte.
Quote: “A territory full of treasures: from silver and gold to the legacy of miners, artists and scientists”

Introduction EN: See the world’s longest recorded fossil trackway of a flying vertebrate—24 paired pterosaur footprints.Visit the Bingling Cave Temple grottoes, a UNESCO World Cultural Heritage site with ancient cliffside sculptures.Experience Hua’er folk songs, a UNESCO-recognised oral tradition shared by nine ethnic groups.
Description: Linxia UNESCO Global Geopark is located in Gansu Province and spans over 2,000 square kilometres across parts of the Loess Plateau and the eastern edge of the Xizang Plateau. The landscape is defined by mid-high mountains, hills, and basins, shaped over millions of years by tectonic activity and erosion. The geopark is particularly noted for its striking Danxia landforms along the Yellow River, where vibrant, layered rock formations have been sculpted by wind, water, and gravity into dramatic cliffs and ridges. The region also contains the Yellow River Three Gorges—an impressive series of valleys and rock outcrops that reveal sedimentary sequences and geomorphological change. Linxia is one of the most fossil-rich areas in China for ancient mammal remains. Among its most significant finds is one of the longest and best-preserved pterosaur trackways on record—24 consecutive paired footprints from an early flying vertebrate. The site also contains valuable Cretaceous dinosaur tracks and extensive late Cenozoic strata, offering critical insights into prehistoric ecosystems and faunal evolution. With 79 identified geosites, Linxia is a key region for understanding the geological history of northern China and remains an important base for research and science education.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: With roots tracing back more than 5,000 years along the Yellow River, Linxia was once a key courier station on the ancient Silk Road. Today, it is equally known for its living cultural traditions. Gansu Province is recognised as the birthplace of Hua’er folk music—a poetic song form shared by nine ethnic groups and inscribed on UNESCO’s Intangible Cultural Heritage list. Hua’er lyrics evolve with the times, offering a vivid oral record of life in northwest China. Linxia’s cultural heritage is also embodied in the Bingling Cave Temple grottoes, a World Cultural Heritage site where Buddhist sculptures are carved directly into the cliffs. Over 30 additional cultural sites reflect the region’s deep ties between geological, ethnic and spiritual history. Education and outreach are central to the geopark’s mission. Twelve local schools are designated as geopark schools, and over 25,000 people participated in science education activities in 2023 alone. Popular events like “My Home Lives in a Geopark” and “Harmonious Coexistence between Human and Nature” connect students and the wider public with geoscience and conservation. At the community level, the geopark has launched 12 designated geopark villages, supporting training in geology, ecology, cultural heritage and disaster preparedness. These communities also help promote the park and co-develop cultural products with Linxia Geopark branding—from carved souvenirs to tea.

Introduction EN: Home to the Reserva Natural Tepesomoto–La Pataste where hundreds of protected species inhabit, there are three emblematic trees: the almond tree of ‘Tere Armijo,’ the Branded Guapino tree, and the 500-year-old Golden Ceiba, sacred for the Mayan people.The area has a rich history, marked by Taguzgalpa heritage, with numerous pre-Hispanic settlements and a few examples of cave art. Spanish conquistadors established the Cuje gold mines in Rio Coco and built the parish church of Santa Maria de Magdalena in Totogalpa (18th and 19th centuries).
Description: Located in the north of Nicaragua, Río Coco is part of the volcanic Central Mountainous Chain, featuring a dynamic landscape of rolling hills, plains, and small valleys, where rivers drain into the Atlantic basin and the Gulf of Fonseca in the Pacific. The region’s highest point, Cerro Volcán de Somoto, rises to 1,730 m, offering breathtaking views of the surrounding terrain. The Río Coco UNESCO Global Geopark is characterised by its elevated and rugged topography, where lookout points reveal ongoing tectonic activity in a landscape of wetlands, highland springs, and cloud forests. Among its standout features is the Somoto Canyon, protected as a National Monument, showcasing the powerful interplay of tectonic forces and erosion. This 190-meter-deep canyon, carved into solid welded ignimbrites during the Pleistocene, is an accessible site where visitors can observe a spectrum of geological phenomena, including volcanic, tectonic, and erosional processes. The geopark’s geological foundation reflects its position on the western part of the Eastern Chortis Terrane, formed during the Jurassic separation of the North and South American plates. The area’s basement comprises Paleozoic metamorphosed siliciclastic sediments, overlaid by Neogene volcanic deposits, including basaltic andesites and late Miocene ignimbrites up to 500 meters thick. These layers, combined with active tectonic processes, have shaped a unique and scientifically significant landscape.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The Río Coco UNESCO Global Geopark is deeply connected to the communities within its diverse landscapes, which include subtropical dry forests, wetlands, cloud forests, and habitats for endangered species. In one of Nicaragua’s smallest and most resource-scarce departments, agriculture and livestock-raising dominate the economy, but the geopark fosters sustainable growth through partnerships, education and geotourism. Indigenous traditions are central to the region’s identity, with handcrafts such as pine needle basket weaving, pottery, and hat-making providing income while preserving ancestral skills. The geopark also supports local products like coffee, “rosquillas” (a traditional snack), and handcrafted goods. Geotourism offers a sustainable pathway to economic growth, showcasing the stunning landscapes of Somoto Canyon and Laguna de Bruja alongside rich cultural narratives. Community engagement is strong, with residents welcoming opportunities for visitors to experience their traditions and participate in local activities. The geopark addresses climate change and natural hazards through initiatives like drought-resistant seeds, based on Indigenous farming knowledge, and community-led reforestation projects in San Lucas. Educational programmes, including the Geoescuelas initiative, teach students about geoheritage and sustainability, while disaster prevention workshops build resilience across municipalities.

Titre EN: Grutas del Palacio UNESCO Global Geopark
Introduction EN: Experience the Creole Stew Festival, a traditional April event held in Centenary Park that showcases ancestral cooking methods using clay and iron pots.Join over 40,000 attendees at the Andresito Sings to the Country Festival, a three-day celebration each January featuring local and international folk musicians by the shores of Andresito Lake.Visit the Fernando Gutiérrez Museum, a national heritage monument with permanent and temporary exhibitions on rocks, fossils, minerals, and a dedicated geopark room.
Description: Located around 200 km north of Montevideo, the Grutas del Palacio UNESCO Global Geopark presents geological features that span all major eons, from the Proterozoic to the Cenozoic. Its central and southern zones consist of Proterozoic crystalline basement rocks—granites, gneisses, and metamorphic belts with magmatic intrusions such as granodiorites, quartzites, hornblendites, and gabbro dykes. To the north, Permian conglomerates and sandstones of the Paraná Basin represent ancient alluvial fan environments, while Mesozoic and Cenozoic sedimentary sequences document fluvial activity and soil formation. This remarkable geodiversity offers a compact yet expansive record of Earth’s evolution over hundreds of millions of years. The region has witnessed some of the planet’s oldest geological events, including the Transamazonian Orogeny (2,140 million years ago) and the breakup of Gondwana (140 million years ago), which led to the opening of the Atlantic Ocean. The landscape reflects morphogenesis processes under changing climatic conditions, alternating between arid and humid periods. Extensive plains, low hills, and granite inselbergs shaped by chemical and physical weathering define the current topography, supporting fertile prairies and significant bodies of freshwater. Among the geopark’s key sites is the Grutas del Palacio cave, formed around 5,000 years ago in sandstone and shaped by erosion to resemble a natural cathedral. Another important geosite, the Chamangá Pictographies, features more than 40 granite boulders painted by Indigenous peoples between 1,000 and 1,500 years ago, marking a deep human connection to the geopark’s geological heritage.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Educational outreach is a central pillar of community engagement. Geotourism Week, held annually, sees university geology students collaborate with geopark guides to lead educational activities, guided tours, and workshops that attract both residents and visitors. The geopark also actively participates in Latin America and Caribbean Geotourism Day, coordinating guided tours and conferences during Easter week, drawing hundreds of participants and strengthening regional ties. The geopark hosts several festivals that foster cultural preservation and local involvement. Each January, the Andresito Lake Festival attracts around 40,000 attendees for performances by national and international folk artists and traditional dance groups. Recognised by the Ministry of Tourism for its national importance, the event helps to promote the geopark’s cultural identity on a broad scale. In April, the Creole Stew Festival takes place in Centenary Park, recreating ancestral cooking techniques using clay and iron pots. Another key event, the Immigrants Festival, has been held for over a decade to celebrate cultural traditions introduced by immigrant communities since the late 19th century. Participants share traditional foods, dances, and clothing, reinforcing intercultural heritage and community identity.
Quote: “A magical bridge between community and science”

Introduction EN: Reach the summit of western France at Mont des Avaloirs (416 metres), with panoramic views and walking trails through heathland, rocks and forest.Discover the long-standing pottery tradition of Ger at the Musée de la Céramique, where workshops and trails explore historic clay extraction and ceramic production.Explore the Neolithic site of the Table au Diable, a collective burial monument dating back to around 2500 BCE.
Description: Normandie-Maine UNESCO Global Geopark lies within a peaceful pastoral region that is rich in hamlets, villages and meadows and reaches into the departments of both Normandy and the Pays de la Loire. Amid the tranquility, you will find remarkable remnants of a geological history spanning 600 million years, including rocky escarpments, sheer cliff drops, white-water rapids and ancient megalithic sites. The oldest rocks formed in marine environments during the Precambrian, when the area lay in the southern hemisphere. Around 550 million years ago, tectonic activity gave rise to the Cadomian mountain chain, leaving traces of ancient volcanic rocks still visible today. Over 300 million years ago, this area was near the equator and witnessed the formation of the Armorican Massif, which reached heights of over 4,000 metres, before gradually eroding into the landscape seen today. The territory has borne witness to the formation of two mountain ranges and the creation of the subsident sedimentary basin known as the Paris Basin, with limestone typical of the region laid down under shallow seas around 170 million years ago.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Today, Normandie-Maine UNESCO Global Geopark works closely with local stakeholders to safeguard biodiversity and promote sustainable territorial development. Restoration of 120 hectares of heathland and 10 hectares of peat bogs has supported fragile ecosystems, home to species such as the Hen Harrier (Circus cyaneus) and European Nightjar (Caprimulgus europaeus). These efforts are carried out in collaboration with local residents, associations and elected officials, ensuring long-term impact and shared responsibility. Education is a central focus of the geopark. Through its “Class’climat” programme, the geopark engages pupils, teachers and municipalities in hands-on climate action. Students carry out diagnostics and propose solutions for their schools or local areas, strengthening links between education and sustainability. The geopark also promotes local heritage through accessible walking circuits. In Domfront, visitors follow marked trails through a medieval city shaped by a thousand years of history. Nearby, the Château de Carrouges—classified as a national monument—offers a striking example of the region’s architectural heritage.

Introduction EN: Enjoy Palóc cuisine and the wines of the Bükk Foothills, where local gastronomy is shaped by the region’s volcanic geology.See the mysterious Beehive Rocks, striking formations shaped by Miocene volcanic activity, and explore basalt pillow lavas formed during deep-sea eruptions.Observe rare species such as the imperial eagle, short-toed snake eagle and black stork in the geopark’s diverse habitats, from karst caves to forested slopes.
Description: The Bükk Region UNESCO Global Geopark in northern Hungary lies in one of the country’s most complex geological environments and comprises a near-continuous sedimentary sequence spanning more than 300 million years, from the Ordovician to the late Jurassic, punctuated by periods of volcanic activity. The geopark features a diverse range of geological formations, including Miocene volcanic rocks in the south and quaternary sediments surrounding the mountain range. Geological highlights include the globally significant Bálvány North geological key section, which records the Permian–Triassic boundary around 252 million years ago, providing valuable insights into the largest mass extinction in Earth’s history. Also notable are pillow basalt lavas formed during deep-sea volcanic eruptions and the beehive rocks shaped by Miocene volcanism. The area is also known for its extensive karst features in Paleozoic–Mesozoic limestones, including more than 1,100 caves—the highest concentration in Hungary—alongside folded Mesozoic sedimentary structures and karst water springs. The region's rich biodiversity includes insect fauna, cave-dwelling bat species and a variety of birdlife, including rare species such as the short-toed snake eagle (Circaetus gallicus), imperial eagle (Aquila heliaca), black stork (Ciconia nigra), and white-throated dipper (Cinclus cinclus).
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The Bükk-Region UNESCO Global Geopark is home to diverse karst formations, exemplified by nearly 1,150 caves—more than a quarter of all caves in Hungary—including the Szeleta Cave, which was inhabited for 130,000 years and gave its name to the Szeleta culture. Archaeological remains from numerous other caves and sites show continuous human presence from the Palaeolithic to the Iron Age.  Educational activities are a central focus of the geopark’s work, including the creation and renovation of interactive trails, guided tours for school groups, and training programmes for local volunteers. One such example is the geopark’s geo-tour guide training for local entrepreneurs, which equips participants with knowledge of the region’s geology and history, enhancing the quality of tourism services. A UNESCO kulturweit volunteer noted the transformative potential of the geopark experience: "These stones carry stories and a soul behind them… there is more science, culture and life than we can imagine."  Tourism-related businesses in the geopark area benefit from regional cooperation initiatives led by the geopark. These efforts aim to combine geological features with local products and experiences, such as wine cellars carved into Miocene volcanic tuff, promoting both geotourism and traditional livelihoods. The integration of geological interpretation with gastronomy, local crafts, and historical heritage enhances visitor experiences while supporting the local economy.

Titre EN: Land of Extinct Volcanoes UNESCO Global Geopark
Introduction EN: Explore the didactic path “Hazel Syncline,” a short 2.5 km trail starting at the Open-Air Mining and Metallurgy Museum in Leszczyna, showcasing remnants of former copper mining and metallurgy with 18 educational boards along the way.Visit the Church of Peace in Jawor, a UNESCO World Heritage Site built in 1654–55 with unique half-timbered construction and an interior richly decorated with over 140 biblical paintings and guild emblems.Discover Rataj forest, home to rare plant species such as the Turk's cap lily and sword-leafed helleborine, and witness the stunning bloom of geophytes in spring.
Description: Situated in the scenic southwest Poland, the Land of Extinct Volcanoes UNESCO Global Geopark encompasses the Kaczawskie Mountains and surrounding foothills. The geopark features distinctive remnants of Paleozoic and Cenozoic volcanoes and lava flows, predominantly from the Oligocene and Miocene (ca. 35 to 15 million years ago), with impressive examples of columnar jointing. Mount Ostrzyca, with its conical basaltic neck, stands as the area's most recognisable landmark. The geopark covers several geological units that are part of the western Sudetes Mountains, themselves forming the northeastern margin of the Bohemian Massif. Key geological structures in the area include the Kaczawa Metamorphic Complex, the North Sudetes Synclinorium, and the Fore-Sudetic Block. These formations span a vast range of time, with rocks dating from the Precambrian to the Quaternary period, showcasing an exceptional variety of lithological features and well-preserved fossils.   The region is characterised by a broad range of volcanic activity, with evidence of eruptions spanning different geological time periods, from the Paleozoic to the Cenozoic. This diversity makes the geopark a valuable area for studying tectonic structures and fossil occurrences, offering significant geological insights into Earth's ancient processes.   One notable geosite within the geopark is Organy Wielisławskie (Wielisław Organs), a former quarry featuring striking Permian rhyolite columns protected as a natural monument. Located at the foot of Wielisławka Hill above the Kaczawa River, this geological site has attracted visitors since the late 18th century. The exposed rhyolites, silica-rich volcanic rocks from the Permian period, display a distinctive columnar structure resembling a large inverted fan. The columns, 20 to 30 cm in diameter, vary in orientation—vertical in the north and gradually shifting to horizontal in the south—suggesting that the lava solidified in a dome-like formation. Organy Wielisławskie is also the starting point for a nature trail leading to the summit of Wielisławka, where remnants of a medieval stronghold and later a small castle, destroyed in the 15th century, can still be found. The area has a rich mining history dating back to the 16th century, with traces of collapsed shafts, spoil heaps, and underground tunnels, the longest of which, Wielisławska Adit, stretches about 100 meters.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The Land of Extinct Volcanoes UNESCO Global Geopark is deeply connected to its mineral-rich history, with a long-standing tradition of gold and copper prospecting that has shaped the livelihoods of local communities for centuries. The legacy of mining is evident in the numerous abandoned quarries that now serve as important geological and cultural landmarks. One such site, the former basalt quarry Wilcza Góra, has been successfully repurposed through community-led conservation efforts, transforming it into a hub for scientific research and educational activities.   The geopark supports sustainable economic opportunities for local communities through initiatives such as the Explorer's Passport programme. This initiative encourages tourists to engage with local businesses by collecting stamps and stickers from participating establishments. Visitors who complete the passport are rewarded with a unique medal crafted by a local artisan, providing an incentive to explore the region while directly supporting local enterprises.

Introduction EN: Explore the watermills of the Cornaga Valley, where 17 historic mills once used the power of the Galvão River to grind cereals into flour, sustaining local communities. Discover the Papôa Islet, a unique geological site showcasing remnants of an ancient volcano and the wreck of the Spanish warship San Pedro de Alcântara, which sank in 1786 carrying gold, silver, and scientific collections from Peru. Experience wine tourism in the Oeste UNESCO Global Geopark with guided tours and tastings at renowned estates such as Quinta do Sanguinhal and Quinta das Cerejeiras.
Description: The Oeste UNESCO Global Geopark, located along Portugal's central west coast, encompasses over 72 km of Atlantic coastline, including more than 15 km of sandy beaches. The exposed geological layers span from the Late Triassic Period (around 230 million years ago) to the Holocene Epoch (beginning 11,700 years ago), a time marked by the opening of the North Atlantic Ocean. The geopark boasts an exceptionally rich palaeontological heritage, with over 180 fossil sites, including remains of 12 distinct dinosaur species. Notably, it is home to two fossilised dinosaur nest sites containing embryos—a globally rare find, with only 12 such occurrences documented worldwide. Within the geopark’s territory, three geological highlights are recognised as internationally important. The Toarcian Global Boundary Stratotype Section and Point (GSSP) serves as a global reference point for the base of the Toarcian Stage (Lower Jurassic). In addition, the discovery of well-preserved Cretaceous plant fossils includes one of the world’s oldest known angiosperm mesofossil assemblages. The region's geological diversity is remarkable, with formations ranging from the end of the Triassic to the Quaternary periods. Jurassic rocks make up 77% of the area's geological units and contain crucial evidence of the Lusitanian Basin’s long evolution and the wide range of organisms that once inhabited it. The geopark includes over 70 geosites, addressing themes such as coastal dynamics, palaeontology, geomorphology, salt tectonics, and geological resources.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Human presence in the region dates back over 5,000 years, with remnants of Castros, ancient, fortified settlements strategically located on high points for defence and shelter. The geopark contains around 13 identified Castros, representing nearly half of all known sites in mainland Portugal. The Serra de Montejunto is believed to have served as a central political and ceremonial site for these early communities. Today, these heritage sites contribute to local identity and tourism, providing insights into the region's prehistoric past. Agriculture has long been linked to the region’s geological heritage. The fertile soils have supported the production of key crops such as Rocha Pears and grapes, both of which play a significant role in the local economy. The region has a strong tradition of milling, with over 200 mills historically utilising wind and water power for cereal processing. Around 20 mills remain operational today, with some open to visitors, showcasing traditional milling techniques and contributing to cultural tourism. The geopark's intangible heritage is rich and diverse, encompassing traditional crafts such as the unique craft of Peniche bobbin lacemaking, traditionally practiced by the wives of fishermen. The region is known for unique cultural events such as the Torres Vedras Carnival, widely regarded as the most traditional in Portugal. The Prego Dourado Programme is an initiative within the Oeste UNESCO Global Geopark that integrates heritage, gastronomy, and local producers to promote the connection between the region's geological, cultural and biological heritage. The programme encourages the creation of geoproducts—local crafts and goods that reflect the geopark's identity—and geodishes—culinary offerings inspired by the area's heritage.

Introduction EN: Begin your archaeological journey at Faid Museum, where exhibits explore the history of the ancient fortress and provide insight into the region’s cultural heritage.Visit Harrat Hutaymah Crater, a volcanic landscape at 888 metres above sea level, with stony terrain and lava fields typical of the region’s harrat formations.Explore Taba Heritage Village, one of the oldest settlements in the Hail Region, set within a volcanic landscape and surrounded by farmlands and traditional houses.
Description: Salma UNESCO Global Geopark, located at the heart of Saudi Arabia, offers a rare and fascinating glimpse into the Earth’s ancient history. With volcanic and magmatic rocks dating back over 740 million years, the geopark serves as an accessible archive of ancient Earth processes. Some of these rocks formed far beneath the Earth’s surface as part of the Arabian Shield, and are now exposed, making them valuable for understanding how continents form and evolve over time. One of the park’s most striking features is the Al-Hutaymah Crater, part of a volcanic field with more than 100 individual vent sites and at least 77 volcanoes. These include broad, shallow craters known as “maars,” which were formed by explosive interactions between magma and groundwater. Some sites also contain spherical volcanic rocks known as “bombs,” ejected during eruptions. These unique formations provide rare insight into how volcanic systems behave in desert regions. The geopark’s landscapes have also been shaped by ancient seas, rivers and lakes, with rock layers showing evidence of the Arabian plate’s movement and flooding during past climate changes. Erosion and weathering have sculpted distinctive features, including “onion-skin” rock formations created by layers peeling off over time. Alongside its geological wealth, the Salma Geopark harbours diverse desert flora and fauna, including the endangered Nubian ibex and Arabian oryx, which are uniquely adapted to survive in the harsh arid environment.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Salma UNESCO Global Geopark also represents a vibrant cultural heritage that includes the Darb Zubaydah, an ancient pilgrimage route once connecting Kufa, a historic city in central Iraq, to Makkah, a city of great religious significance in Saudi Arabia. This route is marked by wells, pools and the celebrated Faid Oasis, which was a critical stop for pilgrims for its pure water and fertile soils. The ancient fortress and its 45 wells stand as enduring symbols of the region’s history. Another key site is Tabah Heritage Village, home to “desert kites,” stone structures that were used to trap wild animals, providing insights into ancient hunting practices and early settlements. Local communities and school children are fully involved with the geopark through an active programme of educational activities. Events such as Iftar dinners during Ramadan, the Darb Zubaydah Walk, tracing the ancient pilgrimage route, and the Tabah Historical Path, where visitors explore the exceptionally preserved archaeological ruins of one of the oldest towns in the region, foster a sense of unity and raise awareness about the region’s cultural heritage.

Introduction EN: Experience the Rebgong June Festival, a vibrant religious and cultural celebration held annually across 22 villages, combining ritual dance and communal participation in a tradition dating back over 1,400 years.Discover the Angla Guomoqie, a giant sesame cake traditionally baked in earth ash on the south bank of the Yellow River, recognised in 2021 as the world's largest baked earthen cake.Visit Gulangti Waterfall, a striking double-layer cascade known as “Youth Waterfall,” celebrated in Tibetan poetry and at its most scenic when apricot blossoms bloom in spring.
Description: Kanbula UNESCO Global Geopark, located on the northeast margin of the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau in Huangnan Tibetan Autonomous Prefecture, sits at the junction of three major orogenic belts: West Qinling, South Qilian, and East Kunlun. This has given rise to a wide diversity of geological features shaped by complex tectonic processes. Key sites include the Maixiu volcanoes, the largest and best-preserved ancient volcanic group in the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, formed during the Mesozoic era (252 million years ago to 66 million years ago). The geopark is also known for the Triassic strata profile of the Longwu River, which reaches nearly 10,000 metres in thickness and offers a comprehensive record of sedimentary and paleogeographic evolution in the central orogenic zone of the region. Other notable features include landslide groups along the Yellow River, ophiolite exposures in Longwu Canyon, Danxia landforms, and fluvial terraces. The uplift of the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau and headward erosion of the Yellow River have helped shape these dramatic landscapes. The Yellow River, one of the longest rivers in the world, continues to play a central role in the region’s geomorphological development. While the geopark protects this exceptional geological heritage, it also supports disaster preparedness by coordinating early warning systems and public awareness efforts related to floods and landslides.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: Culture and tradition are deeply rooted in Kanbula’s landscape, where scientific approaches are enriched by ancestral Tibetan heritage. At the 14th-century Longwusi Monastery, a traditional Tibetan Thang-ga mural tells the story of Earth's evolution – depicting the rise of mountain peaks, volcanic eruptions and the arrival of oceans. Humans and animals are interwoven throughout, and this mural reflects cultural beliefs in a harmonious coexistence with nature – a theme that resonates deeply with local communities. Blending scientific explanations with cultural narratives is central to the geopark’s work. Combining tradition with local economic development, the geopark supports community initiatives such as the Sangjie Thang-ga Art Academy, a cooperative that revitalises traditional Thang-ga skills while empowering women from rural communities through training and sustainable employment. The geopark promotes sustainable tourism through designated scenic areas and ecological corridors, with hiking, cycling and educational trails that integrate conservation and community benefit. Visitors can explore the Lijiaxia Gorge Reservoir by boat and walk along Danxia cliffs at a geohazard education site, or follow the “Oxygen Bar” trail, which introduces local plant biodiversity. The Black Yak Tent initiative, a corporate partner of the geopark, offers immersive experiences in Tibetan culture and cuisine, including overnight stays in traditional tents.

Introduction EN: Visit Hutton’s Unconformity, where James Hutton’s 1787 observations showed that the Earth was far older than previously believed—revealed in the striking meeting point between vertical schist and overlying layers of sandstone.Explore the Lochranza slate quarry, home to 540-million-year-old rocks once quarried for roofing, and spot crystals of pyrite—known as ‘fool’s gold’—among the discarded slate.Visit the Isle of Arran Heritage Museum, housed in former croft buildings at Rosaburn, where exhibits trace the island’s cultural and geological heritage from rural life to scientific discovery.
Description: Arran UNESCO Global Geopark, located off the southwest coast of Scotland, encompasses terrestrial and marine zones that record 600 million years of Earth’s history. This island’s remarkable landscape tells a story of tectonic plate collisions, the shifting of continents from the southern hemisphere, the opening of the Atlantic Ocean, and the sculpting of alpine mountains by glaciers. A wide variety of rock types are exposed across the island—from sedimentary layers spanning most geological periods to ancient metamorphic formations and diverse igneous intrusions—making Arran one of the most geodiverse areas in the British Isles. These geological foundations support equally rich ecosystems. The island is home to three endemic whitebeam tree species, found only in remote mountain gorges; one of them is among the rarest trees on Earth. Since the last glaciers retreated, the landscape has supported more than 1,000 plant species and over 150 bird species. Offshore, the biodiversity continues: the Marine Protected Area around Arran includes Scotland’s first No Take Zone, established through a local campaign to protect marine life. Together, this unique blend of geological and ecological heritage makes Arran a living classroom for understanding Earth’s processes and a refuge for rare species.
Sustaining Local Communities Description: The people of Arran, known as Arranachs, are deeply connected to the land and its traditions. The island’s villages, each with its own unique identity, are united by a strong sense of community. This connection to the land is particularly evident in the island’s climate action efforts. Over 260 hectares of upland peat bogs have been restored across Arran, supported by the National Trust for Scotland and local farmers like Stewart Lambie. Local initiatives have also adjusted grazing levels and reshaped landforms to allow native vegetation to recover, contributing to a more resilient landscape. Tree planting and habitat restoration efforts have also seen more than 40,000 native trees planted to date. These initiatives support both biodiversity and sustainable land use, aligning with broader climate goals. Arran is also home to rich intangible heritage, with local residents working to revive the Gaelic language, which had vanished on the island as a spoken language. Bilingual interpretation panels can be found at key locations, showcasing the Gaelic alphabet alongside the local flora. The island’s cultural traditions are celebrated through events like the Arran Farmers Show, established in 1830, the Brodick Highland Games and the Arran Folk Festival.
